children.title: Irrevocable Online Decisions
children.top_down_role: Online settings in which accepted decisions cannot later be altered.

assumptions_latex: A finite request sequence \(\sigma=(r_1,\ldots,r_T)\) is revealed one request at a time.
For every history \(h_t=(r_1,\ldots,r_t)\), the admissible action set \(A_t(h_t)\) is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_s^{(t)}=x_s^{(s)}\) for every \(1\le s\le t\le T\).

notation.meaning: request history available at time t
decision made for request s as represented after time t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard formalization of irrevocability in online algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines irrevocability of sequential decisions, independently of any competitive-performance guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An online algorithm with irrevocable decisions selects \(x_t^{(t)}\in A_t(h_t)\) after observing \(h_t\), using no future requests. Its state may subsequently change, but every previously selected action is fixed: for all \(s\le t\), \(x_s^{(t)}=x_s^{(s)}\). Thus the final solution \(x^{(T)}\) extends every earlier committed partial solution, and no deletion, replacement, or reassignment of a committed action is permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each action is chosen from the information currently available and remains unchanged after later requests arrive.
knowledge_statements.title: Irrevocable Online Decisions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no inspectable source is cited. A source is also needed to support the stronger, model-dependent assertion that irrevocability universally means extension of a committed partial solution with no deletion, replacement, or reassignment.

children.title: Recourse-Limited Online Decisions
children.top_down_role: Online settings permitting a bounded amount of decision revision.

assumptions_latex: A request sequence \(\sigma=(r_1,\ldots,r_T)\) is revealed sequentially.
Each maintained solution \(x^{(t)}\) is feasible for the prefix \((r_1,\ldots,r_t)\).
A nonnegative edit metric \(d_t\) compares consecutive maintained solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Rec}(x^{(0:T)})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_t(x^{(t-1)},x^{(t)})\le B(T)\).

notation.meaning: feasible solution maintained after request t
allowed total recourse through horizon T

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard cumulative-edit definition of recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses cumulative edit cost; application-specific recourse metrics must be supplied separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A recourse-limited online algorithm maintains a feasible solution \(x^{(t)}\) after each revealed request and may revise earlier choices. Given edit costs \(d_t\), its cumulative recourse is \(\operatorname{Rec}(x^{(0:T)})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_t(x^{(t-1)},x^{(t)})\). The algorithm has recourse budget \(B(T)\) when every permitted input sequence and every realization of its randomness satisfy \(\operatorname{Rec}(x^{(0:T)})\le B(T)\), unless the model explicitly requires only an expected or high-probability bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm may revise earlier choices, but the cumulative cost of all revisions cannot exceed a prescribed budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Recourse-Limited Online Decisions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cumulative-edit definition and content kind fit the leaf, but the record has no citation. In particular, the pathwise requirement over every realization of randomness is one possible recourse convention rather than a universal definition and requires authoritative support or explicit model attribution.

children.title: Recourse Budget Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural transitions caused by differing recourse allowances.

assumptions_latex: For horizon \(T\), \(D(T)>0\) is the maximum recourse allowed by unrestricted replacement under the chosen edit metric.
The admissible budget satisfies \(0\le B(T)\le D(T)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(T)=0\), \(B(T)=o(D(T))\), and \(B(T)=\Theta(D(T))\) define respectively the irrevocable, sublinear-recourse, and unrestricted-order recourse boundaries.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: asymptotic regimes are naturally defined relative to maximum feasible recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies budgets relative to a problem-specific unrestricted-recourse scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Normalize cumulative recourse by \(D(T)\), the maximum edit cost needed to replace the maintained solution freely over \(T\) updates. The irrevocable boundary is \(B(T)=0\). A genuinely recourse-limited asymptotic regime satisfies \(B(T)=o(D(T))\); constant recourse is the special case \(B(T)=O(1)\). Budgets satisfying \(B(T)=\Theta(D(T))\) permit unrestricted-order replacement in the worst case and therefore do not impose an asymptotically smaller recourse scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse regimes are separated by zero, asymptotically submaximal, and full-order budgets relative to unrestricted replacement cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Recourse Budget Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary-style subject fits the leaf, but the proposed trichotomy is not generally valid without a problem-specific definition of D(T). A budget in Theta(D(T)) can still be smaller than the cost required for unrestricted replacement, and O(1) is not necessarily a special case of o(D(T)) unless D(T) tends to infinity. An authoritative source and a specialized model are required.

assumptions_latex: A stream \(a_1,\ldots,a_T\) is read sequentially from an alphabet \(\Sigma\).
All mutable working storage, including output workspace used before the final output is emitted, is included in the memory bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal S_t|\le 2^{M(T)}\) for every \(0\le t\le T\), so a reachable state can be represented using at most \(M(T)\) bits.

notation.meaning: internal state after processing t stream items
set of states reachable after processing t stream items

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard state-space formulation of streaming memory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a one-pass bounded-memory stream; approximation and randomization guarantees are separate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A one-pass bounded-memory streaming algorithm starts in a state \(s_0\) and processes each item according to \(s_t=U_t(s_{t-1},a_t;R)\), where \(R\) denotes optional private randomness. It emits its final output as \(g(s_T;R)\). Let \(\mathcal S_t\) be the set of states reachable after \(t\) items over all admissible stream prefixes and random choices. The algorithm uses at most \(M(T)\) bits of working memory when \(|\mathcal S_t|\le 2^{M(T)}\) for every \(0\le t\le T\), with all mutable working storage included in the state. It is sublinear-space relative to an explicit-stream encoding length \(L(T)\) when \(M(T)=o(L(T))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stream is processed sequentially, and every reachable internal state, including all mutable working storage, can be represented within the stated memory budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Memory Data Streams

children.title: Sublinear Query Access
children.top_down_role: Instance access through a sublinear number of direct queries.

assumptions_latex: An input \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\) is accessible only through indexed queries.
Each query reveals one coordinate value and has unit cost.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard indexed-query model and sublinear query criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concerns direct coordinate access, with computation between queries left unrestricted unless separately bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the indexed-query model, an algorithm chooses indices \(i_1,i_2,\ldots\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\) adaptively, with \(i_t\) determined by its randomness and preceding query-answer pairs, and receives \(x_{i_t}\). It has sublinear query access when its worst-case number of coordinate queries, counting repeated queries, satisfies \(q(N)=o(N)\). The output may be exact or approximate, but its correctness criterion and success probability must be specified independently of the access bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm inspects adaptively chosen input coordinates but makes asymptotically fewer coordinate queries than the input contains, counting repeated queries.
knowledge_statements.title: Sublinear Query Access

children.title: Sublinear Oracle Access
children.top_down_role: Instance access mediated by restricted oracle calls.

assumptions_latex: An object \(F\) is represented only by an oracle \(O_F\) with a specified query domain \(Q_N\).
Each oracle invocation has unit access cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(N)=o(N)\), relative to the declared instance-size parameter \(N\).

notation.meaning: oracle representing the hidden object F

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard black-box oracle model with an explicit query count
size normalization depends on the oracle problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires an explicit oracle interface and size parameter; sublinearity has no meaning without both.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oracle-access algorithm interacts with a hidden object \(F\) only by submitting adaptively selected queries \(z_t\in Q_N\) and receiving \(O_F(z_t)\). It has sublinear oracle access, relative to a declared size parameter \(N\), when the worst-case number of oracle calls is \(q(N)=o(N)\). Local computation and answer lengths are separate resources; a complete model must bound them when oracle-call complexity alone does not control total running time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A black-box algorithm makes asymptotically fewer oracle calls than the declared instance-size parameter, using a specified oracle interface.
knowledge_statements.title: Sublinear Oracle Access

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, and the oracle interface and normalization parameter are introduced. However, no inspectable source supports treating q(N)=o(N) as the relevant sublinear scale for this generic oracle model; that scale is problem dependent.

children.title: Access-Simulation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing transfers between query-based and oracle-based access.

assumptions_latex: Models \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) act on the same instance class and must produce outputs under the same correctness criterion.
A simulator may adapt its queries using all answers already received.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact simulation with overhead \(c(N)\) exists precisely when every primitive query of \(M_2\) can be answered using at most \(c(N)\) queries of \(M_1\); indistinguishable instances violating this condition form a simulation boundary.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: simulation upper bounds and transcript indistinguishability give generic access-model boundaries
claim is model schematic and requires specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States generic sufficient simulation and indistinguishability criteria, not a problem-specific separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Model \(M_1\) simulates model \(M_2\) with overhead \(c(N)\) if every primitive \(M_2\)-query can be answered exactly after at most \(c(N)\) adaptive \(M_1\)-queries; consequently, any \(q(N)\)-query \(M_2\)-algorithm becomes a \(c(N)q(N)\)-query \(M_1\)-algorithm. Simulation fails below budget \(b(N)\) if there exist instances \(I_0,I_1\) requiring different valid outputs such that every \(M_1\)-strategy using fewer than \(b(N)\) queries has identical transcript distributions on \(I_0\) and \(I_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Access models transfer through bounded query simulation; indistinguishable instances with different required outputs certify a lower boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Access-Simulation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the leaf, but the record mixes a definition of query-by-query exact simulation with a sufficient indistinguishability lower-bound certificate. Identical transcript distributions are stronger than necessary for many randomized lower bounds, and the conclusion's 'precisely when' language is not justified for task-level simulation. A source and a more specific access model are required before the mathematical boundary can be fixed.

assumptions_latex: A base instance \(I_0\) undergoes updates \(u_1,\ldots,u_T\).
Each update transforms the current instance rather than creating an independent replacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_t=u_t(I_{t-1})=(u_t\circ\cdots\circ u_1)(I_0)\) for every \(t\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard persistent-state formulation of dynamic instances
persistence terminology can also mean versioned data structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses persistence to mean one evolving instance whose state survives between updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A persistent dynamic instance is a state sequence \(I_0,I_1,\ldots,I_T\) generated by updates \(I_t=u_t(I_{t-1})\). Information not modified by \(u_t\) persists from \(I_{t-1}\) to \(I_t\), and queries at time \(t\) concern the current state \(I_t\). An algorithm may retain auxiliary state between updates; its update time, query time, and memory are measured cumulatively or per operation under an explicitly chosen worst-case, amortized, or randomized convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single instance evolves through updates, with unchanged structure and algorithmic state persisting between successive versions.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Dynamic Instances

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The state-transition formula defines an evolving dynamic instance, but 'persistent' commonly denotes retention and queryability of multiple historical versions, whereas this record permits queries only to the current state. Because the local intended sense cannot be established from the supplied evidence, an authoritative source is required.

children.title: Oblivious Adversaries
children.top_down_role: Adversarial inputs fixed independently of the algorithm's observed behavior.

assumptions_latex: A randomized online algorithm draws a private random seed \(R\).
The adversary selects an input sequence \(\sigma\) from an admissible family \(\mathcal I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma\) is independent of \(R\), equivalently \(\Pr(\sigma=s\mid R=r)=\Pr(\sigma=s)\) whenever the conditional probabilities are defined.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard independence definition of an oblivious adversary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines obliviousness relative to the algorithm's private randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An adversary is oblivious to a randomized online algorithm if it fixes the complete input sequence \(\sigma\in\mathcal I\), or a distribution over such sequences, independently of the algorithm's random seed \(R\) and before observing any random-dependent action. Formally, \(\sigma\) and \(R\) are independent. The adversary may know the algorithm and may choose a worst-case sequence; it is excluded only from conditioning later arrivals on the realized random transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oblivious adversary fixes the input independently of the algorithm's realized randomness and cannot react to random-dependent actions.
knowledge_statements.title: Oblivious Adversaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, quantifiers, notation, and content kind fit the oblivious-adversary leaf. The mathematical formulation is standard, but the candidate supplies no section-, theorem-, definition-, or page-level citation.

children.title: Adaptive Adversaries
children.top_down_role: Adversarial inputs responsive to revealed algorithmic behavior.

assumptions_latex: At round \(t\), the public transcript \(H_{t-1}\) contains all previously revealed requests, responses, and observable actions.
The algorithm may use private randomness not directly included in \(H_{t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_t=\phi_t(H_{t-1},Z_t)\) for an admissible adversarial rule \(\phi_t\) and adversarial randomness \(Z_t\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard filtration-based definition of adaptive adversarial choice
visibility of state and randomness is model dependent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptivity is restricted to the declared observable transcript; private coins remain hidden unless explicitly exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An adversary is adaptive when, at each round \(t\), it selects the next request according to \(r_t=\phi_t(H_{t-1},Z_t)\), where \(H_{t-1}\) is the observable interaction transcript and \(Z_t\) is optional adversarial randomness. Hence later requests may depend on earlier algorithmic actions and revealed random outcomes. The admissibility rules must state whether the adversary observes only outputs, the full internal state, or the current random bits, because these yield distinct adaptive-adversary models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive adversary selects each new request from the observed interaction history, subject to an explicit information policy.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Adversaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the adaptive-adversary leaf and appropriately notes that observability must be declared. No inspectable source is supplied, and the exact adaptive model depends materially on whether actions, state, or random bits are visible.

children.title: Adaptivity Separation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Performance distinctions attributable to adversarial adaptivity.

assumptions_latex: A randomized algorithm induces an observable transcript \(H_t\) from private seed \(R\).
Adaptive adversaries may condition future requests on \(H_t\), while oblivious adversaries must choose independently of \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regimes coincide when \(H_t\) is independent of \(R\) for every \(t\); random-dependent observable transcripts permit adaptive input distributions unavailable to oblivious adversaries.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: transcript dependence identifies the generic boundary between oblivious and adaptive adversaries
no problem-specific performance separation is asserted
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies an information boundary, not a universal competitive-ratio separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed algorithm, the oblivious and transcript-adaptive regimes are behaviorally indistinguishable if every observable history \(H_t\) is independent of the private seed \(R\); conditioning future requests on \(H_t\) then reveals no information about \(R\). A separation becomes possible once some \(H_t\) depends on \(R\): an adaptive adversary may choose \(r_{t+1}=\phi(H_t)\), producing a joint input-seed distribution that no oblivious adversary, whose complete input is independent of \(R\), can realize.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptivity matters when observable actions reveal random-dependent information that can influence later requests; otherwise the two adversary regimes coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptivity Separation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The central boundary claim is false in this generality. Independence of H_t from the private seed R does not make oblivious and adaptive regimes behaviorally indistinguishable: an adaptive adversary may exploit deterministic information in the interaction history, including earlier requests and actions, without learning anything about R. Conversely, dependence of H_t on R alone does not establish a performance separation. The record should not be retained as a generic failure boundary.

children.title: Random-Order Arrivals
children.top_down_role: Inputs presented in a uniformly randomized order.

assumptions_latex: A multiset of \(T\) items \(M=\{e_1,\ldots,e_T\}\) is fixed independently of the algorithm's random seed.
Arrival order is sampled uniformly from all permutations of the indexed items.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(\pi=\rho)=1/T!\) for every \(\rho\in S_T\), and the observed sequence is \((e_{\pi(1)},\ldots,e_{\pi(T)})\).

notation.meaning: symmetric group on T indexed items

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard uniform-permutation random-order arrival model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The item multiset is worst-case fixed; only its permutation is random.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the random-order arrival model, an instance multiset \(M=\{e_1,\ldots,e_T\}\) is fixed independently of the algorithm's random seed. A permutation \(\pi\) is then drawn uniformly from \(S_T\), independently of that seed, and items arrive as \(e_{\pi(1)},\ldots,e_{\pi(T)}\). For repeated item values, the underlying indexed copies are permuted uniformly. Performance is evaluated over the random permutation and any internal algorithmic randomness, with the multiset itself permitted to be worst case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A worst-case fixed collection of indexed items arrives in a uniformly random order independent of the algorithm's randomness.
knowledge_statements.title: Random-Order Arrivals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform-permutation definition, indexed-copy treatment of repeated values, and definition content kind fit the random-order-arrival leaf. The claim is standard and internally consistent, but no inspectable authoritative citation is supplied.

children.title: Secretary Arrivals
children.top_down_role: Selection-oriented arrivals under secretary-style observation constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Secretary Arrivals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical random-permutation, relative-rank secretary model with irrevocable selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}\) be a finite set whose items have distinct, adversarially fixed values \(v:E\to\mathbb R\). The items are revealed in the order \((e_{\pi(1)},\ldots,e_{\pi(n)})\), where \(\pi\) is uniformly distributed over all permutations of \(E\) and is independent of the algorithm's random bits. At time \(t\), the algorithm observes the relative rank of \(e_{\pi(t)}\) among the first \(t\) items and must irrevocably accept or reject it, accepting at most one item. Success means accepting the unique item \(e^*=\operatorname*{argmax}_{e\in E}v(e)\), and performance is the probability of success over the arrival permutation and algorithmic randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct, adversarially ranked items arrive in uniformly random order. After seeing each item's rank among those observed so far, the algorithm irrevocably accepts or rejects it and succeeds by selecting the unique maximum.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 1\) is known to the algorithm.
The item values are distinct and fixed before the random permutation is drawn.
The arrival permutation is uniform and independent of algorithmic randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(\text{the algorithm selects }e^*)\) is the secretary-model performance measure.
review_flags: authoritative secretary-problem source and exact locator required

children.title: Order-Model Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on transferring guarantees between randomized arrival models.

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Model Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates guarantees under uniform random order from guarantees under adversarial or differently distributed orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be an online algorithm, let \(I\) be a finite item instance, and let \(g(A,\mathcal D,I)\) denote its expected reward when the arrival permutation has law \(\mathcal D\). A guarantee \(g(A,U_I,I)\ge \alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) under the uniform permutation law \(U_I\) is an average over all permutations and does not imply \(g(A,\mathcal D_I,I)\ge \alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for an arbitrary alternative law \(\mathcal D_I\). Such a transfer requires an additional comparison or structural hypothesis controlling performance under \(\mathcal D_I\); an adversarial law may concentrate on permutations on which \(A\) performs poorly even though those permutations have small total mass under \(U_I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A guarantee averaged over uniform random arrival order does not automatically hold for an adversarial or differently distributed order, which may concentrate on orders where the algorithm performs poorly.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) makes irrevocable decisions from the revealed prefix.
\(I\) is finite.
The original guarantee is established only under the uniform permutation law \(U_I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without additional hypotheses, \(g(A,U_I,I)\ge\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) does not imply \(g(A,\mathcal D_I,I)\ge\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).

notation.meaning: uniform law on permutations of instance I

review_flags: authoritative transfer result or separating example with exact locator required

children.title: Stochastic Input Models
children.top_down_role: Online inputs governed by specified probabilistic structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Input Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General probability-law formulation for online discrete inputs and observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stochastic input model for a horizon \(T\) is a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) carrying an input process \(X_{1:T}=(X_1,\ldots,X_T)\) and an observation filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\), with \(X_t\) revealed through \(\mathcal F_t\). An admissible online decision \(a_t\) must be \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable and irrevocable when issued. The joint law \(P\) of \(X_{1:T}\)—including its marginals, dependence, and arrival mechanism—is part of the model. For reward \(R(a_{1:T},X_{1:T})\), performance is evaluated by \(\mathbb E_P[R]\), or against a stated offline benchmark under the same realized input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic online model specifies a joint input law and observation filtration; decisions are adapted, and performance is expected reward under that law.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\).
The reward is measurable and integrable under \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Admissibility requires \(a_t\) to be \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable for every \(t\).

notation.meaning: joint law of the input process

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the model container, but it has no citation or inspectable locator. The supplied local inventory does not support stochastic online-input models.

children.title: Independent-Arrival Models
children.top_down_role: Arrival models with independence across revealed items or events.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Arrival Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-law specialization of stochastic online arrivals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An independent-arrival model is a stochastic input model in which \(X_1,\ldots,X_T\) have joint law \[P=P_1\otimes\cdots\otimes P_T,\qquad \mathbb P(X_{1:T}\in B_1\times\cdots\times B_T)=\prod_{t=1}^T P_t(B_t)\] for all measurable sets \(B_t\in\mathcal A_t\). The marginals \(P_t\) may differ, so independence does not imply identical distribution. For the natural filtration \(\mathcal F_t=\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_t)\), each \(X_{t+1}\) is independent of \(\mathcal F_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent arrivals have a product joint law. Their distributions may vary with time, and each next arrival is independent of the observed arrival history.
assumptions_latex: Each \(X_t\) takes values in a measurable space \((\mathcal X_t,\mathcal A_t)\).
The horizon \(T\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t<T\), \(X_{t+1}\) is independent of \(\mathcal F_t\).

notation.meaning: marginal law of the arrival at time t

review_flags: authoritative probability or stochastic online-optimization source with exact locator required

children.title: Dependence-Sensitivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Guarantee changes caused by weakening or violating independence.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependence-Sensitivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies why guarantees using product structure need not extend to dependent arrivals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix marginal laws \(P_1,\ldots,P_T\), an online algorithm \(A\), and an integrable reward \(R\). Define \[\Delta(A)=\sup_{Q\in\mathcal C(P_1,\ldots,P_T)}\left|\mathbb E_Q[R(A,X_{1:T})]-\mathbb E_{P_1\otimes\cdots\otimes P_T}[R(A,X_{1:T})]\right|,\] where \(\mathcal C(P_1,\ldots,P_T)\) is the set of joint laws with the specified marginals. Equality of one-dimensional marginals alone does not transfer a product-law guarantee uniformly to this coupling class: dependence may change conditional future laws after observations and thereby change the value of adaptive decisions. A transfer therefore requires a bound on \(\Delta(A)\) or another dependence-robustness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keeping every one-dimensional marginal fixed need not preserve online performance because dependence changes conditional future laws. Product-law guarantees require an additional dependence-robustness bound.
assumptions_latex: \(R(A,X_{1:T})\) is integrable under every coupling considered.
Every \(Q\in\mathcal C(P_1,\ldots,P_T)\) has the specified one-dimensional marginals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality of marginals alone does not justify uniform transfer from \(P_1\otimes\cdots\otimes P_T\) to \(\mathcal C(P_1,\ldots,P_T)\).

notation.meaning: worst coupling-induced change in expected reward

review_flags: source with exact locator required for the dependence-sensitivity formulation

children.title: Prediction-Augmented Models
children.top_down_role: Online models supplied with predictions about future inputs or outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Prediction-Augmented Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online model with an explicit, potentially inaccurate prediction and measurable error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A prediction-augmented online problem specifies an instance \(I\), an auxiliary prediction \(\widehat z\in\mathcal Z\) available according to a declared access schedule, and an error measure \(\eta(I,\widehat z)\in[0,\infty]\). An online algorithm \(A\) may condition its irrevocable decisions on the revealed history and the available prediction. For a minimization problem, an error-dependent guarantee may take the form \[\operatorname{cost}_A(I,\widehat z)\le f(\eta(I,\widehat z))\operatorname{OPT}(I)+b(I).\] The prediction semantics, error metric, access schedule, and additive term must be fixed as part of the model. Consistency describes performance when \(\eta(I,\widehat z)=0\), whereas robustness describes worst-case performance over admissible predictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prediction-augmented online model supplies a declared prediction and error measure, and states how performance depends on prediction error. Perfect-prediction performance and worst-case robustness are distinct properties.
assumptions_latex: \(\eta(I,\widehat z)=0\) denotes a prediction declared perfect by the model.
\(b(I)\ge0\) is an explicitly stated additive term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Performance may be bounded through the error-dependent factor \(f(\eta(I,\widehat z))\).
review_flags: learning-augmented algorithms source with exact locator required

children.title: Advice-Augmented Models
children.top_down_role: Online models supplied with bounded external advice.

knowledge_statements.title: Advice-Augmented Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online computation with a bounded string supplied by an omniscient oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An advice-augmented online model associates each finite input \(I\) with a finite binary string \(s(I)\in\{0,1\}^*\) supplied by an oracle that knows the complete input. Before processing, or according to a declared access schedule, a deterministic online algorithm reads advice bits and makes irrevocable decisions using only the bits read and the revealed input prefix. If \(r_A(I)\) is the number of advice bits read by algorithm \(A\) on \(I\), its advice complexity is \(b_A(n)=\max_{|I|=n}r_A(I)\). A randomized variant must additionally specify the oracle's access to the algorithm's random bits; absent such access, the advice depends only on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oracle that knows the complete input supplies a finite binary string. Advice complexity is the maximum number of advice bits the online algorithm reads on inputs of a given length.
assumptions_latex: Inputs have finite length \(n\).
The advice-access schedule is fixed by the model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The advice complexity of \(A\) on length-\(n\) inputs is \(b_A(n)=\max_{|I|=n}r_A(I)\).

notation.meaning: oracle advice string for input I
number of advice bits read by A on I
worst-case advice bits read on length-n inputs

review_flags: authoritative online-algorithms-with-advice source with exact locator required

children.title: Lookahead Models
children.top_down_role: Online models exposing a limited window of future input.

knowledge_statements.title: Lookahead Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-window lookahead for sequential, irrevocable decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_{1:T}=(X_1,\ldots,X_T)\) be a finite random input sequence, let \(U\) be an independent random seed, and let \(\ell\ge0\). An \(\ell\)-lookahead algorithm choosing action \(a_t\) at time \(t\) may observe inputs through \(m_t=\min\{T,t+\ell\}\); formally, \(a_t\) must be measurable with respect to \(\sigma(U,X_1,\ldots,X_{m_t})\). The action becomes irrevocable before the window advances. The case \(\ell=0\) is ordinary online access, while \(\ell\ge T-1\) reveals the entire input before the first decision and removes the informational, but not computational, restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With lookahead length ell, the decision at time t may use inputs only through time min(T,t+ell), together with private randomness. Zero lookahead is ordinary online access, while a sufficiently large window reveals the full finite input.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\).
The lookahead length \(\ell\) is fixed and known.
\(U\) is independent of \(X_{1:T}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t\), \(a_t\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(U,X_1,\ldots,X_{\min\{T,t+\ell\}})\).

notation.meaning: last input index visible at time t

review_flags: authoritative lookahead-model source with exact locator required

children.title: Auxiliary-Information Robustness
children.top_down_role: Performance sensitivity to inaccurate, insufficient, or unavailable auxiliary information.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Information Robustness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case protection when predictions, advice, or lookahead information is unhelpful or corrupted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A(I,z)\) be an auxiliary-information algorithm for a minimization problem, where \(z\in\mathcal Z\) is any admissible auxiliary signal. The algorithm is \(\rho\)-robust with additive term \(b(I)\) if \[\sup_{z\in\mathcal Z}\operatorname{cost}_A(I,z)\le \rho\operatorname{OPT}(I)+b(I)\qquad\text{for every instance }I.\] The supremum includes arbitrarily inaccurate, adversarial, or otherwise uninformative signals permitted by the model. Hence robustness is a uniform worst-case guarantee and is logically distinct from consistency under perfect information. For maximization, the corresponding convention is \(\inf_{z\in\mathcal Z}\operatorname{val}_A(I,z)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)/\rho-b(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robustness uniformly bounds performance over every allowed auxiliary signal, including adversarially bad information; it is separate from performance with perfect information.
assumptions_latex: \(b(I)\ge0\) is independent of the auxiliary signal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated bound holds uniformly over \(z\in\mathcal Z\).
review_flags: source required for the chosen uniform robustness convention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the robustness container and is internally coherent, but its uniform treatment of predictions, advice, and lookahead is a chosen convention with no cited source or locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Competitive ratio and strong competitiveness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines competitive performance with an input-independent additive constant and optimality of the achieved ratio among algorithms for the problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma)\) and \(\operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\sigma)\) denote the costs of an online algorithm \(A\) and an optimal offline algorithm on the same input sequence \(\sigma\). The algorithm \(A\) is \(c\)-competitive if there exists a constant \(b\), independent of \(\sigma\), such that for every input sequence \(\sigma\), \[\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma)\le c\operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\sigma)+b.\] Its competitive ratio is \(c_A=\inf\{c:A\text{ is }c\text{-competitive}\}\). The algorithm is strongly competitive if \(c_A\) is the best competitive ratio achievable for the problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An online algorithm is c-competitive when, on every input, its cost is at most c times the optimal offline cost plus an input-independent constant. Its competitive ratio is the infimum of such c, and it is strongly competitive when this is the best ratio achievable for the problem.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is an online algorithm.}
\mathrm{OPT}\text{ is an optimal offline algorithm for the same problem.}
b\text{ is constant and independent of }\sigma.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_A=\inf\left\{c:\exists b\;\forall\sigma,\ \operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma)\le c\operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\sigma)+b\right\}

children.title: Absolute Competitiveness
children.top_down_role: Competitive guarantees applied uniformly across instance sizes.

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute Competitiveness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform competitive guarantee without an asymptotic threshold or additive slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an online minimization problem, an algorithm \(A\) is absolutely \(c\)-competitive if \[\operatorname{cost}_A(I)\le c\operatorname{OPT}(I)\] for every admissible finite instance \(I\), where expectation is taken over the algorithm's randomness when \(A\) is randomized. No additive constant and no restriction to sufficiently large benchmark values are permitted. For a maximization problem, the corresponding convention is \(\operatorname{val}_A(I)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)/c\) for every \(I\). The absolute competitive ratio is the infimum of all \(c\ge1\) for which the relevant uniform inequality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute competitiveness requires the multiplicative comparison with the offline optimum on every finite instance, with neither additive slack nor an asymptotic cutoff.
assumptions_latex: All objective values used in the ratio convention are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The competitive inequality holds for every admissible finite instance without additive slack.

notation.meaning: offline optimal value on instance I

review_flags: authoritative competitive-analysis definition and locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes absolute competitiveness by excluding additive slack and asymptotic cutoffs, but no authoritative competitive-analysis source or exact locator is supplied.

children.title: Asymptotic Competitiveness
children.top_down_role: Competitive guarantees allowing lower-order or bounded-size effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Competitiveness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Competitive guarantee allowing instance-independent additive slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an online minimization problem, an algorithm \(A\) is asymptotically \(c\)-competitive if there exists a constant \(\beta\ge0\), independent of the instance, such that \[\operatorname{cost}_A(I)\le c\operatorname{OPT}(I)+\beta\] for every admissible finite instance \(I\). For randomized \(A\), the left side denotes expected cost. The asymptotic competitive ratio is the infimum of such \(c\ge1\). For maximization, a corresponding convention is \(\operatorname{val}_A(I)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(I)/c-\beta\). The additive term may absorb bounded finite-instance effects but cannot depend on \(I\), its length, or its optimum value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asymptotic competitiveness permits a fixed additive constant while retaining a uniform multiplicative comparison; the constant cannot grow with the instance.
assumptions_latex: Objective values are nonnegative.
The additive constant \(\beta\) is independent of \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\beta\ge0\) such that the competitive inequality holds for every admissible \(I\).
review_flags: authoritative competitive-analysis definition and locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The instance-independent additive-slack definition is coherent and fits the asymptotic competitiveness container, but it lacks an authoritative source and exact locator.

children.title: Finite-Instance Separation
children.top_down_role: Differences between uniform guarantees and eventual large-instance behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Instance Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating absolute from asymptotic competitive guarantees on small-optimum instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, absolute \(c\)-competitiveness implies asymptotic \(c\)-competitiveness by taking \(\beta=0\), but the converse need not hold. Suppose an algorithm \(A\) satisfies \(\operatorname{cost}_A(I)\le c\operatorname{OPT}(I)+\beta\) for every instance, where \(\beta>0\) is instance-independent. If there is a sequence \((I_k)_{k\ge1}\) such that \(\operatorname{OPT}(I_k)>0\), \(\operatorname{OPT}(I_k)\to0\), and \(\operatorname{cost}_A(I_k)\ge\delta\) for some \(\delta>0\), then \(A\) has no finite absolute competitive ratio: for every finite \(c'\), sufficiently large \(k\) satisfies \(\operatorname{cost}_A(I_k)>c'\operatorname{OPT}(I_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute competitiveness implies asymptotic competitiveness. Conversely, an asymptotically competitive algorithm can have no finite absolute ratio when its cost stays bounded away from zero on instances whose positive optimum tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem with nonnegative costs.
\(A\) satisfies an asymptotic bound with an instance-independent \(\beta>0\).
There exist \(\delta>0\) and instances \((I_k)_{k\ge1}\) with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I_k)>0\), \(\operatorname{OPT}(I_k)\to0\), and \(\operatorname{cost}_A(I_k)\ge\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated separating-family hypothesis, \(A\) has no finite absolute competitive ratio despite satisfying an asymptotic competitive bound.

notation.meaning: positive lower bound on algorithmic cost in the separating family

review_flags: canonical separating example or authoritative source with exact locator required

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Competitive-Ratio Transfer Across Adversary Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines adaptive-online and oblivious-adversary guarantees to obtain an adaptive-offline guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{If }G\text{ is }\alpha\text{-competitive against adaptive-online adversaries and there exists an online algorithm }H\text{ that is }\beta\text{-competitive against oblivious adversaries, then }G\text{ is }\alpha\beta\text{-competitive against adaptive-offline adversaries.}
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If G is alpha-competitive against adaptive-online adversaries and some online algorithm H is beta-competitive against oblivious adversaries, then G is alpha beta-competitive against adaptive-offline adversaries.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is an online algorithm that is }\alpha\text{-competitive against adaptive-online adversaries}
\exists H\text{ online that is }\beta\text{-competitive against oblivious adversaries}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is }\alpha\beta\text{-competitive against adaptive-offline adversaries}

children.title: Deterministic Competitiveness
children.top_down_role: Competitive performance for algorithms without internal randomization.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Competitiveness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic competitive ratio for an online minimization problem, allowing an input-independent additive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal I\) be the admissible request sequences of an online minimization problem. A deterministic online algorithm \(A\) is \(c\)-competitive if there exists a constant \(\beta\ge 0\), independent of \(\sigma\), such that
\[
\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma)\le c\,\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)+\beta
\qquad\text{for every }\sigma\in\mathcal I.
\]
Its deterministic competitive ratio is
\[
\operatorname{CR}_{\mathrm{det}}(A)=\inf\{c\ge 1: A\text{ is }c\text{-competitive}\}.
\]
For an algorithm class \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{det}}\), the best achievable ratio is \(\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{det}}}\operatorname{CR}_{\mathrm{det}}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic algorithm is competitive when its cost never exceeds a fixed multiple of offline optimum plus an input-independent additive constant.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)\) is the minimum offline cost on \(\sigma\).
All costs are nonnegative and the problem is a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma)\le c\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)+\beta\) for every admissible \(\sigma\).

notation.meaning: offline optimal algorithm or its cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the deterministic-competitiveness leaf and is mathematically standard, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the additive-constant convention or the stated ratio convention. The local inventory contains no relevant competitive-analysis source.

children.title: Randomized Competitiveness
children.top_down_role: Competitive performance evaluated for randomized online algorithms.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Competitiveness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected competitive ratio against an oblivious adversary for an online minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\) be a randomized online algorithm and let \(\mathcal I\) be the admissible request sequences. Against an oblivious adversary, \(A\) is \(c\)-competitive in expectation if there exists \(\beta\ge 0\), independent of \(\sigma\), such that
\[
\mathbb E_R[\operatorname{cost}_{A(R)}(\sigma)]\le c\,\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)+\beta
\qquad\text{for every }\sigma\in\mathcal I,
\]
where \(R\) is the internal random seed and \(\sigma\) is fixed independently of \(R\). The randomized competitive ratio is the infimum of all such \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized algorithm is competitive against an oblivious adversary when its expected cost satisfies the competitive inequality for every seed-independent request sequence.
assumptions_latex: The adversary fixes \(\sigma\) independently of the algorithm's random seed \(R\).
\(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)\) is the minimum offline cost and is nonrandom for fixed \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_R[\operatorname{cost}_{A(R)}(\sigma)]\le c\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)+\beta\) for every \(\sigma\in\mathcal I\).

notation.meaning: internal random seed of the online algorithm
expectation over the algorithm's random seed

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and statement fit randomized competitiveness, and the oblivious-adversary qualification is explicit. A dedicated source is nevertheless required for the expected-cost definition, adversary convention, and additive constant; none of the inventory entries is relevant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Randomized Online Algorithm and Randomized Competitiveness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The competitive guarantee is evaluated separately on every fixed instance; the expectation is only over the algorithm's random choices. The appropriate inequality direction depends on whether the objective is minimized or maximized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A randomized online algorithm may use random choices when making decisions. It is \(\sigma\)-competitive if, for every fixed instance \(I\), its expected objective value over its internal randomness \(\omega\) is within a factor \(\sigma\) of \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\); conventionally, \[\mathbb{E}_{\omega}[C_A(I;\omega)]\leq \sigma\operatorname{OPT}(I)\] for minimization and \[\mathbb{E}_{\omega}[C_A(I;\omega)]\geq \operatorname{OPT}(I)/\sigma\] for maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized online algorithm can make random choices. It is sigma-competitive when, on every fixed instance, its expected objective value—where expectation is over the algorithm's random choices—is within a factor sigma of the optimal objective value, using the appropriate direction for minimization or maximization.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is an online algorithm with internal randomness }\omega.
I\text{ is an arbitrary fixed instance.
\sigma>0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall I,\quad \mathbb{E}_{\omega}[C_A(I;\omega)]\text{ is within a factor }\sigma\text{ of }\operatorname{OPT}(I).

children.title: Randomization Separation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Problem regimes where randomization changes achievable competitiveness.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomization Separation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for a strict separation between deterministic and randomized competitive performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an online minimization problem \(\Pi\), define
\[
C_{\mathrm{det}}(\Pi)=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{det}}}\operatorname{CR}(A),
\qquad
C_{\mathrm{rand}}^{\mathrm{obl}}(\Pi)=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{rand}}}\operatorname{CR}_{\mathrm{obl}}(A).
\]
Randomization yields a strict competitive separation against oblivious adversaries precisely when
\[
C_{\mathrm{rand}}^{\mathrm{obl}}(\Pi)<C_{\mathrm{det}}(\Pi).
\]
A parameterized family \((\Pi_n)\) has an asymptotic separation when \(C_{\mathrm{rand}}^{\mathrm{obl}}(\Pi_n)=o(C_{\mathrm{det}}(\Pi_n))\); equality of the two quantities marks the no-separation boundary under these conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomization separates the regimes when the optimal randomized competitive ratio against oblivious adversaries is strictly smaller than the optimal deterministic ratio.
assumptions_latex: Deterministic and randomized algorithms receive the same online information and use the same feasibility rules.
Randomized ratios are evaluated against oblivious adversaries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A strict separation holds exactly when \(C_{\mathrm{rand}}^{\mathrm{obl}}(\Pi)<C_{\mathrm{det}}(\Pi)\).

notation.meaning: best randomized ratio against oblivious adversaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the separation-boundary leaf, but the strict, asymptotic, and equality boundary conventions are unsupported. In particular, the little-o criterion is one possible strong asymptotic separation notion rather than a source-free canonical definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Augmented Competitiveness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Competitive analysis comparing an online algorithm with augmented resources against an unaugmented offline optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\rho\ge 1\) be a resource-augmentation factor. Write \(A^{(\rho)}\) for an online algorithm supplied resource level \(\rho\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}^{(1)}\) for an offline optimum restricted to baseline resource level \(1\). For a minimization problem, \(A\) is \((c,\rho)\)-competitive if some \(\beta\ge 0\), independent of the request sequence, satisfies
\[
\operatorname{cost}_{A^{(\rho)}}(\sigma)
\le c\,\operatorname{cost}_{\operatorname{OPT}^{(1)}}(\sigma)+\beta
\qquad\text{for every admissible }\sigma.
\]
The resource-augmented competitive curve is the infimum achievable \(c\) as a function of \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resource augmentation compares an online algorithm with extra capacity or speed against an offline optimum restricted to the baseline resource.
assumptions_latex: The augmentation parameter \(\rho\) changes only the designated resource and not the request sequence or objective.
The problem is a minimization problem with nonnegative costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The performance curve is \(c^*(\rho)=\inf_A\inf\{c:A\text{ is }(c,\rho)\text{-competitive}\}\).

notation.meaning: online algorithm operating with augmented resource

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the node, but resource augmentation is problem dependent: speed, capacity, machine count, and other resources induce different comparison conventions. A relevant source must establish the baseline-versus-augmented formulation and the meaning of the resource factor.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation under Limited Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation guarantee for algorithms whose decisions depend only on a prescribed information transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be an instance, let \(F(x)\) be its feasible solutions, and let \(I(x)\) be the transcript exposed by a limited-information interface. An algorithm has information budget \(b\) if its output is a function only of a transcript satisfying \(|I(x)|\le b\). For a minimization problem, it is an \(\alpha\)-approximation under budget \(b\) when it outputs \(y\in F(x)\) and
\[
\mathbb E[f_x(y)]\le \alpha\operatorname{OPT}(x)
\qquad\text{for every admissible }x,
\]
where the expectation is omitted for deterministic algorithms. The optimal tradeoff is the least achievable \(\alpha\) for each \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The approximation–information tradeoff is the best objective ratio attainable when the algorithm may use only a bounded transcript about each instance.
assumptions_latex: \(f_x(y)\ge 0\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}(x)=\min_{z\in F(x)}f_x(z)\).
The transcript size or query count defining \(b\) is fixed before comparing algorithms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha^*(b)=\inf_A\sup_x \mathbb E[f_x(A(I(x)))]/\operatorname{OPT}(x)\), subject to the information budget.

notation.meaning: information transcript available for instance x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition is too model dependent to validate without a source. Transcript length, query count, bit complexity, adaptivity, and randomized information interfaces are not interchangeable, and the node does not select one of them.

children.title: Space Complexity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Approximation and capability changes under memory restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Space Complexity Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal streaming memory as a function of passes, queries, approximation, and instance size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a streaming problem on instances of size \(n\), an approximation target \(\alpha\), a pass budget \(p\), a permitted auxiliary-query budget \(q\), and failure probability \(\delta\). Define
\[
S^*(n,p,q,\alpha,\delta)
=
\inf_A\max_{x}
\{\text{working-memory bits used by }A\text{ on }x\},
\]
where the infimum ranges over streaming algorithms making at most \(p\) passes and \(q\) permitted queries and returning an \(\alpha\)-approximate feasible solution with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Upper and lower space bounds form a tradeoff when they vary with \(p\), \(q\), or \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The space frontier records the least worst-case working memory needed for a prescribed approximation, pass count, query budget, and failure probability.
assumptions_latex: The stream representation, arrival order, and word or bit model are fixed.
Output storage is either excluded consistently or charged consistently.
Success is required on every admissible instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any feasible algorithm uses at least \(S^*\) bits, and algorithms attaining that order establish matching upper bounds.

notation.meaning: optimal worst-case streaming space in bits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a parameterized optimal-resource definition or representation, not an actual complexity bound, because it supplies no asymptotic upper or lower bound. The mixed streaming-plus-auxiliary-query model and its frontier require a dedicated source; the listed general time-and-space locator does not support them.

children.title: Pass Complexity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Performance changes as the permitted number of data passes varies.

knowledge_statements.title: Pass Complexity Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal number of stream passes under fixed space, query, approximation, and error budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an instance size \(n\), working-space budget \(S\), auxiliary-query budget \(q\), approximation target \(\alpha\), and failure probability \(\delta\). The pass complexity frontier is
\[
P^*(n,S,q,\alpha,
\delta)=
\inf_A\max_x
\{\text{number of complete passes made by }A\text{ on }x\},
\]
where \(A\) ranges over streaming algorithms using at most \(S\) bits and \(q\) permitted queries and producing an \(\alpha\)-approximate feasible solution with probability at least \(1-\delta\). A pass–space tradeoff consists of upper and lower bounds on \(P^*\) as \(S\) varies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pass frontier is the fewest complete scans needed when memory, query count, approximation, and failure probability are fixed.
assumptions_latex: A pass is one sequential scan of the entire stream in the specified arrival order.
The algorithm respects the same memory bound throughout every pass.
Success is required for every admissible input stream.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every qualifying algorithm makes at least \(P^*\) passes in the worst case.

notation.meaning: optimal worst-case number of complete stream passes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record defines an optimal pass measure rather than stating a complexity bound. Its complete-pass convention, auxiliary-query coupling, and pass-space frontier are model-specific and have no relevant cited locator.

children.title: Query Complexity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Performance changes as the permitted number of instance queries varies.

knowledge_statements.title: Query Complexity Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal oracle-query count under fixed streaming space, passes, approximation, and error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let an admissible oracle answer queries about a streaming instance of size \(n\). For space budget \(S\), pass budget \(p\), approximation target \(\alpha\), and failure probability \(\delta\), define
\[
Q^*(n,S,p,\alpha,\delta)
=
\inf_A\max_x
\{\text{number of oracle queries issued by }A\text{ on }x\},
\]
where \(A\) uses at most \(S\) bits, makes at most \(p\) stream passes, and returns an \(\alpha\)-approximate feasible solution with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Query tradeoffs are upper and lower bounds on \(Q^*\) as the other resource budgets vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The query frontier is the least worst-case oracle access needed under fixed memory, pass, approximation, and error requirements.
assumptions_latex: The oracle's legal query set, answer semantics, and answer precision are fixed.
Queries are counted individually, independently of their computational processing cost.
Success is required on every admissible instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every qualifying algorithm issues at least \(Q^*\) oracle queries in the worst case.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record defines an optimal query measure rather than giving a complexity bound. Query complexity is meaningless without a particular oracle and answer model, and no cited source supports combining that oracle with streaming passes and space.

children.title: Cross-Resource Tradeoff Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Interactions among memory, pass count, and query access.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Resource Tradeoff Frontiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto frontier coupling streaming space, passes, queries, approximation, and failure probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed instance size \(n\), let \(\mathcal R_n\) contain every achievable tuple \((S,p,q,\alpha,\delta)\), meaning that some streaming algorithm uses at most \(S\) bits, at most \(p\) passes, and at most \(q\) oracle queries while returning an \(\alpha\)-approximate solution with failure probability at most \(\delta\). Under the order in which smaller \(S,p,q,\alpha,\delta\) is better, the cross-resource frontier is
\[
\mathcal F_n=\{r\in\mathcal R_n:\nexists r'\in\mathcal R_n\text{ with }r'\le r\text{ and }r'\ne r\}.
\]
Every coordinate tradeoff is a projection or slice of \(\mathcal F_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cross-resource frontier consists of achievable performance tuples that cannot improve any resource or error coordinate without worsening another.
assumptions_latex: All algorithms use the same stream, oracle, cost, and success conventions.
Approximation factors follow a minimization convention in which smaller values are better.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_n\) is exactly the set of Pareto-minimal achievable resource-performance tuples.

notation.meaning: space, passes, queries, approximation, and failure tuple

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A Pareto representation fits the frontier leaf, but the achievable region depends on unsourced stream and oracle models. Moreover, a coordinate tradeoff need not equal a projection of the Pareto-minimal set without additional monotonicity and slicing conventions.

children.title: Preprocessing Cost
children.top_down_role: Initial computational investment before dynamic operations begin.

knowledge_statements.title: Preprocessing Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization cost of a dynamic discrete data structure before online operations begin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_0\) be an initial discrete instance and let \(D\) be a dynamic data structure. Its preprocessing cost is the resource usage of the initialization map
\[
\operatorname{Init}_D(x_0)\longmapsto s_0,
\]
where \(s_0\) is the maintained state from which subsequent updates and queries are served. In a time model, define
\[
T_{\mathrm{pre}}(n)=\max_{|x_0|=n}\operatorname{time}(\operatorname{Init}_D(x_0)).
\]
Any randomness, failure probability, memory allocation, and one-time construction work performed before the first operation must be charged according to the declared model rather than to update or query cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preprocessing cost is the worst-case resource needed to convert the initial instance into the maintained state before any update or query.
assumptions_latex: The instance-size measure \(|x_0|=n\) and computational model are fixed.
Initialization ends before the first dynamic operation is issued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{pre}}(n)\) equals the maximum initialization time over size-\(n\) initial instances.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits preprocessing cost, but the accounting rules for initialization, randomness, storage allocation, and deferred work are model-specific. No relevant dynamic-data-structure source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Update Cost
children.top_down_role: Resources consumed when incorporating an instance change.

knowledge_statements.title: Update Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case or amortized resource cost of modifying a maintained dynamic instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(s_{t-1}\) be the state representing instance \(x_{t-1}\), and let \(u_t\) be a legal update producing instance \(x_t\). A dynamic data structure applies
\[
\operatorname{Update}_D(s_{t-1},u_t)\longmapsto s_t.
\]
Its worst-case update time is
\[
T_{\mathrm{upd}}^{\mathrm{wc}}(n)=
\sup_t\sup_{|x_{t-1}|\le n}
\operatorname{time}(\operatorname{Update}_D(s_{t-1},u_t)).
\]
Its amortized update time over every legal sequence of \(m\) updates is the least \(a(n)\) for which total update time is at most \(m a(n)+O(1)\), excluding separately declared preprocessing and query work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Update cost measures the worst-case or amortized resource needed to transform maintained state after one legal instance modification.
assumptions_latex: Each update preserves the declared dynamic problem's admissibility conditions.
Preprocessing and query work are accounted for separately.
The size bound \(n\) applies throughout the update sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update frontier records achievable pairs of update guarantee and maintained solution quality under the fixed model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits update cost, but the worst-case supremum and amortized accounting convention require a source. The conclusion additionally introduces an update-quality frontier that is neither defined nor implied by the preceding statement.

children.title: Query Cost
children.top_down_role: Resources consumed when retrieving information from maintained state.

knowledge_statements.title: Query Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource cost of answering a dynamic query from the currently maintained state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(s_t\) represent the current dynamic instance \(x_t\), and let \(q_t\) be a legal query. The data structure returns
\[

a_t=\operatorname{Query}_D(s_t,q_t).
\]
Its worst-case query time is
\[
T_{\mathrm{qry}}^{\mathrm{wc}}(n)=
\sup_t\sup_{|x_t|\le n}
\operatorname{time}(\operatorname{Query}_D(s_t,q_t)).
\]
For an exact structure, \(a_t\) must equal the specified answer for \((x_t,q_t)\). For an approximate or randomized structure, the approximation factor and failure probability are included as explicit parameters of the query-cost bound. Preprocessing and update work are excluded unless the model expressly charges deferred work to queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Query cost is the worst-case resource needed to answer one legal question about the current maintained instance with the promised accuracy.
assumptions_latex: The maintained state correctly represents the current instance before the query.
The answer specification, approximation convention, and error probability are fixed.
Deferred computation is charged according to a declared accounting rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{qry}}^{\mathrm{wc}}(n)\) is the maximum time for one legal query on an instance of size at most \(n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits query cost and distinguishes exact from approximate or randomized answers, but the accounting of deferred work, error, and approximation is model-specific. No relevant dynamic-data-structure citation or inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Dynamic Cost Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs among preprocessing, update, and query costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Cost Frontiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto frontier for preprocessing, update, and query costs in a fixed dynamic computation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance-size parameter \(n\), a dynamic problem, and a computation model. A resource profile \((P,U,Q)\) is attainable if an algorithm uses preprocessing cost at most \(P(n)\), update cost at most \(U(n)\), and query cost at most \(Q(n)\), with all bounds sharing the stated worst-case or amortized convention. For profiles \(r=(P,U,Q)\) and \(r'=(P',U',Q')\), write \(r'\preceq r\) when each component of \(r'\) is asymptotically no larger than the corresponding component of \(r\). The dynamic cost frontier is the set of attainable profiles for which no distinct attainable profile \(r'\preceq r\) has a strict improvement in at least one component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The frontier consists of attainable preprocessing, update, and query bounds that cannot be improved in one component without worsening another.
assumptions_latex: A fixed dynamic problem and computational model are specified.
Worst-case or amortized cost conventions are fixed consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F=\{r\in\mathcal A:\nexists r'\in\mathcal A\text{ with }r'\preceq r\text{ and }r'\ne r\}.

notation.meaning: set of attainable dynamic resource profiles
preprocessing, update, and query cost functions

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses dynamic data-structure tradeoff frontiers.
Authoritative source needed for the adopted asymptotic Pareto convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the adopted asymptotic Pareto convention. Moreover, the conclusion excludes every distinct dominated profile, whereas the statement requires a strict improvement in at least one component; asymptotically equivalent but syntactically distinct profiles expose the mismatch.

children.title: Recourse Complexity
children.top_down_role: The amount or frequency of discrete solution revision.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial recourse measured by elementary changes between consecutive maintained solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_0,I_1,\ldots,I_T\) be an evolving instance sequence and let \(S_t\subseteq E_t\) be the feasible solution maintained after update \(t\). The recourse at update \(t\) is \(\rho_t=|S_t\triangle S_{t-1}|\), where each insertion or deletion counts once. Total recourse is \(R_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\rho_t\); worst-case recourse is \(\max_{1\le t\le T}\rho_t\); and amortized recourse is \(R_T/T\). A recourse-complexity bound specifies one of these quantities as a function of the instance parameters, update horizon, and required solution quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse counts elementary insertions and deletions needed to transform each maintained solution into the next, measured per update or cumulatively.
assumptions_latex: Each maintained solution is represented as a finite subset of a common labeled universe.
Insertions and deletions are the elementary solution changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}|S_t\triangle S_{t-1}|.
review_flags: No supplied locator supports recourse in evolving combinatorial optimization.
Counting conventions can differ when replacements are treated as one operation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but no source with a specific locator supports symmetric-difference recourse or the convention that a replacement counts as two elementary changes.

children.title: Migration Complexity
children.top_down_role: The volume or cost of reallocating solution components.

knowledge_statements.title: Migration Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted movement cost of reconfiguring a maintained allocation or assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a set of weighted objects, with weights \(w_e\ge 0\), and let \(x_t:E\to L\cup\{\bot\}\) describe their maintained locations after update \(t\). The migration cost of update \(t\) is \(m_t=\sum_{e\in E}w_e\mathbf 1\{x_t(e)\ne x_{t-1}(e)\}\). Total migration is \(M_T=\sum_{t=1}^T m_t\), while worst-case and amortized migration are respectively \(\max_t m_t\) and \(M_T/T\). A migration-complexity bound relates one of these quantities to update size, instance size, or the objective value while preserving the specified feasibility and quality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Migration complexity measures the total weight of objects whose maintained locations change, either per update or over the entire sequence.
assumptions_latex: Objects have fixed nonnegative migration weights.
The maintained solution admits a labeled-location representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{e\in E}w_e\mathbf 1\{x_t(e)\ne x_{t-1}(e)\}.

notation.meaning: maintained object-location assignment after update t
total weighted migration through update T

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses migration in dynamic or online optimization.
The normalization used by migration-factor literature is not fixed by the node path.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted movement definition fits the leaf, but no cited source supports this location-based convention or its relationship to standard migration-complexity normalizations.

children.title: Solution Stability
children.top_down_role: Persistence of solution structure across successive inputs or updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz stability of maintained solutions under changes to the input instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal I,d_{\mathcal I})\) be an instance space, \((\mathcal S,d_{\mathcal S})\) a solution space, and \(A:\mathcal I\to\mathcal S\) a deterministic solution rule. The rule is \(L\)-stable on \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal I\) if every \(I,J\in\mathcal D\) satisfy \(d_{\mathcal S}(A(I),A(J))\le Ld_{\mathcal I}(I,J)\). For a randomized rule, stability in expectation means \(\mathbb E[d_{\mathcal S}(A(I),A(J))]\le Ld_{\mathcal I}(I,J)\) under a specified coupling of its outputs. Stability therefore requires both the input perturbation metric and the solution-change metric to be fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution rule is stable when small instance changes produce proportionally small changes in its output under specified input and solution metrics.
assumptions_latex: The instance and solution spaces carry specified metrics.
For randomized rules, a coupling of outputs is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_{\mathcal S}(A(I),A(J))\le Ld_{\mathcal I}(I,J)\quad\text{for all }I,J\in\mathcal D.
review_flags: No supplied locator supports this metric formulation of solution stability.
Alternative stability notions may use high-probability or local sensitivity guarantees.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metric condition is internally coherent and the content kind fits, but no source establishes that this Lipschitz formulation is the intended solution-stability notion in the local dynamic-optimization context.

children.title: Quality-Stability Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between objective quality and limited solution disruption.

knowledge_statements.title: Quality-Stability Frontiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto boundary between approximation quality and cumulative solution change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a minimization problem, an update horizon \(T\), and a solution-change measure \(R_T\). A pair \((\alpha,r)\) is attainable if an algorithm maintains feasible solutions \(S_t\) satisfying \(c_t(S_t)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I_t)\) for every \(t\) and \(R_T\le r\) under the stated worst-case, expected, or amortized convention. Define \((\alpha',r')\preceq(\alpha,r)\) when \(\alpha'\le\alpha\) and \(r'\le r\). The quality-stability frontier consists of attainable pairs not strictly dominated under \(\preceq\). Thus each frontier point records a solution-quality guarantee that cannot be improved without increasing permitted solution change, or conversely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quality-stability frontier contains nondominated pairs of approximation ratio and permitted recourse or migration.
assumptions_latex: The objective is a nonnegative minimization objective.
The solution-change measure and probabilistic convention are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F_{QS}=\{(\alpha,r)\in\mathcal A:\nexists(\alpha',r')\in\mathcal A\text{ strictly dominating }(\alpha,r)\}.
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses quality-stability tradeoffs.
A source is needed to certify the adopted approximation and domination conventions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the frontier leaf, but the approximation, change-budget, probabilistic, and Pareto conventions lack a supporting citation and locator.

children.title: Distributional Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Hardness obtained from carefully chosen input distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributional Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Average-case lower bounds against deterministic algorithms under a fixed hard input distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be an input set, \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{det}}\) a class of deterministic algorithms, \(C(A,I)\ge 0\) their cost, and \(\mu\) a probability distribution on \(\mathcal I\). The distributional complexity under \(\mu\) is \(D_\mu=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{det}}}\mathbb E_{I\sim\mu}[C(A,I)]\). A distributional lower bound \(L\) is established by exhibiting \(\mu\) such that every admissible deterministic algorithm satisfies \(\mathbb E_{I\sim\mu}[C(A,I)]\ge L\). Error, approximation, and resource restrictions must be incorporated into the admissible algorithm class before taking the infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributional lower bound shows that every admissible deterministic algorithm has large expected cost on one fixed hard distribution.
assumptions_latex: The cost is nonnegative and measurable.
The admissible deterministic algorithm class includes all required error and approximation restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_\mu=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{det}}}\mathbb E_{I\sim\mu}[C(A,I)]\ge L.

notation.meaning: cost of algorithm A on input I

review_flags: No supplied locator concerns distributional complexity or randomized lower bounds.
A relevant complexity-theory source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is a plausible definition of distributional deterministic complexity, but no relevant source specifies the admissible algorithm, error, approximation, or cost conventions.

children.title: Minimax Lower-Bound Transfers
children.top_down_role: Transfers from distributional hardness to randomized worst-case limitations.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimax Lower-Bound Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Yao minimax transfer from deterministic distributional bounds to randomized worst-case bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
