Let \(\mathcal I\) and \(\mathcal A\) be finite sets of inputs and deterministic algorithms, and let \(C:\mathcal A\times\mathcal I\to\mathbb R\) be bounded. A randomized algorithm is a distribution \(\rho\) on \(\mathcal A\). Then
\[
\min_{\rho\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\max_{I\in\mathcal I}\mathbb E_{A\sim\rho}[C(A,I)]
=
\max_{\mu\in\Delta(\mathcal I)}\min_{A\in\mathcal A}\mathbb E_{I\sim\mu}[C(A,I)].
\]
Consequently, if some distribution \(\mu\) gives every deterministic algorithm expected cost at least \(L\), then every randomized algorithm has some input on which its expected cost is at least \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite bounded games, a hard distribution against every deterministic algorithm transfers to a worst-case expected lower bound for randomized algorithms.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal I and \mathcal A are finite.
C is a bounded real-valued cost function.
Randomization is represented by a distribution over deterministic algorithms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\rho}\max_I\mathbb E_{A\sim\rho}C(A,I)=\max_{\mu}\min_A\mathbb E_{I\sim\mu}C(A,I).

notation.meaning: probability simplex over a finite set X

review_flags: Standard finite minimax result, but no relevant source locator was supplied.
The exact treatment of bounded-error algorithms requires source-specific admissibility conventions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite minimax equality and stated transfer are mathematically standard and fit the theorem leaf, but no authoritative source with a theorem, section, or page locator is cited.

children.title: Minimax Applicability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions limiting distributional-to-randomized transfers.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimax Applicability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unrestricted minimax equality on infinite, noncompact strategy spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Finiteness, compactness, or comparable tightness conditions cannot be omitted indiscriminately. Let the input and deterministic-action sets both be \(\mathbb N\), and define \(C(a,i)=\mathbf 1\{a<i\}\). For every probability distribution \(\rho\) on actions, \(\sup_{i\in\mathbb N}\mathbb E_{a\sim\rho}[C(a,i)]=1\). Conversely, for every probability distribution \(\mu\) on inputs, \(\inf_{a\in\mathbb N}\mathbb E_{i\sim\mu}[C(a,i)]=0\). Hence
\[
\inf_{\rho}\sup_i\mathbb E_\rho C(a,i)=1>0=\sup_\mu\inf_a\mathbb E_\mu C(a,i),
\]
so the finite minimax transfer fails on this noncompact infinite game.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On infinite noncompact strategy spaces, the randomized worst-case value can exceed every deterministic distributional value, invalidating an unrestricted minimax transfer.
assumptions_latex: Both strategy sets are the positive integers.
All probability distributions are countably additive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{\rho}\sup_i\mathbb E_\rho C(a,i)=1>0=\sup_\mu\inf_a\mathbb E_\mu C(a,i).

notation.meaning: indicator cost that the chosen action is below the input

review_flags: The counterexample is directly checkable but lacks an external source locator.
A minimax reference is needed to contextualize sufficient compactness and convexity conditions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is coherent and correctly illustrates failure on a noncompact infinite game, but it has no source locator establishing the example or contextualizing the omitted minimax hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Complexity Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound transfer by simulating an algorithm as a two-party communication protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\times Y\to Z\) have randomized communication complexity \(R_\varepsilon(f)\). Suppose every algorithm for a target problem using resource \(T\) can, on an encoding \(g(x,y)\), be simulated by a public-coin protocol that computes \(f(x,y)\) with error at most \(\varepsilon\) and communicates at most \(cT+b\) bits, where \(c>0\). Then every such algorithm satisfies
\[
T\ge \frac{R_\varepsilon(f)-b}{c}.
\]
The reduction must preserve the relevant input promise, approximation gap, adaptivity, and error convention; otherwise the communication lower bound does not transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a low-resource algorithm would yield a low-communication protocol for a hard function, communication lower bounds imply an algorithmic resource lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The simulation communicates at most cT+b bits.
The protocol preserves the source problem's promise and error bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\ge (R_\varepsilon(f)-b)/c.

notation.meaning: randomized communication complexity of f at error epsilon
resource usage of the target algorithm

review_flags: No supplied locator concerns communication complexity.
A relevant source is needed for model-specific reduction requirements.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-bound transfer principle fits the topic, but no communication-complexity source supports the model-specific simulation, randomness, error, and promise-preservation requirements.

children.title: Indistinguishability Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Hard instances whose observable transcripts remain difficult to distinguish.

knowledge_statements.title: Indistinguishability Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary transcript-testing lower bound expressed through total variation distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be uniform on \(\{0,1\}\), and let a fixed algorithm produce transcript \(\Pi\) whose conditional distributions are \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) under \(V=0\) and \(V=1\). For every estimator \(\widehat V=\phi(\Pi)\),
\[
\Pr(\widehat V\ne V)\ge \frac{1-\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1)}{2}.
\]
Therefore, success probability at least \(1-\varepsilon\) requires \(\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1)\ge1-2\varepsilon\). Any resource restriction forcing the two transcript laws to have smaller total variation consequently proves a resource lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two cases induce nearby transcript distributions, no transcript-based algorithm can reliably distinguish them; high success requires large total variation distance.
assumptions_latex: The two hypotheses have equal prior probability.
The estimator depends only on the observed transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(\widehat V\ne V)\ge \bigl(1-\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1)\bigr)/2.

notation.meaning: conditional law of the transcript under hypothesis v

review_flags: Standard binary testing inequality, but no relevant source locator was supplied.
Transcript measurability and testing conventions require source certification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary testing inequality is standard and correctly scoped, but no authoritative source with a specific locator supports the total-variation convention and theorem statement.

children.title: Information-Theoretic Bounds
children.top_down_role: Limitations derived from restricted information acquisition or retention.

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Theoretic Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fano lower bound for identifying one of finitely many equiprobable hidden instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be uniform on a set of cardinality \(M\ge2\), let \(Y\) be an observation or algorithm transcript, and let \(\widehat V=\phi(Y)\). With natural logarithms and error probability \(P_e=\Pr(\widehat V\ne V)\), Fano's inequality gives
\[
P_e\ge 1-\frac{I(V;Y)+\log 2}{\log M}.
\]
Consequently, any procedure with \(P_e\le\varepsilon\) must reveal
\[
I(V;Y)\ge(1-\varepsilon)\log M-\log 2.
\]
An upper bound on information obtainable per query, update, sample, or communicated bit therefore yields a corresponding resource lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reliable identification among many equiprobable instances requires the observation transcript to contain information proportional to the logarithm of the family size.
assumptions_latex: V is uniform on M hypotheses with M at least 2.
The estimate is a measurable function of Y.
Logarithms are natural.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_e\ge1-\frac{I(V;Y)+\log 2}{\log M}.

notation.meaning: mutual information between the hidden index and observation

review_flags: Standard Fano inequality, but no information-theory locator was supplied.
A source is required to certify the precise logarithm and constant convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated Fano bound and its rearranged information requirement are standard, but the precise logarithm and additive-constant convention require an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Transcript-Information Connections
children.top_down_role: Relations between observational similarity and information limitations.

knowledge_statements.title: Transcript-Information Connections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information revealed by a discrete transcript is bounded by its entropy and encoded length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be hidden input data, \(R\) public randomness independent of \(X\), and \(\Pi\) a discrete interactive transcript. Then
\[
I(X;\Pi\mid R)\le H(\Pi\mid R).
\]
If, conditional on every value of \(R\), transcripts are represented by a binary prefix-free encoding with length \(L(\Pi)\), then
\[
H(\Pi\mid R)\le\mathbb E[L(\Pi)].
\]
Thus a protocol or algorithm communicating an expected \(b\) bits reveals at most \(b\) bits of conditional information about \(X\). Together with an information requirement, this converts transcript-length upper bounds into communication or query lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prefix-free transcript reveals no more information than its entropy, and its entropy is no greater than its expected encoded length.
assumptions_latex: R is independent of X.
The transcript is discrete.
Conditional transcript encodings are binary and prefix-free.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I(X;\Pi\mid R)\le H(\Pi\mid R)\le\mathbb E[L(\Pi)].

notation.meaning: public randomness independent of the hidden input

review_flags: Standard entropy and coding inequalities, but no relevant source locator was supplied.
The prefix-free qualification is essential for the expected-length inequality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inequalities are standard under a conditional binary prefix-free code, but no source is cited and the entropy and mutual-information logarithm base must be specified as base two to justify the numerical claim in bits.

children.title: Cell-Probe Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Data-structure limitations measured through memory-cell access.

assumptions_latex: The data structure stores words of \(w\) bits and answers each operation using at most \(t\) adaptive cell probes.
A reduction maps an instance of a communication problem to one data-structure operation and simulates every probe using at most \(c w\) communicated bits.
The communication problem has lower bound \(L\) bits under the same deterministic, randomized, or distributional convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[t\ge \frac{L}{cw}.\]
review_flags: exact source and model convention require certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Communication-reduction form of a cell-probe lower bound, with computation between probes free.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a cell-probe data structure have word size \(w\) and worst-case probe complexity \(t\). Suppose a reduction from a communication problem simulates each probe by a protocol exchanging at most \(cw\) bits, so a data-structure operation induces communication at most \(ctw\). If every protocol of the corresponding type and error guarantee requires at least \(L\) bits, then \(ctw\ge L\), and hence \[t\ge \frac{L}{cw}.\] The reduction must preserve preprocessing, update/query order, randomization, and error conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A communication lower bound transfers to cell-probe complexity when each memory probe can be simulated with bounded communication.
knowledge_statements.title: Cell-Probe Lower Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role and conditional transfer formula are coherent, but no inspectable citation certifies the communication simulation, preprocessing, randomization, and error conventions.

children.title: Fine-Grained Conditional Bounds
children.top_down_role: Dynamic or sublinear limitations conditioned on fine-grained hardness hypotheses.

assumptions_latex: Problem \(P\) on size \(n\) is conjectured to require time \(n^{a-o(1)}\).
A reduction transforms \(P\) instances into \(Q\) instances of size \(N=O(n^c)\) in time \(n^{a-o(1)}\).
The reduction preserves correctness and the relevant randomized or deterministic error convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), an \(O(N^{a/c-\varepsilon})\)-time algorithm for \(Q\) would refute the conjecture for \(P\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard fine-grained reduction exponent transfer
specific conjecture and reduction class are not fixed by the node
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exponent-preserving conditional lower bound rather than a bound tied to one hardness conjecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the fine-grained conjecture that problem \(P\) on size \(n\) has no algorithm running in time \(n^{a-\delta}\) for any \(\delta>0\). Let a correctness-preserving reduction produce an instance of \(Q\) having size \(N=O(n^c)\), with reduction overhead \(n^{a-o(1)}\). If \(Q\) admitted time \(O(N^{a/c-\varepsilon})\) for some \(\varepsilon>0\), composition would solve \(P\) in time \(O(n^{a-c\varepsilon})+n^{a-o(1)}\), contradicting the conjectured exponent whenever the overhead is correspondingly subcritical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exponent-preserving reduction turns a sufficiently faster algorithm for the target problem into a violation of the source hardness conjecture.
knowledge_statements.title: Fine-Grained Conditional Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed contradiction does not follow with reduction overhead merely n^{a-o(1)}, which can dominate the target-algorithm term without yielding n^{a-δ} time. A sourced, quantitatively subcritical overhead condition is required.

children.title: Model-Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on transferring hardness between cell-probe and fine-grained settings.

assumptions_latex: A word-RAM operation performs at most \(c\) probes to \(w\)-bit memory cells.
Cell-probe computation between probes is free, whereas the word-RAM charges for arithmetic and control operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A cell-probe lower bound \(L\) implies word-RAM time at least \(L/c\), but a word-RAM time lower bound need not imply any comparable cell-probe bound.

notation.meaning: maximum probes performed by one word-RAM operation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard containment of cell-probe cost by word-RAM time
machine instruction and word-size conventions require a source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way transfer boundary between cell-probe and word-RAM lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each operation of a \(w\)-bit word-RAM accesses at most \(c\) memory cells. Any word-RAM algorithm taking time \(T\) induces a cell-probe algorithm using at most \(cT\) probes. Consequently, a cell-probe lower bound \(L\) yields \(T\ge L/c\) for that RAM model. The converse transfer is invalid without additional hypotheses: a word-RAM lower bound may charge computation that is free in the cell-probe model, so it alone supplies no comparable lower bound on probes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cell-probe lower bounds transfer to bounded-access RAMs, but RAM lower bounds generally do not transfer back because cell-probe computation is free.
knowledge_statements.title: Model-Transfer Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, and the one-way transfer is conditionally correct, but the RAM instruction, memory-access, and word-size conventions require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Online Discrete Optimization
children.top_down_role: Classical and modern discrete problems in which decisions precede knowledge of future requests or items.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Chapter 13, paging, k-server, metrical task systems, load balancing, and routing
Foundational examples, task systems, server problems, and request-answer games

children.title: Ski-Rental Problems
children.top_down_role: Canonical online decisions between continued rental and irreversible purchase.

assumptions_latex: Rent costs \(r>0\) per day and purchase costs \(B>0\).
The unknown horizon is an integer \(T\ge1\), and buying at the start of a day eliminates that day's rental cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The threshold rule has cost at most \(2\operatorname{OPT}(T)\) for every horizon \(T\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical deterministic ski-rental threshold theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical deterministic, discrete-time ski-rental theorem with known rent and purchase prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k=\lceil B/r\rceil\). The deterministic threshold algorithm rents on days \(1,\ldots,k-1\) and, if day \(k\) occurs, buys at its start. For horizon \(T<k\), its cost is \(rT=\operatorname{OPT}(T)\). For \(T\ge k\), its cost is \(r(k-1)+B<2B\), while \(\operatorname{OPT}(T)=\min\{rT,B\}=B\). Therefore its competitive ratio is strictly below \(2\), and in particular its cost is at most \(2\operatorname{OPT}(T)\) for every \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rent until accumulated rental cost approaches the purchase price, then buy; this deterministic policy is 2-competitive.
knowledge_statements.title: Ski-Rental Problems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The discrete deterministic threshold theorem is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no authoritative theorem locator is supplied and the statement includes proof-style derivation.

children.title: Rent-or-Buy Problems
children.top_down_role: Generalized online acquisition settings with temporary and permanent commitments.

assumptions_latex: A finite action set contains a rental action with recurring cost and a purchase action with one-time cost.
The stopping horizon is selected without being revealed to the online algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is to minimize online cost relative to the clairvoyant minimum over all feasible rent-and-purchase schedules.

notation.meaning: online and offline costs on horizon T

review_flags: formal variant and authoritative source remain unspecified
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract irreversible rent-or-buy problem, encompassing ski rental but allowing general feasible cost schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rent-or-buy problem is an online minimization problem with an unrevealed stopping horizon \(T\). Before purchase, the algorithm repeatedly chooses feasible rental actions and pays their recurring costs; at a chosen time it may irrevocably purchase and thereafter receives the contracted service without further rental charges. For algorithm \(A\), let \(C_A(T)\) be its cost and let \(C^*(T)\) be the minimum cost of a schedule knowing \(T\). The algorithm is \(\rho\)-competitive if some constant \(\beta\ge0\) satisfies \(C_A(T)\le \rho C^*(T)+\beta\) for every \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rent-or-buy asks an online algorithm to choose when to replace recurring payments by an irreversible purchase without knowing the stopping time.
knowledge_statements.title: Rent-or-Buy Problems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits, but the abstraction allows general rental actions and schedules without fixing their feasibility and cost conventions. A source for this precise rent-or-buy variant is needed.

children.title: Purchase-Threshold Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes governing transitions from rental to purchase.

assumptions_latex: Time is continuous, rental rate is \(r>0\), purchase price is \(B>0\), and the horizon is adversarial.
A threshold policy buys at time \(\tau=\alpha B/r\) if the process has not stopped, where \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Its competitive ratio is \(1+1/\alpha\) for \(0<\alpha\le1\) and \(1+\alpha\) for \(\alpha\ge1\), uniquely minimized at \(\alpha=1\) with value \(2\).
review_flags: continuous-time convention and source require certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-time deterministic threshold regimes, normalized by the break-even time \(B/r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the policy that rents until \(\tau=\alpha B/r\) and then buys, the worst-case competitive ratio is \[R(\alpha)=\begin{cases}1+1/\alpha,&0<\alpha\le1,\\1+\alpha,&\alpha\ge1.\end{cases}\] Indeed, purchase at \(\tau\) is compared with rental cost \(r\tau\) when \(\alpha\le1\), and with purchase cost \(B\) when \(\alpha\ge1\). Thus \(R(\alpha)\ge2\), with equality exactly at the break-even threshold \(\alpha=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Buying at the break-even time is the optimal deterministic threshold regime; earlier or later normalized thresholds have a worse worst-case ratio.
knowledge_statements.title: Purchase-Threshold Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The piecewise ratio is correct under the stated continuous-time convention and the property role fits the regime leaf, but that convention lacks a source and the statement contains proof text.

children.title: Online Search
children.top_down_role: Sequential search problems requiring commitment under incomplete price information.

assumptions_latex: Prices \(p_1,dots,p_n\) arrive online in \([m,M]subset(0,infty), with \(m<M\).
Exactly one price must be accepted, and the final price is forced if no earlier price was accepted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepting the first price at least \(\sqrt{mM}\) is \(\sqrt{M/m}\)-competitive for maximizing the accepted price.

notation.meaning: known lower and upper price bounds

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical reservation-price algorithm for online search
authoritative source and adversary convention required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic online search with known price interval and compulsory acceptance of the last offer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set the reservation price \(q=\sqrt{mM}\). Inspect \(p_1,p_2,dots,p_n\) sequentially, accept and stop at the first \(p_i\ge q\), and accept \(p_n\) if no earlier price qualifies. If the algorithm accepts at least \(q\), the offline maximum is at most \(M\), giving ratio at most \(M/q\). Otherwise every earlier price is below \(q\), so the offline maximum is below \(q\) while the forced price is at least \(m\), giving ratio at most \(q/m\). Both bounds equal \(\sqrt{M/m}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With known price bounds, accept the first offer reaching their geometric mean; otherwise take the last offer.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reservation-price algorithm and bound are standard, but no authoritative source is supplied. The assumptions contain malformed TeX, and the explanatory case analysis incorrectly says the offline maximum is below the threshold without separately handling a qualifying terminal price.

children.title: One-Way Trading
children.top_down_role: Sequential conversion problems with an irreversible trading direction.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Way Trading
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional one-way currency conversion with known rate bounds, compulsory terminal conversion, and no conversion back.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In one-way trading, exchange rates \(p_1,\dots,p_n\in[m,M]\subset(0,\infty)\) are revealed sequentially. After observing \(p_i\), an online strategy irrevocably converts a fraction \(x_i\ge 0\) of its initial source currency, where \(x_i\) depends only on the revealed prefix. Feasibility requires \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=1\), with any balance remaining before the final period converted at \(p_n\). The final proceeds are \(V=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i p_i\), whereas the clairvoyant optimum is \(V^*=\max_{1\le i\le n}p_i\). Multiplicative performance is measured by \(V^*/V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-way trading allocates a divisible asset across sequential exchange rates, forces any remaining balance to be converted at the final rate, and compares the proceeds with conversion entirely at the best rate.
assumptions_latex: Exchange rates \(p_1,\dots,p_n\in[m,M]\subset(0,\infty)\) arrive sequentially.
The trader starts with one unit of source currency; conversions are divisible, irreversible, and free of transaction costs.
Any balance remaining before period \(n\) is converted at the terminal rate \(p_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[V=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i p_i,\qquad V^*=\max_{1\le i\le n}p_i.\]

notation.meaning: fraction of the initial source currency converted at time i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard fractional one-way trading model
authoritative source for the compulsory terminal-conversion convention is required

children.title: Price-Range Information Regimes
children.top_down_role: Performance regimes determined by available bounds or distributions for prices.

assumptions_latex: Every revealed price lies in a known interval \([m,M] with \(0<m\le M<infty\).
Performance is measured by a multiplicative competitive ratio.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After normalization by \(m\), the regime is determined by the uncertainty ratio \(\theta=M/m\); common rescaling of all prices leaves every multiplicative competitive ratio unchanged.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scale invariance of multiplicative online price models
precise information-regime taxonomy requires a source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Known positive lower and upper bounds under multiplicative competitive analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<m\le p_i\le M<\infty\) and define \(\theta=M/m\). Replacing every price and both bounds by \(ap_i\), \(am\), and \(aM\), where \(a>0\), multiplies online and offline rewards by the same factor and therefore preserves their ratio. Hence normalization \(m=1\) loses no information for multiplicative analysis, and the bounded-range regime is parametrized by \(\theta\). Allowing \(m=0\) or \(M=\infty\) destroys this finite normalization and may preclude a uniform finite competitive guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For multiplicative analysis, a known positive price interval matters only through its upper-to-lower uncertainty ratio; unbounded regimes can lose finite guarantees.
knowledge_statements.title: Price-Range Information Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Scale invariance under positive common rescaling is correct and fits the information-regime leaf. The assumptions contain malformed TeX, and the claim about loss of finite guarantees in unbounded regimes requires a model-specific source.

children.title: List Update
children.top_down_role: Online maintenance of linear order under access and rearrangement costs.

assumptions_latex: Requests address items in a fixed unsorted list, and accessing position \(i\) costs \(i\).
After access, the requested item may move toward the front freely; every other adjacent transposition costs one.
The offline comparator obeys the same paid-exchange rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Move-to-front satisfies \(C_{\mathrm{MTF}}(\sigma)\le2C_{mathrm{OPT}}(\sigma)+K\) for every request sequence \(\sigma\), where \(K\) depends only on the initial lists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical deterministic list-update theorem in the paid adjacent-exchange model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each request, move-to-front accesses the requested item and then moves it to the first position at no cost. In the list-update model where access to position \(i\) costs \(i\), moving the accessed item forward is free, and every other adjacent exchange costs one, there is a constant \(K\) depending only on the initial online and comparator lists such that, for every request sequence \(\sigma\), \[C_{\mathrm{MTF}}(\sigma)\le2C_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\sigma)+K.\] Thus move-to-front is deterministically \(2\)-competitive against the optimal offline update schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the standard paid-exchange list model, moving every requested item to the front is 2-competitive up to an initial-state constant.
knowledge_statements.title: List Update

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role and 2-competitive claim fit the list-update leaf, but an exact theorem locator for this paid-exchange model is absent. The conclusion also writes C_{mathrm{OPT}} rather than C_{\mathrm{OPT}}.

children.title: Self-Organizing Structures
children.top_down_role: Adaptive structures that reorganize in response to observed access patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Organizing Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-state model for adaptive structures whose total cost combines request service and state reorganization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A self-organizing structure is an online state system \((S,a,d)\). Starting from \(s_0\in S\), request \(x_t\) is served in state \(s_{t-1}\) at cost \(a(s_{t-1},x_t)\). The algorithm then chooses \(s_t\in S\) and pays reorganization cost \(d(s_{t-1},s_t)\). The choice of \(s_t\) may depend only on \(x_1,\dots,x_t\). Its total cost through time \(T\) is \[\sum_{t=1}^T\bigl(a(s_{t-1},x_t)+d(s_{t-1},s_t)\bigr),\] and it is compared with the minimum cost of a state sequence that knows all requests in advance and obeys the same cost rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A self-organizing structure adapts its state after each request, balancing access costs against reorganization costs and comparing its online choices with an offline state sequence.
assumptions_latex: A finite state space \(S\) represents the admissible organizations of stored items.
Each request \(x_t\) has access cost \(a(s,x_t)\) when served in state \(s\).
Changing state from \(s\) to \(s'\) incurs reorganization cost \(d(s,s')\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C=\sum_{t=1}^T\bigl(a(s_{t-1},x_t)+d(s_{t-1},s_t)\bigr).\]

notation.meaning: cost of serving request x in state s
cost of reorganizing from state s to state s'

review_flags: authoritative source and intended structure class remain unspecified

children.title: Reorganization Cost Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural effects of free, paid, or restricted reorganization.

knowledge_statements.title: Reorganization Cost Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paid adjacent-exchange regime for list reorganization, with free forward movement of the accessed item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the standard list-update reorganization regime, serving a request to an item at position \(i\) incurs access cost \(i\). Immediately afterward, the accessed item may be moved any distance toward the front at zero reorganization cost. Every other adjacent transposition costs one. Thus a schedule on request sequence \(\sigma\) has cost \[C(\sigma)=A(\sigma)+E(\sigma),\] where \(A(\sigma)\) is its total positional access cost and \(E(\sigma)\) is its number of paid adjacent exchanges. Online and offline schedules must use the same free-move convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regime charges positional access costs and all adjacent exchanges except the free forward movement of the item that was just accessed.
assumptions_latex: Items occupy positions in a linear list.
Accessing the item at position \(i\) costs \(i\).
After an access, the accessed item may move toward the front freely; every other adjacent exchange costs one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C(\sigma)=A(\sigma)+E(\sigma).\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard free-exchange and paid-exchange list-update convention
authoritative source distinguishing alternative full-cost conventions is required

children.title: Online Graph Exploration
children.top_down_role: Discovery of initially unknown graph structure through sequential movement.

knowledge_statements.title: Online Graph Exploration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines exploration when graph incidence information is revealed only at visited vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite connected graph with nonnegative edge lengths \(\ell:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) and start vertex \(s\in V\). Initially an algorithm knows only \(s\). Upon first visiting \(v\), it learns the edges incident to \(v\), their lengths, and their opposite endpoints. An online exploration walk starts at \(s\), traverses only revealed edges, and must visit every vertex. Its cost is the total traversed length; in the return variant it must also finish at \(s\). Performance is measured against a shortest offline walk satisfying the same endpoint requirement with full knowledge of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An online explorer learns each vertex’s incident edges upon arrival and must visit the entire graph, minimizing travel relative to an omniscient optimal exploration walk.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and connected.
\(\ell(e)\ge 0\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exploration cost is \(\operatorname{cost}(W)=\sum_{e\in W}\ell(e)\), compared with the corresponding offline optimum \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{exp}}(G,s)\).

notation.meaning: online exploration walk, with repeated edges counted

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no citation supports the particular local-incidence revelation model, endpoint convention, or offline comparator.

children.title: Online Graph Navigation
children.top_down_role: Movement toward destinations under incrementally revealed graph information.

knowledge_statements.title: Online Graph Navigation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines point-to-point navigation in an incrementally revealed weighted graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite connected graph with lengths \(\ell:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), start \(s\), and designated target \(t\). The algorithm initially knows \(s\) and the identity of \(t\), but not the unrevealed graph. When it visits a vertex, all incident edges, their lengths, and opposite endpoints are revealed. An online navigation algorithm chooses a walk from \(s\) until it first reaches \(t\). Its competitive ratio is the least \(c\) for which its travel cost is at most \(c\,d_G(s,t)+b\) on every admissible instance, where \(b\ge 0\) is an allowed additive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Online navigation seeks a designated target while local graph information is revealed during travel, and compares traveled length with the fully known shortest-path distance.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and connected.
\(s,t\in V\) and \(\ell(e)\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The offline benchmark is the shortest-path distance \(d_G(s,t)\).

notation.meaning: shortest-path distance from start to target

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The navigation concept fits the leaf, but the meaning of knowing the target's identity in an otherwise unrevealed graph and the additive-constant competitive convention require an exact source and model specification.

children.title: Exploration-Navigation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions between learning graph structure and reaching designated locations.

knowledge_statements.title: Exploration-Navigation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the bicriteria frontier between information acquisition and target-directed travel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an online walk \(W\) from \(s\) to a target \(t\), let \(X(W)\) be the length spent before acquiring the prescribed graph information and let \(N(W)\) be its total length until reaching \(t\). For an instance class \(\mathcal G\), the achievable tradeoff region is \[\mathcal R(\mathcal G)=\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^2:\exists A\ \forall G\in\mathcal G,\ X(A,G)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{exp}}(G),\ N(A,G)\le\beta d_G(s,t)\}.\] Its exploration-navigation frontier is the set of coordinatewise minimal points of \(\mathcal R(\mathcal G)\); moving along it exchanges exploration overhead for navigation quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tradeoff is the Pareto frontier of simultaneously attainable exploration and target-navigation competitive factors over a fixed graph and revelation model.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\) fixes a common revelation model and endpoint convention.
Both offline benchmarks are positive on the instances considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pair \((\alpha,\beta)\) is Pareto-optimal exactly when it belongs to \(\mathcal R(\mathcal G)\) and no distinct feasible pair is coordinatewise smaller.

notation.meaning: cost incurred before reaching the target

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes this particular bicriteria representation. The prescribed information defining X, the instance-dependent arguments of both costs, and the common endpoint conventions are not specified precisely enough to determine the claimed frontier.

children.title: Single-Choice Secretary Problems
children.top_down_role: Secretary selection with capacity for one accepted item.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Choice Secretary Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical random-order, adversarial-value secretary algorithm for selecting one maximum-value item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge 2\) distinct-valued items arrive in a uniformly random permutation, with their values fixed before the permutation. Set \(r=\max\{1,\lfloor n/e\rfloor\}\). Reject the first \(r\) arrivals and let \(M\) be their maximum value. Thereafter accept the first item whose value exceeds \(M\); if no such item arrives, accept nothing. Every decision is irrevocable and at most one item is accepted. Success means accepting the unique maximum-valued item. If \(P_n\) denotes the success probability, then \(\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n=1/e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Observe about the first fraction 1/e of a uniformly random arrival order, then accept the first later item better than every observed item; the probability of selecting the maximum approaches 1/e.
assumptions_latex: The arrival order is a uniformly random permutation.
Item values are distinct and fixed before the permutation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(P_n\) is the probability of accepting the maximum-valued item, then \(\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n=1/e\).

notation.meaning: largest value in the observation phase
probability of selecting the maximum-valued item

children.title: Multiple-Choice Secretary Problems
children.top_down_role: Secretary selection with capacity for multiple accepted items.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Choice Secretary Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines cardinality-capacitated secretary selection with random arrival and irrevocable decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\) items with nonnegative values \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) arrive in a uniformly random permutation, and let \(1\le k\le n\). On each arrival an online algorithm observes the item's value and irrevocably accepts or rejects it, while maintaining at most \(k\) accepted items. Its reward is the sum of accepted values. The offline benchmark is \[\operatorname{OPT}_k(v)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}v_{(j)},\] where \(v_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge v_{(n)}\). An algorithm is \(c\)-competitive when its expected reward is at least \(c\operatorname{OPT}_k(v)\) for every fixed value vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple-choice secretary algorithm may irrevocably accept up to k random-order items and is compared with the sum of the k largest values.
assumptions_latex: Values are nonnegative and fixed before arrival.
The arrival permutation is uniform and independent of the values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible outputs are subsets \(S\) with \(|S|\le k\), and their reward is \(\sum_{i\in S}v_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit cardinality-capacitated secretary selection, but no cited source with a specific locator supports the chosen weighted top-k formulation and competitive convention.

children.title: Choice-Capacity Transitions
children.top_down_role: Performance changes as the number of permitted selections varies.

knowledge_statements.title: Choice-Capacity Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records monotonicity and normalization across cardinality capacities in secretary selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed nonnegative value vector, define \(\operatorname{OPT}_k=\sum_{j=1}^{k}v_{(j)}\) for \(0\le k\le n\), with \(\operatorname{OPT}_0=0\). Then \(\operatorname{OPT}_{k+1}-\operatorname{OPT}_k=v_{(k+1)}\ge0\), so the offline benchmark is nondecreasing in capacity and has nonincreasing marginal increments. Every policy feasible with capacity \(k\) remains feasible with capacity \(k+1\). Consequently, the optimal expected online reward is also nondecreasing in \(k\). The endpoint \(k=1\) is single-choice selection, whereas \(k=n\) permits acceptance of every item and removes the feasibility scarcity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing choice capacity enlarges the online feasible set; both online and offline optimal rewards increase, while the offline marginal value of another slot decreases.
assumptions_latex: Item values satisfy \(v_i\ge0\).
All capacities use the same arrival and information model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(0\le k<n\), \(\operatorname{OPT}_k\le\operatorname{OPT}_{k+1}\) and \(v_{(k+2)}\le v_{(k+1)}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotonicity and diminishing offline increments are correct for nonnegative sorted values and fit the transition leaf, but the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Matroid Secretary Problems
children.top_down_role: Secretary selection subject to matroid feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Secretary Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines weighted secretary selection subject to matroid independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid and let nonnegative weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) be fixed adversarially. Elements of \(E\) arrive in a uniformly random permutation. When \(e\) arrives, its identity and weight are revealed, and an online algorithm irrevocably accepts or rejects it while keeping the accepted set in \(\mathcal I\). Its reward is the accepted weight. The offline benchmark is \[\operatorname{OPT}(M,w)=\max_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}w(e).\] A randomized algorithm is \(c\)-competitive if its expected reward is at least \(\operatorname{OPT}(M,w)/c\) for every \(M\) and \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid secretary selection accepts random-order weighted elements irrevocably while preserving independence, compared with a maximum-weight independent set known offline.
assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid.
Weights are nonnegative and fixed before a uniform random arrival order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted set \(S\) must satisfy \(S\in\mathcal I\), and its value is \(w(S)=\sum_{e\in S}w(e)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted random-order matroid secretary definition fits the leaf, but the revelation of element identity, access to the matroid, and the competitive-ratio convention require a cited source.

children.title: Constraint Secretary Problems
children.top_down_role: Secretary selection under non-matroid combinatorial constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Secretary Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines secretary selection over a general downward-closed feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) be nonempty and downward closed: if \(S\in\mathcal F\) and \(T\subseteq S\), then \(T\in\mathcal F\). Nonnegative element weights are fixed before elements arrive in a uniformly random permutation. Upon observing an element and its weight, an online algorithm irrevocably accepts or rejects it and must maintain an accepted set in \(\mathcal F\). The benchmark is \[\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal F,w)=\max_{S\in\mathcal F}\sum_{e\in S}w(e).\] A competitive guarantee compares the algorithm's expected accepted weight with this benchmark uniformly over admissible weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint secretary problems replace a cardinality or matroid rule by a general downward-closed family while retaining random arrival and irrevocable weighted selection.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and \(\mathcal F\) is downward closed.
Weights are nonnegative and the arrival permutation is uniform.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At every time the accepted set \(A\) satisfies \(A\in\mathcal F\), and the offline comparator is \(\operatorname{OPT}(\mathcal F,w)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement coherently defines a downward-closed weighted secretary problem, but no source confirms that this is the intended constraint-secretary model or specifies how feasibility information is accessed online.

children.title: Feasibility-System Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Guarantee changes across alternative combinatorial feasibility systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-System Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies heredity as the boundary permitting irrevocable feasibility maintenance by local acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an irrevocable acceptance process, downward closure ensures that every partial accepted set remains feasible whenever the final accepted set is feasible. If downward closure is removed, this implication can fail. For example, let \(E=\{a,b\}\) and \(\mathcal F=\{\varnothing,\{a,b\}\}\). The set \(\{a,b\}\) is feasible, but after accepting only \(a\), the partial set \(\{a\}\) is infeasible. Thus the usual secretary requirement that feasibility hold after every arrival cannot realize the feasible terminal set without allowing temporary infeasibility, bundled decisions, or recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without downward closure, a feasible final selection can have infeasible prefixes, so ordinary irrevocable secretary acceptance no longer models the constraint faithfully.
assumptions_latex: Accepted elements cannot be revoked.
Feasibility is required after each arrival.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system \(\mathcal F=\{\varnothing,\{a,b\}\}\) demonstrates failure of prefix-feasible construction when heredity is absent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly shows that a non-hereditary feasible terminal set need not admit feasible acceptance prefixes, and failure_boundary is appropriate. A source or explicit standard-field rationale is nevertheless required for the broader modeling-boundary claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Secretary Order-Model Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates uniform random arrival from adversarial arrival in the classical secretary model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider selecting the maximum of \(n\ge2\) distinct items using only relative ranks and at most one irrevocable acceptance. Under a uniformly random arrival order, the classical sample-then-select rule has success probability tending to \(1/e\). Under adversarial order, no randomized algorithm can guarantee a constant success probability uniformly over \(n\): choose the maximum's position uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) after fixing an order consistent with indistinguishable rank histories; the algorithm's total probability of stopping at the designated maximum position is at most \(1/n\) in the corresponding hard distribution. Thus random-order symmetry is essential to the classical constant guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical constant success probability relies on uniform random arrival; adversarial ordering can reduce worst-case success to a quantity vanishing with the number of items.
assumptions_latex: Only relative ranks of arrived items are observed.
Exactly one item may be accepted and rejection is irrevocable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform random order permits asymptotic success \(1/e\), whereas the adversarial-order worst-case guarantee is not bounded below by a positive constant independent of \(n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The adversarial-order conclusion depends on whether the adversary is oblivious or adaptive and on what value or rank information is observed. The stated hard-distribution argument does not define these choices sufficiently to support the 1/n assertion.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Resource Prophet Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical prophet inequality for at most one irrevocable selection from independent nonnegative observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be independent nonnegative random variables with known distributions and finite expectations, observed sequentially in a fixed order. Define \(X_\infty=0\), where \(\tau=\infty\) represents accepting no observation. There exists a stopping time \(\tau\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\cup\{\infty\}\), adapted to the observed values, such that \[\mathbb E[X_\tau]\ge \frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb E\!\left[\max_{1\le i\le n}X_i\right].\] Equivalently, a single-resource online selector that irrevocably accepts at most one observation can obtain at least half the expected reward of a prophet who sees all realizations before choosing. A possibly randomized threshold rule with appropriate tie handling suffices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent nonnegative observations from known distributions, an online rule selecting at most one observation earns at least half the expected maximum available to an omniscient prophet.
assumptions_latex: The variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are independent and nonnegative.
Their distributions are known and their expectations are finite.
The observations are revealed sequentially in a fixed order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists an adapted stopping time \(\tau\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\cup\{\infty\}\) such that \(\mathbb E[X_\tau]\ge\tfrac12\mathbb E[\max_{1\le i\le n}X_i]\), with \(X_\infty=0\).

notation.meaning: online stopping time, with infinity denoting no acceptance
zero reward when no observation is accepted

children.title: Matroid Prophet Selection
children.top_down_role: Prophet selection subject to matroid feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Prophet Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines prophet selection with independent values and matroid feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid. Each element \(e\in E\) has an independent nonnegative random value \(X_e\) drawn from a known distribution, and elements are revealed in a specified online order. Upon seeing \(X_e\), an algorithm irrevocably accepts or rejects \(e\), maintaining an accepted set in \(\mathcal I\). Its prophet benchmark is \[\operatorname{PROPHET}(M)=\mathbb E\!\left[\max_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}X_e\right].\] An algorithm has approximation factor \(c\ge1\) if its expected reward is at least \(\operatorname{PROPHET}(M)/c\) for every admissible collection of distributions and orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid prophet selection chooses independent random-valued elements online while preserving matroid independence, compared with the expected omniscient maximum-weight independent set.
assumptions_latex: \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is a finite matroid.
The values \(X_e\) are independent, nonnegative, and drawn from known distributions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The online output \(S\) satisfies \(S\in\mathcal I\) and is compared with \(\operatorname{PROPHET}(M)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits matroid prophet selection, but 'specified online order' and a guarantee over every admissible order do not identify whether order is fixed, adversarial, adaptive, or random. The intended variant and benchmark require an exact source.

children.title: Downward-Closed Prophet Selection
children.top_down_role: Prophet selection under general downward-closed feasibility.

assumptions_latex: The ground set \(E\) is finite and \(\varnothing\ne\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\) is downward closed.
The values \((V_e)_{e\in E}\) are independent, nonnegative random variables with known distributions.
Elements arrive sequentially in a specified order, and decisions are irrevocable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A policy is \(\alpha\)-competitive when \(\mathbb E[\sum_{e\in S}V_e]\ge \alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{prophet}}\).

notation.meaning: Downward-closed family of feasible selected sets.
Set selected irrevocably by the online policy.
Expected value of the offline feasible optimum.

review_flags: No supplied source locator supports the downward-closed prophet-selection model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard independent-values, known-distribution formulation with an arbitrary hereditary feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A downward-closed prophet-selection instance consists of \(E\), \(\mathcal F\), and values \((V_e)_{e\in E}\), where \(A\in\mathcal F\) and \(B\subseteq A\) imply \(B\in\mathcal F\). Upon observing an arriving element's realized value, an online policy irrevocably accepts or rejects it while maintaining \(S\in\mathcal F\). The prophet benchmark is \[\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{prophet}}=\mathbb E\!\left[\max_{A\in\mathcal F}\sum_{e\in A}V_e\right].\] The policy has prophet factor \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) if its expected selected value is at least \(\alpha\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{prophet}}\) on every instance in the stated model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Downward-closed prophet selection compares an irrevocable feasible online selection against the expected offline optimum under a hereditary constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Downward-Closed Prophet Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the selected independent-values, known-distribution model.

children.title: Constraint-Generalization Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on extending matroid guarantees to broader downward-closed systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Generalization Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates arbitrary hereditary constraints from the matroid subclass used by stronger prophet guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{1,2,3\}\) and \(\mathcal F=\{\varnothing,\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{1,2\}\}\). This family is downward closed but is not a matroid. The feasible sets \(A=\{3\}\) and \(B=\{1,2\}\) satisfy \(|A|<|B|\), while \(A\cup\{b\}\notin\mathcal F\) for every \(b\in B\setminus A\). Thus downward closure alone does not supply the exchange structure required by matroid-specific prophet results.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This three-element downward-closed system fails matroid augmentation, so matroid-specific prophet results do not automatically extend to arbitrary hereditary constraints.
assumptions_latex: The ground set is \(E=\{1,2,3\}\).
The feasible family is \(\mathcal F=\{\varnothing,\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{1,2\}\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Downward closure alone does not imply the matroid exchange axiom.

notation.meaning: Two feasible sets witnessing augmentation failure.

review_flags: An authoritative locator for the hereditary-system versus matroid boundary is required.

children.title: Correlation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Performance limitations caused by dependence among item values or arrivals.

assumptions_latex: Both coordinates have the Bernoulli distribution with success probability \(1/2\).
The prophet may select at most one of the two coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Marginal distributions do not determine either \(\mathbb E[\max\{X_1,X_2\}]\) or the relevant prophet instance.

notation.meaning: A Bernoulli random variable with parameter one half.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports correlation-sensitive prophet inequalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why marginal distribution knowledge cannot replace a specified joint dependence model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\). Under the positively correlated coupling \((X_1,X_2)=(Z,Z)\), both marginals are Bernoulli with parameter \(1/2\), but \(\mathbb E[\max\{X_1,X_2\}]=1/2\). Under the negatively correlated coupling \((X_1,X_2)=(Z,1-Z)\), the same two marginals are retained while \(\mathbb E[\max\{X_1,X_2\}]=1\). Hence marginal laws alone neither specify the prophet benchmark nor justify an independence-based threshold guarantee; a correlation model or a guarantee uniform over an explicit coupling class is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two reward vectors can have identical marginals but different prophet benchmarks, making the dependence model an essential part of the problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Correlation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coupling counterexample is correct and fits a correlation failure boundary, but no inspectable citation supports its use in the prophet setting.

children.title: Distribution-Knowledge Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Performance limitations caused by partial or absent distributional knowledge.

assumptions_latex: Rewards arrive sequentially and selection decisions are irrevocable.
The admissible distribution class \(\mathcal P\) is specified before performance is assessed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A distributional prophet guarantee is meaningful only relative to the information supplied about \(P\in\mathcal P\).

notation.meaning: Number of training samples available from a law.

review_flags: The taxonomy does not select one canonical sample-based or prior-independent model.
No supplied source locator supports these distribution-information regimes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact-law, sample-access, and distribution-oblivious prophet models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the known-distribution regime, the policy receives an exact description of \(P\in\mathcal P\) before arrivals. In the sample-access regime, it receives \(m\ge0\) independent training samples from \(P\), separate from the online realization. In the distribution-oblivious regime, it receives neither \(P\) nor samples and may use only structural information defining \(\mathcal P\). A competitive claim must quantify over \(P\), specify which of these information objects the policy receives, and state whether its expectation includes training-sample randomness, online rewards, and internal randomization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prophet guarantees must specify whether the policy knows the exact law, receives samples, or has only structural distributional information.
knowledge_statements.title: Distribution-Knowledge Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regimes are clearly distinguished, but the taxonomy does not determine this particular three-way information model and no source establishes it as the intended formulation.

children.title: Robust Prophet Regimes
children.top_down_role: Prophet-selection settings designed for dependence or distributional uncertainty.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a nonempty ambiguity class of reward laws on a common measurable space.
For every \(P\in\mathcal P\), both the policy value and prophet value are finite.
The policy uses only the information declared available in the robust model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Robust prophet performance is the worst-case ratio \(\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathrm{ALG}(P)/\mathrm{OPT}(P)\).

notation.meaning: Ambiguity class of possible reward distributions.
Expected reward of the online policy under a law.
Expected offline prophet reward under a law.

review_flags: No supplied locator identifies a canonical robust prophet ambiguity model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributionally robust competitive-ratio formulation over an explicitly declared ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A policy is robustly \(\alpha\)-competitive over \(\mathcal P\) if \[\mathrm{ALG}(P)\ge \alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}(P)\qquad\text{for every }P\in\mathcal P.\] Equivalently, when \(\mathrm{OPT}(P)>0\) throughout the class, its robust ratio is \[\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}\frac{\mathrm{ALG}(P)}{\mathrm{OPT}(P)}.\] The ambiguity class must encode all permitted changes in marginals, dependence, and distributional parameters. Randomness in rewards, training data, and the policy is included in \(\mathrm{ALG}(P)\); the same law \(P\) defines the offline benchmark.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A robust prophet policy achieves one competitive factor uniformly over every reward law in a declared ambiguity class.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Prophet Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform competitive condition is internally consistent and the condition kind is defensible, but the ambiguity model is not canonical without a supporting source.

children.title: Threshold Methods
children.top_down_role: Online selection organized around value or density thresholds.

knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density-threshold policy for single-budget online selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(b_1=B\). For each arriving item \(t\), choose \(\lambda_t\ge0\) using only pre-arrival information and set \[x_t=\mathbf 1\!\left\{c_t\le b_t\ \text{ and }\ \frac{v_t}{c_t}\ge\lambda_t\right\}.\] Update \(b_{t+1}=b_t-c_tx_t\). After the final arrival, output \(S=\{t:x_t=1\}\), whose total value is \(\sum_t v_tx_t\) and whose total cost is at most \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept an arriving item exactly when it fits and its value-to-cost ratio reaches a threshold fixed from prior information.
assumptions_latex: Items arrive as pairs \((c_t,v_t)\) with \(c_t>0\) and \(v_t\ge0\).
The initial budget is \(B>0\).
Each threshold \(\lambda_t\) is determined before observing the current item.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update always returns a feasible online packing with total cost at most \(B\).
review_flags: A relevant source for density-threshold online budgeted selection is required.

children.title: Reservation Methods
children.top_down_role: Online selection that preserves capacity for anticipated future opportunities.

assumptions_latex: Items arrive as pairs \((c_t,v_t)\) with \(c_t>0\) and \(v_t\ge0\).
The reserve \(\rho_t\) and eligibility decision are based only on information available at time \(t\).
The reserve satisfies \(0\le\rho_t\le b_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted item preserves at least \(\rho_t\) units of budget for future arrivals.

notation.meaning: Budget remaining before the current decision.
Budget reserved after the current decision.
Predictable eligibility predicate for the current item.

review_flags: Reservation method is not uniquely specified by the node path.
No supplied source locator supports online budget-reservation selection.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic capacity-reservation family with an explicit eligibility rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(b_1=B\). Before deciding on item \(t\), compute a reserve \(\rho_t\in[0,b_t]\) and an eligibility predicate \(q_t(c_t,v_t)\in\{0,1\}\) from currently available information. Set \[x_t=\mathbf 1\!\left\{q_t(c_t,v_t)=1\ \text{ and }\ c_t\le b_t-\rho_t\right\},\qquad b_{t+1}=b_t-c_tx_t.\] After the last arrival, output \(S=\{t:x_t=1\}\). The reserve rule controls how much present capacity may be consumed, while \(q_t\) supplies the policy's value or priority criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reservation policy accepts an eligible item only when doing so leaves a prescribed amount of budget for future arrivals.
knowledge_statements.title: Reservation Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is feasible and matches the reservation-method leaf, but the eligibility-and-reserve formulation is one generic design rather than a source-established canonical method.

children.title: Threshold-Reservation Hybrids
children.top_down_role: Method families combining admission thresholds with reserved capacity.

assumptions_latex: Each item has cost \(c_t>0\) and value \(v_t\ge0\), and the initial budget is \(B>0\).
The threshold \(\lambda_t\) and reserve \(\rho_t\) use no future observations.
The reserve obeys \(0\le\rho_t\le b_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hybrid enforces both a value-density cutoff and a future-capacity reservation.
review_flags: No supplied source locator supports this online threshold-reservation hybrid.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical intersection of density screening and remaining-capacity reservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(b_1=B\). At arrival \(t\), compute predictable controls \(\lambda_t\ge0\) and \(\rho_t\in[0,b_t]\), then set \[x_t=\mathbf 1\!\left\{\frac{v_t}{c_t}\ge\lambda_t\ \text{ and }\ c_t\le b_t-\rho_t\right\}.\] Update \(b_{t+1}=b_t-c_tx_t\) and output all accepted items after the final arrival. Thus an item must simultaneously clear the value-density threshold and leave the designated reserve. Taking \(\rho_t=0\) recovers a pure threshold rule, while taking \(\lambda_t=0\) recovers reservation with universal nonnegative-value eligibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hybrid accepts an item only when it clears a density threshold and leaves the prescribed budget reserve.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold-Reservation Hybrids

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hybrid algorithm is internally consistent and correctly specializes to its two component rules, but no source supports this particular formulation as the intended hybrid family.

children.title: Fractional Knapsack Regimes
children.top_down_role: Online knapsack settings permitting fractional acceptance.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Knapsack Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Offline fractional relaxation underlying budget-scale and integrality comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For items indexed by \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the fractional knapsack value is \[\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{frac}}=\max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n v_ix_i:\sum_{i=1}^n c_ix_i\le B,\ 0\le x_i\le1\right\}.\] Relabel the items so that \(d_1\ge d_2\ge\cdots\ge d_n\), where \(d_i=v_i/c_i\). Some optimal solution selects successive items fully until either all items are selected or the next item would exceed the residual capacity. In the latter case, it selects exactly the residual-capacity fraction of that next item and assigns zero to all later items. Hence some optimal solution has at most one coordinate in \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional knapsack processes items in decreasing value-density order; it either takes every item or has at most one partially selected cutoff item.
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many items indexed by \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(c_i>0\), \(v_i\ge0\), and budget \(B>0\).
Fractional decisions satisfy \(0\le x_i\le1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal fractional solution may be chosen in nonincreasing density order with at most one strictly fractional coordinate.
review_flags: A relevant authoritative locator for the fractional-knapsack representation is required.

children.title: Integral Knapsack Regimes
children.top_down_role: Online knapsack settings requiring indivisible acceptance decisions.

assumptions_latex: There are finitely many items with costs \(c_i>0\), values \(v_i\ge0\), and budget \(B>0\).
Every decision is indivisible: \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible integral selections are precisely the subsets whose total cost is at most \(B\).

notation.meaning: Binary indicator that item i is selected.

review_flags: Standard integral-knapsack definition lacks a relevant supplied locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-budget, indivisible-item knapsack regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The integral knapsack problem is \[\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}=\max\left\{\sum_i v_ix_i:\sum_i c_ix_i\le B,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\] Equivalently, it selects a subset \(S\) maximizing \(\sum_{i\in S}v_i\) subject to \(\sum_{i\in S}c_i\le B\). Unlike the fractional regime, unused capacity may remain even when an unselected item has positive value, because no fraction of that item may be used. In an online version, each binary coordinate is fixed irrevocably when its item arrives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral knapsack selects whole items only, maximizing total value while keeping their total cost within the budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Knapsack Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integral-knapsack definition is precise, standard, and suitable for the leaf, but the candidate supplies no authoritative section or page locator.

children.title: Budget-Scale Regimes
children.top_down_role: Behavior distinguished by budget size relative to item demands.

knowledge_statements.title: Budget-Scale Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized item-size classification for sequences of budgeted-selection instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each knapsack instance, define \[\delta=\frac{\max_i c_i}{B}.\] A sequence of instances is in the small-item, or scale-free large-budget, regime when \(\delta\to0\). It is uniformly small-item when a declared constant \(\bar\delta<1\) satisfies \(c_i\le\bar\delta B\) for every item in every instance. It is in a large-item regime when \(\limsup\delta>0\). Any asymptotic guarantee invoking a large budget must state whether it assumes absolute growth \(B\to\infty\) or the scale-free condition \(\delta\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Budget scale is measured by the largest item cost divided by capacity; the small-item regime requires this ratio to vanish.
assumptions_latex: Every relevant item has cost \(0<c_i\le B\).
The normalized maximum item size is \(\delta=\max_i c_i/B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The small-item regime is characterized by \(\delta\to0\), whereas a large-item regime has \(\limsup\delta>0\).

notation.meaning: Maximum cost as a fraction of the budget.

review_flags: A source specifying the intended budget-scaling convention is required.

children.title: Integrality Gap Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on transferring fractional performance to integral decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Gap Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive boundary between the standard fractional relaxation and integral knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the same items and budget, the standard fractional and integral knapsack optima satisfy \[0\le \mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{frac}}-\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}\le v_{\max}.\] If \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}>0\) and \(v_{\max}\le\varepsilon\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}\) for some \(\varepsilon\ge0\), then \[\frac{\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{frac}}}{\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}}\le1+\varepsilon.\] Without a condition making \(v_{\max}/\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}\) small, the additive bound does not imply a small relative integrality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fractional optimum exceeds the integral optimum by at most the largest item value, but a small relative gap additionally requires that no item dominate the integral optimum.
assumptions_latex: Items satisfy \(0<c_i\le B\) and \(v_i\ge0\).
The quantities \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{frac}}\) and \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}\) use the same items and budget.
Let \(v_{\max}=\max_i v_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The additive relaxation gap is at most \(v_{\max}\), and it is relatively negligible only when \(v_{\max}/\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}\) is small.

notation.meaning: Declared upper bound on the largest-item value relative to the integral optimum.

review_flags: A relevant authoritative locator for the additive knapsack relaxation gap is required.

children.title: Random-Priority Methods
children.top_down_role: Online matching methods driven by randomized offline-side priorities.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(U,V,E)\) is bipartite, \(U\) is known initially, and vertices of \(V\) arrive sequentially with their incident edges.
Each offline vertex may be matched at most once, and assignments are irrevocable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the matching formed by the stated random-priority rule.

notation.meaning: Independent random priority of offline vertex u
Currently unmatched neighbors of an arriving vertex v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard random-ranking formulation for online bipartite matching
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random permutation priorities on the offline side under irrevocable online arrivals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initially sample independent continuous random variables \(R_u\) for all \(u\in U\), independently of the arrival sequence. When \(v\in V\) arrives, let \(A_v=\{u\in U:(u,v)\in E\text{ and }u\text{ is unmatched}\}\). If \(A_v=\varnothing\), reject \(v\). Otherwise choose \(u_v\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in A_v}R_u\), add \((u_v,v)\) to the matching, and permanently mark \(u_v\) matched. Continuity makes the minimizer unique with probability one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign every offline vertex an independent random priority, then match each arrival to its available neighbor of highest priority, rejecting it if no neighbor remains.
knowledge_statements.title: Random-Priority Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited source supports the online Ranking rule. The canonical random-permutation interpretation also requires identically distributed continuous priorities, not merely independent continuous variables.

children.title: Rank-Greedy Methods
children.top_down_role: Online matching methods selecting feasible partners according to maintained ranks.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(U,V,E)\) is an online bipartite graph with offline side \(U\).
A fixed total priority order on \(U\) is chosen before arrivals begin.

children.title: Rounding Loss Boundaries

assumptions_latex: A naive rule independently proposes edge \((u,v)\) with probability \(x_{uv}\) and accepts it only if \(u\) remains free.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For this naive rule, uniform marginal retention greater than \(1/e\) is impossible, and exact marginal preservation fails.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp marginal-loss mechanism for naive independent proposals with first-acceptance contention resolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider one offline vertex and \(n\) sequential neighbors, with \(x_j=1/n\) for every \(j\). Under independent proposals and first-acceptance contention resolution, \(p_j=(1/n)(1-1/n)^{j-1}\). Hence \(p_n/x_n=(1-1/n)^{n-1}\to e^{-1}\). Therefore this rounding rule cannot guarantee \(p_j\geq\alpha x_j\) uniformly for any \(\alpha>1/e\), and it cannot preserve all marginals exactly despite the fractional feasibility equation \(\sum_{j=1}^n x_j=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent edge proposals lose marginals through earlier collisions: on one resource with n equal fractions, the final edge's retention ratio approaches one over e.
knowledge_statements.title: Rounding Loss Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The single-resource calculation correctly gives an asymptotic 1/e upper boundary for the stated naive rule, but the nontrivial failure claim has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Weight-Placement Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Differences caused by locating weights on vertices rather than edges.

assumptions_latex: The online instance is bipartite, with offline vertices known before arrivals and online vertices revealed sequentially.

It is edge-weighted when arrival of \(j\) reveals every incident value \(w_{ij}\ge 0\), and matching \((i,j)\) earns \(w_{ij}\). assumptions_latex: The feasible allocations are described by a nonnegative online packing system.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between coordinatewise capacities and requests that jointly consume multiple resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The capacity constraints are \(Ax\le B\) with \(A\ge 0\). If every column of \(A\) has at most one positive entry, accepting a request reduces exactly one resource coordinate, so feasibility decomposes by resource apart from the choice among requests. If some request \(t\) has \(a_{it}>0\) and \(a_{kt}>0\) for distinct resources \(i\) and \(k\), its single decision \(x_t\) simultaneously changes both residual capacities. Consequently the feasible decision set is not a Cartesian product of independent per-resource decision sets, and any rule that accepts independently for each coordinate can issue incompatible decisions for that request.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A request consuming multiple resources couples their residual capacities, so independently feasible per-resource decisions need not form one feasible allocation.
