children.title: Fairness-Partition Interactions
children.top_down_role: Compatibility and tension between fairness criteria and partition restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Fairness-Partition Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact aggregate compatibility for integer cardinality bounds, excluding item eligibility and temporal prefix constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a group, and let \(\ell_i,u_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) with \(\ell_i\le u_i\) be the individual cardinality bounds for every \(i\in G\). Let \(L_G,U_G\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) with \(L_G\le U_G\) be the group quota. There exist integers \(y_i\) satisfying \(\ell_i\le y_i\le u_i\) for all \(i\in G\) and \(L_G\le\sum_{i\in G}y_i\le U_G\) if and only if \(\max\{L_G,\sum_{i\in G}\ell_i\}\le\min\{U_G,\sum_{i\in G}u_i\}\). This condition must hold for every group in the partition. It certifies only aggregate cardinality compatibility; item eligibility, indivisibility, and online prefix constraints may impose additional obstructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer individual allocation bounds and an integer group quota are compatible at the aggregate-count level exactly when their attainable total intervals overlap; eligibility and online constraints may still prevent an allocation.
assumptions_latex: Agents form a fixed partition into groups.
Every individual lower and upper cardinality bound is a nonnegative integer, with \(\ell_i\le u_i\).
Every group lower and upper quota is a nonnegative integer, with \(L_G\le U_G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Aggregate compatibility for each group \(G\) is equivalent to \(\max\{L_G,\sum_{i\in G}\ell_i\}\le\min\{U_G,\sum_{i\in G}u_i\}\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative integer lower and upper allocation bounds for agent i
Nonnegative integer lower and upper quotas for group G
Integer number of items assigned to agent i

children.title: Online Dual Growth
children.top_down_role: Dual-variable growth techniques for online optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Online Dual Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible dual-coordinate growth for an online covering LP with row arrivals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the covering relaxation 
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\geq \mathbf 1,\ x\geq 0\}\]
with dual 
\[\max\{\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\leq c,\ y\geq0\}.\]
Initialize \(y=0\). When row \(a_t\) arrives, append \(y_t=0\) and continuously increase only \(y_t\) until either a prescribed stopping condition holds or some constraint \(\sum_{s\leq t}a_{sj}y_s\leq c_j\) becomes tight. Invoke the associated primal augmentation rule on newly tight coordinates, never decreasing earlier primal or dual coordinates. After each arrival, output the current primal action and dual vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raise each newly revealed dual variable while preserving dual feasibility, and augment the irrevocable primal solution whenever a dual constraint becomes tight.
assumptions_latex: \(c\in\mathbb R_{>0}^n\) and every revealed row satisfies \(a_t\in\mathbb R_+^n\).
The primal augmentation rule uses only information revealed through time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At every time \(t\), the maintained vector satisfies \(y^{(t)}\geq0\) and \(A_{1:t}^{\mathsf T}y^{(t)}\leq c\).

notation.meaning: covering row revealed at time t
dual coordinate associated with the arriving row

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf, but the stopping condition and primal augmentation rule are unspecified, and no online primal–dual source supports this generic procedure.

children.title: Competitive Dual Fitting
children.top_down_role: Dual-fitting analyses used to establish competitive guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Competitive Dual Fitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Competitive certificate obtained by scaling an online dual vector into feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an online minimization algorithm, suppose its final cost \(C_{\mathrm{alg}}\) and a constructed vector \(y\geq0\) satisfy
\[C_{\mathrm{alg}}\leq \alpha\sum_{t=1}^T y_t\]
for some \(\alpha\geq1\). If a fitting factor \(\beta\geq1\) satisfies
\[A^{\mathsf T}(y/\beta)\leq c,\]
then \(y/\beta\) is feasible for the dual covering relaxation. Weak duality therefore makes the pair consisting of the charging inequality and the fitted dual vector a verifiable competitive certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If algorithmic cost is charged to a dual vector whose constraint violations are at most β, scaling the vector proves an αβ competitive ratio.
assumptions_latex: The offline covering relaxation and its dual are feasible and obey weak duality.
\(C_{\mathrm{alg}}\leq\alpha\sum_t y_t\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\leq\beta c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C_{\mathrm{alg}}\leq \alpha\beta\,\mathrm{OPT}.\]

notation.meaning: cost incurred by the online algorithm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role and αβ conclusion are mathematically plausible, but A, c, and the precise primal–dual pair are not introduced within the record, and no dual-fitting source is cited.

children.title: Dual-Growth–Fitting Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Structural similarities, differences, and applicability boundaries between the two techniques.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Growth–Fitting Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of direct feasible growth and post-hoc dual fitting under a common charging inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two analyses establish the same charging inequality \(C_{\mathrm{alg}}\leq\alpha\sum_t y_t\). Direct dual growth maintains \(A^{\mathsf T}y\leq c\), so its fitting factor is \(1\) and it certifies ratio \(\alpha\). Dual fitting permits \(A^{\mathsf T}y\nleq c\) during construction but requires a number \(\beta\geq1\) such that \(A^{\mathsf T}y\leq\beta c\); scaling then certifies ratio \(\alpha\beta\). Thus fitting trades the invariant of immediate dual feasibility for an explicit multiplicative loss determined by the maximum normalized dual load.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible dual growth gives factor α directly; dual fitting tolerates violations but multiplies the bound by the required scaling factor β.
assumptions_latex: Both analyses use the same covering dual and cost-charging factor \(\alpha\).
The fitted vector has finite violation factor \(\beta=\max_j (A^{\mathsf T}y)_j/c_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certified factors are \(\alpha\) for feasible growth and \(\alpha\beta\) for fitting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the comparison leaf, but defining β as the maximum normalized load can yield β<1, conflicting with β≥1; the intended definition is typically bounded below by 1. No comparative source is cited.

children.title: Fractional Online Updates
children.top_down_role: Online maintenance of fractional solutions before integral conversion.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Online Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone fractional response to sequentially revealed covering constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x^{(0)}=0\). When a nonnegative covering row \(a_t\) arrives, retain \(x^{(t)}=x^{(t-1)}\) if \(a_t^{\mathsf T}x^{(t-1)}\geq1\). Otherwise choose, using only the revealed history, a measurable velocity \(v_t(\tau)\in\mathbb R_+^n\) and evolve
\[x(\tau)=x^{(t-1)}+\int_0^\tau v_t(s)\,ds\]
until the first time \(\tau_t\) at which \(a_t^{\mathsf T}x(\tau_t)=1\); set \(x^{(t)}=x(\tau_t)\). The output after each arrival is the current fractional vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increase fractional resource variables, without decreasing past decisions, until every newly arrived covering constraint is satisfied.
assumptions_latex: Every arriving row satisfies \(a_t\in\mathbb R_+^n\) and has at least one positive coordinate.
The selected velocity reaches the new constraint in finite time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(s\leq t\), \(a_s^{\mathsf T}x^{(t)}\geq1\) and \(x^{(t)}\geq x^{(t-1)}\geq0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but an arbitrary measurable velocity subject only to finite attainment is an update template rather than a fully specified algorithm. No source supports the selected formulation.

children.title: Randomized Online Rounding
children.top_down_role: Randomized conversion of evolving fractional solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Online Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent-threshold rounding of a monotone fractional online allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Independently sample \(\theta_j\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) once for each resource \(j\). Given monotone fractional states \(x^{(t)}\in[0,1]^n\) and a scale \(\lambda>0\), initialize \(z^{(0)}=0\) and set
\[z_j^{(t)}=\mathbf 1\!\left\{\theta_j\leq\min\{1,\lambda x_j^{(t)}\}\right\}.\]
The same thresholds are retained at every time, so decisions are irrevocable. Output \(z^{(t)}\) after each update. For every coordinate and time, \(\Pr[z_j^{(t)}=1]=\min\{1,\lambda x_j^{(t)}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample one threshold per resource and select it irrevocably when its scaled fractional value crosses that threshold.
assumptions_latex: The fractional trajectory is coordinatewise nondecreasing and lies in \([0,1]^n\).
Thresholds are mutually independent and independent of any oblivious arrival sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rounded trajectory is coordinatewise monotone and satisfies \(\mathbb E[c^{\mathsf T}z^{(t)}]\leq\lambda c^{\mathsf T}x^{(t)}\) for \(c\geq0\).

notation.meaning: persistent random threshold for resource j
integral selection vector at time t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Persistent-threshold rounding and its marginal cost bound are coherent, but the record does not state that the fractional trajectory is independent of the sampled thresholds. No online-rounding source is cited.

children.title: Deterministic Online Rounding
children.top_down_role: Deterministic conversion regimes for online fractional solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Online Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold rounding for sparse binary covering rows and monotone fractional states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume each revealed binary covering row has support \(S_t\) with \(|S_t|\leq d\), and a monotone fractional algorithm maintains \(\sum_{j\in S_t}x_j^{(t)}\geq1\). Initialize \(z^{(0)}=0\) and update
\[z_j^{(t)}=\max\left\{z_j^{(t-1)},\mathbf 1\!\left\{x_j^{(t)}\geq\frac1d\right\}\right\}.\]
Once selected, a resource remains selected. After each arrival, output \(z^{(t)}\). Since every feasible row contains a coordinate of value at least \(1/d\), the rounded solution covers that row immediately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For rows containing at most d resources, permanently select every resource whose fractional value reaches 1/d; all revealed rows are then covered.
assumptions_latex: Each row is binary and has support size at most \(d\geq1\).
The fractional states are monotone and satisfy all revealed covering rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For all \(s\leq t\), \(\sum_{j\in S_s}z_j^{(t)}\geq1\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}z^{(t)}\leq d\,c^{\mathsf T}x^{(t)}\) for \(c\geq0\).

notation.meaning: support of the binary row arriving at time t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic algorithm role, feasibility statement, and d-factor cost bound are internally consistent under the stated binary row-sparsity and monotonicity assumptions, but no supporting source is supplied.

children.title: Element-Arrival Covering
children.top_down_role: Covering problems in which elements arrive online.

knowledge_statements.title: Element-Arrival Covering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Row-arrival model for online set covering with a fixed purchasable family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An element-arrival covering instance consists of a fixed family of purchasable sets \(\mathcal S=\{S_1,\ldots,S_n\}\) with costs \(c_j>0\), together with elements \(e_1,
ldots,e_T\) revealed sequentially. On arrival of \(e_t\), the algorithm learns \(J_t=\{j:e_t\in S_j\}\) and must irrevocably enlarge its purchased index set \(B_t\supseteq B_{t-1}\) until \(B_t\cap J_t\neq\varnothing\). Its cost is \(\sum_{j\in B_T}c_j\), compared with the minimum-cost subfamily covering every revealed element.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elements arrive one by one; their incident sets become known, and irrevocable set purchases must cover each element immediately.
assumptions_latex: The family \(\mathcal S\) and costs are fixed before arrivals.
Every arriving element belongs to at least one set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires \(B_{t-1}\subseteq B_t\) and \(B_t\cap J_s\neq\varnothing\) for all \(s\leq t\).

notation.meaning: sets containing the element arriving at time t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the arrival-regime leaf, but the element sequence contains “ldots” rather than a valid ellipsis, and no source is cited for the information-revelation convention.

children.title: Set-Arrival Covering
children.top_down_role: Covering problems in which candidate sets arrive online.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Arrival Covering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column-arrival covering model with fixed requirements and irrevocable acceptance decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set-arrival covering instance has a fixed requirement universe \(U=\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}\). At time \(t\), a set \(S_t\subseteq U\) and cost \(c_t>0\) are revealed, after which the algorithm irrevocably chooses \(z_t\in\{0,1\}\). At the declared terminal time \(T\), feasibility requires
\[\sum_{t:e_i\in S_t}z_t\geq1\qquad(i=1,\ldots,m).\]
The online cost is \(\sum_{t=1}^T c_tz_t\), compared with the minimum-cost cover formed from all sets revealed by time \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sets and costs arrive sequentially; each acceptance decision is irrevocable, and the accepted sets must cover the fixed universe at termination.
assumptions_latex: The universe \(U\) and terminal-feasibility convention are known initially.
The complete revealed family admits a cover of \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid terminal output satisfies \(z\in\{0,1\}^T\) and covers every \(e_i\in U\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent, but terminal-only feasibility is one of several possible set-arrival conventions and materially affects the model. A specific source is required.

children.title: Mixed-Arrival Covering
children.top_down_role: Models combining multiple arrival types or alternating revelation regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Arrival Covering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online covering model allowing both requirement rows and purchasable columns to arrive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-arrival covering instance evolves through row events and column events. A row event reveals a new requirement with its incidences to currently available resources; a column event reveals a new resource, its cost, and incidences to revealed requirements. The algorithm may purchase only revealed resources, purchases are irrevocable, and after every row event its purchased set must cover every revealed requirement. The input is promised to make this immediate-feasibility condition attainable. Performance compares total purchase cost with an offline solution that knows the complete event sequence but respects the specified resource-availability convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both covering requirements and purchasable resources may arrive; irrevocable purchases must cover all current requirements using resources available at that time.
assumptions_latex: Each event reveals all incidences between the new object and previously revealed objects.
After every row event, the available resources contain a feasible cover of all revealed rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At each time \(t\), the purchased resources form a cover of every requirement revealed by time \(t\).

notation.meaning: event index in the mixed arrival sequence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits, but mixed arrival is not canonical and the offline resource-availability convention is left unspecified. These choices require an explicit source before the model is reliable.

children.title: Fractional Online Covering
children.top_down_role: Online covering problems maintained in a fractional solution space.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Online Covering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone fractional algorithm for a row-arrival covering linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given costs \(c\in\mathbb R_{>0}^n\), initialize \(x^{(0)}=0\). When row \(a_t\in\mathbb R_+^n\) arrives, choose a nonnegative update \(\Delta_t\), using only rows revealed through time \(t\), such that
\[x^{(t)}=x^{(t-1)}+\Delta_t,\qquad a_t^{\mathsf T}x^{(t)}\geq1.\]
The update may minimize a prescribed local potential or follow a continuous primal-dual rule, but it may not decrease previous coordinates. Output \(x^{(t)}\) after every arrival; its incurred fractional cost is \(c^{\mathsf T}x^{(t)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a covering row arrives, increase fractional purchases online until it is satisfied, while preserving all earlier allocations and constraints.
assumptions_latex: Every revealed row is nonnegative and individually coverable.
Fractional purchases are irrevocable, so updates satisfy \(\Delta_t\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For all \(s\leq t\), \(a_s^{\mathsf T}x^{(t)}\geq1\), and the cost after time \(t\) is \(c^{\mathsf T}x^{(t)}\).

notation.meaning: fractional purchases after t row arrivals
nonnegative response to the new row
covering row arriving at time t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the calculus leaf, but merely requiring an arbitrary feasible nonnegative update does not specify a particular fractional algorithm or performance guarantee. No source is cited.

children.title: Randomized Covering Rounding
children.top_down_role: Randomized integral conversion for fractional covering solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Covering Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability online rounding for finitely many binary covering rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x^{(t)}\in[0,1]^n\) be monotone and satisfy each binary row \(\sum_{j\in S_t}x_j^{(t)}\geq1\). For known horizon \(T\) and \(0<\delta<1\), set \(\lambda=\ln(T/\delta)\), sample independent \(\theta_j\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), and define
\[z_j^{(t)}=\mathbf 1\!\left\{\theta_j\leq\min\{1,\lambda x_j^{(t)}\}\right\}.\]
Retain every selection permanently. Output \(z^{(t)}\). Each row is uncovered with probability at most \(e^{-\lambda}\); hence all \(T\) rows are covered with probability at least \(1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale a feasible fractional cover and apply persistent independent thresholds; all rows are covered with high probability at logarithmic expected cost inflation.
assumptions_latex: There are at most \(T\) binary covering rows and the arrival sequence is oblivious.
The fractional states are coordinatewise monotone and satisfy every revealed row.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr[\forall t,\ \sum_{j\in S_t}z_j^{(t)}\geq1]\geq1-\delta\) and \(\mathbb E[c^{\mathsf T}z^{(T)}]\leq\lambda c^{\mathsf T}x^{(T)}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The high-probability claim is coherent for a fractional trajectory fixed independently of the thresholds and an oblivious sequence, but that independence is not explicit. No online covering-rounding source is supplied.

children.title: Deterministic Covering Rounding
children.top_down_role: Deterministic integral conversion for fractional covering solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Covering Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic online rounding of row-sparse binary fractional covers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose every binary covering row has support \(S_t\) of size at most \(d\), and the fractional trajectory is monotone with \(\sum_{j\in S_t}x_j^{(t)}\geq1\). Initialize \(z^{(0)}=0\). After each fractional update, set
\[z_j^{(t)}=1\quad\text{if}\quad z_j^{(t-1)}=1\ \text{or}\ x_j^{(t)}\geq 1/d,
\]
and otherwise set \(z_j^{(t)}=0\). Output the resulting irrevocable integral cover. Every revealed row contains a selected coordinate, while each selected coordinate satisfies \(1\leq d x_j^{(t)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Threshold at 1/d when each row has at most d entries; the integral cover is feasible and costs at most d times the fractional cover.
assumptions_latex: Every row is binary with support size at most \(d\geq1\).
The fractional cover is feasible after every arrival and is coordinatewise nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t\), \(\sum_{j\in S_t}z_j^{(t)}\geq1\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}z^{(t)}\leq d\,c^{\mathsf T}x^{(t)}\) for \(c\geq0\).

notation.meaning: maximum number of resources in any row

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic algorithm role and stated feasibility and d-factor bounds are consistent under monotone fractional states and binary row sparsity, but the record has no supporting citation.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and facilities may be opened only at points of \(X\).
Requests \(x_1,x_2,\ldots\in X\) arrive sequentially, and opening a facility costs \(f>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{t-1}\subseteq F_t\) for every \(t\), and the total cost is \(f|F_T|+\sum_{t=1}^T d(x_t,F_t)\).

notation.meaning: Facilities open after request t is processed.
Distance from x to its nearest point in F.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the online facility-location formulation; authoritative source required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated metric facility location with permanent opening decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An irrevocable facility-opening algorithm maintains sets \(F_t\subseteq X\). After observing request \(x_t\), it chooses \(F_t\supseteq F_{t-1}\); hence no opened facility can later be closed. Request \(x_t\) is assigned to a facility in \(F_t\), incurring minimum connection cost \(d(x_t,F_t)\). For a finite horizon \(T\), its objective is
\[
\operatorname{cost}_T=f|F_T|+\sum_{t=1}^T d(x_t,F_t).
\]
The decision defining \(F_t\) may depend on \(x_1,\ldots,x_t\) but not on future requests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facilities may be opened after each arriving demand, but never closed; total cost combines facility-opening charges with distances from demands to their assigned open facilities.
knowledge_statements.title: Irrevocable Facility Opening

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and its content kind fit irrevocable online facility opening, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports the precise timing, assignment, and cost convention. The record therefore requires an authoritative online facility-location source.

children.title: Online Metric Clustering
children.top_down_role: Metric clustering under sequentially revealed demand.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(k\geq 1\), and requests \(x_1,x_2,\ldots\in X\) arrive sequentially.
Center sets may be changed after each arrival, subject to the chosen recourse or migration model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At time \(t\), the clustering service cost is \(\Phi_t(S_t)=\sum_{i=1}^t d(x_i,S_t)\), with \(|S_t|\leq k\).

notation.meaning: Center set selected after request t arrives.
Distance from x to its nearest selected center.
Clustering service cost at time t.

review_flags: The sequence notation has been repaired, but an authoritative source with a specific locator is still required for this timing convention and metric k-median formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online metric \(k\)-median formulation underlying recourse-aware variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In online metric clustering, after the prefix \(x_1,\ldots,x_t\) is revealed, an algorithm selects a center set \(S_t\subseteq X\) with \(|S_t\leq k\), using no information about later requests. Each revealed request is served by its nearest center. In the metric \(k\)-median version, the service objective for the current prefix is
\[
\Phi_t(S_t)=\sum_{i=1}^t d(x_i,S_t).
\]
A recourse-aware model additionally charges or constrains transitions from \(S_{t-1}\) to \(S_t\); the base clustering objective itself is \(\Phi_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After every demand arrival, an online algorithm chooses at most k metric centers and pays the sum of current-prefix distances to nearest centers.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Metric Clustering

children.title: Bounded-Recourse Clustering
children.top_down_role: Online clustering subject to limits on solution revisions.

assumptions_latex: Each solution \(S_t\) is a set of exactly \(k\) centers.
The recourse allowance \(R_T\) is specified either cumulatively or through per-update bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires \(\sum_{t=1}^T r_t\leq R_T\), or \(r_t\leq b_t\) for every update under per-step budgets.

notation.meaning: Number of center replacements at update t under the set-replacement convention.
Cumulative recourse permitted through time T.

review_flags: The intersection notation and set-model assumption have been repaired, but a source is still needed to establish that center-set replacement is the intended recourse convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Center-replacement recourse for fixed-cardinality online clustering solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For center sets \(S_{t-1},S_t\subseteq X\) of cardinality \(k\), define update recourse by
\[
r_t=k-|S_{t-1}\cap S_t|=\tfrac12|S_t\mathbin{\triangle}S_{t-1}|.
\]
A clustering sequence has cumulative recourse budget \(R_T\) through time \(T\) when \(\sum_{t=1}^T r_t\leq R_T\). Under a per-update model with allowances \(b_t\), the condition is instead \(r_t\leq b_t\) for every \(t\). Centers retained at the same metric point incur no replacement; each removed-and-added pair counts once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded-recourse clustering limits how many centers may be replaced, either at each update or cumulatively over the request sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Recourse Clustering

children.title: Clustering Migration Costs
children.top_down_role: Costs induced by moving centers or reassigning clustered demand.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and every center configuration contains \(k\) centers, counted with multiplicity.
A nonnegative coefficient \(\lambda\) converts movement distance into objective cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transition cost is \(M(S_{t-1},S_t)=\min_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_k}\sum_{j=1}^k d(s_{t-1,j},s_{t,\pi(j)})\).

notation.meaning: Minimum matching distance between successive center configurations.
Permutation group on k center labels.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports this matching-based center-migration convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric matching cost for moving unlabeled centers between successive configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write successive center multisets as \(S_{t-1}=(s_{t-1,1},\ldots,s_{t-1,k})\) and \(S_t=(s_{t,1},\ldots,s_{t,k})\). Their migration cost is the minimum perfect-matching distance
\[
M(S_{t-1},S_t)=\min_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_k}\sum_{j=1}^k d(s_{t-1,j},s_{t,\pi(j)}).
\]
For horizon \(T\), a migration-aware clustering objective has the form \(\sum_{t=1}^T \Phi_t(S_t)+\lambda\sum_{t=1}^T M(S_{t-1},S_t)\), where \(\Phi_t\) is the stipulated service cost. Matching makes the cost independent of arbitrary center labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Migration cost is the minimum total metric distance needed to match old centers to new centers, optionally added to clustering service cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Clustering Migration Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matching formula is internally coherent for multisets of exactly k centers, and `definition` fits the leaf. However, no source establishes that this terminal uses minimum perfect-matching migration rather than labeled-center movement, Hausdorff movement, or another transition model.

assumptions_latex: Items of sizes \(s_t\in(0,1]\) arrive sequentially.
Bins have unit capacity, and each item must be assigned immediately and irrevocably.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A packing is feasible exactly when \(\sum_{t:a_t=b}s_t\leq1\) for every bin \(b\); its cost is the number of used bins.

notation.meaning: Number of bins used through time T.

review_flags: The supplied locators concern matching and network optimization, not online bin packing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical one-dimensional online bin packing with unit-capacity bins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In one-dimensional online bin packing, item \(t\) reveals a size \(s_t\in(0,1]\). Before seeing \(s_{t+1}\), the algorithm assigns it to a bin \(a_t\), and this assignment cannot subsequently change. Feasibility requires
\[
\sum_{t:a_t=b}s_t\leq1
\]
for every bin \(b\). For a sequence of length \(T\), the cost \(B_T\) is the number of bins containing at least one item. Competitive performance compares \(B_T\) with the minimum number \(\operatorname{OPT}(s_1,\ldots,s_T)\) achievable by an offline packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Items arrive with sizes at most one and must be placed permanently into unit bins; the objective is to minimize the number of used bins.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Bin-Packing Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly defines classical one-dimensional online bin packing and the definition role is suitable for the family container. The available inventory does not contain a bin-packing source or locator, so the formulation and competitive-comparison convention remain unsupported.

children.title: Machine Load Balancing
children.top_down_role: Online assignment problems with scalar machine loads.

assumptions_latex: There are \(m\geq1\) machines and jobs arrive sequentially.
On arrival, job \(t\) reveals nonnegative processing times \(p_{t,i}\) for all machines \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is the makespan \(C_{max}=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\sum_{t:a_t=i}p_{t,i}\).

notation.meaning: Processing time of job t on machine i.

review_flags: The supplied source inventory does not identify an online scheduling or load-balancing section.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online unrelated-machine makespan minimization; identical machines arise when processing times are machine-independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In online machine load balancing, job \(t\) arrives with processing-time vector \((p_{t,1},\ldots,p_{t,m})\in\mathbb R_+^m\). The algorithm immediately and irrevocably chooses a machine \(a_t\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). After \(T\) jobs, machine \(i\) has load \(L_i(T)=\sum_{t:a_t=i}p_{t,i}\), and the objective is
\[
C_{\max}(T)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}L_i(T).
\]
The identical-machine specialization has \(p_{t,i}=p_t\) for every \(i\); arbitrary \(p_{t,i}\) give unrelated machines.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each arriving job is assigned permanently to a machine; the objective minimizes the largest resulting sum of processing times on any machine.
knowledge_statements.title: Machine Load Balancing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is a coherent definition of online makespan minimization on unrelated machines and explicitly identifies the identical-machine specialization. Because the leaf title alone does not determine that unrelated-machine scope, a specific online scheduling source is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential-potential assignment for online unrelated-machine load balancing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online scalar machine assignment using a positive known upper bound on the offline optimum; the extract contains correctable index inconsistencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \sigma=\langle p(1),\ldots,p(k)\rangle, where assigning job j to machine i adds p_i(j)\ge 0, and let l_i(j)=\sum_{1\le r\le j:\,r\in S_i}p_i(r). Assume \operatorname{cost}_{OPT}(\sigma)\le\Lambda with \Lambda>0, and write \widetilde{x}=x/\Lambda. For fixed a>1 and threshold parameter \beta=O(\log n), algorithm U assigns job j to a machine i minimizing a^{\widetilde l_i(j-1)+\widetilde p_i(j)}-a^{\widetilde l_i(j-1)}. It declares failure if the selected assignment satisfies l_i(j-1)+p_i(j)\ge\beta\Lambda.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a positive upper bound on the offline optimum, assign each arriving job to the machine producing the smallest increase in an exponential potential of normalized loads. Declare failure if that assignment reaches the threshold beta times the bound.
assumptions_latex: p_i(j)\ge0
0<\Lambda\text{ and }\operatorname{cost}_{OPT}(\sigma)\le\Lambda
\widetilde{x}=x/\Lambda
\beta=O(\log n)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: i_j\in\arg\min_i\left(a^{\widetilde l_i(j-1)+\widetilde p_i(j)}-a^{\widetilde l_i(j-1)}\right),\quad U\text{ fails if }l_{i_j}(j-1)+p_{i_j}(j)\ge\beta\Lambda.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Removes advance knowledge of the offline bound from algorithm U; positive initialization or separate handling of a zero-cost case is necessary.

children.title: Vector Load Balancing
children.top_down_role: Online assignment problems with multidimensional loads.

assumptions_latex: There are \(m\geq1\) identical machines and load dimension \(d\geq1\).
Each arriving job reveals a nonnegative load vector \(v_t\in\mathbb R_+^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is \(L_{max}=\max_{i\in[m],\,q\in[d]}\sum_{t:a_t=i}v_{t,q}\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative d-dimensional load of job t.
Coordinatewise load vector accumulated by machine i.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the vector-scheduling model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online vector scheduling on identical machines under the coordinatewise maximum norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In online vector load balancing, job \(t\) reveals \(v_t=(v_{t,1},\ldots,v_{t,d})\in\mathbb R_+^d\). Before later vectors are known, the algorithm assigns it irrevocably to a machine \(a_t\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Machine \(i\) accumulates the coordinatewise load \(L_i=\sum_{t:a_t=i}v_t\). The maximum-load objective is
\[
L_{\max}=\max_{i\in[m]}\|L_i\|_\infty
=\max_{i\in[m],\,q\in[d]}\sum_{t:a_t=i}v_{t,q}.
\]
The case \(d=1\) is scalar identical-machine load balancing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each job contributes load in several coordinates and is assigned permanently to one machine; performance is the largest coordinate load on any machine.
knowledge_statements.title: Vector Load Balancing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vector-scheduling definition, domains, irrevocable assignment rule, and infinity-norm objective are internally consistent, and `definition` fits the leaf. No cited source or locator supports this precise identical-machine vector-load model.

children.title: Dimensionality-Sensitive Load Balancing
children.top_down_role: Load-balancing behavior governed by vector dimension or norm choice.

assumptions_latex: For each \(d\geq1\), \(\mathrm{CR}_d\) is the optimal competitive ratio for the same vector-load model in dimension \(d\).
Zero coordinates are admissible and do not affect feasibility or objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(1\leq d\leq d'\), \(\mathrm{CR}_d\leq\mathrm{CR}_{d'}\); in particular \(\mathrm{CR}_1\leq\mathrm{CR}_d\).

notation.meaning: Best achievable competitive ratio in dimension d.
Zero-padding embedding from dimension d into dimension d-prime.

review_flags: The monotonicity claim is standard but the supplied inventory lacks a source for the precise competitive model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension monotonicity obtained by embedding lower-dimensional vector instances via zero padding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d'\geq d\) and embed every load vector \(v\in\mathbb R_+^d\) as \(E(v)=(v,0,\ldots,0)\in\mathbb R_+^{d'}\). Every assignment has exactly the same coordinatewise maximum load before and after this embedding, and the offline optimum is unchanged. Consequently, every \(d\)-dimensional instance is a \(d'\)-dimensional instance of equal value. If \(\mathrm{CR}_d\) denotes the infimum competitive ratio over algorithms in dimension \(d\), then
\[
\mathrm{CR}_d\leq\mathrm{CR}_{d'}.
\]
Thus dimension-dependent guarantees cannot improve merely by enlarging the admissible dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-padding embeds every lower-dimensional load instance into a higher dimension without changing costs, so the best competitive ratio cannot improve with dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimensionality-Sensitive Load Balancing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-padding monotonicity property is mathematically coherent when every dimension uses the same online model, admissible algorithm class, adversary convention, and definition of competitive ratio. Those conventions and the property have no supporting citation, so source uncertainty is material.

assumptions_latex: A cache holds at most \(k\geq1\) unit-size pages.
Requests \(r_1,r_2,\ldots\) are revealed sequentially, and a miss costs one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: LRU evicts, on each full-cache miss, the resident page whose most recent request time is smallest.

notation.meaning: Cache contents immediately after request t is served.
Most recent request time of page p before time t.

review_flags: No caching source or locator was supplied for the LRU rule and deterministic paging model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least-recently-used eviction for unit-size, unit-cost paging.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(C_0=\varnothing\). At time \(t\), if \(r_t\in C_{t-1}\), set \(C_t=C_{t-1}\). If \(r_t\notin C_{t-1}\) and \(|C_{t-1}|<k\), set \(C_t=C_{t-1}\cup\{r_t\}\). Otherwise choose
\[
p_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{p\in C_{t-1}}\tau_t(p)
\]
and set \(C_t=(C_{t-1}\setminus\{p_t\})\cup\{r_t\}\). Here \(\tau_t(p)\) is the last request time of \(p\), with a fixed deterministic tie rule. Output is the resulting cache sequence; each miss incurs unit cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Least recently used keeps requested pages and, on a full-cache miss, deterministically evicts the page whose last request occurred earliest.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Eviction Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly specifies LRU as a deterministic paging algorithm, and `algorithm` is the correct role for that method. It covers one method within the broader plural container rather than the whole family, and no caching source with a locator supports the rule or paging model.

assumptions_latex: A cache holds \(k\geq1\) unit-size pages and every miss costs one.
Random choices are made against an obliviously fixed request sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Within each phase, requested pages are marked; when a request would be the \((k+1)\)-st distinct page of the phase, all marks are cleared before processing it, and eviction on a full-cache miss is uniform among currently unmarked resident pages.

notation.meaning: Pages marked in the current phase after request t.

review_flags: The phase transition has been moved before eviction so that the set of eligible unmarked pages is nonempty; a source with a specific locator is still required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical randomized marking algorithm for paging against an oblivious request sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(C_0=M_0=\varnothing\). Upon request \(r_t\), if \(r_t\notin M_{t-1}\) and \(|M_{t-1}|=k\), begin a new phase by clearing all marks. Let \(M'_{t-1}=\varnothing\) after such a phase change and \(M'_{t-1}=M_{t-1}\) otherwise. If \(r_t\notin C_{t-1}\) and the cache is full, evict a page chosen uniformly from \(C_{t-1}\setminus M'_{t-1}\). Insert \(r_t\) when absent, and then set \(M_t=M'_{t-1}\cup\{r_t\}\); if no eviction or insertion is needed, retain the cache contents. Thus a page marked in the current phase is never evicted during that phase. The output is the randomized cache sequence, and cost equals the number of misses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The marking algorithm partitions requests into phases of at most k distinct pages, clears marks before processing the first new page of a phase, and on a full-cache miss randomly evicts an unmarked cached page.

children.title: Weighted Caching
children.top_down_role: Caching models with nonuniform retrieval or eviction costs.

assumptions_latex: Every page has unit size and the cache has capacity \(k\).
Fetching page \(p\) after a miss incurs a fixed cost \(w_p>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The total cost through time \(T\) is \(\sum_{t=1}^T w_{r_t}\mathbf 1\{r_t\notin C_{t-1}\}\).

notation.meaning: Cache contents immediately before request t.

review_flags: The provided locator hints do not address weighted caching.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-size paging with page-dependent retrieval costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In weighted caching, a request sequence \(r_1,r_2,\ldots\) names unit-size pages. Immediately before request \(t\), the cache contains \(C_{t-1}\) with \(|C_{t-1}|\leq k\). If \(r_t\in C_{t-1}\), service is free. Otherwise the algorithm pays \(w_{r_t}\), inserts \(r_t\), and, if necessary, evicts pages so the resulting cache \(C_t\) has at most \(k\) pages. Evictions themselves are free. The objective through time \(T\) is
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T w_{r_t}\mathbf 1\{r_t\notin C_{t-1}\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted caching assigns each unit-size page its own retrieval cost; a request incurs that cost exactly when the page is absent from cache.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Caching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record consistently defines unit-size weighted caching with page-dependent retrieval costs, free evictions, and a miss-cost objective. The content kind fits, but no authoritative caching source or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: File Caching
children.top_down_role: Caching models with variable-size objects.

assumptions_latex: The cache has capacity \(K>0\).
Each file \(p\) has size \(s_p\in(0,K]\) and retrieval cost \(w_p>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires \(\sum_{p\in C_t}s_p\leq K\), and misses cost \(w_{r_t}\).

notation.meaning: Size and retrieval cost of file p.
Set of resident files after request t.

review_flags: The supplied source inventory lacks a locator for variable-size file caching.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-size, nonuniform-retrieval-cost caching with whole-file admission and eviction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In file caching, each file \(p\) has size \(s_p\in(0,K]\) and retrieval cost \(w_p>0\). On request \(r_t\), cost is zero if \(r_t\in C_{t-1}\); otherwise the algorithm pays \(w_{r_t}\) and loads the entire file. It may evict any resident files, without retrieval credit, to produce \(C_t\) satisfying
\[
\sum_{p\in C_t}s_p\leq K.
\]
Admission and eviction decisions use only requests revealed through time \(t\). The objective is the sum of retrieval costs over misses; weighted caching is the special case of equal file sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Files have individual sizes and retrieval costs; each missing requested file is loaded whole, with evictions maintaining the cache-capacity constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: File Caching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variable-size, weighted whole-file caching definition is internally consistent and distinguishes it from unit-size weighted caching. No source supports the whole-file admission, free-eviction, and retrieval-cost conventions, so the precise model remains unreliable without a locator.

children.title: Rental Caching
children.top_down_role: Caching models that charge for retaining objects over time.

knowledge_statements.title: Rental Caching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard rental-caching model with capacity, retrieval cost, and per-time holding rent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the cache have capacity \(k\), and let requests \(r_1,\ldots,r_T\) arrive online. Each item \(p\) has retrieval cost \(c_p\ge 0\) and rental rate \(\lambda_p\ge 0\). Before serving request \(r_t=p\), an algorithm must place \(p\) in the cache if absent, paying \(c_p\), and may evict items without charge. During each time interval it pays \(\lambda_p\) for every cached item \(p\), while maintaining at most \(k\) items. The rental-caching objective is to minimize total retrieval cost plus total rental cost over the request sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rental caching minimizes retrieval charges plus time-dependent holding charges while serving every request from a cache of bounded capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(k\ge 1\).
All retrieval costs and rental rates are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cost}=\sum_t \operatorname{retrieval}_t+\sum_t\sum_{p\in C_t}\lambda_p\) is minimized subject to \(|C_t|\le k\).

notation.meaning: cache contents during time interval t

knowledge_statements.title: Metrical Task Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state metrical task systems with movement paid before processing each revealed task.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A metrical task system consists of a finite metric space \((X,d)\), an initial state \(x_0\in X\), and an online sequence of nonnegative task-cost functions \(c_t:X\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). After \(c_t\) is revealed, an online algorithm chooses \(x_t\in X\) and incurs movement cost \(d(x_{t-1},x_t)\) and service cost \(c_t(x_t)\). Its total cost through time \(T\) is \[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(d(x_{t-1},x_t)+c_t(x_t)\bigr).\] The objective is to minimize this cost relative to an offline state sequence knowing all tasks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An online controller moves among metric states and pays both movement distance and the revealed processing cost at its chosen state.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a finite metric space.
Each \(c_t\) is revealed before \(x_t\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible decision at time \(t\) is any \(x_t\in X\), with cost \(d(x_{t-1},x_t)+c_t(x_t)\).

notation.meaning: task-cost function revealed at time t

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metrical task system and schedule cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines task systems, causal online schedules, movement and processing costs, the offline optimum, and the symmetry condition for a metrical task system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A task system consists of a finite state set \(S\), distances \(d_{ij}\) satisfying \(d_{ii}=0\) and the triangle inequality, and a set \(\mathcal T\) of nonnegative task-cost vectors \(T:S\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). Given \(\sigma=(T^1,\ldots,T^N)\) and a fixed initial state \(\pi(0)\), a schedule \(\pi:\{1,\ldots,N\}\to S\) has cost \[\operatorname{cost}(\pi,\sigma)=\sum_{i=1}^N d_{\pi(i-1),\pi(i)}+\sum_{i=1}^N T^i(\pi(i)).\] An online schedule chooses \(\pi(j)\) using only \(T^1,\ldots,T^j\), and \[\operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\sigma)=\min_{\pi}\operatorname{cost}(\pi,\sigma).\] If \(d_{ij}=d_{ji}\) for every \(i,j\in S\), the task system is a metrical task system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A task system has finitely many states, distances satisfying zero self-distance and the triangle inequality, and nonnegative state-dependent processing costs. A schedule pays movement and processing costs. An online schedule can use only tasks revealed so far, while the offline optimum minimizes total schedule cost. Symmetric distances make it a metrical task system.
assumptions_latex: |S|<\infty.
d_{ii}=0\quad\forall i\in S.
d_{ik}\le d_{ij}+d_{jk}\quad\forall i,j,k\in S.
T(i)\ge0\quad\forall T\in\mathcal T,\ i\in S.
\pi(0)\in S\text{ is fixed.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\sigma)=\min_{\pi}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N d_{\pi(i-1),\pi(i)}+\sum_{i=1}^N T^i(\pi(i))\right],\qquad \left(\forall i,j,\ d_{ij}=d_{ji}\right)\Rightarrow\text{metrical task system}

knowledge_statements.title: Work-Function Algorithm Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical work-function algorithm for the finite-metric k-server problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite metric space \((X,d)\), request prefix \(\sigma_t=(r_1,\ldots,r_t)\), and initial \(k\)-server configuration \(S_0\), define \(w_t(S)\) as the minimum offline movement cost that serves \(\sigma_t\) and ends in configuration \(S\). Initialize the online configuration as \(A_0=S_0\). After request \(r_t\) arrives, choose a configuration \[A_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{S:\,r_t\in S}\bigl(w_t(S)+D(A_{t-1},S)\bigr),\] move the servers from \(A_{t-1}\) to \(A_t\) along a minimum matching, and output the resulting configuration. Ties are resolved by a fixed rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The work-function algorithm moves to a request-containing configuration minimizing offline prefix cost plus distance from its current configuration.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is finite and \(1\le k\le |X|\).
Configurations are multisets of \(k\) points, with matching distance \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each update produces \(A_t\) containing \(r_t\) and incurs movement cost \(D(A_{t-1},A_t)\).

notation.meaning: minimum prefix-serving cost ending at configuration S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Duality Lemma for Work-Function Request Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-cost attainment and persistence of request minimizers under a work-function update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\sigma_t=r\), and suppose that the feasible configuration \(X\) satisfies
\[
X\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{Y}\left\{\operatorname{opt}_{t-1}(\sigma,Y)-\sum_{y\in Y}d(r,y)\right\}.
\]
Then \(X\) attains the extended cost of the request:
\[
X\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{Y}\left\{\operatorname{opt}_{t}(\sigma,Y)-\operatorname{opt}_{t-1}(\sigma,Y)\right\}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
X\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{Y}\left\{\operatorname{opt}_{t}(\sigma,Y)-\sum_{y\in Y}d(r,y)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A request minimizer for the work function immediately before request r attains that request's extended cost and remains a request minimizer after the work function is updated.
assumptions_latex: \(\sigma_t=r\).
\(X\) and \(Y\) are feasible \(k\)-server configurations.
X\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{Y}\left\{\operatorname{opt}_{t-1}(\sigma,Y)-\sum_{y\in Y}d(r,y)\right\}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{Y}\left\{\operatorname{opt}_{t}(\sigma,Y)-\operatorname{opt}_{t-1}(\sigma,Y)\right\}\quad\text{and}\quad X\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{Y}\left\{\operatorname{opt}_{t}(\sigma,Y)-\sum_{y\in Y}d(r,y)\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multi-Configuration Potential for WFA Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary potential obtained by minimizing a work-function expression over one principal and k auxiliary configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\) and \(B_i=(b_{i1},\ldots,b_{ik})\), \(i=1,\ldots,k\), be feasible configurations. Define
\[
\psi(\operatorname{opt}_t,U,B_1,\ldots,B_k)
= k\,\operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,U)
+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\left[\operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,B_i)-\sum_{j=1}^{k}d(u_i,b_{ij})\right].
\]
The potential is
\[
\phi_t=\min_{U,B_1,\ldots,B_k}\psi(\operatorname{opt}_t,U,B_1,\ldots,B_k),
\]
with the minimum taken over feasible configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The potential is the minimum over one principal configuration U and k auxiliary configurations of k times the work value at U, plus the auxiliary work values, minus the specified distance sums.
assumptions_latex: U=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\text{ is a feasible }k\text{-server configuration}.
B_i=(b_{i1},\ldots,b_{ik})\text{ is a feasible }k\text{-server configuration for each }i=1,\ldots,k.
\(d\) is the underlying metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi_t=\min_{U,B_1,\ldots,B_k}\left\{k\,\operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,U)+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\left[\operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,B_i)-\sum_{j=1}^{k}d(u_i,b_{ij})\right]\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasi-Convexity of Configuration-Indexed Optimum Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exchange-based quasi-convexity definition for the configuration-indexed optimum functions used in k-server work-function analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The functions \operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,\cdot) are quasi-convex if and only if, for every pair of configurations A,B, there exists a bijection h:A\to B such that h(r)=r for every r\in A\cap B and, for every X,Y\subseteq A satisfying A=X\cup Y and X\cap Y=\varnothing,\n\[\operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,A)+\operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,B)\geq \operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,X\cup h(Y))+\operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,h(X)\cup Y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The functions are quasi-convex exactly when every pair of configurations admits an intersection-fixing bijection for which the stated exchange inequality holds for every bipartition of the first configuration.
assumptions_latex: A,B \text{ are configurations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall A,B\;\exists h:A\to B\text{ bijective such that }\bigl(\forall r\in A\cap B,\ h(r)=r\bigr)\text{ and }\forall X,Y\subseteq A,\ \bigl(A=X\cup Y\land X\cap Y=\varnothing\bigr)\Rightarrow \operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,A)+\operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,B)\geq \operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,X\cup h(Y))+\operatorname{opt}_t(\sigma,h(X)\cup Y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential Comparison Under Request-Minimizer Substitution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A substitution inequality for the multi-configuration potential used in WFA analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume
\[
\phi_t=\psi(\operatorname{opt}_t,\widetilde U,\widetilde B_1,\ldots,\widetilde B_k),
\]
where \(\widetilde U=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\), let \(\sigma_t=r\), and let \(A\) be a minimizer of \(r\) with respect to \(\operatorname{opt}_{t-1}(\sigma,\cdot)\). For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), define
\[
\psi_t^{(i)}=\psi\!\left(\operatorname{opt}_t,\widetilde U-u_i+r,\widetilde B_1,\ldots,\widetilde B_{i-1},A,\widetilde B_{i+1},\ldots,\widetilde B_k\right).
\]
Then
\[
\phi_t\geq \psi_t^{(i)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the listed configurations attain the potential, then for each index i, replacing the ith point of the principal configuration by the current request and the ith auxiliary configuration by a preceding-work-function request minimizer yields a psi value no greater than the potential.
assumptions_latex: \phi_t=\psi(\operatorname{opt}_t,\widetilde U,\widetilde B_1,\ldots,\widetilde B_k).
\widetilde U=(u_1,\ldots,u_k).
\sigma_t=r.
A\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{X}\left\{\operatorname{opt}_{t-1}(\sigma,X)-\sum_{x\in X}d(r,x)\right\}.
i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi_t\geq\psi\!\left(\operatorname{opt}_t,\widetilde U-u_i+r,\widetilde B_1,\ldots,\widetilde B_{i-1},A,\widetilde B_{i+1},\ldots,\widetilde B_k\right).

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Metric Server Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The k-server problem restricted to shortest-path metrics of weighted trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,\ell)\) be a connected tree with edge lengths \(\ell_e>0\), and let \(d_G(u,v)\) be the length of the unique \(u\)-to-\(v\) path. A tree-metric \(k\)-server instance specifies an initial multiset \(S_0\) of \(k\) vertices and reveals requests \(r_t\in V\) online. To serve \(r_t\), an algorithm moves servers along tree paths until some server occupies \(r_t\), paying the total traversed edge length. The objective is to minimize cumulative movement cost, conventionally compared with the offline optimum under the same initial configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tree-metric k-server restricts requests and server movement to the shortest-path metric induced by a weighted tree.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a connected tree with strictly positive edge lengths.
\(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and requests occur at vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Serving \((r_t)_{t=1}^T\) costs the sum of all server-movement distances in \((V,d_G)\).

knowledge_statements.title: General-Metric Server Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical k-server problem on an arbitrary metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(S_0\) be a multiset of \(k\) initial server locations. Requests \(r_1,r_2,\ldots\in X\) are revealed sequentially. After seeing \(r_t\), an online algorithm must move servers so that at least one occupies \(r_t\); moving a server from \(x\) to \(y\) costs \(d(x,y)\). Servers not needed for service may also move, and the step cost is the sum of all movement distances. The general-metric \(k\)-server objective is to minimize cumulative movement cost relative to an offline optimum with the same \(S_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The general-metric k-server problem serves each revealed point by moving one or more of k servers and paying total metric distance.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space.
\(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(S_0\) contains exactly \(k\) locations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After every request \(r_t\), the resulting server configuration contains \(r_t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The general-metric k-server definition is coherent and fits the container, but it lacks an inspectable authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General-metric k-server problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines sequential request service by k mobile servers in a fixed metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M,d)\) be a fixed metric space known to the online algorithm, and let \(k\) mobile servers occupy points of \(M\). Requests \(x_1,x_2,\ldots\in M\) arrive sequentially, and each request must be served before the next appears. A request at \(x_t\) is served by having a server at \(x_t\); if none is present, the algorithm moves a server from some point \(a_t\) to \(x_t\), incurring cost \(d(a_t,x_t)\). The objective is to minimize the total distance moved by all servers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The k-server problem has k mobile servers in a fixed metric space known in advance. Each sequentially revealed request must be served before the next request appears by placing a server at the requested point. Moving a server costs the distance moved, and the objective is to minimize total movement.
assumptions_latex: (M,d)\text{ is a fixed metric space known to the online algorithm.}
k\text{ mobile servers occupy points of }M.
x_t\in M\text{ is revealed sequentially and must be served before }x_{t+1}\text{ appears.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\sum_t d(a_t,x_t)\quad\text{subject to serving every request before the next request appears}

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Embedding Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Competitive-ratio transfer through a dominating random embedding into tractable metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\\) be a finite metric space, and suppose a distribution over embeddings \(f:X\to Y_f\) into metrics \((Y_f,d_f)\) satisfies \(d(x,y)\le d_f(f(x),f(y))\) for all \(x,y\in X\) and \(\mathbb{E}[d_f(f(x),f(y))]\le Dd(x,y)\). If an online \(k\)-server algorithm on every \((Y_f,d_f)\) has expected cost at most \(\rho\operatorname{OPT}_f+\beta\), then sampling \(f\), running that algorithm, and projecting its moves back yields \[\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{cost}_X]\le \rho D\operatorname{OPT}_X+\beta,\] provided server configurations and requests admit cost-nonincreasing projection to \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dominating embedding with expected distortion D transfers a rho-competitive server algorithm to an expected rho-D competitive algorithm on the original metric.
assumptions_latex: The embedding is noncontractive and has expected pairwise stretch at most \(D\).
The target algorithm is randomized \(\rho\)-competitive.
Projection preserves request service without increasing movement cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{cost}_X]\le \rho D\operatorname{OPT}_X+\beta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed competitive-ratio transfer depends on a precise coupling and projection theorem not supplied here. Pairwise expected stretch alone does not transparently justify the stated online transfer, and the opening metric expression contains a stray LaTeX line-break command.

children.title: Completion-Time Objectives
children.top_down_role: Online scheduling criteria based on job completion times.

knowledge_statements.title: Completion-Time Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted and unweighted total completion-time objectives in online scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For jobs \(J\), job \(j\) has release time \(r_j\), processing requirement \(p_j>0\), and optional weight \(w_j\ge 0\). Under a feasible schedule, its completion time is \(C_j=\inf\{t:\text{all processing of job }j\text{ is finished by }t\}\). The total completion-time objective is \[\sum_{j\in J} C_j,\] and its weighted form is \[\sum_{j\in J} w_jC_j.\] In online scheduling, each job's parameters become known no earlier than \(r_j\), and the schedule minimizes the selected objective subject to the specified machine and preemption constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Completion-time objectives minimize the sum, or weighted sum, of the absolute times at which jobs finish.
assumptions_latex: Every job has finite positive processing requirement.
The schedule satisfies the ambient machine, release-time, and preemption rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is \(\min\sum_{j\in J}C_j\) or \(\min\sum_{j\in J}w_jC_j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted and unweighted completion-time objectives are standard and fit the leaf, but no source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Flow-Time Objectives
children.top_down_role: Online scheduling criteria based on time spent within the system.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Time Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted and unweighted job flow time measured from release until completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each job \(j\) with release time \(r_j\) and completion time \(C_j\ge r_j\), define its flow time by \(F_j=C_j-r_j\). The total flow-time objective is \[\sum_{j\in J}F_j=\sum_{j\in J}(C_j-r_j),\] and the weighted total flow-time objective is \[\sum_{j\in J}w_jF_j,\] where \(w_j\ge 0\). For a time horizon containing all releases and completions, total flow time also equals the integral of the number of released but unfinished jobs; the weighted version integrates their total weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flow time measures how long each job remains in the system after release; the objective sums these durations or their weighted values.
assumptions_latex: Each job completes at a finite time \(C_j\ge r_j\).
Weights, when present, satisfy \(w_j\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\sum_j(C_j-r_j)\), or \(\min\sum_jw_j(C_j-r_j)\), is the flow-time objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The flow-time formulas and integral interpretation are coherent and appropriately classified, but they lack a cited source and locator.

children.title: Delay Objectives
children.top_down_role: Online scheduling criteria emphasizing waiting or service delay.

knowledge_statements.title: Delay Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General nondecreasing penalties applied to job waiting or flow durations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each released job \(j\), let \(C_j\) be its completion time and let \(g_j:\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) be a nondecreasing delay-penalty function with \(g_j(0)=0\). The job's delay is measured by its residence time \(C_j-r_j\), and the generalized delay objective is \[\sum_{j\in J}g_j(C_j-r_j).\] Equivalently, if \(g_j\) is absolutely continuous, this equals the integral over time of the instantaneous delay rates \(g_j'(t-r_j)\) of released unfinished jobs. Linear \(g_j(u)=w_ju\) recovers weighted flow time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A delay objective charges each job a nondecreasing penalty based on time elapsed between its release and completion.
assumptions_latex: Every \(g_j\) is nonnegative, nondecreasing, and satisfies \(g_j(0)=0\).
Every job eventually completes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The schedule minimizes \(\sum_{j\in J}g_j(C_j-r_j)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is one valid generalized flow-delay convention, but the broader title admits other delay models; a source is needed to establish the intended local convention and integral representation.

children.title: Deadline Objectives
children.top_down_role: Online scheduling criteria centered on deadline satisfaction.

knowledge_statements.title: Deadline Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard-deadline feasibility and soft tardiness penalties for released jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign each job \(j\) a release time \(r_j\), processing requirement \(p_j>0\), and deadline \(d_j\ge r_j\). A schedule meets the hard-deadline condition precisely when \[C_j\le d_j\qquad\text{for every required job }j.\] When deadline violations are permitted, define tardiness \(T_j=(C_j-d_j)_+\). Standard soft-deadline objectives minimize \(\sum_j T_j\), \(\sum_j w_jT_j\), or the number or weight of late jobs, \(\sum_j w_j\mathbf{1}\{C_j>d_j\}\). In an online model, job data are disclosed at release, and later decisions cannot anticipate unreleased jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hard deadlines require every job to finish on time; soft variants minimize tardiness or the number or weight of late jobs.
assumptions_latex: \(d_j\ge r_j\) and \(p_j>0\) for every job.
Weights used in soft penalties are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hard feasibility is \(C_j\le d_j\) for all required jobs; soft violations are quantified by \((C_j-d_j)_+\) or \(\mathbf{1}\{C_j>d_j\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record combines a hard feasibility condition with several distinct soft-deadline objectives, while the terminal container is an objective family. An authoritative source is needed to determine the intended variant before correcting its mathematical role.

children.title: Throughput Objectives
children.top_down_role: Online scheduling criteria centered on completed workload or value.

knowledge_statements.title: Throughput Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completed-job count or value under deadlines and scheduling constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each job \(j\) have release time \(r_j\), processing requirement \(p_j>0\), deadline \(d_j\), and value \(v_j\ge 0\). For a feasible schedule, define \(U_j=1\) if job \(j\) completes by \(d_j\), and \(U_j=0\) otherwise. The unweighted throughput is \[\sum_{j\in J}U_j,\] while weighted throughput is \[\sum_{j\in J}v_jU_j.\] The throughput objective maximizes the applicable quantity; jobs not completed by their deadlines contribute zero, although the model must separately specify whether rejected or tardy processing consumes machine capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Throughput scheduling maximizes the number or total value of jobs completed by their deadlines.
assumptions_latex: Job parameters become available at their release times.
Values satisfy \(v_j\ge 0\).
Completion and rejection follow the ambient scheduling model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is \(\max\sum_jU_j\) or \(\max\sum_jv_jU_j\), where \(U_j=\mathbf{1}\{C_j\le d_j\}\).

notation.meaning: indicator that job j meets its deadline
value of completing job j on time

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The throughput formulas fit the leaf, but the treatment of rejected, abandoned, or tardily processed jobs is model-dependent and no source locator is supplied.

children.title: Energy Objectives
children.top_down_role: Online scheduling criteria centered on energy consumption.

knowledge_statements.title: Energy Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Speed-scaling energy objective with convex power consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a speed-scalable processor model, a schedule selects a measurable speed \(s(t)\ge 0\). Executing at speed \(s(t)\) performs \(s(t)\,dt\) units of work during \(dt\) and consumes power \(P(s(t))\), where \(P:\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) is nondecreasing and convex with \(P(0)=0\). The schedule's energy is \[E=\int_0^{\infty}P(s(t))\,dt.\] An energy objective minimizes \(E\) subject to release times, processing requirements, deadlines, and machine constraints; a common model uses \(P(s)=s^{\alpha}\) for \(\alpha>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Energy-aware scheduling chooses processor speed over time to minimize integrated power while completing required work under scheduling constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(s\) is measurable and the required work is feasibly scheduled.
\(P\) is nonnegative, nondecreasing, convex, and satisfies \(P(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is \(\min E=\min\int_0^{\infty}P(s(t))\,dt\) over feasible schedules.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The speed-scaling energy definition fits the leaf, but the processor model, feasibility requirements, and assumptions on the power function require a specific authoritative citation.
