children.title: Online Path Routing
children.top_down_role: Online selection of routes for sequential connection requests.

assumptions_latex: A directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) has capacities \(u_e>0\).
Requests \(r_t=(s_t,d_t)\) arrive sequentially, and the decision for request \(t\) is made before future requests are revealed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each accepted request is assigned a feasible path when it arrives.

notation.meaning: load placed on edge e after processing t requests
path selected for request t when accepted

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral, irrevocable path selection for sequential unit-demand requests.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Path Flows and Conformal Decomposition p. 7
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An online path-routing policy receives requests \(r_t=(s_t,d_t)\) sequentially. On arrival of \(r_t\), using only \(r_1,\ldots,r_t\), it chooses \(a_t\in\{0,1\}\); if \(a_t=1\), it also chooses an \(s_t\)-to-\(d_t\) path \(P_t\subseteq E\). Decisions are irrevocable. The induced edge load is \(L_e(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{t}a_j\mathbf 1\{e\in P_j\}\). A capacity-feasible policy satisfies \(L_e(t)\le u_e\) for every \(e\in E\) and every time \(t\). Variants may instead minimize the maximum normalized load \(\max_{e\in E}L_e(T)/u_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Requests arrive one at a time. The policy immediately rejects each request or assigns it one path, while respecting capacities or controlling maximum normalized edge load.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Path Routing

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Path Flows and Conformal Decomposition p. 7
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit Online Path Routing, and the notation is internally coherent. However, the cited locator supports path-flow concepts rather than sequential revelation, irrevocable acceptance, online capacity feasibility, or comparison with an offline congestion objective. A direct online-routing source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Online Multicommodity Routing
children.top_down_role: Online routing with multiple commodities sharing network capacity.

assumptions_latex: A directed capacitated graph \(G=(V,E)\) is fixed.
Commodity \(k_t=(s_t,d_t,b_t)\), with demand \(b_t\ge0\), is revealed at time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The online decisions induce simultaneous commodity flows satisfying conservation and the selected capacity convention.

notation.meaning: flow of commodity j on edge e
total load on edge e through time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential fractional multicommodity flow with irrevocable acceptance and routing decisions.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Multicommodity Flow Problems p. 17
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In online multicommodity routing, commodity \(k_t=(s_t,d_t,b_t)\) is revealed at time \(t\). The policy irrevocably chooses \(x_t\in[0,1]\) and a nonnegative flow \((f_e^t)_{e\in E}\) of value \(x_tb_t\) from \(s_t\) to \(d_t\). Thus flow conservation holds at every vertex other than \(s_t,d_t\), with net outflow \(x_tb_t\) at \(s_t\) and net inflow \(x_tb_t\) at \(d_t\). The aggregate load is \(L_e(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{t}f_e^j\); strict feasibility requires \(L_e(t)\le u_e\) for all \(e\) and \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each arriving commodity is fractionally accepted and routed as a flow. All commodity flows jointly obey conservation and the chosen edge-capacity constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Multicommodity Routing

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Multicommodity Flow Problems p. 17
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fractional-flow definition and its content kind fit Online Multicommodity Routing. The cited multicommodity-flow section can support conservation and aggregate capacities, but it does not establish the sequential, history-dependent, irrevocable online model. A direct source for online multicommodity routing is required.

children.title: Online Unsplittable-Flow Routing
children.top_down_role: Online routing regimes requiring each demand to use a single route.

assumptions_latex: A directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) has edge capacities \(u_e>0\).
Request \(t\) reveals terminals \((s_t,d_t)\) and demand \(b_t>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted demand is carried wholly on one path, so no accepted commodity is split among routes.

notation.meaning: single path assigned to accepted request t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral single-path routing of demands that arrive sequentially.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Path Flows and Conformal Decomposition p. 7
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An online unsplittable-flow policy processes request \((s_t,d_t,b_t)\) using only information available through time \(t\). It irrevocably chooses \(a_t\in\{0,1\}\); when \(a_t=1\), it selects one \(s_t\)-to-\(d_t\) path \(P_t\) and sends all \(b_t\) units on that path. Hence \(L_e(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{t}a_jb_j\mathbf 1\{e\in P_j\}\). Capacity feasibility means \(L_e(t)\le u_e\) for every edge and time. Unlike fractional multicommodity routing, a request cannot be divided across multiple paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An accepted request sends its entire demand along one irrevocably selected path; splitting the demand across paths is forbidden.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Unsplittable-Flow Routing

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Path Flows and Conformal Decomposition p. 7
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes unsplittable routing from fractional multicommodity routing and fits the leaf. The cited path-flow section does not support the defining online and irrevocable single-path-demand model. A source specifically treating online unsplittable-flow routing is required.

children.title: Congestion Minimization
children.top_down_role: Online network optimization centered on limiting capacity overload.

assumptions_latex: A capacitated graph \(G=(V,E,u)\) and a finite sequence of routed demands are given.
Each routed demand has a specified nonnegative amount.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Congestion minimization selects feasible routes attaining the smallest possible maximum capacity-normalized edge load.

notation.meaning: total routed load on edge e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax edge congestion under fractional or integral routing constraints.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Multicommodity Flow Problems p. 17
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an admissible routing \(f\in\mathcal F\), let \(L_e(f)\) be the total load placed on edge \(e\). Its congestion is \(\rho(f)=\max_{e\in E}L_e(f)/u_e\). The congestion-minimization problem is \[\rho^*=\min_{f\in\mathcal F}\max_{e\in E}\frac{L_e(f)}{u_e}.\] The feasible family \(\mathcal F\) specifies flow conservation, served demands, and whether routing is fractional or unsplittable. In the online version, routing decisions are made irrevocably as demands arrive, and performance is compared with the offline value \(\rho^*\) for the complete demand sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose admissible routes that minimize the largest ratio of edge load to edge capacity; online performance is compared with the complete-information optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Congestion Minimization

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Multicommodity Flow Problems p. 17
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimax formula is recognizable as congestion minimization, but the cited multicommodity-flow locator does not support the online benchmark formulation. In addition, writing a minimum and claiming that routes attain it requires finiteness, compactness, or another attainment hypothesis; otherwise an infimum is the generally valid formulation. A direct source and a corrected attainment convention are required.

children.title: Online Admission Control
children.top_down_role: Online acceptance or rejection of resource-consuming requests.

assumptions_latex: Requests \(r_t=(s_t,d_t,b_t,w_t)\) arrive sequentially on a capacitated graph.
A routing decision for an accepted request must be fixed at its arrival.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy maximizes accepted value subject to maintaining capacity-feasible irrevocable routes.

notation.meaning: residual edge capacity before request t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immediate accept-or-reject control with capacity-feasible routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize residual capacities by \(c_e(1)=u_e\). When request \(r_t=(s_t,d_t,b_t,w_t)\) arrives, an online admission-control policy uses only the revealed history to choose \(a_t\in\{0,1\}\). If \(a_t=1\), it must select an admissible route whose added load does not exceed \(c_e(t)\) on any edge; it then subtracts that load from the residual capacities. If no such route is selected, set \(a_t=0\) and leave capacities unchanged. Decisions are irrevocable. After the final request, output the accepted set and routes, with throughput value \(\sum_t a_tw_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each arrival, immediately accept and feasibly route the request or reject it. The objective is the total value of accepted requests.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Admission Control

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No inspectable source is supplied. The statement defines the online admission-control model but gives no acceptance or route-selection rule, so it is not an algorithm. It also says the policy maximizes accepted value, although an arbitrary online policy need not attain that maximum; total accepted value is the objective. A sourced model definition or a fully specified sourced algorithm is required.

children.title: Throughput–Congestion Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural compromises between accepted demand and network congestion.

assumptions_latex: For each input sequence \(\sigma\), a policy produces throughput \(W_A(\sigma)\) and congestion \(\rho_A(\sigma)\).
The offline benchmark has throughput \(W^*(\sigma)\) under unit congestion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bicriteria guarantee records the simultaneous throughput loss and permitted congestion augmentation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bicriteria comparison with an offline unit-congestion throughput optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An online routing or admission policy \(A\) has an \((\alpha,\beta)\) throughput-congestion guarantee on an input class \(\Sigma\) if, for every \(\sigma\in\Sigma\), \[W_A(\sigma)\ge \frac{1}{\alpha}W^*(\sigma)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \rho_A(\sigma)\le\beta.\] Here \(W^*(\sigma)\) is the maximum offline throughput achievable with congestion at most \(1\). Smaller \(\alpha\) means greater retained throughput, while smaller \(\beta\) means less capacity augmentation. A family of attainable pairs is downward preferable in both coordinates; its nondominated boundary expresses the throughput-congestion tradeoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bicriteria pair states how much offline throughput the online policy retains and how much capacity-normalized congestion it may incur.
knowledge_statements.title: Throughput–Congestion Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits a throughput-congestion guarantee, and the displayed inequalities are coherent under the declared unit-congestion benchmark. Because no citation is supplied, the exact bicriteria convention, benchmark, and frontier interpretation cannot be validated for this online-routing leaf.

assumptions_latex: For every instance \(I\), an algorithm receives a prediction \(\widehat z\) and incurs cost \(C_A(I,\widehat z)\).
The benchmark cost is \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consistency controls performance under correct predictions, whereas robustness controls the worst prediction-dependent performance.

notation.meaning: correct prediction associated with instance I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention for algorithms augmented with untrusted predictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A prediction-augmented minimization algorithm \(A\) is \(c\)-consistent if \(C_A(I,z(I))\le c\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every instance \(I\) when the supplied prediction is correct. It is \(r\)-robust if \(C_A(I,\widehat z)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every instance \(I\) and every admissible prediction \(\widehat z\). A consistency-robustness tradeoff is a parameterized family \((A_\lambda)_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\) with guarantee pairs \((c(\lambda),r(\lambda))\), where improving \(c(\lambda)\) may worsen \(r(\lambda)\). The meaningful frontier consists of pairs not dominated in both coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consistency measures performance with correct advice; robustness measures worst-case performance with arbitrary advice. A parameterized algorithm family trades one guarantee against the other.
knowledge_statements.title: Consistency–Robustness Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the topic, and the minimization-form consistency and robustness quantifiers are explicit. No source is provided for the chosen conventions or the claimed tradeoff-frontier framing, so the record requires an authoritative learning-augmented algorithms citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Prediction-Error Measures
children.top_down_role: Measures used to classify prediction quality in learning-augmented algorithms.

assumptions_latex: The true information sequence is \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_T)\) and its prediction is \(\widehat z=(\widehat z_1,\ldots,\widehat z_T)\).
A nonnegative local discrepancy \(d_t\) is specified for each time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The chosen prediction-error functional vanishes on exact predictions and quantifies deviation at the scale relevant to the online problem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic cumulative and worst-coordinate error measures for sequential predictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given nonnegative discrepancies \(d_t(z_t,\widehat z_t)\), two standard sequence-level prediction errors are \[\eta_1(z,\widehat z)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_t(z_t,\widehat z_t),\qquad \eta_\infty(z,\widehat z)=\max_{1\le t\le T}d_t(z_t,\widehat z_t).\] A valid discrepancy satisfies \(d_t(x,x)=0\), so both measures vanish for exact predictions. The local loss \(d_t\) must reflect the prediction object: absolute error for scalars, symmetric-difference weight for sets, or an appropriate metric for structured decisions. Any error-dependent competitive guarantee must state which functional and normalization it uses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prediction error aggregates local discrepancies between true and predicted information, commonly by their sum or maximum; the local discrepancy depends on the predicted object.
knowledge_statements.title: Prediction-Error Measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulas correctly define generic sum and maximum aggregations of declared local discrepancies, and the definition kind fits the leaf. No source supports calling these the relevant standard prediction-error measures in this taxonomy context; the appropriate discrepancy and normalization are problem dependent and require a direct citation.

children.title: Misspecified Prediction Models
children.top_down_role: Model mismatch affecting prediction-assisted online decisions.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm is designed for predictions generated by a model class \(\mathcal M\).
The realized joint law or prediction mechanism need not belong to \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Model-relative guarantees need not control performance under misspecification unless they include an explicit discrepancy or worst-case robustness term.

notation.meaning: distance from P to the model class

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of model-conditional guarantees outside the assumed prediction class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be the class of prediction mechanisms under which an online guarantee is established. The model is misspecified when the true law \(P\notin\mathcal M\), equivalently when \(\delta(P,\mathcal M)=\inf_{Q\in\mathcal M}D(P,Q)>0\) for a declared discrepancy \(D\). A guarantee quantified only over \(Q\in\mathcal M\) imposes no performance bound at such a \(P\). Consequently, without either a uniform worst-case guarantee or a bound that degrades with \(\delta(P,\mathcal M)\), arbitrarily accurate in-model performance is compatible with arbitrarily poor cost on out-of-model instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is misspecified when the true prediction mechanism lies outside the assumed class. In-model guarantees alone then provide no out-of-model performance control.
knowledge_statements.title: Misspecified Prediction Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container, but the mathematical statement is not reliable as written. The condition P not in M is not equivalent to positive distance from M unless the discrepancy separates points and M is suitably closed. Moreover, the claim of compatibility with arbitrarily poor out-of-model cost needs a quantified construction or theorem, not merely the observation that an in-model guarantee is silent outside M. A direct source is required before correction.

children.title: Robustness Under Distribution Shift
children.top_down_role: Algorithm behavior when deployment inputs depart from the prediction model.

assumptions_latex: Training and deployment laws \(P\) and \(Q\) are defined on the same instance space.
An online algorithm has nonnegative cost \(C_A(I)\) and benchmark \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A distribution-shift guarantee controls deployment performance by a training-law term plus an explicit penalty depending on the shift size.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected normalized-cost stability under a declared distributional divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a specified divergence \(D\), algorithm \(A\) is \(\Phi\)-robust under distribution shift on a class \(\mathcal Q\) if, for every deployment law \(Q\in\mathcal Q\), \[\mathbb E_{I\sim Q}\!\left[\frac{C_A(I)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}\right]\le \mathbb E_{I\sim P}\!\left[\frac{C_A(I)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}\right]+\Phi(D(Q,P)),\] where \(\Phi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]\) is nondecreasing and \(\Phi(0)=0\). The definition is meaningful only when the expectations are finite and the divergence, admissible deployment class, and normalization are fixed explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deployment performance is stable if its expected normalized cost is bounded by training performance plus a stated penalty increasing with distributional shift.
knowledge_statements.title: Robustness Under Distribution Shift

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is plausible, but the displayed inequality is a proposed stability definition rather than a generally established consequence of distribution shift. Its validity and meaning depend on the divergence, integrability, loss scale, deployment class, and assumptions connecting expectations under P and Q. No source is supplied for this exact formulation.

children.title: Recourse Budgets
children.top_down_role: Limits on the number or magnitude of online solution revisions.

assumptions_latex: After each arrival \(t\), an algorithm maintains a feasible discrete solution \(x^t\).
A nonnegative change measure \(d(x^{t-1},x^t)\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A recourse budget bounds either every update, the total solution change, or an amortized change rate over the sequence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-update, cumulative, and amortized bounds on discrete solution changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^t\) be the maintained feasible solution after update \(t\), and let \(R_t=d(x^{t-1},x^t)\) count the permitted elementary changes, such as insertions, deletions, or reassigned items. Total recourse is \(R_{1:T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}R_t\). A per-update budget \(B\) requires \(R_t\le B\) for every \(t\); a cumulative budget \(B_T\) requires \(R_{1:T}\le B_T\); and an amortized budget \(\bar B\) requires \(R_{1:T}/T\le\bar B\). The change measure and accounting horizon are part of the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse counts changes between consecutive maintained solutions and may be bounded per update, cumulatively, or on average over time.
knowledge_statements.title: Recourse Budgets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Recourse Budgets, and the per-update and cumulative formulas are coherent for a declared change measure. The term amortized recourse can denote a worst-case prefix bound, an expectation, or a sequence-average guarantee in different models; the record fixes one convention without a source. An authoritative online-recourse citation is required.

children.title: Migration Costs
children.top_down_role: Costs charged for relocating or reassigning previously placed objects.

assumptions_latex: At times \(t=0,\ldots,T\), a feasible solution assigns objects to locations or resources.
Moving object \(i\) from assignment \(x_i^{t-1}\) to \(x_i^t\) has nonnegative cost \(m_i(x_i^{t-1},x_i^t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Migration cost is the accumulated weighted cost of changing assignments over time.

notation.meaning: assignment of object i after update t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted recourse for reassignment of objects between maintained solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For assignment vectors \(x^0,x^1,\ldots,x^T\), the migration cost at update \(t\) is \[M_t=\sum_i m_i(x_i^{t-1},x_i^t),\] and total migration cost is \(M_{1:T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}M_t\). The functions \(m_i\) are nonnegative and satisfy \(m_i(a,a)=0\); they may encode object size, transfer distance, or resource-specific movement penalties. An algorithm has migration budget \(B\) when \(M_{1:T}\le B\). Unweighted recourse is recovered by taking \(m_i(a,b)=\mathbf 1\{a\ne b\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Migration cost weights each reassignment by its movement expense and sums these expenses across objects and updates; ordinary recourse is the unit-cost special case.
knowledge_statements.title: Migration Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Migration Costs, and the weighted reassignment formula is internally consistent. No source is supplied for this migration model, its budget convention, or the asserted reduction to ordinary recourse. A direct citation with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Recourse–Quality Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Relationships between revision allowances and solution quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse–Quality Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto tradeoff between objective quality and cumulative solution change in online minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let requests through time \(T\) induce feasible sets \(\mathcal F_t\), nonnegative costs \(c_t:\mathcal F_t\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and optima \(\mathrm{OPT}_t=\min_{x\in\mathcal F_t}c_t(x)\). An online algorithm outputs \(x_t\in\mathcal F_t\). For a change metric \(d\), its cumulative recourse is \(R_T=\sum_{t=2}^{T}d(x_{t-1},x_t)\). A pair \((\alpha,B)\) is achievable if every admissible request sequence satisfies \(c_t(x_t)\le \alpha\mathrm{OPT}_t\) for all \(t\) and \(R_T\le B\). The recourse–quality tradeoff is the Pareto boundary of achievable pairs: improving \(\alpha\) may require increasing \(B\), and conversely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tradeoff records which approximation factors and cumulative solution-change budgets an online algorithm can guarantee simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_t\ne\varnothing\) and \(\mathrm{OPT}_t>0\) whenever a multiplicative guarantee is evaluated.
\(d\) is a nonnegative change-cost metric or application-specific recourse measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T=\{(\alpha,B):c_t(x_t)\le\alpha\mathrm{OPT}_t\ \forall t,\ R_T\le B\}\), ordered by simultaneous minimization of \(\alpha\) and \(B\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the recourse-quality tradeoff leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no source or inspectable locator supports this particular cumulative-recourse and pointwise-approximation formulation.

children.title: Sublinear-Summary Discrete Optimization Family
children.top_down_role: One-pass and few-pass optimization using sublinear summaries, with graph and set-system applications.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Models, graph summaries, connectivity, matching, sparsification, and lower bounds
7.4–7.5, sparse certificates for directed and undirected graphs

children.title: Insertion-Only Streams
children.top_down_role: Streaming settings restricted to positive insertions.

knowledge_statements.title: Insertion-Only Streams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frequency-vector formulation of streams containing additions but no deletions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a universe \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An insertion-only stream is a sequence of updates \((i_t,\Delta_t)\) with \(i_t\in[n]\) and \(\Delta_t\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\). Starting from \(f^{(0)}=0\), the frequency vector after prefix \(t\) is \(f^{(t)}=f^{(t-1)}+\Delta_t e_{i_t}\). Consequently every coordinate is monotone: \(f_i^{(t)}\ge f_i^{(t-1)}\ge0\). A streaming algorithm processes the updates sequentially while retaining only its internal summary, and its output is a prescribed function or approximation of \(f^{(m)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An insertion-only stream consists solely of positive frequency updates, so every item count is nonnegative and nondecreasing.
assumptions_latex: The universe \([n]\) is fixed during the stream.
Updates are processed in one specified sequential order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{(t)}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{n}\) and \(f^{(t)}\ge f^{(t-1)}\) coordinatewise for every \(t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The frequency-vector definition is standard, precise, and appropriate for the insertion-only leaf, but it has no cited authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Random-Order Streams
children.top_down_role: Streaming settings with randomly ordered input items.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Order Streams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformly random permutation model for a fixed multiset of stream items or updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\) be a fixed multiset of stream items or updates chosen independently of the algorithm's random bits. In the random-order model, the observed stream is \((u_{\pi(1)},\ldots,u_{\pi(m)})\), where \(\pi\) is uniformly distributed over all permutations of \([m]\). Probability and expected performance are taken over \(\pi\) and, when applicable, the algorithm's independent internal randomness. The adversary may choose \(U\), but it does not choose the realized arrival permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed adversarial multiset arrives in a uniformly random order independent of the algorithm’s private randomness.
assumptions_latex: The stream length \(m\) and update multiset \(U\) are fixed before the permutation is sampled.
The permutation and the algorithm's private random bits are independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr[\pi=\sigma]=1/m!\) for every permutation \(\sigma\) of \([m]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniformly random permutation model matches the random-order stream leaf, but no cited source with an inspectable locator supports the stated adversary and independence conventions.

children.title: Arrival-Order Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of streaming performance on adversarial versus random arrival order.

knowledge_statements.title: Arrival-Order Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case variation of an algorithm’s expected loss over permutations of identical updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a multiset \(U\) of \(m\) updates and a streaming algorithm \(A\). For each permutation \(\pi\), let \(L_A(U,\pi)\ge0\) be the expected loss of \(A\) on the ordered stream \(U_\pi\), with expectation over its private randomness. The multiplicative arrival-order sensitivity is \(\mathrm{AS}_A(U)=\sup_{\pi,\sigma}L_A(U,\pi)/L_A(U,\sigma)\), provided all denominator losses are positive. The algorithm is order-oblivious for this loss when \(\mathrm{AS}_A(U)=1\) for every \(U\); values above one quantify deterioration caused solely by reordering the same updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arrival-order sensitivity measures how much an algorithm’s expected loss can change when the same updates are permuted.
assumptions_latex: \(L_A(U,\pi)>0\) for every evaluated permutation \(\pi\).
The multiset \(U\) is unchanged between compared streams.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{AS}_A(U)\ge1\), with equality exactly when \(L_A(U,\pi)\) is permutation-invariant.

notation.meaning: Expected loss under arrival permutation pi.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record is locally relevant, but the multiplicative ratio of expected losses is not a uniquely standard definition of arrival-order sensitivity. A source is required to establish this normalization and its intended scope.

children.title: Strict-Turnstile Streams
children.top_down_role: Turnstile streams whose represented frequencies remain nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Turnstile Streams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Turnstile updates constrained to keep every prefix frequency vector nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a universe \([n]\). A strict-turnstile stream is a sequence \((i_t,\Delta_t)\), where \(i_t\in[n]\) and \(\Delta_t\in\mathbb Z\), defining \(f^{(0)}=0\) and \(f^{(t)}=f^{(t-1)}+\Delta_t e_{i_t}\). Positive and negative updates are permitted, but legality requires \(f_i^{(t)}\ge0\) for every coordinate \(i\) and every prefix \(t\). Thus deletions may only remove multiplicity currently present, and the terminal frequency vector belongs to \(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{n}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict-turnstile stream permits insertions and deletions but never allows any item’s prefix frequency to become negative.
assumptions_latex: The universe \([n]\) is fixed.
Frequencies and update increments are integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{(t)}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{n}\) for all \(t\), although individual coordinates need not be monotone.

notation.meaning: Signed multiplicity update at time t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The prefix-nonnegative signed-update definition correctly fits strict-turnstile streams, but it lacks an authoritative citation and specific locator.

children.title: General-Turnstile Streams
children.top_down_role: Turnstile streams permitting signed intermediate frequencies.

knowledge_statements.title: General-Turnstile Streams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed-update streams without the prefix nonnegativity restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a universe \([n]\). A general-turnstile stream is a sequence of signed updates \((i_t,\Delta_t)\in[n]\times\mathbb Z\), with \(f^{(0)}=0\) and \(f^{(t)}=f^{(t-1)}+\Delta_t e_{i_t}\). No nonnegativity constraint is imposed on prefix frequencies: coordinates of \(f^{(t)}\) may be positive, zero, or negative. A streaming problem in this model specifies a function on the admissible terminal vector \(f^{(m)}\in\mathbb Z^n\), together with any separate promise required by that function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general-turnstile stream applies arbitrary signed updates and permits negative item frequencies at intermediate and terminal times.
assumptions_latex: The universe \([n]\) is fixed.
Update increments are integral and may have either sign.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{(t)}\in\mathbb Z^n\) with no coordinatewise sign restriction.

notation.meaning: Signed frequency vector after t updates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unrestricted signed-frequency definition fits the general-turnstile leaf, but no source with a section, page, or definition locator is cited.

children.title: Fully Dynamic Graph Streams
children.top_down_role: Graph streams containing both edge insertions and deletions.

knowledge_statements.title: Fully Dynamic Graph Streams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-stream model supporting both edge insertion and edge deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a fixed vertex set and let \(E_t\) denote the edge set after update \(t\). A fully dynamic simple-graph stream consists of updates \((e_t,s_t)\), where \(e_t\in\binom{V}{2}\) and \(s_t\in\{+1,-1\}\). Starting from \(E_0=\varnothing\), an insertion sets \(E_t=E_{t-1}\cup\{e_t\}\), while a deletion sets \(E_t=E_{t-1}\setminus\{e_t\}\). Legal streams insert only absent edges and delete only present edges. The algorithm must summarize the evolving graph using its prescribed streaming space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fully dynamic graph stream maintains a graph under legal edge insertions and deletions processed sequentially.
assumptions_latex: The vertex set \(V\) is fixed throughout the stream.
The stated version concerns undirected simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_t=(V,E_t)\) is well-defined after every legal update and may both gain and lose edges.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly describes one common fully dynamic simple-graph stream model, but the legality convention and exclusion of multigraph or multiplicity-based variants require a cited source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Sliding-Window Streams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Streaming model whose query depends only on the most recent fixed-length suffix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((u_1,u_2,\ldots)\) be a stream and fix a window length \(W\ge1\). At time \(t\), the active window is \(\mathcal W_t=(u_{\max\{1,t-W+1\}},\ldots,u_t)\). A sliding-window streaming algorithm must output, exactly or approximately, a specified function \(F(\mathcal W_t)\) while processing each item once and using bounded state. Items older than \(W\) positions expire automatically and must have no effect on the correct current answer, although the algorithm need not store expiration updates explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each time, a sliding-window algorithm summarizes only the most recent W stream items; older items have expired.
assumptions_latex: The window length \(W\) is fixed and known to the algorithm.
Items have discrete arrival positions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal W_t=(u_j)_{j=\max\{1,t-W+1\}}^{t}\), and the target output is \(F(\mathcal W_t)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-count suffix definition fits sliding-window streams and clearly excludes time-based windows, but no authoritative source with an inspectable locator supports that selected variant.

children.title: Semi-Streaming Space Regime
children.top_down_role: Graph-stream computation under semi-streaming memory bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Semi-Streaming Space Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-stream space between vertex-linear and edge-linear storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph stream on \(n\) vertices, the semi-streaming regime permits at most \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) bits of working memory, usually with one or a constant number of sequential passes. This space is sufficient to store a polylogarithmic amount of information per vertex but is \(o(n^2)\), and hence cannot explicitly store an arbitrary dense simple graph. Random bits, counters, sketches, and retained edges all count toward the working-memory bound unless the computational model states otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semi-streaming graph algorithms use roughly linear-in-vertices memory, far less than storing all edges of a dense graph.
assumptions_latex: The input is a graph stream on a known vertex set of size \(n\).
Space is measured in bits of mutable working memory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(n)=O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) bits and \(S(n)=o(n^2)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The roughly vertex-linear space description fits the semi-streaming regime, but the bit-based O(n polylog n) convention and pass qualification need an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Multi-Pass Stream Regime
children.top_down_role: Streaming computation allowed multiple scans of the input.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Pass Stream Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential streaming model allowing repeated complete scans of the same input order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u_1,\ldots,u_m\) be a fixed stream and let \(p\ge1\). A \(p\)-pass streaming algorithm reads the sequence from \(u_1\) to \(u_m\) exactly \(p\) times. Its bounded internal state persists between passes, but within a pass it receives updates only sequentially and has no random access to unretained input. The algorithm outputs after the final pass, or at prescribed intermediate points. Its resources are reported as the pair \((p,S)\), where \(S\) is the maximum working space used at any time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multi-pass streaming algorithm repeatedly scans the same ordered stream while retaining only bounded state between scans.
assumptions_latex: Every pass observes the same fixed stream in the same order.
Input storage is read-only and is not charged as working memory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{passes}(A)=p\) and \(\max_t\operatorname{space}_A(t)\le S\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the multi-pass streaming leaf, but the same-order rescanning, persistent-state, and read-only-input conventions are model choices that require a cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Pass–Space Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Relationships between scan count and memory requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Pass–Space Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Achievable resource frontier relating sequential passes and working memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a streaming problem, input-size parameter \(N\), accuracy \(\varepsilon\), and failure bound \(\delta\). A resource pair \((p,S)\) is achievable if an algorithm using at most \(p\) complete sequential passes and \(S\) bits of working memory returns an \(\varepsilon\)-valid answer with probability at least \(1-\delta\) on every admissible input. The pass–space tradeoff is the Pareto boundary of the achievable set \(\mathcal R_{N,\varepsilon,\delta}\). A lower bound excludes a region by proving that every valid algorithm satisfies a relation such as \(S\ge L(N,p,\varepsilon,\delta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pass–space tradeoff describes which combinations of stream scans and working memory can attain a specified accuracy and success probability.
assumptions_latex: Passes are sequential scans under a fixed stream-access convention.
Space is the maximum mutable memory measured in bits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R_{N,\varepsilon,\delta}=\{(p,S):\Pr[A\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-valid}]\ge1-\delta\}\), ordered by simultaneous minimization of \(p\) and \(S\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The achievable-region definition is appropriate for a pass-space tradeoff leaf, but no source supports the stated randomized worst-case-input convention or the generic lower-bound formulation.

children.title: Reservoir Sampling
children.top_down_role: Fixed-capacity sampling from sequential data.

assumptions_latex: Random choices \(J_t\) are mutually independent and uniform on their stated ranges.
Sampling is over stream positions, so repeated item values remain distinct occurrences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr[R=S]=1/\binom{t}{k}\) for every \(S\subseteq[t]\) with \(|S|=k\).

notation.meaning: Uniform replacement index at arrival t.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-pass uniform sampling without replacement from a stream of unknown length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a stream \(u_1,u_2,\ldots\) and capacity \(k\ge1\), initialize reservoir \(R\) with the first \(k\) observed items, or with all observed items while fewer than \(k\) have arrived. For each arrival \(u_t\) with \(t>k\), draw \(J_t\) uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,t\}\). If \(J_t\le k\), replace reservoir position \(J_t\) by \(u_t\); otherwise leave \(R\) unchanged. After any time \(t\ge k\), output \(R\). The resulting reservoir is a uniformly distributed \(k\)-element subset of the first \(t\) stream positions, so each position is retained with probability \(k/t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reservoir sampling maintains a uniform sample of k observed positions in one pass without knowing the final stream length.
knowledge_statements.title: Reservoir Sampling

children.title: Priority Sampling
children.top_down_role: Priority-based sampling for weighted streaming data.

assumptions_latex: \(n>k\ge 1\) and every item weight satisfies \(w_i>0\).
The random variables \(u_i\) are independent and uniformly distributed on \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a size-\(k\) weighted sample with threshold-based adjusted weights.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-size priority sampling for positive weighted items.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each arriving item \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), generate \(u_i\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) independently and assign priority \(q_i=w_i/u_i\). Maintain the \(k\) items having the largest priorities, together with the next-largest priority. After the stream, let \(S\) be the retained set and let \(\tau\) be the \((k+1)\)-st largest priority. Output \(S\), \(\tau\), and adjusted weights \(\widehat w_i=\max\{w_i,\tau\}\) for \(i\in S\), with \(\widehat w_i=0\) for \(i\notin S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign each weighted item a random priority, retain the k largest priorities, and estimate retained weights using the next-largest priority as a threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Priority Sampling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and content kind fit the Priority Sampling leaf, and the threshold and adjusted-weight formulas are mathematically coherent. No cited source or inspectable locator supports the selected fixed-size variant, so source review is required.

children.title: Edge Sampling
children.top_down_role: Sampling mechanisms specialized to graph edges.

assumptions_latex: Each edge \(e\) has a fixed inclusion probability \(p_e\in(0,1]\) known when it arrives.
The edge hash values are mutually independent uniform random variables on \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each sampled edge represents its original weight by the unbiased value \(w_e/p_e\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent weighted edge sampling in an insertion-only graph stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(E_s=\varnothing\). When a weighted edge \(e\) of weight \(w_e\) arrives, draw \(u_e\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\). If \(u_e\le p_e\), insert \(e\) into \(E_s\) with stored weight \(\widetilde w_e=w_e/p_e\); otherwise discard it. The output is the weighted sampled graph \((V,E_s,\widetilde w)\). For every edge, \(\mathbb E[\widetilde w_e\mathbf 1_{\{e\in E_s\}}]=w_e\), so every fixed linear sum of edge weights has an unbiased sampled estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independently retain each arriving edge with its prescribed probability and divide retained weights by that probability to preserve linear edge statistics in expectation.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge Sampling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The independent Horvitz-Thompson edge-sampling algorithm is correct and fits the leaf, but Edge Sampling admits several streaming variants. No source establishes that this is the intended local variant or supports its stated guarantee.

children.title: Importance Sampling
children.top_down_role: Sampling based on contribution-sensitive probabilities.

assumptions_latex: \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) are vectors in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, and \(A=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\).
The probabilities satisfy \(p_i>0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\).
The sample size satisfies \(m\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The estimator satisfies \(\mathbb E[\widehat A]=A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Importance sampling for estimating a finite vector-valued sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a probability vector \(p=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\). Draw \(I_1,\ldots,I_m\) independently with \(\mathbb P(I_t=i)=p_i\), and output \[\widehat A=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{t=1}^m\frac{a_{I_t}}{p_{I_t}}.\] Then \(\mathbb E[\widehat A]=A\). Moreover, \[\mathbb E\!\left[\left\lVert\frac{a_{I_1}}{p_{I_1}}\right\rVert^2\right]=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\lVert a_i\rVert^2}{p_i},\] and probabilities proportional to \(\lVert a_i\rVert\) minimize this expression over positive probability vectors when every \(a_i\ne 0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample summands independently from a nonuniform distribution and divide each sampled summand by its probability. Averaging the reweighted samples gives an unbiased estimate of the full sum; when all summands are nonzero, norm-proportional probabilities minimize the displayed second moment.
knowledge_statements.title: Importance Sampling

children.title: Leverage-Score Sampling
children.top_down_role: Sampling based on leverage-derived importance measures.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\) has rank \(r\ge1\), with row vectors \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\).
Parameters satisfy \(\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a row-sampled, rescaled matrix determined by the statistical leverage scores of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent row sampling using exact statistical leverage scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute \(\tau_i=a_i^{\mathsf T}(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{\dagger}a_i\) for every row. For a chosen absolute constant \(c>0\), set \(p_i=\min\{1,c\tau_i\log(r/\delta)/\varepsilon^2\}\). Independently retain row \(i\) with probability \(p_i\); if retained, place \(a_i^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{p_i}\) in \(\widetilde A\), and otherwise omit it. Equivalently, with a diagonal sampling matrix \(D\) having \(D_{ii}=1/\sqrt{p_i}\) upon retention and \(D_{ii}=0\) otherwise, output \(\widetilde A=DA\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute each row's leverage score, sample rows at probabilities proportional to those scores, and rescale retained rows by the inverse square root probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Leverage-Score Sampling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-leverage row-sampling procedure is coherent and algorithm is the correct content kind. Because no conclusion asserts a subspace-embedding theorem, leaving the absolute constant unspecified does not make the algorithm internally false, but a source is required to support this precise probability formula and parameter dependence.

children.title: Approximate-Score Sampling
children.top_down_role: Sampling regimes using estimated importance or leverage scores.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\) has rank \(r\ge 1\) and exact row leverage scores \(\tau_i\).
The available scores satisfy \(\tau_i\le\widetilde\tau_i\le\alpha\tau_i\) for every \(i\), where \(\alpha\ge1\).
Parameters satisfy \(\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1)\), and \(c>0\) is a chosen absolute constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every row, \(p_i^{\star}\le p_i\le\alpha p_i^{\star}\), and hence \(\sum_i p_i\le\alpha\sum_i p_i^{\star}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent row sampling from multiplicative overestimates of leverage scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \[p_i=\min\!\left\{1,\frac{c\widetilde\tau_i\log(r/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}\right\},\qquad p_i^{\star}=\min\!\left\{1,\frac{c\tau_i\log(r/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}\right\}.\] Independently retain row \(i\) with probability \(p_i\) and rescale each retained row by \(1/\sqrt{p_i}\). The score inequalities imply \(p_i^{\star}\le p_i\le\alpha p_i^{\star}\) for every \(i\). Consequently, \[\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\le\alpha\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^{\star}\le\frac{\alpha c r\log(r/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2},\] where \(\sum_i\tau_i=r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample and rescale rows using certified multiplicative overestimates of their leverage scores. Each resulting inclusion probability lies between the exact-score probability and alpha times that probability, so the expected sample size increases by at most factor alpha.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Score Sampling

children.title: Frequency Sketches
children.top_down_role: Sketches supporting point-frequency estimation.

assumptions_latex: The turnstile stream defines \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) through updates \((i,\Delta)\) applying \(x_i\leftarrow x_i+\Delta\).
Parameters satisfy \(0<\varepsilon<1\) and \(0<\delta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point query has one-sided additive error at most \(\varepsilon\lVert x\rVert_1\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\) in the nonnegative model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Count-Min frequency sketch for nonnegative point queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(d=\lceil\log(1/\delta)\rceil\) pairwise-independent hash functions \(h_j:[n]\to[w]\), where \(w=\lceil e/\varepsilon\rceil\), and initialize \(C\in\mathbb R^{d\times w}\) to zero. On update \((i,\Delta)\), add \(\Delta\) to every \(C_{j,h_j(i)}\). For a point query, output \(\widehat x_i=\min_j C_{j,h_j(i)}\). If all final frequencies are nonnegative and all updates are nonnegative, then \(x_i\le\widehat x_i\le x_i+\varepsilon\lVert x\rVert_1\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Count-Min hashes each update into several counter rows and answers a frequency query by their minimum, giving one-sided additive error for nonnegative streams.
knowledge_statements.title: Frequency Sketches

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Count-Min algorithm and insertion-only point-query guarantee are mathematically coherent and fit Frequency Sketches as a representative algorithm. The assumptions correctly narrow the guarantee to nonnegative updates, but no authoritative source with a locator is supplied.

children.title: Frequency-Moment Sketches
children.top_down_role: Sketches supporting aggregate frequency-moment estimation.

assumptions_latex: The turnstile stream defines \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and the target moment is \(F_2=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\).
Parameters satisfy \(0<\varepsilon<1\) and \(0<\delta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The median-of-means estimate satisfies \(\mathbb P(|\widehat F_2-F_2|\le\varepsilon F_2)\ge1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: AMS-type linear sketch for the second frequency moment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each independent copy, choose a four-wise independent sign map \(\sigma:[n]\to\{-1,1\}\). Maintain \(Z=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma(i)x_i\) by applying \(Z\leftarrow Z+\sigma(i)\Delta\) on update \((i,\Delta)\), and let the copy report \(Z^2\). Average \(s=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-2})\) independent reports in each group and take the median of \(g=\Theta(\log(1/\delta))\) independent group averages. For suitable absolute constants in \(s\) and \(g\), the output \(\widehat F_2\) satisfies \[\mathbb P\!\left(|\widehat F_2-F_2|\le\varepsilon F_2\right)\ge1-\delta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain independent signed linear counters, square them to estimate the second frequency moment, average enough independent copies, and take a median across groups to obtain a relative-error estimate with high probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Frequency-Moment Sketches

children.title: Heavy-Hitter Sketches
children.top_down_role: Sketches supporting recovery of high-frequency items.

assumptions_latex: The turnstile stream defines \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
The sketch width and depth satisfy \(w\ge2\) and \(d\ge1\).
Within each row, the hash map and sign map are independent; different rows are mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each row estimate is unbiased and satisfies \(\mathbb E[(Y_{j,i}-x_i)^2]\le\lVert x_{[n]\setminus\{i\}}\rVert_2^2/w\); median aggregation supports heavy-coordinate estimation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: CountSketch signed-hashing estimates used to identify heavy coordinates in a turnstile stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each row \(j\in[d]\), choose a pairwise-independent hash map \(h_j:[n]\to[w]\) and an independent pairwise-independent sign map \(s_j:[n]\to\{-1,1\}\). Initialize \(C\in\mathbb R^{d\times w}\) to zero. On update \((i,\Delta)\), set \(C_{j,h_j(i)}\leftarrow C_{j,h_j(i)}+s_j(i)\Delta\) for every \(j\in[d]\). For coordinate \(i\), define \(Y_{j,i}=s_j(i)C_{j,h_j(i)}\) and \(\widehat x_i=\operatorname{median}_{j\in[d]}Y_{j,i}\). For every row, \[\mathbb E[Y_{j,i}]=x_i,\qquad \mathbb E[(Y_{j,i}-x_i)^2]\le\frac{\lVert x_{[n]\setminus\{i\}}\rVert_2^2}{w}.\] Heavy-hitter recovery uses these median estimates to distinguish coordinates whose magnitudes dominate the collision error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CountSketch uses independent signed hashing in several rows. Each row gives an unbiased coordinate estimate with collision variance controlled by the squared mass of the other coordinates, and the median estimates support identification of heavy coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Hitter Sketches

children.title: Sparse-Recovery Sketches
children.top_down_role: Linear summaries supporting recovery of sparse vectors or updates.

assumptions_latex: The signal satisfies \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
The sketching matrix satisfies \(S\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and the decoder is \(D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\).
The approximation factor and failure probability satisfy \(C\ge1\) and \(0<\delta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With probability at least \(1-\delta\), decoding \(Sx\) returns an approximation whose \(\ell_2\) error is at most \(C\) times the best \(k\)-term \(\ell_2\) error.

notation.meaning: best k-sparse approximation to x in the Euclidean norm

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stable randomized linear sparse recovery in the \(\ell_2/\ell_2\) formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A distribution over pairs \((S,D)\), where \(S\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is linear and \(D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\) is a decoder, is a stable \(k\)-sparse-recovery sketch with factor \(C\) and failure probability \(\delta\) if, for every fixed \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), the maintained summary is \(y=Sx\) and \[\mathbb P_{(S,D)}\!\left(\lVert D(Sx)-x\rVert_2\le C\min_{\lVert z\rVert_0\le k}\lVert x-z\rVert_2\right)\ge1-\delta.\] A best \(k\)-sparse approximation \(x_k\) is any minimizer in the displayed expression. In a turnstile stream, update \((i,\Delta)\) changes the summary by \(y\leftarrow y+\Delta Se_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable sparse-recovery sketch is a randomized linear summary and decoder that, for every fixed signal, reconstructs it within a constant factor of its best k-sparse approximation error with the prescribed success probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Recovery Sketches

children.title: Support-Sampling Sketches
children.top_down_role: Linear summaries supporting sampling from nonzero support.

assumptions_latex: The turnstile stream defines a nonzero vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
The requested failure probability satisfies \(0<\delta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditioned on not returning \(\mathsf{FAIL}\), the output is uniform on \(\operatorname{supp}(x)\), and the unconditional failure probability is at most \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear \(\ell_0\)-sampling from the support of a turnstile vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \(\ell_0\)-sampling sketch is a randomized linear map \(S\) with a decoder that, from \(Sx\), outputs either an index \(I\in[n]\) or \(\mathsf{FAIL}\). For every nonzero \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), it never outputs an index outside \(\operatorname{supp}(x)\), satisfies \[\mathbb P\!\left(I=i\mid I\ne\mathsf{FAIL}\right)=\frac{1}{\lVert x\rVert_0}\quad\text{for every }i\in\operatorname{supp}(x),\] and has \(\mathbb P(I=\mathsf{FAIL})\le\delta\). Under update \((i,\Delta)\), its stored state changes by \(Sx\leftarrow Sx+\Delta Se_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support-sampling sketch is a randomized linear summary that returns a uniformly random nonzero coordinate of a turnstile vector, never returns a zero coordinate, and may declare failure only with bounded probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Sampling Sketches

children.title: Recovery Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Noise, density, or update regimes that limit reliable recovery.

assumptions_latex: The matrix satisfies \(S\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m<n\).
The decoder is an arbitrary map \(D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\) that observes only \(Sx\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(D(Sx)\ne x\); hence universal exact recovery is impossible.

notation.meaning: decoder using only the linear summary
number of measurements and ambient dimension

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic failure of exact universal recovery from compressed deterministic linear measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be deterministic with \(m<n\). For every decoder \(D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\), there exists an input \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) for which \(D(Sx)\ne x\). Equivalently, no deterministic linear sketch with fewer than \(n\) measurements permits exact recovery of every vector in \(\mathbb R^n\) from its summary alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No deterministic linear sketch with fewer measurements than ambient coordinates allows any decoder to recover every input vector exactly from the sketch alone.
knowledge_statements.title: Recovery Failure Regimes

children.title: Cut Sketches
children.top_down_role: Graph sketches specialized to cut queries or cut recovery.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is an undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights \(w_e\).
Parameters satisfy \(0<\varepsilon<1\) and \(0<\delta<1\).
The queried set \(U\subseteq V\) is fixed independently of the sketch randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every fixed cut query \(U\), the estimate has relative error at most \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: weight of the cut induced by U

knowledge_statements.scope_note: For-each multiplicative cut estimation from a linear, mergeable graph summary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A randomized \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) cut sketch consists of a linear summary map \(\mathcal S\) on the graph's edge-weight update vector and a query procedure. For every graph \(G=(V,E,w)\) and every fixed \(U\subseteq V\), the estimate \(\widehat c(U)\) computed from \(\mathcal S(G)\) satisfies \[\mathbb P\!\left((1-\varepsilon)c_G(U)\le\widehat c(U)\le(1+\varepsilon)c_G(U)\right)\ge1-\delta,\] where \[c_G(U)=\sum_{\substack{\{u,v\}\in E\\ |\{u,v\}\cap U|=1}}w_{uv}.\] Linearity implies that summaries of edge-update substreams add to the summary of their combined stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut sketch is a randomized linear graph summary that, for every fixed vertex cut chosen independently of the sketch randomness, estimates its crossing weight within the prescribed relative error and failure probability. Linear summaries combine additively across edge-update substreams.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut Sketches

children.title: Incidence Sketches
children.top_down_role: Linear summaries built from graph incidence structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Incidence Sketches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertexwise linear sketches whose aggregation cancels internal edges and represents a cut boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an orientation of the possible edges of a graph and let \(B\in\{-1,0,1\}^{V\times E}\) be its signed incidence matrix. For an edge-frequency vector \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\), vertex \(v\) has signed incidence vector \(a_v\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\), where \((a_v)_e=B_{v,e}x_e\). Given a linear map \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^{E}\to\mathbb{R}^{r}\), its incidence sketch is \(s_v=\Phi a_v\). For every \(S\subseteq V\), linearity gives \[\sum_{v\in S}s_v=\Phi\!\left(\sum_{v\in S}a_v\right).\] Coordinates of edges internal to \(S\) cancel, so the argument on the right is supported exactly on the cut \(\delta(S)\), with signs determined by the orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex stores a linear sketch of its signed incident edges. Summing sketches over vertices cancels internal edges and leaves a sketch of the boundary cut.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected graph with an arbitrary fixed orientation.
\(\Phi\) is linear over the field containing the edge frequencies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in S}s_v\) is a linear sketch of the signed edge-frequency vector supported on \(\delta(S)\).

notation.meaning: signed incidence-frequency vector of vertex v

review_flags: No supplied source locator directly covers incidence sketches or their cancellation identity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the leaf, and the cancellation identity is standard, but no inspectable source is cited. Moreover, when zero edge frequencies are permitted, the aggregated incidence vector is supported within the cut, not necessarily exactly on every coordinate of the cut. An authoritative linear-sketch or dynamic-graph-stream source is required to settle the intended frequency model and wording.

children.title: Graph Recovery from Linear Sketches
children.top_down_role: Recovery of graph structure or certificates from linear summaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Recovery from Linear Sketches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery of a sparse graph frequency vector from a fixed linear measurement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N=\binom{|V|}{2}\) index the possible undirected edges, let \(x\in\mathbb{F}^{N}\) be the final edge-frequency vector, and maintain \(y=Ax\) under updates \((e,\Delta)\) by setting \(y\leftarrow y+\Delta A_e\). Suppose every nonzero \(h\in\ker A\) satisfies \(\|h\|_0>2k\). When \(\|x\|_0\le k\), decode \[\widehat{x}\in\mathop{\arg\min}_{z\in\mathbb{F}^{N}}\{\|z\|_0:Az=y\}.\] Output the graph whose nonzero weighted edges are the coordinates of \(\widehat{x}\). The kernel condition makes \(x\) the unique feasible vector with at most \(k\) nonzero coordinates, hence the decoded graph is exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain linear measurements of edge updates, then select the sparsest consistent edge vector. A suitable kernel condition ensures exact recovery of any graph with at most k edges.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) has at most \(k\) nonzero edge coordinates.
Every nonzero \(h\in\ker A\) has \(\|h\|_0>2k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat{x}=x\), so the final weighted graph is recovered exactly from \(Ax\).

notation.meaning: edge-frequency vector of the final graph

review_flags: No supplied source locator covers sparse graph recovery from linear measurements.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits exact graph recovery, and the stated kernel condition is the standard uniqueness condition for k-sparse recovery. However, the dimensions and codomain of A, the domain of update increments, and the admissible values of k are not introduced explicitly, and no source supports this computationally intractable l0 decoder as the intended graph-recovery algorithm.

knowledge_statements.title: Merge–Reduce Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-counter organization of mergeable summaries with controlled reduction error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition an insertion stream into base blocks and assign each block a level-zero summary. Maintain at most one summary \(C_i\) at every level \(i\ge0\), representing \(2^i\) consecutive base blocks. When two level-\(i\) summaries collide, merge their represented weighted sets and replace them by \[C_{i+1}=\operatorname{Reduce}(C_i^{(1)}\uplus C_i^{(2)},\varepsilon_i).\] Repeat carries until every level is singly occupied. At query time, output the disjoint union of all occupied summaries. If a reduction at level \(i\) changes every query cost multiplicatively by a factor in \([1-\varepsilon_i,1+\varepsilon_i]\), then a represented item crosses at most one reduction per level, and the final multiplicative distortion is bounded by the corresponding product of level factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summaries are merged like carries in a binary counter and reduced after each collision. Per-level errors combine multiplicatively along any item’s reduction path.
assumptions_latex: The objective is defined on weighted disjoint unions and the summary routine accepts weighted inputs.
Each call to \(\operatorname{Reduce}\) satisfies its stated uniform query guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maintained output uses one reduced summary per occupied level and has distortion bounded by \(\prod_i(1\pm\varepsilon_i)\) along each active reduction path.

notation.meaning: reduction error allocated to level i

review_flags: No supplied source locator covers the merge–reduce streaming framework.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the Merge-Reduce Framework leaf. The binary-counter organization is plausible, but the expression product_i(1 plus-or-minus epsilon_i) is not a precise pair of lower and upper bounds, and the assumptions do not fully specify how query costs combine across occupied summaries. A source specifying the merge-reduce invariant and accumulated-error theorem is required.

children.title: Composable Coresets
children.top_down_role: Coreset families designed for combination across partitions or stream segments.

knowledge_statements.title: Composable Coresets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong composability for additive objectives over disjoint input partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=X_1\uplus\cdots\uplus X_m\) be a weighted disjoint union, let \(Q\) be a query family, and suppose \(\operatorname{cost}_X(q)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\operatorname{cost}_{X_j}(q)\ge0\). A coreset constructor \(C\) is strongly \(\varepsilon\)-composable if, for every such partition, each \(C(X_j)\) is weighted and their union \(C^*=\biguplus_{j=1}^{m}C(X_j)\) satisfies \[(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{cost}_X(q)\le \operatorname{cost}_{C^*}(q)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cost}_X(q)\qquad\text{for every }q\in Q.\] The definition requires the same error parameter after arbitrary merging; it does not permit error to grow with the number of parts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coresets built independently on disjoint parts remain an epsilon-coreset after union, provided the objective adds across parts.
assumptions_latex: \(X_1,\ldots,X_m\) are pairwise disjoint weighted inputs.
Query costs are nonnegative and additive across the partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\biguplus_j C(X_j)\) approximates every query cost on \(X\) within multiplicative error \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: weighted coreset of partition part j
union of the independently constructed coresets

review_flags: No supplied source locator directly defines composable coresets.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf and the formula is internally coherent for nonnegative additive objectives. No source is supplied, however, and the term strongly epsilon-composable is convention-dependent; composable-coreset definitions may use separate local and composition approximation factors or probabilistic guarantees. A specific definition locator is required.

children.title: Streaming Kernels
children.top_down_role: Compact streaming instances preserving optimization-relevant structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Streaming Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-pass kernelization for parameterized problems presented as data streams.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameterized decision problem \(\Pi\), a streaming kernelization is a one-pass algorithm that receives an encoded instance \(I\) as a stream together with parameter \(k\), uses working memory bounded by a function of \(k\) and logarithmic encoding terms, and outputs an instance \((I',k')\) such that \[(I,k)\in\Pi\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(I',k')\in\Pi.\] There must exist computable functions \(f\) and \(g\), independent of the stream length, for which \(|I'|\le f(k)\) and \(k'\le g(k)\). If the algorithm is randomized, the equivalence must hold with its declared success probability for every valid stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A streaming kernel is a one-pass, parameter-bounded reduction to an equivalent small instance whose size does not depend on stream length.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) is a parameterized decision problem with a fixed stream encoding.
The stream and parameter \(k\) describe a valid instance \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \((I',k')\) is equivalent to \((I,k)\), with \(|I'|\le f(k)\) and \(k'\le g(k)\).
review_flags: The supplied locators do not address streaming parameterized kernelization.

children.title: Composition Quality Under Merging

knowledge_statements.title: Composition Quality Under Merging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of relative coreset error when summaries of disjoint parts are united.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=X_1\uplus\cdots\uplus X_m\), and assume query costs are nonnegative and additive. If, for every \(j\) and every \(q\in Q\), \[(1-\varepsilon_j)\operatorname{cost}_{X_j}(q)\le\operatorname{cost}_{C_j}(q)\le(1+\varepsilon_j)\operatorname{cost}_{X_j}(q),\] then for \(C=\biguplus_j C_j\) and \(\varepsilon=\max_j\varepsilon_j\), \[(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{cost}_X(q)\le\operatorname{cost}_{C}(q)\le(1+\varepsilon)
\operatorname{cost}_X(q)\qquad\text{for every }q\in Q.\] Thus parallel merging does not sum relative errors; sequential re-reduction may introduce additional distortion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For additive nonnegative costs, merging coresets of disjoint parts incurs the largest component error, not their sum. Later reductions may add distortion.
assumptions_latex: \(X_1,\ldots,X_m\) are pairwise disjoint.
Both input and summary costs add under weighted disjoint union.
Each \(C_j\) uniformly approximates \(X_j\) with relative error \(\varepsilon_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\biguplus_j C_j\) is a \(\max_j\varepsilon_j\)-coreset for \(\biguplus_j X_j\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports coreset composition under merging.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind correctly matches the leaf, and the maximum-error composition formula is mathematically valid when both original and summary costs are nonnegative and additive over the disjoint union. No inspectable source or locator supports the property, so it cannot pass evidence review.

children.title: Connectivity Certificates
children.top_down_role: Streaming graph summaries preserving component connectivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sparse subgraph certifying every pairwise connectivity relation of an undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a connectivity certificate is a subgraph \(H=(V,F)\) with \(F\subseteq E\) such that, for all \(u,v\in V\), \[u	ext{ and }v	ext{ are connected in }H\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u	ext{ and }v	ext{ are connected in }G.\] Equivalently, \(G\) and \(H\) induce the same partition of \(V\) into connected components. A certificate is sparse when \(|F|=O(|V|)\). It is verifiable by computing the component labels of \(H\) and checking that every edge of \(G\) has endpoints receiving the same label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A connectivity certificate is a spanning subgraph with exactly the same connected components as the original graph; a sparse one has only linearly many edges.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(H=(V,F)\) is a spanning subgraph of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\) certifies precisely the connectivity equivalence relation induced by \(G\).
review_flags: The supplied connectivity locators do not specifically state the certificate definition or verification criterion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the terminal container, and the connectivity-equivalence and verification criteria are coherent for a spanning subgraph. The inventory contains general connectivity material but no cited locator that states this certificate definition or verification criterion.

children.title: Spanning-Forest Certificates
children.top_down_role: Streaming graph summaries preserving a spanning forest.

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Forest Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A minimum-size connectivity certificate formed by one spanning tree per component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have \(c(G)\) connected components. A spanning-forest certificate is a subgraph \(F=(V,T)\) such that \(F\) is acyclic and, for each connected component \(U\subseteq V\) of \(G\), the restriction \(F[U]\) is a spanning tree of \(G[U]\). Consequently, \[|T|=|V|-c(G)\] and two vertices are connected in \(F\) exactly when they are connected in \(G\). A proposed \(F\) can be checked by testing \(T\subseteq E\), acyclicity, and equality of the component partitions of \(F\) and \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One spanning tree from each connected component forms an acyclic connectivity certificate with exactly the minimum number of edges.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(F=(V,T)\) is a spanning subgraph of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a connectivity certificate with \(|T|=|V|-c(G)\).

notation.meaning: number of connected components of G
subgraph of F induced by component vertex set U

children.title: Certificate Recovery Under Deletions
children.top_down_role: Certificate maintenance or recovery in deletion-capable streams.

assumptions_latex: The stream is strict-turnstile, so every final edge frequency is nonnegative.
The incidence sketches and support-sampling decoders are dimensioned for the fixed vertex set \(V\).
With probability at least \(1-\delta\), every support-sampling call needed throughout all recovery phases returns a valid outgoing edge whenever one exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With probability at least \(1-\delta\), the recovered acyclic edge set is a spanning forest of the final graph.

notation.meaning: signed update of magnitude Delta to edge e

review_flags: The mathematical and LaTeX defects are repaired, but a source must still specify the sketch, decoder, independence, space, and overall success guarantee.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion-safe spanning-forest recovery from linear incidence sketches in a strict-turnstile graph stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite vertex set \(V\). Process strict-turnstile updates \((e,\Delta)\) to an edge-frequency vector \(x\), maintaining linear sketches of signed vertex-incidence vectors. At recovery, initialize one component per vertex. In each Boruvka phase, sum the vertex sketches within every current component and apply a support-sampling decoder to each resulting component sketch. For every component from which an outgoing edge is recovered, select recovered edges subject to preserving acyclicity, add them to the forest, and contract the resulting forest components. Stop when no current component yields an outgoing edge. Assume that, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), all decoder calls required during the complete recovery return an outgoing edge whenever the queried component has one. Under this joint success event, the output is a spanning forest of the final graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain linear incidence sketches through strict-turnstile insertions and deletions, then use repeated outgoing-edge recovery and contraction to construct a spanning forest. If all decoder calls needed by the recovery succeed jointly with probability at least 1-delta, the final forest is correct with that probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Recovery Under Deletions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted subgraphs preserving every undirected cut within uniform multiplicative error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be a finite undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights, and let \(0<\varepsilon<1\). A weighted graph \(H=(V,F,\widetilde w)\), usually with \(F\subseteq E\), is an \(\varepsilon\)-cut sparsifier of \(G\) if, for every \(S\subseteq V\), \[(1-\varepsilon)w_G(\delta(S))\leq \widetilde w_H(\delta(S))\leq(1+\varepsilon)w_G(\delta(S)).\] Here each cut value is the sum of the weights of edges having exactly one endpoint in \(S\). The approximation requirement is simultaneous over all \(S\subseteq V\); sparsity refers to \(|F|\ll |E|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-cut sparsifier is a weighted graph on the same vertices that simultaneously approximates the weight of every cut within relative error epsilon and uses substantially fewer edges when it is sparse.

For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), a weighted graph \(H=(V,F,\widetilde w)\) with Laplacian \(L_H\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-spectral sparsifier of \(G\) if \[(1-\varepsilon)x^{\mathsf T}L_Gx\leq x^{\mathsf T}L_Hx\leq(1+\varepsilon)x^{\mathsf T}L_Gx\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^{V}.\] Equivalently, \[(1-\varepsilon)L_G\preceq L_H\preceq(1+\varepsilon)L_G.\] The condition simultaneously approximates every graph energy \(x^{\mathsf T}L_Gx=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}w_{uv}(x_u-x_v)^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-spectral sparsifier is a weighted graph on the same vertices whose Laplacian quadratic form approximates that of the original graph within relative error epsilon for every real vertex vector.
