children.top_down_role: Sparse streaming subgraphs preserving approximate distances.

assumptions_latex: The stream is insertion-only and describes a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E,w)\).
Every edge weight is positive.
The stretch parameter satisfies \(t\geq1\).
The exact current distance \(d_H(u,v)\) is available when each edge \(\{u,v\}\) is processed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(u,v\in V\), the output satisfies \(d_G(u,v)\leq d_H(u,v)\leq t\,d_G(u,v)\), so \(H\subseteq G\) is a multiplicative \(t\)-spanner of \(G\).

notation.meaning: shortest-path distance in the maintained subgraph
positive weight of arriving edge e

review_flags: LaTeX is repaired and proof-like justification is removed, but no supplied source supports the greedy streaming algorithm or its guarantee.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Insertion-only greedy construction of a multiplicative spanner for a positively weighted graph stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an insertion-only stream describe a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E,w)\) with positive edge weights, and fix \(t\geq1\). Initialize \(H=(V,\varnothing)\). When an edge \(e=\{u,v\}\) of weight \(w(e)\) arrives, compute the current shortest-path distance \(d_H(u,v)\), taking it to be \(+\infty\) when \(u\) and \(v\) are disconnected. Insert \(e\) into \(H\) if and only if \(d_H(u,v)>t\,w(e)\). After processing the stream, output \(H\). The output satisfies \[d_G(u,v)\leq d_H(u,v)\leq t\,d_G(u,v)\qquad\text{for every }u,v\in V.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an insertion-only positively weighted graph stream, retain an arriving edge exactly when the current maintained graph has no path between its endpoints of length at most t times the edge weight. The final subgraph is a multiplicative t-spanner.
knowledge_statements.title: Streaming Graph Spanners

children.title: Streaming Distance Oracles
children.top_down_role: Streaming summaries supporting approximate distance queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Streaming Distance Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query interface for an insertion-only weighted-graph stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=[n]\), let \((e_t,w_t)_{t=1}^m\) be an insertion-only stream of edges with nonnegative weights, and let \(G\) be the final graph. For \(\alpha\ge 1\), an \(\alpha\)-stretch streaming distance oracle consists of a state \(\Sigma\), updated sequentially without retaining the entire stream, and a query map \(Q_\Sigma:V\times V\to[0,+\infty]\). With its declared success probability, one event guarantees simultaneously for all \(u,v\in V\) that \[d_G(u,v)\le Q_\Sigma(u,v)\le \alpha d_G(u,v).\] If \(u\) and \(v\) are disconnected, then \(d_G(u,v)=Q_\Sigma(u,v)=+\infty\). The space usage is the maximum number of bits in \(\Sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alpha-stretch streaming distance oracle retains a compact state and, with its declared success probability, simultaneously returns for every vertex pair an extended distance between the true distance and alpha times that distance, returning infinity for disconnected pairs.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is the final graph of an insertion-only stream.
\(w(e)\ge 0\) for every streamed edge.
\(\alpha\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_G(u,v)\le Q_\Sigma(u,v)\le \alpha d_G(u,v)\) for all \(u,v\in V\), with extended value \(+\infty\) on disconnected pairs.

notation.meaning: Extended shortest-path distance in the final graph.
State retained after processing the stream.
Multiplicative stretch factor, with alpha at least one.
Distance-query map determined by the retained state.

children.title: Stretch–Space Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Relationships between distance distortion and summary size.

knowledge_statements.title: Stretch–Space Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-oracle tradeoff inherited from a stored streaming spanner.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a streaming algorithm stores a weighted subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) having \(s\) edges and satisfying \(d_G(u,v)\le d_H(u,v)\le \alpha d_G(u,v)\) for all vertex pairs. Storing adjacency lists for \(H\), with polynomially bounded integer weights, uses \(O((n+s)\log n)\) bits. Answering a query by computing \(d_H(u,v)\) therefore gives stretch \(\alpha\). Consequently, any attainable spanner pair \((\alpha,s)\) induces the same stretch–space tradeoff for a streaming distance oracle, apart from representation overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alpha-stretch streaming spanner with s edges directly yields an alpha-stretch distance oracle using space proportional to its stored vertices and edges.
assumptions_latex: \(H\subseteq G\) preserves every distance within factor \(\alpha\).
Vertex identifiers and edge weights require \(O(\log n)\) bits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{space}=O((n+s)\log n)\) bits and \(d_G(u,v)\le d_H(u,v)\le\alpha d_G(u,v)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction from a stored spanner is mathematically plausible and the complexity-bound kind fits the leaf, but the streaming tradeoff and bit bound require a source and an explicit weight-encoding model.

children.title: Connected-Component Recovery
children.top_down_role: Streaming recovery of component memberships and connectivity partitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Connected-Component Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery from an insertion–deletion stream defining a final simple graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let updates \((\{u,v\},\Delta)\), where \(\Delta\in\{-1,+1\}\), define a strict-turnstile stream whose final edge multiplicities belong to \(\{0,1\}\). A connected-component recovery procedure maintains a state \(\Sigma\) and, after the stream, outputs a labeling \(c:V\to\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying \[c(u)=c(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\text{ and }v\text{ are connected in the final graph }G.\] For a randomized procedure, this simultaneous equivalence must hold with its declared success probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component recovery outputs labels that agree exactly for vertices connected in the graph remaining after all insertions and deletions.
assumptions_latex: Updates form a strict-turnstile stream.
The final graph is simple and undirected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(u)=c(v)\iff u\) and \(v\) lie in the same component of \(G\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and matches exact component recovery, but no inspectable source supports the dynamic-stream model or simultaneous randomized guarantee.

children.title: Spanning-Forest Recovery

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Forest Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact forest certificate for the final graph of a dynamic stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a strict-turnstile stream defining a final undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a recovered set \(F\subseteq E\) is a spanning-forest certificate when \((V,F)\) is acyclic and, for every \(u,v\in V\), \[u\text{ and }v\text{ are connected in }(V,F)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\text{ and }v\text{ are connected in }G.\] Equivalently, the restriction of \(F\) to each nontrivial connected component of \(G\) is a tree spanning that component, while isolated vertices remain isolated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recovered spanning-forest certificate uses final graph edges, is acyclic, and induces exactly the same connected components as the final streamed graph.
assumptions_latex: The strict-turnstile stream defines a final simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq E\), \((V,F)\) is acyclic, and \(\operatorname{cc}(V,F)=\operatorname{cc}(G)\).

notation.meaning: Partition of vertices into connected components of G.

children.title: Recovery Consistency Across Components

knowledge_statements.title: Recovery Consistency Across Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition between recovered labels and a recovered spanning forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c:V\to\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be recovered component labels and let \(F\) be a recovered forest. The two outputs are component-consistent exactly when \[c(u)=c(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\text{ and }v\text{ are connected in }(V,F)\] for every \(u,v\in V\). If either output is already correct for the final graph \(G\), this condition holds if and only if the other output induces the same connected-component partition as \(G\). Thus consistency is simultaneously checkable by traversing \((V,F)\) and comparing labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovered labels and forest are consistent precisely when their induced partitions of the vertex set coincide.
assumptions_latex: \((V,F)\) is a forest on the streamed vertex set.
\(c\) assigns one label to every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(u)=c(v)\iff u\leftrightarrow_F v\) for every \(u,v\in V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Spanning-Tree Streaming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-pass insertion-only algorithm maintaining an MST of every stream prefix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an insertion-only stream of weighted edges on fixed vertex set \(V\). Initialize \(F_0=(V,\varnothing)\). On receiving \(e_t=\{u,v\}\), set \(F_t=F_{t-1}+e_t\) if \(u,v\) are disconnected in \(F_{t-1}\). Otherwise let \(f\) be a maximum-weight edge on the unique \(u\)-to-\(v\) path in \(F_{t-1}\); set \(F_t=F_{t-1}+e_t-f\) when \(w(e_t)<w(f)\), and set \(F_t=F_{t-1}\) otherwise. After the stream, output \(F_m\), a minimum spanning forest of the final graph; it is an MST when that graph is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a prefix minimum spanning forest, replacing the heaviest edge on a newly formed cycle whenever the arriving edge is lighter.
assumptions_latex: Edges arrive once in an insertion-only stream.
Weights are totally ordered, using a fixed tie-breaking rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_m\) is a minimum spanning forest of the final graph and stores at most \(n-1\) edges.

notation.meaning: Maintained forest after the first t edges.
Maximum-weight edge on the created cycle path.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a stream of weighted-edge updates define a final undirected graph \(G=(V,E,w)\). An \(\varepsilon\)-approximate cut-query summary is a retained state \(\Sigma\) with a query procedure that, for every \(S\subseteq V\), returns \(\widetilde c(S)\) satisfying \[(1-\varepsilon)c_G(S)\le \widetilde c(S)\le(1+\varepsilon)c_G(S),\qquad c_G(S)=\sum_{uv\in E:\,|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1}w(uv).\] The guarantee must specify whether it holds simultaneously for all cuts, per fixed query, or against adaptive queries, since these are distinct streaming requirements.

\(0<\varepsilon<1\).

children.title: Terminal-Cut Streaming

knowledge_statements.title: Terminal-Cut Streaming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Streaming summary for minimum cuts separating prescribed terminal subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix terminals \(K\subseteq V\). For each \(A\subseteq K\), define the terminal-cut value \[\lambda_G(A)=\min\{c_G(S):S\subseteq V,\ S\cap K=A\}.\] An \(\varepsilon\)-approximate terminal-cut streaming summary retains a state \(\Sigma\) from the edge stream and returns \(\widetilde\lambda(A)\) such that \((1-\varepsilon)\lambda_G(A)\le\widetilde\lambda(A)\le(1+\varepsilon)\lambda_G(A)\) for every covered terminal query. Its specification must state whether all \(2^{|K|-1}\) complementary query pairs are covered simultaneously or only individually.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A terminal-cut summary approximates the cheapest graph cut whose terminal side equals the queried subset of designated terminals.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is an undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights.
\(K\subseteq V\) is fixed before streaming.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1-\varepsilon)\lambda_G(A)\le\widetilde\lambda(A)\le(1+\varepsilon)\lambda_G(A)\) for covered \(A\subseteq K\).

notation.meaning: Minimum cut realizing terminal side A.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The terminal-cut definition is mathematically coherent, including complementary query pairs, but the streaming guarantee and assumption that terminals are fixed before streaming require a source.

children.title: Cut-Query Family Separations

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Query Family Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-query correctness does not imply correctness for arbitrary post-stream cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{1,2,3\}\) and fix the sole supported query \(S_0=\{1\}\). Consider \(G_0\), containing only edge \(12\) of weight \(1\), and \(G_M\), containing edges \(12\) of weight \(1\) and \(23\) of weight \(M>0\). A summary storing only \(c_G(S_0)\) has identical state \(1\) on both graphs and answers its fixed query exactly. Nevertheless \(c_{G_0}(\{3\})=0\) while \(c_{G_M}(\{3\})=M\). Hence fixed-query correctness alone cannot certify arbitrary or simultaneously quantified cut queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two graphs can agree on a predetermined cut but differ arbitrarily on another, so a fixed-query summary need not support arbitrary cuts.
assumptions_latex: The summary is required to support only the predetermined cut \(S_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactness for \(S_0\) does not imply any finite multiplicative guarantee for the query \(\{3\}\).

notation.meaning: Graph whose edge 23 has weight M.

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Cut Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global minimum-cut approximation induced by simultaneous cut preservation.

Define \(\widetilde\lambda=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}\widetilde c(S)\) and \(\lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}c_G(S)\). Then \[(1-\varepsilon)\lambda(G)\le\widetilde\lambda\le(1+\varepsilon)\lambda(G).\] Thus an all-cuts streaming certificate also certifies the global minimum-cut value.

\(0<\varepsilon<1\) and edge weights are nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut–Flow Transfer Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier conditions under which cut approximation transfers to flow values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a terminal pair \((s,t)\), cut-to-flow transfer is valid when one event guarantees \[(1-\varepsilon)c_G(S)\le\widetilde c(S)\le(1+\varepsilon)c_G(S)\] for every \(s\)-\(t\) cut \(S\) over which the minimum is taken. A merely per-cut probabilistic guarantee is insufficient without a simultaneous-event or query-validity argument. Transfer to all terminal pairs requires the same preservation event for every relevant cut; transfer to one fixed pair requires only its \(s\)-\(t\) cut family. Under the applicable event, minimizing estimates preserves the corresponding maximum-flow value within factor \(1\pm\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut estimates transfer to flow values only when their guarantee simultaneously covers the entire cut family defining each requested flow minimum.

children.title: Greedy Streaming Matching
children.top_down_role: Greedy selection strategies for matching in edge-arrival streams.

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Streaming Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Insertion-only, adversarial-order, unweighted graph streams.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(M\leftarrow\varnothing\). When an edge \(e=\{u,v\}\) arrives, insert \(e\) into \(M\) if and only if neither \(u\) nor \(v\) is incident to an edge already in \(M\); otherwise discard \(e\). After the final edge, output \(M\). For every admissible stream, the output is a maximal matching and satisfies \(|M|\geq\nu(G)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept each arriving edge whose endpoints are both unmatched. The resulting matching is maximal and has at least half as many edges as a maximum matching.
assumptions_latex: The input is an insertion-only stream of edges of a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\).
Edges are processed once in their arrival order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned set \(M\) is a maximal matching and satisfies \(|M|\geq \nu(G)/2\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: insertion-only greedy matching is a standard streaming specialization

children.title: Semi-Streaming Matching
children.top_down_role: Matching algorithms operating within semi-streaming memory budgets.

assumptions_latex: The streamed graph has \(n\) vertices and polynomially bounded vertex identifiers.
The algorithm makes a constant number of sequential passes over the edge stream.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The working memory is \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) bits, excluding read-only stream storage.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the stated memory scale is the conventional semi-streaming regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conventional graph semi-streaming resource model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matching algorithm is semi-streaming if it reads the edges of an \(n\)-vertex graph sequentially, uses at most \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) bits of mutable working memory, and makes \(p=O(1)\) passes unless another pass bound is stated. The input stream itself is read-only and is not charged as memory. The algorithm must output a matching represented either explicitly by its edges or implicitly by enough stored information to enumerate them. Randomized algorithms additionally specify a success probability, conventionally at least \(2/3\), over their internal randomness for every fixed admissible stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semi-streaming matching uses near-linear memory in the number of vertices, sequential access, and ordinarily only a constant number of passes.
knowledge_statements.title: Semi-Streaming Matching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semi-streaming memory scale is standard, but no inspectable source supports the asserted constant-pass default, output representation, or randomized-success convention.

children.title: Greedy Performance Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Approximation and ordering limitations specific to greedy streaming choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Performance Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp adversarial-order boundary for irrevocable greedy acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every admissible graph and arrival order, greedy acceptance returns a matching \(M\) satisfying \(|M|\geq\nu(G)/2\). This factor is tight. On the path with vertices \(v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\), present \(\{v_2,v_3\}\) before \(\{v_1,v_2\}\) and \(\{v_3,v_4\}\). Greedy returns only \(\{v_2,v_3\}\), while a maximum matching has size \(2\). Hence the worst-case value of \(|M|/\nu(G)\) is \(1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy is always a one-half approximation, and a four-vertex path arriving middle-edge first makes this guarantee tight.
assumptions_latex: Edges of an unweighted graph arrive in adversarial order.
The algorithm irrevocably accepts an edge exactly when both endpoints are currently unmatched.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case approximation ratio is exactly \(1/2\) under the convention \(|M|/\nu(G)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: maximal matching and the four-vertex path give the classical sharp boundary

assumptions_latex: The dynamic stream consists of updates \((e,\Delta)\) with \(\Delta\in\mathbb Z\).
The final edge-frequency vector represents a simple graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maintained state is \(y=Lx\), and every update is processed as \(y\leftarrow y+\Delta L\mathbf e_e\).

notation.meaning: edge-frequency vector indexed by the universe of possible edges

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Turnstile linear-sketch representation, without fixing a recovery approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an edge universe \(\mathcal U\) and encode the current graph by \(x\in\mathbb Z^{\mathcal U}\), where an update \((e,
\Delta)\) replaces \(x_e\) by \(x_e+\Delta\). A dynamic-stream graph sketch is a randomized linear map \(L:\mathbb Z^{\mathcal U}\to\mathcal R\) whose maintained state is \(y=Lx\). Because of linearity, an insertion or deletion is processed without retaining the edge set by applying \(y\leftarrow y+\Delta L\mathbf e_e\). A matching sketch couples this state with a decoder that, from \(y\) and the public randomness, outputs a matching in the final graph with a separately specified approximation and failure probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic matching sketch linearly summarizes turnstile edge updates and later decodes a matching without storing the complete graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Stream Matching Sketches

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the topic, but linearity and scalar multiplication require an explicitly suitable codomain, and no source supports the matching-sketch decoder formulation.

children.title: Weighted Streaming Matching
children.top_down_role: Streaming matching under edge-weighted objectives.

assumptions_latex: Each streamed edge \(e\) has a nonnegative weight \(w(e)\).
The final graph is finite and undirected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is \(\operatorname{OPT}_w(G)=\max\{\sum_{e\in M}w(e):M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weighted matching objective is standard, but its streaming formulation needs a dedicated source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization problem and approximation convention for weighted edge streams.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In weighted streaming matching, the input is a sequential stream describing a graph \(G=(V,E)\) together with weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\). A feasible output is a matching \(M\subseteq E\), and its value is \(w(M)=\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\). The optimum is \(\operatorname{OPT}_w(G)=\max\{w(N):N\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}\). For \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), an \(\alpha\)-approximation must output \(M\) satisfying \(w(M)\geq\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_w(G)\), with the stated success probability when the algorithm is randomized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted streaming matching seeks a matching of maximum total arriving-edge weight; an alpha approximation captures at least an alpha fraction of optimum weight.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Streaming Matching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted-matching objective and approximation convention are precise, but the stream type is not fixed and the cited inventory does not support this streaming formulation.

children.title: Multi-Pass Streaming Matching
children.top_down_role: Matching algorithms using repeated access to the stream.

assumptions_latex: The stream is replayable in the same order.
Persistent state between passes is charged to the memory bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A \(p\)-pass algorithm performs at most \(p\) complete sequential scans and uses no random access to stream positions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: replayable sequential passes are the conventional multi-pass model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replayable-stream model with persistent bounded memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(p\)-pass streaming matching algorithm processes the input through at most \(p\) complete sequential scans. During a scan, edges are encountered in stream order; the algorithm may update an internal state of at most \(s\) bits but may not access an arbitrary stream position. The state may persist between scans, and the next scan begins at the start of the same replayable stream. After the last scan, the algorithm outputs a matching in the graph represented by the stream. Pass count, memory \(s\), approximation ratio, and failure probability are separate resource parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multi-pass matching algorithm may rescan a replayable edge stream sequentially while retaining only its bounded state between scans.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Pass Streaming Matching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The replayable sequential-pass definition fits the leaf, but it selects a particular multi-pass model without an inspectable streaming-model source.

children.title: Weighted Multi-Pass Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Approximation, memory, and pass tradeoffs for weighted matching.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm attains approximation factor \(\alpha\) using at most \(p\) passes and \(s\) bits.
Unused passes and memory may be ignored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(p'\geq p\) and \(s'\geq s\), the same factor \(\alpha\) is attainable within resources \((p',s')\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: resource-monotonicity follows directly from the streaming model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource monotonicity underlying weighted multi-pass tradeoff curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A(p,s)\) be the supremum approximation factor attainable for weighted matching by algorithms using at most \(p\) passes and at most \(s\) bits of working memory under a fixed stream and success model. If \(p'\geq p\) and \(s'\geq s\), every algorithm feasible for \((p,s)\) remains feasible for \((p',s')\) by leaving the additional resources unused. Hence \(\mathcal A(p',s')\geq\mathcal A(p,s)\). Equivalently, the minimum memory required for a fixed factor is nonincreasing in the permitted pass count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing more passes or memory cannot worsen the best achievable weighted-matching approximation; required memory is nonincreasing with the pass budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Multi-Pass Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Generic resource monotonicity does not capture a weighted multi-pass matching tradeoff and is independent of weighted matching. The exact leaf requires a substantive weighted approximation/pass/memory tradeoff statement.

assumptions_latex: The final graph has nonnegative edge lengths.
The stream model and pass bound are fixed before processing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is specified by update type, pass count, memory, queried distance family, approximation parameters, and success probability.

notation.meaning: shortest-path distance in the final graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource-model definition encompassing exact and approximate streamed distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A shortest-path streaming regime fixes an insertion-only or turnstile stream representing a length-weighted graph \(G=(V,E,\ell)\), a pass budget \(p\), and a working-memory bound. It also fixes the requested output, such as one-source, selected-pair, all-pairs, eccentricity, or diameter distances. Under the one-sided \((\alpha,\beta)\)-stretch convention, every reported finite distance \(\widehat d(u,v)\) must satisfy \(d_G(u,v)\leq\widehat d(u,v)\leq\alpha d_G(u,v)+\beta\). A randomized regime additionally states the probability with which all required inequalities hold simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shortest-path streaming regime fixes updates, passes, memory, requested distances, approximation error, and randomized success probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Path Streaming Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regime definition is coherent, but no source supports the combined update, pass, memory, output-family, stretch, and simultaneous-success conventions.

children.title: Diameter Approximation
children.top_down_role: Streaming approximation of graph diameter.

assumptions_latex: The final graph \(G=(V,E)\) is connected and has nonnegative edge lengths.
Distance estimates use one-sided \((\alpha,\beta)\)-stretch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(G)\leq\widehat D\leq\alpha D(G)+\beta\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the standard one-sided stretch predicate specialized to diameter
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided multiplicative-additive diameter approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a connected length-weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), define its diameter by \(D(G)=\max_{u,v\in V}d_G(u,v)\). A streaming output \(\widehat D\) is an \((\alpha,\beta)\) one-sided diameter approximation, where \(\alpha\geq1\) and \(\beta\geq0\), precisely when \(D(G)\leq\widehat D\leq\alpha D(G)+\beta\). For a randomized algorithm claiming simultaneous success probability at least \(1-\delta\), this inequality must hold with probability at least \(1-\delta\) over its internal randomness for every fixed admissible stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-sided diameter estimate never underestimates the true diameter and exceeds it by at most the declared multiplicative and additive error.
knowledge_statements.title: Diameter Approximation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically precise and fits diameter approximation, but the selected one-sided multiplicative-additive convention lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Pairwise-Distance Approximation
children.top_down_role: Streaming approximation of selected or aggregate pairwise distances.

assumptions_latex: The queried vertices \(u,v\) are connected in the final nonnegatively weighted graph.
The approximation uses one-sided stretch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_G(u,v)\leq\widehat d(u,v)\leq\alpha d_G(u,v)+\beta\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the conventional one-sided multiplicative-additive distance predicate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided approximation for designated vertex-pair distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For specified vertices \(u,v\in V\) with finite shortest-path distance, an estimate \(\widehat d(u,v)\) has one-sided \((\alpha,\beta)\)-stretch if \(d_G(u,v)\leq\widehat d(u,v)\leq\alpha d_G(u,v)+\beta\), where \(\alpha\geq1\) and \(\beta\geq0\). If a set \(Q\subseteq V\times V\) of pairs is requested, a simultaneous pairwise-distance approximation requires this inequality for every \((u,v)\in Q\) in the same successful execution. A randomized guarantee must state the probability of that simultaneous event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each requested pairwise estimate lies between the true distance and its declared multiplicative-plus-additive upper bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise-Distance Approximation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pairwise condition and simultaneous-event quantification are precise, but the one-sided stretch convention and streaming interpretation are unsupported by a citation.

children.title: Eccentricity Approximation
children.top_down_role: Streaming approximation of vertex eccentricities and radius-related quantities.

assumptions_latex: The final graph \(G=(V,E)\) is connected and has nonnegative edge lengths.
Estimates are required for a specified vertex set \(U\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(u\in U\), \(\operatorname{ecc}_G(u)\leq\widehat e(u)\leq\alpha\operatorname{ecc}_G(u)+\beta\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: eccentricity is the maximum pairwise distance from a fixed vertex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous one-sided eccentricity approximation on requested vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(u\in V\), define \(\operatorname{ecc}_G(u)=\max_{v\in V}d_G(u,v)\). Given requested vertices \(U\subseteq V\), estimates \(\widehat e(u)\) form a simultaneous one-sided \((\alpha,\beta)\) eccentricity approximation when, for every \(u\in U\), \(\operatorname{ecc}_G(u)\leq\widehat e(u)\leq\alpha\operatorname{ecc}_G(u)+\beta\), with \(\alpha\geq1\) and \(\beta\geq0\). For a randomized streaming algorithm, all inequalities must hold together with at least the declared success probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every requested eccentricity estimate simultaneously lies between the true maximum distance from that vertex and its declared stretch bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Eccentricity Approximation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simultaneous eccentricity condition fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the one-sided stretch and randomized simultaneous-success formulation.

children.title: Cardinality-Constrained Maximization
children.top_down_role: Streaming submodular maximization subject to cardinality limits.

assumptions_latex: The ground set \(N\) is finite and its elements arrive sequentially.
The objective \(f:2^N\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) is accessed through a value oracle.
The cardinality budget satisfies \(k\in\{0,1,\ldots,|N|\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_k(f)=\max\{f(S):S\subseteq N,\ |S|\leq k\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform-cardinality constrained submodular maximization is a standard optimization model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Streaming formulation of the uniform-cardinality feasibility constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Cardinality-constrained submodular maximization is the problem \(\operatorname{OPT}_k(f)=\max\{f(S):S\subseteq N,\ |S|\leq k\}\), where \(f\) is submodular: for all \(A\subseteq B\subseteq N\) and \(e\in N\setminus B\), \(f(A\cup\{e\})-f(A)\geq f(B\cup\{e\})-f(B)\). In the streaming version, elements of \(N\) arrive sequentially, the algorithm has bounded working memory, and its final output must be a retained or recoverable set \(S\) satisfying \(|S|\leq k\). Monotonicity or normalization of \(f\) must be stated separately when an approximation theorem requires them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose at most k streamed elements to maximize a submodular objective; monotonicity and normalization are additional assumptions, not part of the cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality-Constrained Maximization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The optimization problem, submodularity condition, and separation of monotonicity assumptions are precise, but the value-oracle streaming formulation and recoverable-output convention require a dedicated source.

children.title: Knapsack-Constrained Maximization
children.top_down_role: Streaming submodular maximization subject to budgeted item costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack-Constrained Maximization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-pass submodular maximization subject to one additive budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite ground set arriving as a stream, let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) be submodular, and assign each \(e\in V\) a cost \(c_e\ge 0\). Given a budget \(B>0\), knapsack-constrained streaming maximization asks an algorithm using sublinear memory to output a retained set \(S\subseteq V\) satisfying \[\sum_{e\in S}c_e\le B\] and maximizing \(f(S)\). For approximation factor \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), the guarantee is \(f(S)\ge \alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}\), where \(\mathrm{OPT}=\max\{f(T):T\subseteq V,\ \sum_{e\in T}c_e\le B\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select streamed elements whose total cost fits one budget and whose submodular value approximates the best feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and its elements arrive sequentially.
\(f\) is nonnegative and submodular.
Costs are nonnegative and \(B>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\subseteq V\), \(\sum_{e\in S}c_e\le B\), and \(f(S)\ge\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}\).

notation.meaning: Submodular objective accessed during the stream.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical definition matches single-knapsack streaming submodular maximization, but no cited source supports the streaming formulation, approximation convention, or memory model. A specific authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Multiple-Budget Constraint Regimes
children.top_down_role: Streaming regimes with multiple cardinality or knapsack-style budgets.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Budget Constraint Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Streaming submodular maximization under finitely many additive budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) arrive as a stream and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) be submodular. For \(d\ge1\), each element \(e\) has costs \(c_{j,e}\ge0\) under budgets \(B_j>0\), where \(j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A feasible output \(S\subseteq V\) obeys \[\sum_{e\in S}c_{j,e}\le B_j\qquad(j=1,\ldots,d).\] The multiple-budget streaming problem maximizes \(f(S)\) using sublinear memory. Its regime records whether \(d\) is constant or input-dependent, since approximation and space guarantees may depend on \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a high-value streamed set satisfying every additive budget, while explicitly tracking whether the number of budgets is fixed or variable.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and streamed sequentially.
\(f\) is nonnegative and submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\subseteq V\) and \(\sum_{e\in S}c_{j,e}\le B_j\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\).

notation.meaning: Cost of element e against budget j.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasibility system correctly represents multiple additive budgets and the definition fits the container. No source supports the streaming formulation or the distinction between constant and input-dependent numbers of budgets.

children.title: Matroid-Constrained Streaming
children.top_down_role: Streaming submodular maximization over matroid-feasible selections.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid-Constrained Streaming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Streaming submodular maximization with matroid-independent outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(V,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid whose ground elements arrive sequentially, and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) be submodular. A matroid-constrained streaming algorithm maintains a sublinear-space state and, after its prescribed passes, returns \(S\in\mathcal I\). For approximation factor \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), its required guarantee is \[f(S)\ge\alpha\max\{f(T):T\in\mathcal I\}.\] Feasibility queries test membership in \(\mathcal I\); the objective may be accessed through a value oracle unless another access model is specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process streamed elements in limited memory and return a matroid-independent set approximating the best feasible submodular value.
assumptions_latex: \(M=(V,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid.
\(f\) is nonnegative and submodular.
Elements of \(V\) arrive in a prescribed stream order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\mathcal I\) and \(f(S)\ge\alpha\max_{T\in\mathcal I}f(T)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly defines matroid-feasible streaming submodular maximization, but the pass, oracle, order, and memory conventions are not backed by a cited source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Nonmonotone Streaming Objectives
children.top_down_role: Streaming maximization for nonmonotone submodular objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Streaming Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Streaming objectives for which adding elements can reduce value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite streamed ground set. A nonmonotone streaming submodular objective is a function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) satisfying \[f(A)+f(B)\ge f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B)\qquad(A,B\subseteq V),\] but not satisfying monotonicity: there exist \(A\subseteq B\subseteq V\) with \(f(A)>f(B)\). Consequently, accepting an arriving element can reduce the objective, so a streaming maximization algorithm must permit rejection, replacement, or postprocessing rather than relying solely on positive marginal gains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonmonotone streamed submodular objective has diminishing returns but may lose value when an element is added.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) is submodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists A,B\subseteq V\) such that \(A\subseteq B\) and \(f(A)>f(B)\).

notation.meaning: Set-valued objective evaluated on streamed elements.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed submodularity and strict nonmonotonicity conditions are mathematically precise. A source is required, particularly for the additional claim that streaming algorithms must use rejection, replacement, or postprocessing, which does not follow as a formal exhaustive requirement from nonmonotonicity alone.

children.title: Nonmonotone Matroid Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximation and resource behavior when matroid feasibility meets nonmonotonicity.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Matroid Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization regimes combining nonmonotone submodularity with matroid feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonmonotone matroid maximization instance is a triple \((V,\mathcal I,f)\), where \((V,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid and \(f:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) is submodular but need not be monotone. Its optimum is \[\mathrm{OPT}=\max\{f(S):S\in\mathcal I\}.\] A streaming regime additionally specifies the number of passes, stream-order assumption, memory bound, objective-access oracle, and independence oracle. An \(\alpha\)-approximate regime requires its output \(S\in\mathcal I\) to satisfy \(f(S)\ge\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}\), deterministically or with the stated success probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximize a possibly value-decreasing submodular function over matroid-independent sets under an explicitly specified streaming and oracle model.
assumptions_latex: \((V,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid.
\(f\) is nonnegative and submodular, without monotonicity.
The streaming and oracle model is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\mathcal I\) and \(f(S)\ge\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}\) under the declared guarantee mode.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The optimization regime is plausible, but no source supports it. The source must also clarify whether “nonmonotone” means that monotonicity is not assumed, as stated here, or that the objective is strictly nonmonotone, as used by the sibling record.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) and the streamed family are finite.
Universe weights are nonnegative.
\(k\in\{0,\ldots,m\}\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|I|\le k\) and \(F(I)\ge\alpha\max\{F(J):J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\},\ |J|\le k\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Streaming selection of boundedly many sets for maximum union weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite universe with weights \(w:U\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), and let sets \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq U\) arrive sequentially. Given \(k\in\{0,\ldots,m\}\), streaming maximum coverage asks for an index set \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with \(|I|\le k\) maximizing \[F(I)=\sum_{u\in\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i}w(u).\] For \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), an \(\alpha\)-approximate algorithm outputs such an \(I\) with \[F(I)\ge\alpha\max\{F(J):J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\},\ |J|\le k\},\] while using memory sublinear in an explicitly specified representation of the stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: From a stream of sets, retain at most k sets whose weighted union approximates the largest achievable coverage.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Coverage Streams

assumptions_latex: \(U\) and the streamed set family are finite, and the family covers \(U\).
\(p\in\mathbb{N}\), \(p\ge1\), \(s\ge0\), \(\rho\ge1\), and \(\delta\in[0,1)\).
The pass and output-storage conventions are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr[\bigcup_{A\in C}A=U\ \land\ |C|\le\rho\tau]\ge1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: Pass limit and working-memory limit in bits.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pass and memory parameters for streaming set cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a universe of \(n\) elements, and let \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq U\) form a streamed family whose union is \(U\). Fix \(p\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(p\ge1\), \(s\ge0\), \(\rho\ge1\), and \(\delta\in[0,1)\). A \((p,s,\rho,\delta)\) set-cover streaming regime permits at most \(p\) sequential passes and at most \(s\) bits of working memory, and outputs a subfamily \(C\subseteq\{A_1,\ldots,A_m\}\) satisfying \[\bigcup_{A\in C}A=U,\qquad |C|\le\rho\tau\] with probability at least \(1-\delta\), where \(\tau=\min\{|D|:D\subseteq\{A_1,\ldots,A_m\},\ \bigcup_{A\in D}A=U\}\). The regime must state whether output storage is charged to \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-cover streaming regime records its pass limit, memory limit, approximation ratio, failure probability, and whether output storage is charged to memory.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Cover Pass–Space Regimes
Streaming Clustering Coresets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composable weighted summaries preserving clustering costs throughout a stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite weighted point set in a metric space and let \(\Phi_P(C)=\sum_{x\in P}w_x d(x,C)^z\), where \(z\ge1\) and \(C\) ranges over center sets of size at most \(k\). A weighted summary \(Q\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-coreset if, simultaneously for every such \(C\), \[(1-\varepsilon)\Phi_P(C)\le\Phi_Q(C)\le(1+\varepsilon)\Phi_P(C).\] A streaming coreset algorithm maintains such a summary using space determined by \(k\), \(\varepsilon\), and logarithmic stream parameters rather than storing all of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a small weighted summary that approximates every candidate k-clustering cost within a multiplicative factor.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a finite weighted metric point set.
Weights are nonnegative and \(z\ge1\).
Candidate center sets have cardinality at most \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1-\varepsilon)\Phi_P(C)\le\Phi_Q(C)\le(1+\varepsilon)\Phi_P(C)\) for every admissible \(C\).

notation.meaning: Clustering cost of centers C on P.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simultaneous multiplicative coreset condition is a valid definition, but the asserted streaming-space behavior is not justified for an arbitrary metric space and may require dimension, metric-family, composability, or stream-model hypotheses. A source is needed to determine the correct scope.

knowledge_statements.title: Pass–Space–Approximation Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal lower-bound predicate coupling passes, memory, and approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a streaming optimization problem \(\Pi\), input size \(n\), pass budget \(p\), approximation target \(\rho\), and success probability \(1-\delta\). A pass–space–approximation lower bound \(L(n,p,\rho,\delta)\) means that every randomized streaming algorithm which, on every valid instance, uses at most \(p\) passes and returns a \(\rho\)-approximate solution with probability at least \(1-\delta\), must use at least \[L(n,p,\rho,\delta)\] bits of working memory on some instance. The stream order, output accounting, and adversary model are part of the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Such a lower bound says every algorithm attaining specified passes, approximation, and success must consume a stated amount of memory.
assumptions_latex: The streaming problem and valid-input family are fixed.
Pass, approximation, success, and stream-order conventions are fixed.
Working memory is measured in bits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\ge L(n,p,\rho,\delta)\) for some valid instance faced by every qualifying algorithm.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This lower-bound leaf requires a complexity-bound statement, but the candidate is only a generic definition of what a lower bound would mean and supplies no problem-specific bound. Accepting it as a definition would place the wrong mathematical role in the terminal container.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Sketch Dimension Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension lower bounds for randomized linear summaries of frequency vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let inputs be frequency vectors \(x\in\mathbb{F}^n\). A linear sketch of dimension \(r\) stores \(Ax\in\mathbb{F}^r\), where the matrix \(A\) may be randomly chosen independently of \(x\), and a decoder estimates a target \(g(x)\). A dimension lower bound \(R(n,\varepsilon,\delta)\) asserts that any such sketch satisfying \[\Pr[\widehat g(Ax)\in\mathcal A_\varepsilon(g(x))]\ge1-\delta\qquad\text{for every valid }x\] must have \(r\ge R(n,\varepsilon,\delta)\). The field, validity domain, and approximation relation \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\) must be fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-sketch lower bound requires a minimum number of stored linear measurements for uniform approximation at the stated success probability.
assumptions_latex: The field and valid frequency-vector domain are fixed.
The sketch matrix is selected independently of the input.
The approximation and probability conventions are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\ge R(n,\varepsilon,\delta)\) for every qualifying linear sketch.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The candidate defines a linear sketch and a placeholder lower-bound predicate but states no actual dimension lower bound for any target problem. The exact leaf calls for a complexity bound, not a generic definition, and no supporting citation is supplied.

children.title: Deletion-Sensitive Streaming Barriers
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound phenomena caused by deletions invalidating insertion-only summaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Deletion-Sensitive Streaming Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of summaries that cannot retract contributions after deletions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider updates to a frequency vector \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\). A summary is deletion-insensitive if processing \((i,-1)\) never retracts information contributed by an earlier \((i,+1)\). For distinct coordinates \(i,j\), compare \(\sigma_1=((i,+1),(j,+1),(j,-1))\) with \(\sigma_2=((i,+1),(j,+1))\). Their final supports are respectively \(\{i\}\) and \(\{i,j\}\). If the summary states coincide because the deletion is ignored, no decoder can correctly compute every support-sensitive objective on both streams. Thus insertion-only monotone summaries require explicit deletion handling in turnstile streams.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A summary that cannot retract deleted contributions confuses streams with different final supports and therefore fails for support-sensitive objectives.
assumptions_latex: Updates have the form \((i,\Delta)\) with \(\Delta\in\{-1,+1\}\).
The target distinguishes \(\{i\}\) from \(\{i,j\}\).
The summary ignores or cannot retract deletions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{state}(\sigma_1)=\mathrm{state}(\sigma_2)\) implies that one common decoder output is incorrect on at least one stream.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional indistinguishability argument is coherent only for summaries whose deletion behavior actually makes the two states coincide. Because that model condition is central to the claimed failure boundary and no source is cited, authoritative support is required before fixing the statement's scope.

children.title: Turnstile-Stream Barriers
children.top_down_role: Space and approximation limitations in streams with signed frequency updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Turnstile-Stream Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary created by signed updates and cancellation in turnstile streams.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the turnstile model, a stream consists of signed updates \((i,\Delta)\) producing the final vector \(x=\sum_t\Delta_t e_{i_t}\). Any algorithm whose decision is an irrevocable function of whether an item has ever appeared can fail: the streams \(\sigma=((i,+1),(i,-1))\) and the empty stream have the same final vector \(x=0\), although \(i\) appears in only the first. Hence a correct algorithm for a function depending solely on the final vector must be invariant under insertion–deletion cancellation; insertion-only acceptance rules lacking retraction do not extend directly to turnstile streams.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Turnstile cancellation makes appearance-based irreversible decisions invalid because a nonempty update sequence can have the same final vector as an empty stream.
assumptions_latex: Updates are signed and aggregate additively.
The target is a function only of the final frequency vector.
The challenged rule records an appearance irreversibly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(\sigma)=x(\varnothing)=0\), so any correct final-vector algorithm must return identical answers on \(\sigma\) and \(\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: An insertion followed by its cancelling deletion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cancellation example correctly identifies a failure of irreversible appearance-based rules for final-vector functions, and failure_boundary is the appropriate content kind. It is a model-conditional barrier rather than a general turnstile lower bound, and it lacks a supporting turnstile-streaming citation.

children.title: Strict-Turnstile Separations
children.top_down_role: Complexity gaps between strict-turnstile and general-turnstile models.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Turnstile Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary between strict and unrestricted turnstile lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For updates \((i_t,\Delta_t)\) and frequencies \(f^{(t)}=\sum_{s\le t}\Delta_s e_{i_s}\), a strict-turnstile stream satisfies \(f^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n\) for every \(t\); an unrestricted turnstile stream need not. Hence the strict model is a proper restriction of the unrestricted model. An algorithm proved only for strict streams need not handle unrestricted streams, while a lower bound proved only over unrestricted streams does not establish the same bound for strict streams unless its hard instances preserve coordinatewise nonnegativity at every prefix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict streams maintain nonnegative frequencies at every prefix. Consequently, unrestricted-turnstile lower bounds transfer to the strict model only when their hard streams satisfy this promise.
assumptions_latex: Each update has \(i_t\in[n]\) and \(\Delta_t\in\mathbb{R}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unrestricted-turnstile lower bounds do not automatically imply strict-turnstile lower bounds.

notation.meaning: frequency vector after the first t updates

review_flags: exact separation theorem depends on the streaming problem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The model-containment and lower-bound-transfer boundary is mathematically precise and fits the failure-boundary container, but no source supports the strict-turnstile convention or any problem-specific separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Query Failures for Sketches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel-based failure mechanism for a fixed linear sketch under adaptive interrogation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}\) have \(r<n\), and suppose answers about \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) depend only on \(Ax\). If an adaptive interaction identifies \(0\ne z\in\ker A\), then every pair \(z,\lambda z\), with \(\lambda>0\), produces the identical sketch \(0\). For any \(c\ge1\), choosing \(\lambda>c^2\) makes the admissible multiplicative-approximation intervals for \(\lVert z\rVert_2\) and \(\lVert\lambda z\rVert_2\) disjoint. Thus no decoder of the fixed sketch can be a \(c\)-approximation on both adaptive queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once adaptive queries expose a nonzero kernel direction, scaled vectors have identical sketches but arbitrarily different norms, forcing any fixed-sketch norm decoder to fail.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}\) with \(r<n\)
The decoder observes only \(Ax\)
Approximation factor \(c\ge1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recovery of a nonzero vector in \(\ker A\) yields an adaptive multiplicative-approximation failure.

notation.meaning: nonzero kernel vector exposed by the interaction

review_flags: source needed for an adaptive procedure that recovers a kernel direction
statement records the failure mechanism, not an adaptive-query complexity theorem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional kernel-scaling obstruction is correct, but the record supplies no source or adaptive procedure showing that an interaction can identify the required nonzero kernel vector. It therefore does not yet support an adaptive-query failure result.

children.title: Dense-Graph Access

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjacency-matrix query model for arbitrary simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=[n]\), dense-graph access is provided by an adjacency oracle \(\mathsf{Adj}_G\). On an unordered pair \(\{u,v\}\subseteq V\) with \(u\ne v\), the oracle returns \(1\) exactly when \(\{u,v\}\in E\), and returns \(0\) otherwise. Each invocation costs one query, independent of \(n\), the degrees, or \(|E|\). Algorithms may choose successive pairs adaptively from previous answers and internal randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense-graph access reveals whether any requested vertex pair is an edge, at unit cost per adjacency query.
assumptions_latex: \(G=([n],E)\) is simple and undirected
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathsf{Adj}_G(u,v)=\mathbf{1}[\{u,v\}\in E]\) defines the dense-graph oracle.

children.title: Bounded-Degree Graph Access

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Degree Graph Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-list oracle model with a known maximum-degree bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a simple undirected graph with \(V=[n]\) and maximum degree at most \(d\). Bounded-degree access consists of \(\mathsf{Deg}_G(v)=\deg_G(v)\) and an incidence-list oracle \(\mathsf{Nbr}_G(v,i)\), where \(i\in[d]\). After fixing an arbitrary ordering of every neighborhood, \(\mathsf{Nbr}_G(v,i)\) returns the \(i\)-th neighbor when \(i\le\deg_G(v)\), and \(\bot\) otherwise. Each oracle invocation has unit query cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-degree graph is accessed through degree and indexed-neighbor queries, with an explicit maximum degree bound.

\(\max_{v\in V}\deg_G(v)\le d\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathsf{Deg}_G,\mathsf{Nbr}_G)\) defines bounded-degree access with query indices in \([d]\).

children.title: Dense–Sparse Access Separations
children.top_down_role: Query-complexity differences induced by dense and bounded-degree representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense–Sparse Access Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case query separation between adjacency-matrix and bounded-degree incidence access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an unknown simple graph and a fixed vertex \(u\) promised to have degree at most one. Using only adjacency queries \(\mathsf{Adj}_G(u,v)\), any deterministic algorithm that must return the unique neighbor of \(u\), or \(\bot\) if none exists, requires \(n-1\) queries in the worst case. Conversely, under bounded-degree access with degree bound \(d\), an adjacency query \(\mathsf{Adj}_G(u,v)\) can be simulated by inspecting at most \(d\) indexed neighbors of \(u\). Thus unit-cost access in one representation can cost \(\Theta(n)\) or \(O(d)\) in the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finding a possible unique neighbor costs n−1 adjacency probes, whereas bounded-degree neighbor access simulates adjacency in at most d probes.
assumptions_latex: \(G=([n],E)\) is simple and undirected
Algorithms require exact answers
Queries may be chosen adaptively
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neighbor discovery has worst-case cost \(n-1\) under dense adjacency access, while adjacency testing costs at most \(d\) bounded-degree neighbor queries.
review_flags: elementary adversary bound stated without supplied access-model source
randomized and approximate variants are outside scope

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic exact-query bounds are mathematically plausible and the complexity-bound kind fits the separation leaf, but neither the access conventions nor the adversary and simulation bounds have cited support.

knowledge_statements.title: Degree Queries

knowledge_statements.title: Neighbor Queries

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Sampling Queries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact uniform edge-sampling oracle for finite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), an exact edge-sampling query returns an edge \(e\in E\) with probability \(1/|E|\), independently of previous calls conditional on the fixed graph. If \(E=\varnothing\), it returns \(\bot\). The orientation of a returned undirected edge is immaterial; if an ordered representation is required, a fixed canonical ordering of its endpoints is used. One returned sample counts as one oracle query.

children.title: Cut Queries

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Queries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact oracle returning the cardinality or weight of a requested cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be a finite undirected graph with weights \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\). For \(S\subseteq V\), define \(\delta_G(S)=\{\{u,v\}\in E:u\in S,\ v\in V\setminus S\}\). A cut query returns \(\mathsf{Cut}_G(S)=\sum_{e\in\delta_G(S)}w(e)\). In an unweighted graph, take \(w(e)=1\), so the response is \(|\delta_G(S)|\). Each exact response counts as one query, irrespective of \(|S|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut query returns the total weight, or number, of edges crossing from a requested vertex set to its complement.

\(w(e)\ge0\) for every \(e\in E\)

knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Set Queries

children.title: Cut–Independent-Set Access Separations
children.top_down_role: Simulation costs and query-complexity gaps between the two interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut–Independent-Set Access Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact simulation asymmetry between cut-value and independent-set oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an unweighted simple graph, cut queries decide whether \(S\subseteq V\) is independent using \(|S|+1\) calls: obtain every \(\deg_G(v)=\mathsf{Cut}_G(\{v\})\), obtain \(\mathsf{Cut}_G(S)\), and compute \(|E(S)|=(\sum_{v\in S}\deg_G(v)-\mathsf{Cut}_G(S))/2\). Conversely, fix \(S\) with \(|S|=a\). Across graphs containing only edges between \(S\) and \(V\setminus S\), the cut value has \(a(n-a)+1\) possibilities. Since each independent-set answer is one bit, every deterministic exact procedure computing that cut value requires at least \(\lceil\log_2(a(n-a)+1)\rceil\) queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut queries simulate an independent-set test in |S|+1 calls, while exact cut recovery from Boolean independent-set answers needs logarithmically many calls.
assumptions_latex: \(G=([n],E)\) is simple, undirected, and unweighted
Oracle answers are exact
The reverse-simulation algorithm is deterministic
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cut access decides independence in \(|S|+1\) queries, whereas exact reverse simulation needs at least \(\lceil\log_2(a(n-a)+1)\rceil\) queries on the stated family.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matroid rank-oracle access model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid with rank function \(r_M(S)=\max\{|I|:I\subseteq S,\ I\in\mathcal I\}\). Query complexity counts evaluations of \(O_r\).

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Size Estimation

knowledge_statements.title: Local Matching Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stateless local access to one fixed matching through vertex-mate queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A local matching oracle is a map \(\mathcal O_M:V\to V\cup\{\bot\}\) for which there exists a matching \(M\subseteq E\) such that \(\mathcal O_M(v)=u\) exactly when \(\{u,v\}\in M\), and \(\mathcal O_M(v)=\bot\) exactly when \(v\) is unmatched in \(M\). Thus every non-null answer satisfies \(\{v,\mathcal O_M(v)\}\in E\) and \(\mathcal O_M(\mathcal O_M(v))=v\). Repeated queries must return the same answer and must not depend on query order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local matching oracle reports each vertex's mate, or unmatched, while all answers describe one fixed matching independently of query order.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists M\subseteq E\text{ a matching such that }\mathcal O_M(v)=u\iff \{u,v\}\in M\).

notation.meaning: null answer indicating an unmatched vertex

Repeated answers are invariant under query order, so all membership queries expose the same global cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle answers whether a queried vertex belongs to a single fixed vertex cover, consistently across all queries.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\{v\in V:\mathcal O_C(v)=1\}\text{ satisfies }(\forall\{u,v\}\in E)\,[u\in C\lor v\in C]\).

knowledge_statements.title: Matching–Cover Oracle Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition induced by taking endpoints of a maximal matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O_M\) represent a maximal matching \(M\) of a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(\mathcal O_C:V\to\{0,1\}\). The matching and cover oracles are endpoint-consistent when, for every \(v\in V\), \(\mathcal O_C(v)=1\) if and only if \(\mathcal O_M(v)\neq\bot\). Equivalently, the represented set is \(C=\bigcup_{e\in M}e\). Under maximality, this condition makes \(C\) a vertex cover and gives \(|C|=2|M|\); hence \(|C|\leq 2\tau(G)\), where \(\tau(G)\) is the minimum vertex-cover size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cover oracle selects exactly the endpoints of one maximal matching, yielding a valid cover whose size is at most twice optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
\(\mathcal O_M\) represents a maximal matching \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_C(v)=1\iff\mathcal O_M(v)\neq\bot\), and consequently \(C\text{ is a vertex cover with }|C|\leq2\tau(G)\).

notation.meaning: minimum cardinality of a vertex cover of G
set selected by the cover oracle

knowledge_statements.title: Local Independent-Set Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Membership-query access to one fixed independent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A local independent-set oracle is a map \(\mathcal O_I:V\to\{0,1\}\) for which the represented set \(I=\{v\in V:\mathcal O_I(v)=1\}\) is independent. Repeated answers refer to the same set and are invariant under query order.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.

knowledge_statements.title: Independence–Coloring Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility obtained by identifying the independent set with one color class.

The represented set \(I=\mathcal O_\chi^{-1}(\{c_\star\})\) is then independent because adjacent vertices receive distinct colors.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Partitioning Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pair-query access to the equivalence relation of one fixed vertex partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite set. A local partitioning oracle is a map \(\mathcal O_P:V\times V\to\{0,1\}\) for which there exists a partition \(P\) of \(V\) such that \(\mathcal O_P(u,v)=1\) exactly when \(u\) and \(v\) lie in the same block of \(P\). Consequently, \(\mathcal O_P\) is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive: \(\mathcal O_P(u,u)=1\), \(\mathcal O_P(u,v)=\mathcal O_P(v,u)\), and two positive answers on \((u,v)\) and \((v,w)\) force a positive answer on \((u,w)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle decides whether two queried vertices occupy the same block of one fixed partition.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\sim_Pv\iff\mathcal O_P(u,v)=1\text{ defines an equivalence relation on }V\).

notation.meaning: represented partition of the vertex set

knowledge_statements.title: Local Clustering Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local label and boundary access to one fixed graph clustering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)[0m be a finite undirected graph. Thus the label fibers form a partition of \(V\), while the boundary oracle identifies precisely the edges crossing between distinct clusters. Both maps are fixed independently of query order.

\(L\) is a set of cluster labels.

children.title: Partition–Cluster Boundary Consistency
