knowledge_statements.title: Partition–Cluster Boundary Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Agreement between same-block queries, cluster labels, and boundary-edge answers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), let \(\mathcal O_P:V\times V\to\{0,1\}\) represent a partition, and let \(\lambda:V\to L\) and \(\mathcal O_\partial:E\to\{0,1\}\) represent a clustering. The interfaces are boundary-consistent when, for all \(u,v\in V\), \(\mathcal O_P(u,v)=1\) if and only if \(\lambda(u)=\lambda(v)\), and, for every \(\{u,v\}\in E\), \(\mathcal O_\partial(\{u,v\})=1-\mathcal O_P(u,v)\). Hence an edge is declared boundary-crossing exactly when its endpoints occupy different blocks of the represented partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition, label, and boundary answers are consistent exactly when equal labels mean one block and boundary edges join different blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
All three oracles use the same vertex set \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_P(u,v)=1\iff\lambda(u)=\lambda(v)\), and \(\mathcal O_\partial(\{u,v\})=1-\mathcal O_P(u,v)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the correct role for this consistency leaf, and the formulas are coherent for the proposed interfaces. Those interfaces and the exact complement convention for boundary answers are not cited, so their intended local meaning cannot be verified.

children.title: Cross-Query Consistency
children.top_down_role: Global compatibility requirements across locally answered queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Query Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite transcripts must extend to one legal global solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be a query set, \(Arac{0}{0}\) an answer set, and \(\mathscr S\subseteq A^Q\) the legal global solutions. An oracle transcript \(T=((q_1,a_1),\ldots,(q_m,a_m))\) is cross-query consistent when there exists \(s\in\mathscr S\) such that \(s(q_i)=a_i\) for every \(i\). In particular, repeated occurrences of one query have equal answers. An oracle is cross-query consistent when every finite transcript it produces has this extension property, including transcripts formed by adaptively chosen or concurrently issued queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite collection of oracle answers must be jointly extendable to one legal global solution, regardless of query order or adaptivity.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) and \(A\) are query and answer sets.
\(\mathscr S\subseteq A^Q\) is the specified family of legal global solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall T)\,(\exists s\in\mathscr S)\,(\forall(q,a)\in T)\;s(q)=a\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-extension formulation is a plausible condition, but it needs a formal local-computation source, especially because requiring a possibly different global solution for every finite transcript is weaker than requiring one fixed global solution across an unbounded execution. The fragment `\(Arac{0}{0}\)` is also a corrupted or undefined command where the answer set `\(A\)` is evidently intended.

children.title: Parallel Oracle Simulation
children.top_down_role: Parallel execution models for batches of local oracle queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Oracle Simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Round-based evaluation of dependency-compatible query batches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite query batch \(B\subseteq Q\), a shared seed \(\rho\), and a directed acyclic dependency graph \(D=(B,F)\). Initialize the answered set as \(R_0=\varnothing\). In round \(t\geq1\), evaluate in parallel every unanswered query whose predecessors in \(D\) lie in \(R_{t-1}\), using the same deterministic oracle simulation parameterized by \(\rho\); append all resulting answers simultaneously to the transcript and obtain \(R_t\). Stop when \(R_t=B\), and output the answers in a fixed canonical order. Shared state may be committed only between rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Queries whose dependencies are already resolved run together, using one shared seed and round-boundary commits to preserve a common transcript.
assumptions_latex: \(B\subseteq Q\) is finite.
\(D=(B,F)\) is acyclic.
The seeded oracle simulation is deterministic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_T=B\text{ after at most }1+\max_{q\in B}\operatorname{depth}_D(q)\text{ rounds}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is an appropriate content kind, but the proposed precedence-DAG scheduler is not sourced as a parallel local-oracle simulation. Determinism under a shared seed and round-boundary commits alone do not establish that its answers extend to one legal global solution; the required oracle-state and consistency assumptions must be sourced and stated.

children.title: Consistency–Parallelism Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Query, locality, and synchronization costs of preserving consistent parallel outputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Consistency–Parallelism Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Round complexity determined by the query-dependency partial order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite batch \(B\) with dependency directed acyclic graph \(D=(B,F)\), let \(h(D)\) be the maximum number of vertices on a directed path. Any faithful simulation that answers a query only after all of its predecessors are fixed requires at least \(h(D)\) sequential rounds. A level-synchronous simulation attains exactly \(h(D)\) rounds by processing each antichain of currently minimal unanswered queries in parallel. Thus stronger cross-query dependencies reduce available parallelism; if each query costs at most \(W\) local work, total work is at most \(W|B|\), while parallel depth is \(h(D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The longest dependency chain fixes the necessary and sufficient number of synchronous rounds; incomparable queries can be evaluated in parallel.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a finite query batch.
\(D=(B,F)\) is an acyclic precedence graph.
Each query requires at most \(W\) local work after its predecessors are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rounds}=h(D)\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{work}\leq W|B|\).

notation.meaning: number of vertices on a longest directed path in D

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity bound is the correct role for the tradeoff leaf, and the height bound is valid for the stipulated precedence model. However, that model is not sourced as a consistency-parallelism tradeoff for local oracles. The work bound also counts only per-query local work and needs explicit assumptions excluding synchronization, dependency-discovery, and shared-state overhead.

knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Value-Oracle Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-ground-set maximization model with black-box function access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(f(A)+f(B)\ge f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B)\) for all \(A,B\subseteq V\). A value oracle returns \(f(S)\) when queried with \(S\subseteq V\). Given a feasible family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^V\), value-oracle submodular maximization seeks \(S\in\mathcal F\) maximizing \(f(S)\), while charging one query for each oracle evaluation. An \(\alpha\)-approximation returns \(S\in\mathcal F\) satisfying \(f(S)\ge\alpha\max_{T\in\mathcal F}f(T)\), under any separately stated sign, monotonicity, and access assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize a submodular set function over a feasible family using only queried function values, measuring both approximation quality and oracle-query cost.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(\mathcal F\subseteq2^V\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(S)\ge\alpha\max_{T\in\mathcal F}f(T)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical finite submodular value-oracle model

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the terminal topic, and the finite value-oracle model is mathematically coherent. However, no citation or inspectable locator supports the oracle model or approximation convention, so source verification is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Independence-Oracle Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Black-box matroid feasibility model for discrete optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid. An independence oracle accepts \(S\subseteq E\) and returns whether \(S\in\mathcal I\). Independence-oracle optimization seeks an independent set maximizing a specified objective \(g:\mathcal I\to\mathbb R\), with feasibility information obtained only through these oracle answers. For explicit weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), the standard objective is \(g(S)=\sum_{e\in S}w(e)\). Query complexity counts oracle calls, while computation on explicit elements and weights is accounted for separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize over a matroid when independence is accessible only through yes-or-no subset queries; query complexity is separated from ordinary computation.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite.
\((E,\mathcal I)\) satisfies the matroid axioms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{S\in\mathcal I}g(S)\).
review_flags: supplied matroid locator does not explicitly support the oracle formulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the terminal topic, but the record does not state how the general objective g is represented or evaluated. The supplied inventory concerns matroid optimization but does not specifically support this independence-oracle formulation, and the candidate cites no source.

children.title: Sampling-Supported Oracles
children.top_down_role: Oracle interfaces backed by random samples from the input or solution space.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Supported Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle answers computed from fresh random observations rather than exact stored values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For query set \(\mathcal Q\), instance \(x\), and target response \(F(x,q)\), a sampling-supported oracle has access to a distribution \(P_{x,q}\). On query \(q\in\mathcal Q\), it draws \(m\) fresh observations \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m\sim P_{x,q}\) and returns an estimator \(\widehat F_m(q)=A_q(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)\). It is an \((\varepsilon,\delta,m)\) sampling oracle when \(\Pr[d(\widehat F_m(q),F(x,q))\le\varepsilon]\ge1-\delta\) for every permitted \(x\) and \(q\), where the probability is over the fresh samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each query is answered by an estimator built from fresh samples, with an explicit accuracy, failure probability, and sample budget.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal Y,d)\) is the response metric space.
Fresh observations follow \(P_{x,q}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr[d(\widehat F_m(q),F(x,q))\le\varepsilon]\ge1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: accuracy, failure probability, and sample budget

review_flags: node does not specify a particular sampling model

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition has the correct role and is internally coherent as a pointwise sampling-oracle model. The terminal title does not determine independence, repeated-query, or simultaneous-query conventions, and no source with a specific locator supports the selected formulation.

children.title: Sketch-Supported Oracles
children.top_down_role: Oracle interfaces backed by compact linear or nonlinear summaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Sketch-Supported Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Queries answered from a compact randomized summary of the instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathcal X\), let \(F(x,q)\) be the desired response for \(q\in\mathcal Q\), and let \(R\) be preprocessing randomness. A sketch-supported oracle stores \(K=\operatorname{Sketch}(x;R)\) using at most \(s\) bits and answers \(q\) by \(D(K,q)\), without further access to \(x\). It has \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) accuracy when, for every fixed \(x,q\), \(\Pr_R[d(D(K,q),F(x,q))\le\varepsilon]\ge1-\delta\). Simultaneous accuracy instead requires this event to hold for every query in a stated query family under the same sketch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact randomized summary replaces the original instance, and a decoder answers queries with stated pointwise or simultaneous accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal Y,d)\) is the response metric space.
The decoder accesses only \(K\) and \(q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr_R[d(D(\operatorname{Sketch}(x;R),q),F(x,q))\le\varepsilon]\ge1-\delta\).
review_flags: node does not specify pointwise versus simultaneous guarantees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the sketch-supported-oracle container and correctly distinguishes pointwise from simultaneous accuracy. A source is needed to determine which guarantee and query model belong to this taxonomy leaf; no citation or locator is supplied.

Conditional on \(x,q\), fresh observations follow \(P_{x,q}\).

children.title: Rare-Witness Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds driven by informative witnesses occurring with low probability.

knowledge_statements.title: Rare-Witness Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical search lower bound when one uniformly hidden query reveals the witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) contain \(N\) possible queries. Under the null instance every answer is \(0\); under instance \(I_W\), where \(W\) is uniform on \(Q\), the answer is \(1\) exactly at query \(W\). Any possibly randomized adaptive algorithm making at most \(q\) distinct queries observes the witness with probability at most \(q/N\). Consequently, distinguishing the null instance from \(I_W\) with success probability at least \(2/3\) under the equal mixture requires \(q\ge N/3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If only one uniformly hidden query differs from the null instance, seeing that witness has probability at most the queried fraction of the domain.
assumptions_latex: \(W\) is uniform on \(Q\).
The algorithm makes at most \(q\) distinct queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr[\text{witness observed}]\le q/N\), and equal-prior distinguishing success \(\ge2/3\) requires \(q\ge N/3\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary rare-marked-item query lower bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role is correct, and the stated rare-witness calculation and N/3 equal-prior consequence are coherent. No cited lower-bound source or inspectable locator supports this canonical construction.

children.title: Hidden-Structure Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds driven by planted structure concealed from limited queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden-Structure Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional indistinguishability bound for structures revealed only by low-hazard queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be a random hidden structure and suppose oracle answers equal a fixed null transcript until a revealing query occurs. Assume that, conditional on every unrevealing history, any next query reveals \(\Theta\) with probability at most \(p\). If every output determined from the null transcript is correct for at most a \(\beta\) fraction of structures, then any adaptive algorithm using at most \(q\) queries has success probability at most \(qp+\beta\). Thus success at least \(1-\delta\) requires \(q\ge(1-\delta-\beta)/p\) whenever the numerator is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When each query has small conditional probability of exposing hidden structure, success is bounded by total revelation probability plus null-transcript guessing success.
assumptions_latex: Each unrevealing history has conditional revelation hazard at most \(p\).
Null-transcript outputs succeed with probability at most \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr[\text{success}]\le qp+\beta\), hence \(q\ge(1-\delta-\beta)/p\) for success \(1-\delta\).
review_flags: specific hidden-structure family is not identified

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf, and the hazard-based indistinguishability template is plausible. The meaning of correctness over hidden structures and the admissible instance family depend on an unstated distributional model, and no source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Witness-Visibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Access conditions controlling whether decisive witnesses or planted structures become observable.

knowledge_statements.title: Witness-Visibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by cumulative probability that adaptive queries expose a correctness witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance distribution and an adaptive algorithm. Conditional on no earlier witness, let \(p_t\) be the probability that round \(t\)'s query reveals a witness. The witness visibility through \(q\) queries is \(v(q)=1-\prod_{t=1}^q(1-p_t)\). A family is uniformly low-visibility at scale \(q\) if \(v(q)=o(1)\) for every admissible algorithm; it is constant-visibility if some admissible algorithm has \(v(q)\ge c\) for an absolute constant \(c>0\). In particular, \(p_t\le p\) implies \(v(q)\le qp\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Visibility is the cumulative conditional chance that queries expose a witness; low- and constant-visibility regimes are distinguished by whether this probability vanishes.
assumptions_latex: The event of first witness revelation is measurable after each query.
\(p_t\) is conditioned on no previous revelation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(q)=1-\prod_{t=1}^q(1-p_t)\), and \(p_t\le p\) implies \(v(q)\le qp\).

notation.meaning: conditional revelation probability at query t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: hazard-based formalization of witness visibility
taxonomy does not specify the admissible algorithm class

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role is appropriate, and the cumulative-hazard formula is coherent when p_t denotes the scalar conditional hazard given survival. The low-visibility and constant-visibility classifications depend on an unspecified admissible algorithm class and asymptotic family, with no source fixing those conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Access-Model Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic comparison of query power between two representations of the same instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For access models \(\mathsf A\) and \(\mathsf B\), problem family \(\Pi_n\), and fixed accuracy and success requirements, let \(Q_{\mathsf A}(n)\) and \(Q_{\mathsf B}(n)\) be their minimum worst-case query complexities. The family exhibits an \(h(n)\)-fold separation favoring \(\mathsf A\) when \(Q_{\mathsf B}(n)/Q_{\mathsf A}(n)=\Omega(h(n))\). It exhibits a polynomial-versus-sublinear separation when \(Q_{\mathsf B}(n)=\Omega(n^c)\) for some \(c>0\) while \(Q_{\mathsf A}(n)=o(n^c)\), with identical input promises and output guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An access-model separation compares optimal query complexities for the same promised problem and guarantee, recording an asymptotic advantage of one representation.
assumptions_latex: Both models solve the same family \(\Pi_n\).
Accuracy and success requirements are identical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathsf B}(n)/Q_{\mathsf A}(n)=\Omega(h(n))\).

notation.meaning: optimal query complexity in model A
optimal query complexity in model B

review_flags: specific access models are not named

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is a suitable role for the general separation concept, and the ratio-based definition is coherent. The phrase polynomial-versus-sublinear is not tied to a conventional input-size scale, the access models are unnamed, and no citation or locator supports the selected terminology.

assumptions_latex: Queries inside each round are issued nonadaptively.
Accuracy \(\varepsilon\) and failure probability \(\delta\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{r+1}(n;\varepsilon,\delta)\le Q_r(n;\varepsilon,\delta)\).

notation.meaning: optimal query complexity using at most r rounds

review_flags: no problem-specific tradeoff theorem is identified
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto profile relating oracle-query count to the number of adaptive rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For problem family \(\Pi_n\), let \(Q_r(n;\varepsilon,\delta)\) be the minimum worst-case number of oracle queries used by an algorithm with at most \(r\) adaptive rounds, whose queries within each round are fixed before that round's answers arrive, and which returns an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate output with probability at least \(1-\delta\). The adaptivity–query tradeoff is the profile \(r\mapsto Q_r(n;\varepsilon,\delta)\). It is monotone: \(Q_{r+1}(n;\varepsilon,\delta)\le Q_r(n;\varepsilon,\delta)\), because every algorithm using at most \(r\) rounds is also admissible under an at-most-\(r+1\)-round bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tradeoff profile records the fewest queries achievable with at most a bounded number of adaptive batches; allowing another round cannot increase this optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptivity–Query Tradeoffs

children.title: Noisy-Oracle Failures
children.top_down_role: Optimization failures caused by corrupted or unstable oracle responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Noisy-Oracle Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adversarial additive noise destroys identifiability when the objective gap does not exceed twice the noise radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{a,b\}\), let feasible outputs be \(\{a\}\) and \(\{b\}\), and suppose a query \(S\subseteq E\) returns \(y(S)=f(S)+\eta(S)\) with adversarial \(|\eta(S)|\le\Delta\). Consider modular objectives \(f_1(S)=2\Delta\mathbf1\{a\in S\}\) and \(f_2(S)=2\Delta\mathbf1\{b\in S\}\). Every subset query admits the same valid response under both instances: use \(0\) for \(S=\varnothing\), \(2\Delta\) for \(S=E\), and \(\Delta\) for either singleton. Hence no algorithm can select an optimum with probability greater than \(1/2\) on both instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With adversarial additive error, two opposite optima separated by twice the noise radius can generate identical transcripts, preventing reliable optimization.
assumptions_latex: Noise may be chosen adversarially within \([-\Delta,\Delta]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{i\in\{1,2\}}\Pr[\widehat S\in\operatorname*{argmax}f_i]\le1/2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is correct, and the two modular instances admit the stated common adversarial-noise transcript. The conclusion correctly expresses that no algorithm can exceed one-half success on both instances, but no authoritative noisy-oracle lower-bound citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Approximate-Oracle Failures
children.top_down_role: Optimization failures caused by bounded-accuracy oracle responses.

assumptions_latex: Oracle errors may be adversarial within the multiplicative interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{i\in\{1,2\}}\Pr[f_i(\widehat S)/\max_T f_i(T)\le\kappa^{-2}]\ge1/2\).
review_flags: approximate-oracle convention is not specified by the node
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided multiplicative oracle error incurs a squared ambiguity in attainable optimization ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{a,b\}\), let feasible outputs be the two singletons, and let \(\kappa>1\). Suppose the oracle may return any \(\widetilde f(S)\) satisfying \(f(S)/\kappa\le\widetilde f(S)\le\kappa f(S)\). Define modular objectives by \(f_1(\{a\})=\kappa\), \(f_1(\{b\})=1/\kappa\), with the values reversed for \(f_2\). A common valid transcript returns \(1\) on each singleton and \(\kappa+1/\kappa\) on \(E\). Therefore some instance makes any algorithm choose the inferior singleton with probability at least \(1/2\), attaining ratio only \(1/\kappa^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-sided factor-κ value oracle can make opposite optima indistinguishable, so a better-than-κ⁻² ratio cannot be guaranteed with probability greater than one half on every instance.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Oracle Failures

children.title: Noise–Approximation Interaction Failures
children.top_down_role: Failure regimes where response noise compounds approximation error.

assumptions_latex: \(\eta>0\), and oracle errors are adversarial within the stated bound.
The multiplicative guarantee must hold uniformly over both instances.
For randomized algorithms, success probability is taken over the algorithm's internal randomness against the common admissible oracle transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every deterministic algorithm, one of the two instances violates \(f(\widehat{x})\leq\rho\operatorname{OPT}\) for every finite \(\rho\); for every randomized algorithm, the minimum of its success probabilities on the two instances is at most \(1/2\).

notation.meaning: Two objective functions consistent with the same oracle transcript.
Solution returned by the oracle algorithm.

review_flags: randomized guarantee clarified as a worst-instance success bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive oracle noise obstructs multiplicative approximation when the optimum has no positive scale separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{a,b\}\), let \(\eta>0\), and suppose an oracle returns \(y(x)\) satisfying \(|y(x)-f(x)|\leq\eta/2\) for every queried \(x\in X\). Consider the minimization instances \(f_0(a)=0\), \(f_0(b)=\eta\) and \(f_1(a)=\eta\), \(f_1(b)=0\). The common transcript \(y(a)=y(b)=\eta/2\) is admissible for both instances, so an oracle algorithm cannot distinguish them. Every deterministic output has positive value on one instance although that instance has optimum zero; hence no finite multiplicative approximation factor holds uniformly. For a randomized algorithm, if \(p\) is the probability of outputting \(a\) under this transcript, its success probabilities on \(f_0\) and \(f_1\) are respectively \(p\) and \(1-p\), so their minimum is at most \(1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same bounded-noise transcript can hide which of two solutions has zero cost. Consequently no deterministic algorithm has a finite uniform multiplicative factor, and every randomized algorithm has success probability at most one half on at least one of the two instances.
knowledge_statements.title: Noise–Approximation Interaction Failures

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Update Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard edge-insertion model for dynamic graph problems on a fixed vertex universe.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An incremental graph-update model consists of a fixed vertex set \(V\), an initial graph \(G_0=(V,E_0)\), and updates \(u_1,\ldots,u_T\), where every \(u_t\) inserts an edge \(e_t\notin E_{t-1}\). The state after update \(t\) is \(G_t=(V,E_t)\) with \(E_t=E_{t-1}\cup\{e_t\}\). A dynamic algorithm preprocesses \(G_0\), processes the insertions in order, and maintains or reports the prescribed graph solution or query answer for each current graph \(G_t\). No edge deletion is permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incremental model starts from a graph and permits only edge insertions while maintaining answers for each resulting graph.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is fixed throughout the update sequence.
Each inserted edge is absent immediately before its insertion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_0\subseteq E_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq E_T\).

children.title: Fully Dynamic Update Models

knowledge_statements.title: Fully Dynamic Update Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard dynamic graph model allowing edge insertions and deletions in one online sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fully dynamic graph-update model consists of a fixed vertex set \(V\), an initial graph \(G_0=(V,E_0)\), and a valid sequence \(u_1,\ldots,u_T\) of edge insertions and deletions. An insertion of \(e_t\) gives \(E_t=E_{t-1}\cup\{e_t\}\), while a deletion gives \(E_t=E_{t-1}\setminus\{e_t\}\). Updates of both types may occur in arbitrary order. A dynamic algorithm preprocesses \(G_0\), processes each update, and maintains or reports the required solution or query answer for the current graph \(G_t=(V,E_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fully dynamic model permits an arbitrary valid mixture of edge insertions and deletions while answers are maintained online.

Each event is either a valid update, which produces a new graph state, or a query \(q\) designating a graph state \(G_t\). If \(Q(G_t,q)\) denotes the prescribed answer to query \(q\) on state \(G_t\), the algorithm must report \(Q(G_t,q)\) for every query event. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph sensitivity model with parameter \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) preprocesses a fixed base graph \(G=(V,E)\). A request then supplies a collection \(U\) of at most \(k\) valid elementary edge updates of the types permitted by the model. children.title: Batch-Update Models

knowledge_statements.title: Batch-Update Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic model in which each update operation changes a bounded or variable set of graph elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A batch-update graph model presents updates \(B_1,\ldots,B_T\), where each \(B_t\) is a finite set of mutually consistent elementary insertions and deletions applied atomically to \(G_{t-1}\), producing \(G_t=B_t(G_{t-1})\). The algorithm must maintain or report the required solution for \(G_t\) after completing the batch. If \(b_t=|B_t|\), complexity may be stated per batch as a function of \(b_t\), or over the sequence in terms of \(\sum_{t=1}^T b_t\); it must not silently treat a batch as one elementary update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A batch-update model applies several consistent elementary changes atomically and measures work with the batch size made explicit.
assumptions_latex: Each \(B_t\) is finite and valid for \(G_{t-1}\).
Answers are required only after the complete batch is applied.

children.title: Amortized Complexity Measures
children.top_down_role: Update costs averaged across operation sequences.

assumptions_latex: \(T\geq1\), and the update sequence is valid.

All operation costs are measured in one specified computational or oracle model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a sequence-level average resource measure for dynamic updates, with preprocessing accounted for separately unless explicitly included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a declared size parameter \(n\) and a valid sequence of \(T\geq1\) updates. Let \(c_t\) be the charged resource cost of processing update \(t\), including required post-update maintenance, and let \(P\) be preprocessing cost. An amortized update-complexity upper bound \(A(n,T)\) means that every valid sequence with the declared parameters satisfies \(\sum_{t=1}^T c_t\leq T A(n,T)\). Preprocessing is excluded from the amortized update cost unless the convention explicitly instead bounds \(P+\sum_{t=1}^T c_t\). Individual update costs may exceed \(A(n,T)\); the constraint is on total sequence cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Amortized update complexity is a sequence-level measure: total charged update work over every valid sequence is at most the number of updates times the declared amortized bound, even though individual updates may cost more.
knowledge_statements.title: Amortized Complexity Measures

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a declared size parameter \(n\). For every valid dynamic history \(\sigma\) whose relevant instance size is at most \(n\), and every admissible next update \(u\), let \(c(\sigma,u)\) be the charged resource cost of processing \(u\), including all maintenance required before the next operation. A worst-case update-complexity upper bound \(W(n)\) means that \(c(\sigma,u)\leq W(n)\) for every such pair \((\sigma,u)\). Unlike an amortized measure, this condition constrains each operation separately. Worst-case query complexity is defined analogously over every valid update history and admissible query.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case dynamic complexity is a uniform per-operation measure that bounds each admissible update or query after every valid history of the declared size.

children.title: Exact Dynamic Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dynamic maintenance requiring exact objective values or solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Dynamic Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic optimization requiring an optimal feasible solution or exact optimum value after every update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each current instance \(G_t\), let \(\mathcal{F}(G_t)\) be its feasible solutions and let \(f_t\) be the objective. An exact dynamic optimization regime requires the maintained output \(x_t\) to belong to \(\mathcal{F}(G_t)\) and attain the optimum after every update. Thus, for minimization, \(f_t(x_t)=\min_{x\in\mathcal{F}(G_t)}f_t(x)\); for maximization, \(f_t(x_t)=\max_{x\in\mathcal{F}(G_t)}f_t(x)\). If only an objective value is requested, the reported value must equal this optimum exactly under the model's arithmetic convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact dynamic regime must maintain a genuinely optimal solution or exact optimal value after every update.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{F}(G_t)\neq\varnothing\) after every update.
The objective and arithmetic convention determine an attained finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_t(x_t)=\operatorname{OPT}(G_t)\) for every \(t\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set for the current instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Dynamic Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative solution-quality regime for dynamic optimization with nonnegative objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\alpha\geq1\). For each current instance \(G_t\), let \(\mathcal{F}(G_t)\neq\varnothing\) and assume the objective \(f_t\) is nonnegative. An \(\alpha\)-approximate dynamic regime maintains \(x_t\in\mathcal{F}(G_t)\) after every update such that, for minimization, \(f_t(x_t)\leq\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(G_t)\), and for maximization, \(f_t(x_t)\geq\operatorname{OPT}(G_t)/\alpha\). If the algorithm is randomized, the statement must additionally specify whether the guarantee holds surely, in expectation, or with a declared success probability against a declared update adversary.

All objective values are nonnegative.

children.title: Bounded-Recourse Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dynamic maintenance limiting changes to the maintained solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Recourse Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines per-update and amortized recourse for dynamically maintained discrete solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_0,I_1,\ldots\) be instances and let \(S_t\in\mathcal F(I_t)\) be the maintained feasible solution after update \(t\). Given an elementary-edit distance \(d\) on solutions, the recourse of update \(t\) is \(r_t=d(S_{t-1},S_t)\). The regime has worst-case recourse at most \(R\) if \(r_t\le R\) for every update. It has amortized recourse at most \(R\) if, for every \(T\ge1\), \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_t\le RT+O(1)\). A bounded-recourse regime additionally specifies a solution-quality requirement, such as \(c(S_t)\le\alpha\,\operatorname{OPT}(I_t)\), that must hold after each update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic algorithm has bounded recourse when each update, or every update sequence on average, changes only a bounded number of elementary solution components while preserving feasibility and stated quality.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F(I_t)\neq\varnothing\) after every update.
\(d\) counts the designated elementary changes between feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_t\le R\) for all \(t\), or \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_t\le RT+O(1)\) for every \(T\ge1\).

children.title: Link–Cut Tree Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Dynamic-tree access through path-oriented link–cut representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Link–Cut Tree Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract interface for path-oriented maintenance of a dynamic forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a vertex-weighted forest \(F\) through operations \(\operatorname{makeTree}(v)\), \(\operatorname{link}(u,v)\), \(\operatorname{cut}(u,v)\), \(\operatorname{makeRoot}(v)\), \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\), \(\operatorname{update}(v,a)\), and \(\operatorname{pathQuery}(u,v)\). Each represented tree is decomposed into preferred paths stored as balanced auxiliary trees. Accessing a vertex changes preferred edges, splits and concatenates auxiliary paths, and propagates lazy reversals and aggregate summaries. If summaries form a constant-time composable monoid, a successful path query returns the ordered aggregate over the unique \(u\)-to-\(v\) path. For a forest of at most \(n\) vertices, every operation takes amortized \(O(\log n)\) time and \(O(n)\) total space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Link–cut trees maintain a changing forest through path-centered operations, supporting links, cuts, rerooting, connectivity, and composable path aggregates in amortized logarithmic time.
assumptions_latex: Every \(\operatorname{link}(u,v)\) joins distinct trees and every \(\operatorname{cut}(u,v)\) removes an existing forest edge.
Aggregate composition and lazy-action updates take \(O(1)\) time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each interface operation costs amortized \(O(\log n)\) time and the representation uses \(O(n)\) space.

notation.meaning: aggregate query on the unique forest path

children.title: Top-Tree Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Dynamic-tree access through recursively maintained top-tree clusters.

knowledge_statements.title: Top-Tree Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract interface for boundary-cluster maintenance of a dynamic forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a dynamic forest \(F\) by a balanced binary hierarchy of connected edge clusters, each having at most two boundary vertices. Leaves represent edges; an internal cluster is obtained by \(\operatorname{join}(A,B)\) when child clusters share exactly one admissible boundary, and \(\operatorname{split}\) reverses that join. The interface provides \(\operatorname{link}\), \(\operatorname{cut}\), and \(\operatorname{expose}(u,v)\), after which the cluster containing the \(u\)-to-\(v\) path has boundaries \(u,v\). If a cluster summary is recomputable from two child summaries in \(O(1)\) time, each forest update or exposure changes \(O(\log n)\) clusters and therefore costs \(O(\log n)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A top tree stores a forest as balanced one- or two-boundary clusters; link, cut, and expose modify logarithmically many clusters when summaries merge in constant time.
assumptions_latex: The cluster hierarchy has height \(O(\log n)\).
Each legal join, split, and summary recomputation costs \(O(1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{link}\), \(\operatorname{cut}\), and \(\operatorname{expose}\) require \(O(\log n)\) time.
review_flags: Supplied sources do not cover top trees, cluster legality, or exposure bounds.

children.title: Path–Cluster Interface Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Operation and augmentation tradeoffs between path-oriented and cluster-oriented interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Path–Cluster Interface Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts path exposure with bounded-boundary cluster decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a dynamic forest on \(n\) vertices, a path-oriented interface makes the unique path \(P(u,v)\) the primary aggregate object, whereas a cluster-oriented interface maintains summaries of connected subtrees with at most two boundary vertices. With constant-time summary composition and balanced auxiliary structures, both interfaces support link and cut in \(O(\log n)\) time. Path orientation directly supports associative ordered aggregates on \(P(u,v)\); cluster orientation additionally supports any statistic closed under legal boundary-cluster joins. The latter generality requires defining summaries for every permitted join type, while the former requires defining concatenation, reversal, and lazy actions on path sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Path interfaces simplify ordered path aggregates; cluster interfaces admit broader bounded-boundary subtree summaries but require more join cases. Balanced implementations give logarithmic forest updates.
assumptions_latex: Both representations remain balanced with height \(O(\log n)\).
All required path or cluster summary transformations take \(O(1)\) time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Forest updates cost \(O(\log n)\), with expressiveness determined respectively by path composition or legal cluster joins.

notation.meaning: unique path between connected vertices u and v

review_flags: The precise interface comparison and admissible summary classes need a dynamic-tree source.

children.title: Euler-Tour Tree Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Dynamic-forest access through maintained Euler-tour sequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Euler-Tour Tree Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence-based interface for dynamic-forest connectivity and component aggregates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each tree of a forest \(F\), store an Euler-tour occurrence sequence in a balanced split–join sequence structure. The interface supports \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\), \(\operatorname{link}(u,v)\), \(\operatorname{cut}(u,v)\), vertex or edge updates, and \(\operatorname{componentQuery}(v)\). Linking reroots two tour sequences and concatenates them with the new edge occurrences; cutting splits at the two occurrences of the deleted edge and rejoins the remaining pieces. Values duplicated across occurrences use a designated representative or compensated contribution. With constant-time sequence-summary composition, every operation costs \(O(\log n)\) time and component queries return the aggregate of the tree containing \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euler-tour trees encode each dynamic tree as a balanced sequence, giving logarithmic link, cut, connectivity, and component-aggregate operations, with explicit handling of duplicated occurrences.
assumptions_latex: Every link preserves acyclicity and every cut removes a present forest edge.
Sequence split, join, search, and summary recomputation take \(O(\log n)\) time in total per operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each update or query costs \(O(\log n)\) time and component aggregates are maintained correctly.

notation.meaning: aggregate over the tree containing v

children.title: Cluster-Tree Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Dynamic-forest access through hierarchical cluster representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Cluster-Tree Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic bounded-boundary cluster hierarchy for dynamic forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cluster-tree representation of a forest \(F\) is a rooted hierarchy whose leaves correspond to forest edges and whose nodes represent connected subgraphs. Each internal cluster \(C\) is the edge-disjoint union \(C=C_1\cup C_2\) of adjacent child clusters, and its boundary \(\partial C\) consists of vertices incident both to \(C\) and to edges outside \(C\). The interface permits only joins satisfying \(|\partial C|\le b\) for a fixed constant \(b\), stores a summary \(\sigma(C)=M(\sigma(C_1),\sigma(C_2))\), and supplies split and join primitives. A balanced hierarchy with constant-time \(M\) propagates any leaf change through \(O(\log n)\) summaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cluster tree recursively combines adjacent connected edge sets with bounded boundary, storing composable summaries so a local edge change affects logarithmically many balanced-hierarchy nodes.
assumptions_latex: The boundary bound \(b\) is constant.
The hierarchy is balanced and the merge map \(M\) takes \(O(1)\) time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A leaf update requires recomputation of \(O(\log n)\) cluster summaries.

children.title: Tour–Cluster Representation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Update, query, and augmentation distinctions between tour-based and cluster-based representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Tour–Cluster Representation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares sequence tours with bounded-boundary cluster representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An Euler-tour representation linearizes every tree component into a sequence and reduces structural updates to sequence splits and joins; consequently, any aggregate decomposable over tour intervals is directly maintainable. A cluster representation instead decomposes the tree into connected subgraphs with bounded boundary and directly maintains any summary closed under its legal cluster joins. Under balanced representations and constant-time summary composition, either approach processes a forest update through \(O(\log n)\) summary changes. Tour representations require accounting for repeated vertex and edge occurrences, whereas cluster representations require boundary-indexed states and multiple join types.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tours offer uniform sequence operations but duplicate occurrences; clusters avoid linearization and support boundary-aware summaries but require richer merge states. Balanced versions update logarithmically many summaries.
assumptions_latex: The tour sequence or cluster hierarchy has height \(O(\log n)\).
Every relevant summary merge takes \(O(1)\) time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either representation yields \(O(\log n)\) update propagation, subject to its distinct summary-encoding requirements.
review_flags: The comparative expressiveness claim requires a source treating both representation families.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits, but the claimed classes of directly maintainable summaries and the shared O(log n) propagation bound need a source comparing the two representation families.

children.title: Level-Based Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Dynamic decompositions organized by discrete levels or scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Based Hierarchies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested subgraph hierarchy indexed by discrete maintenance levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be dynamic and assign each edge a level \(\ell(e)\in\{0,\ldots,L\}\). For every \(i\), define \(E_{\ge i}=\{e\in E:\ell(e)\ge i\}\) and \(G_i=(V,E_{\ge i})\). Then \(G_{i+1}\subseteq G_i\), so every connected component of \(G_{i+1}\) lies in a unique component of \(G_i\); these components form a laminar hierarchy. An update interface changes edges and promotes or demotes selected edges while restoring specified level invariants. If \(L=O(\log n)\) and restoration touches bounded work per affected level, the hierarchical overhead per update is \(O(\log n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge levels induce nested subgraphs whose connected components form a laminar hierarchy. With logarithmically many levels and bounded repair per level, hierarchy overhead is logarithmic.
assumptions_latex: \(L=O(\log n)\).
The maintenance algorithm performs \(O(1)\) hierarchy work at each affected level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The components of \(G_0,\ldots,G_L\) are laminar and maintenance overhead is \(O(\log n)\) per update.

notation.meaning: subgraph induced by edges at level at least i

children.title: Cluster-Based Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Dynamic decompositions organized by nested graph clusters.

knowledge_statements.title: Cluster-Based Hierarchies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Laminar dynamic decomposition into bounded-size or bounded-boundary clusters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cluster-based hierarchy for a dynamic graph \(G\\) is a rooted laminar family \(\mathcal C\) containing singleton base objects and a root for each maintained component. Every nonleaf cluster is the disjoint union of its children and stores a summary determined by the children and their interface data. Fix thresholds \(s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_L\); a level-\(i\) cluster must satisfy the chosen size or boundary invariant at scale \(s_i\). After an update, violating clusters are split or adjacent clusters are merged until all invariants hold. If the hierarchy has height \(O(\log n)\) and only \(O(1)\) clusters change per level, repair changes \(O(\log n)\) summaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cluster hierarchy recursively groups graph objects at increasing scales. Local split-and-merge repairs affect logarithmically many summaries when height and changes per level are bounded.
assumptions_latex: The cluster family is laminar and has height \(O(\log n)\).
At most \(O(1)\) clusters are created, removed, or modified at each affected level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each graph update changes \(O(\log n)\) cluster summaries.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but the size-or-boundary invariant is not concretely specified or sourced. The fragment \(G\\\) is also malformed LaTeX and must be corrected when a sourced model is supplied.

children.title: Level–Cluster Coupling
children.top_down_role: Maintenance regimes linking level assignments to evolving cluster structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Level–Cluster Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility invariant linking discrete levels to laminar clusters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each maintained object \(x\) have a level \(\ell(x)\in\{0,ldots,L\}\), and let \(\mathcal C_i\) be the cluster partition at level \(i\). A level–cluster coupling is valid when: (i) \(\mathcal C_{i+1}\) refines \(\mathcal C_i\); (ii) every level-\(i\) object has all endpoints or incidences inside one cluster of \(\mathcal C_i\); and (iii) changing an object from level \(i\) to \(j\) invalidates summaries only on the ancestor chains of clusters containing that object between those levels. If each partition is represented by a height-\(O(\log n)\) cluster forest, one promotion or demotion affects \(O(|i-j|+\log n)\) cluster records.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Levels and clusters are coupled when higher-level partitions refine lower ones, each object is contained at its level, and level changes have localized ancestor-chain effects.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal C_i)_{i=0}^{L}\) consists of nested partitions.
Every cluster forest has height \(O(\log n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A level change from \(i\) to \(j\) affects \(O(|i-j|+\log n)\) cluster records.
review_flags: The taxonomy does not identify a canonical coupling convention or algorithm.
A source is needed to validate the stated locality bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits, but the coupling convention and O(|i-j|+log n) locality bound are not established. The domain \(\{0,ldots,L\}\) also contains a TeX typo and should be \(\{0,\ldots,L\}\).

children.title: Periodic Rebuilding Schedules
children.top_down_role: Scheduled reconstruction strategies for maintaining dynamic hierarchical structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Rebuilding Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amortized schedule for replacing a deteriorating dynamic representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a representation serve updates in time at most \(U(n)\) while its age \(a\), the number of updates since its last rebuild, satisfies \(a<B\). Initialize by building the representation in time \(P(n)\). After each update increment \(a\); when \(a=B\), rebuild the entire representation from the current instance and reset \(a=0\). Over any \(T\) updates, at most \(\lceil T/B\rceil\) rebuilds occur, so total time is \(O(TU(n)+(T/B+1)P(n))\). Thus the amortized update cost is \(O(U(n)+P(n)/B)\), although a rebuilding update may cost \(\Theta(P(n))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rebuild after every B updates. This adds rebuild cost divided by B to amortized update time, but an individual rebuilding update can still incur the full cost.
assumptions_latex: A fresh representation can be constructed in \(P(n)\) time.
The active representation remains correct for fewer than \(B\) intervening updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The amortized update cost is \(O(U(n)+P(n)/B)\), with worst-case rebuilding latency \(\Theta(P(n))\).
review_flags: No supplied source covers periodic rebuilding or its amortized accounting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits and the amortized accounting is plausible, but no source is cited. Moreover, a rebuild cost bounded above by P(n) supports O(P(n)) latency, not Theta(P(n)), unless a matching lower bound is assumed.

children.title: Deamortized Rebuilding
children.top_down_role: Techniques that distribute reconstruction work across updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Deamortized Rebuilding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental two-copy schedule converting periodic rebuild work into bounded latency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a full rebuild costs at most \(P(n)\) elementary steps and the active representation remains valid for \(B\) updates. Maintain an active copy and, at the start of each epoch, initialize a shadow copy for the epoch's target state. During every subsequent update, apply the update to the active copy, record or apply it to the shadow copy, and execute at most \(q=\lceil P(n)/B\rceil\) pending rebuild steps. At the epoch boundary, replay any bounded update backlog, verify the shadow timestamp, and atomically make it active. If synchronization costs \(O(q)\) per update, rebuilding adds worst-case \(O(P(n)/B)\) time rather than a single \(P(n)\)-time pause.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build a shadow copy incrementally, spending a fixed rebuild budget per update, then switch copies only after synchronizing all intervening updates. This bounds rebuilding latency per update.
assumptions_latex: The rebuild decomposes into at most \(P(n)\) resumable elementary steps.
The shadow copy can absorb or replay intervening updates within the per-update budget.
The active copy remains correct throughout the \(B\)-update epoch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case rebuilding overhead per update is \(O(P(n)/B)\).

notation.meaning: number of elementary steps in a full rebuild

review_flags: No supplied source supports the two-copy deamortization schedule.
Correctness depends on an application-specific synchronization mechanism.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but correctness and latency depend on an unspecified application-specific shadow-copy synchronization mechanism. Because q=ceil(P(n)/B), the stated O(P(n)/B) overhead also needs an assumption such as P(n)>=B or must retain the ceiling/additive constant.

children.title: Rebuilding Latency Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions among update latency, reconstruction frequency, and maintenance overhead.

assumptions_latex: \(B,L\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(L\ge 1\).
Rebuilding work is preemptible and divisible into unit operations.
After each update, the scheduler performs the prescribed rebuilding allocation whenever rebuilding work remains.
Buffered updates preserve correctness until rebuilding finishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{rebuild}}^{\mathrm{update}}\le \lceil B/L\rceil\), and the rebuilt representation is available within \(L\) updates.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary work-spreading bound under explicit divisibility and scheduling assumptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic incremental deamortization of a divisible rebuilding task.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose rebuilding a representation requires at most \(B\) unit operations and may be performed incrementally during the next \(L\ge 1\) updates. After each update, while work remains, let the scheduler execute the smaller of \(\lceil B/L\rceil\) and the number of remaining rebuilding operations. Then rebuilding finishes within \(L\) updates and contributes at most \(\lceil B/L\rceil\) worst-case work per update. For \(L'\ge L\), the corresponding scheduled load \(\lceil B/L'\rceil\) is no greater than \(\lceil B/L\rceil\), provided correctness is maintained meanwhile by the old representation together with an update buffer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning up to the prescribed positive share of divisible rebuilding work after every update completes rebuilding within the latency limit; allowing a larger limit weakly decreases the worst-case rebuilding work per update.

children.title: Dynamic Connectivity Certificates
children.top_down_role: Sparse maintained representations supporting connectivity queries under graph updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Connectivity Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact undirected connectivity certificates maintained under edge updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each time \(t\), let \(G_t=(V,E_t)\) be an undirected graph. A dynamic connectivity certificate is a maintained spanning forest \(F_t\subseteq E_t\) satisfying, for every \(u,v\in V\), \(u\) and \(v\) are connected in \((V,F_t)\) if and only if they are connected in \(G_t\). Its size is at most \(|V|-1\). The certificate is verifiable by checking that \((V,F_t)\) is a forest, every forest edge belongs to \(E_t\), and every edge of \(E_t\) has endpoints in one forest component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maintained spanning forest exactly records the connected components of every current graph and has at most one fewer edge than vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G_t=(V,E_t)\) is a finite undirected graph after each update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\leftrightarrow_{G_t}v\iff u\leftrightarrow_{(V,F_t)}v\) for all \(u,v\in V\), with \(|F_t|\le |V|-1\).

children.title: Dynamic Cut Certificates
children.top_down_role: Maintained sparse structures preserving cut information relevant to dynamic optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Cut Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact truncated cut certificates for unweighted undirected multigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer \(k\ge 1\). For each time \(t\), a subgraph \(H_t=(V,E'_t)\) of the unweighted undirected multigraph \(G_t=(V,E_t)\) is a dynamic \(k\)-cut certificate when every nonempty proper set \(S\subset V\) satisfies \(\min\{k,|\delta_{H_t}(S)|\}=\min\{k,|\delta_{G_t}(S)|\}\). Consequently, every cut of size less than \(k\) is preserved exactly, while every larger cut retains at least \(k\) certificate edges. The invariant must hold after each completed graph update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic k-cut certificate preserves every cut smaller than k exactly and retains at least k edges across every larger cut.
assumptions_latex: \(G_t\) is a finite unweighted undirected multigraph.
\(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(k\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{k,|\delta_{H_t}(S)|\}=\min\{k,|\delta_{G_t}(S)|\}\) for every \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\).

notation.meaning: edges of G with exactly one endpoint in S

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Cut functions and connectivity concepts p. 19

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Cut functions and connectivity concepts p. 19

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The truncated-cut equality is mathematically precise and the certificate kind fits the leaf, but the cited general section on cut functions and connectivity does not establish the exact k-cut-certificate invariant or its dynamic maintenance. A direct sparse-certificate source with a specific theorem or definition locator is required.

children.title: Certificate Update Coupling
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships between connectivity preservation and cut preservation during updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Update Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic coupling condition between graph updates and maintained certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C(G,H)\) denote the required certificate predicate. A graph-update procedure and certificate-maintenance procedure are update-coupled if every update \(\Delta_t\) induces a transition \((G_t,H_t)\mapsto(G_{t+1},H_{t+1})\) such that \(G_{t+1}=\Delta_t(G_t)\), \(H_{t+1}\subseteq G_{t+1}\), and \(C(G_{t+1},H_{t+1})\) holds before any query observes time \(t+1\). Intermediate states may be exposed only when they also satisfy the certificate predicate; otherwise the transition must be atomic with respect to queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph and certificate updates are coupled when every query-visible state contains a valid certificate for the corresponding current graph.
assumptions_latex: \(C(G_t,H_t)\) holds initially.
Updates and queries have a specified linearization order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(G_t,H_t)\) holds at every query-visible time \(t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly expresses query-visible invariant preservation and the condition kind fits the coupling leaf. No inspectable source supports the atomicity and linearization formulation, so the record must remain source-blocked.

children.title: Dynamic Graph Sparsifiers
children.top_down_role: Sparse dynamic representations preserving selected graph quantities.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Graph Sparsifiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic spectral sparsifiers of weighted undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_t=(V,E_t,w_t)\) be a weighted undirected graph with Laplacian \(L_{G_t}\). A dynamic \(\varepsilon\)-spectral sparsifier is a maintained weighted graph \(H_t\) on \(V\), usually with substantially fewer edges, such that after every update and for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\), \((1-\varepsilon)x^{\mathsf T}L_{G_t}x\le x^{\mathsf T}L_{H_t}x\le(1+\varepsilon)x^{\mathsf T}L_{G_t}x\). This quadratic-form condition simultaneously approximates all cuts because indicator vectors are admissible choices of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic spectral sparsifier is a sparse weighted graph whose Laplacian quadratic form approximates that of the current graph for every vector.
assumptions_latex: All edge weights are nonnegative.
\(0<\varepsilon<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1-\varepsilon)L_{G_t}\preceq L_{H_t}\preceq(1+\varepsilon)L_{G_t}\) after every update.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The spectral approximation invariant is standard and internally correct, and representation fits the leaf. However, no source is supplied, and the statement describes having substantially fewer edges only informally rather than giving a sourced sparsity requirement or bound. A direct dynamic spectral-sparsification definition is needed.

children.title: Dynamic Graph Spanners
children.top_down_role: Maintained sparse subgraphs offering controlled distance distortion.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Graph Spanners
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative spanners maintained for weighted undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each time \(t\), let \(G_t=(V,E_t,w_t)\) have nonnegative edge lengths. A dynamic \(\alpha\)-spanner is a maintained subgraph \(H_t=(V,E'_t,w_t|_{E'_t})\), where \(E'_t\subseteq E_t\), such that for all \(u,v\in V\), \(d_{G_t}(u,v)\le d_{H_t}(u,v)\le\alpha d_{G_t}(u,v)\), with infinite distances interpreted componentwise. The lower inequality follows from the subgraph requirement; the upper inequality is the stretch invariant that must hold after every update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic alpha-spanner is a maintained subgraph whose pairwise distances stretch current graph distances by at most alpha.
assumptions_latex: Edge lengths are nonnegative.
\(\alpha\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{G_t}(u,v)\le d_{H_t}(u,v)\le\alpha d_{G_t}(u,v)\) for every \(u,v\in V\) after each update.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The noncontractive multiplicative-distance inequalities follow correctly for a maintained subgraph with nonnegative lengths, and representation is the correct kind. No authoritative source or inspectable locator is supplied for the dynamic spanner definition.

children.title: Dynamic Graph Emulators
children.top_down_role: Maintained sparse surrogate graphs whose edges need not belong to the input graph.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Graph Emulators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noncontractive distance emulators maintained under graph updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each time \(t\), a dynamic \(\alpha\)-emulator of a nonnegatively weighted graph \(G_t=(V,E_t,w_t)\) is a maintained weighted graph \(H_t=(V,F_t,\ell_t)\) whose edges need not belong to \(E_t\), and which satisfies \(d_{G_t}(u,v)\le d_{H_t}(u,v)\le\alpha d_{G_t}(u,v)\) for every \(u,v\in V\). Unlike a spanner, an emulator may use auxiliary edges between original vertices, but their weights must preserve the stated global noncontraction and stretch inequalities after every update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic emulator preserves all current graph distances within multiplicative stretch while allowing maintained edges absent from the original graph.
assumptions_latex: Graph and emulator edge lengths are nonnegative.
\(\alpha\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{G_t}\le d_{H_t}\le\alpha d_{G_t}\) pointwise on \(V\times V\) after every update.

notation.meaning: emulator edge set, not necessarily contained in the graph

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated noncontractive multiplicative emulator invariant is coherent and representation fits the leaf. Emulator conventions vary, including multiplicative-additive guarantees and restrictions on auxiliary-edge weights, so the selected convention requires a direct authoritative source.

children.title: Local Exchange Repair
children.top_down_role: Solution repair based on bounded local substitutions after an update.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Exchange Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-radius exchange repair for a changing finite feasible family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite ground set \(U\), a new feasible family \(\mathcal F_t\subseteq2^U\), objective \(f_t\), previous solution \(S_{t-1}\), and radius \(r\), initialize \(S\leftarrow S_{t-1}\). Repeatedly choose \(S'\in\mathcal F_t\) with \(|S\triangle S'|\le r\) that strictly improves \(f_t\), preferring a feasible repair when \(S\notin\mathcal F_t\), and set \(S\leftarrow S'\). Stop when \(S\in\mathcal F_t\) and no improving feasible radius-\(r\) exchange exists; report failure if no permitted move can restore feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local exchange repair repeatedly changes at most r elements until the updated solution is feasible and locally optimal, or reports that such repair fails.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(\mathcal F_t\) are finite.
Objective comparisons and feasibility tests are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Satisfaction on success: \(S\in\mathcal F_t\) and \(f_t(S')\ge f_t(S)\) for every \(S'\in\mathcal F_t\) with \(|S\triangle S'|\le r\), for minimization.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: abstract bounded-neighborhood local-search repair scheme

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the appropriate kind, but the procedure requires every feasible repair move from an infeasible state to strictly improve the objective. A feasible radius-r repair can therefore exist yet be incorrectly rejected when it does not improve the objective value of the infeasible incumbent. A problem-class-specific source is needed to determine the intended feasibility and improvement ordering before the algorithm can be corrected reliably.

children.title: Augmentation-Based Repair
children.top_down_role: Solution improvement through maintained augmenting structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Augmentation-Based Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repair through improving augmentations in a finite state-transition system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_t\) be the updated feasible states, let \(z_{t-1}\) be the previous state, and let \(\mathcal A_t(z)\) be the admissible augmentations from \(z\). Initialize \(z\leftarrow z_{t-1}\). While \(z\notin\mathcal F_t\) or an objective-improving augmentation exists, select \(a\in\mathcal A_t(z)\), replace \(z\leftarrow z\oplus a\), and require either a strict decrease of a nonnegative infeasibility measure or, once feasible, a strict objective improvement. Stop at a feasible state with no improving augmentation; report failure if infeasibility remains and no admissible augmentation exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augmentation repair follows admissible improving transitions, first eliminating infeasibility and then improving the objective until no augmentation remains.
assumptions_latex: The state space is finite.
Each selected augmentation strictly decreases infeasibility or strictly improves the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure terminates at \(z\in\mathcal F_t\) with no improving \(a\in\mathcal A_t(z)\), or returns a repair-failure certificate.

notation.meaning: state obtained by applying augmentation a

children.title: Exchange–Augmentation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem settings favoring exchange repair, augmentation repair, or their coordinated use.

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange–Augmentation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal regime separating bounded exchange repair from general augmentation repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an updated feasible family \(\mathcal F_t\), previous solution \(S_{t-1}\), and exchange bound \(r\). The update lies in the local-exchange regime if some \(S_t\in\mathcal F_t\) satisfies \(|S_t\triangle S_{t-1}|\le r\). It lies in the augmentation regime relative to an augmentation system \(\mathcal A_t\) if no such bounded exchange exists but a finite sequence \(a_1,\ldots,a_q\) yields a feasible state from \(S_{t-1}\). If neither condition holds, the specified repair system cannot repair the update without rebuilding or enlarging its move set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An update is locally exchange-repairable within radius r, augmentation-repairable only through a move sequence, or unrepairable by the specified moves.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_t\subseteq2^U\) is the updated feasible family.
The exchange radius and augmentation system are fixed before classification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly the stated predicates determine bounded-exchange repairability, augmentation repairability, or failure relative to the chosen move system.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formal classification induced by two specified repair neighborhoods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is a plausible kind for this classification leaf, but the action of the augmentation sequence on the state is not formally specified, and the terminology and boundary between the two regimes are unsupported. A source is needed before choosing a reliable formal version.

children.title: Warm-Start Reoptimization
children.top_down_role: Reuse of previously maintained solutions as starting points after updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Start Reoptimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-simplex warm start after changing an LP right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the updated linear program \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b',\ x\ge0\}\). Input a basis \(B\) that was optimal before the right-hand-side change and remains dual feasible, meaning its reduced costs satisfy \(\bar c_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\ge0\). Initialize \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b'\). While some basic component is negative, perform a dual-simplex pivot that preserves \(\bar c_N\ge0\) and removes primal infeasibility. Stop when \(x_B\ge0\); then output the resulting basis and basic solution, or declare infeasibility when the ratio test admits no entering variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After a right-hand-side change, dual simplex reuses the old dual-feasible basis and pivots only until primal feasibility is restored.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular.
The old basis remains dual feasible for the updated linear program.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the procedure reaches \(x_B\ge0\) while preserving \(\bar c_N\ge0\), the resulting basic solution is optimal for the updated program.

children.title: Dual-Solution Repair
children.top_down_role: Maintenance or restoration of dual solution information after instance changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Solution Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate primal–dual repair certificate for an updated linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the updated primal program \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and dual program \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}\), a repaired pair \((x',y')\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal primal–dual certificate when \(Ax'=b\), \(x'\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y'\le c\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}x'-b^{\mathsf T}y'\le\varepsilon\). These conditions are directly checkable. Weak duality then places the updated optimum between the two displayed objective values, so the repaired primal solution has additive error at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A repaired feasible primal–dual pair with gap at most epsilon certifies that the updated primal solution is epsilon-optimal.
assumptions_latex: The updated primal and dual programs are feasible.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le c^{\mathsf T}x'-\operatorname{OPT}\le c^{\mathsf T}x'-b^{\mathsf T}y'\le\varepsilon\).

children.title: Bounded-Recourse Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Limits on how much a maintained solution may change per update.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Recourse Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case and amortized recourse for repairing a feasible discrete solution after each update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_0,I_1,\ldots,I_T\) be instances and let \(S_t\) be the feasible solution output after update \(t\). For a prescribed edit metric \(d\), an algorithm has worst-case recourse \(r\) if \[d(S_{t-1},S_t)\le r\qquad(1\le t\le T).\] It has amortized recourse \(r\) if \[\sum_{t=1}^{T}d(S_{t-1},S_t)\le rT.\] For set-valued solutions, the standard unit-edit convention is \(d(A,B)=|A\mathbin{\triangle}B|\). A bounded-recourse guarantee must hold together with the stated feasibility and approximation guarantees for every permitted update sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse bounds how many solution elements may change per update, either individually or in total, while preserving feasibility and the claimed solution quality.
assumptions_latex: \(S_t\) is feasible for \(I_t\) after every permitted update.
The edit metric \(d\) and update model are fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(S_{t-1},S_t)\le r\) worst-case, or \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}d(S_{t-1},S_t)\le rT\) amortized.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The worst-case and amortized formulas are coherent and fit the bounded-recourse leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied for the recourse convention, edit metric, or requirement that recourse accompany feasibility and approximation guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjoint-Set Union Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Union-by-rank disjoint-set union with path compression for incremental connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite vertex set \(V\), initialize \(\operatorname{parent}(v)=v\) and rank zero for every \(v\in V\). The operation \(\operatorname{Find}(v)\) follows parent pointers to a root, makes every visited vertex point directly to that root, and returns it. The operation \(\operatorname{Union}(u,v)\) computes the two roots and, when they differ, attaches the lower-rank root below the higher-rank root, breaking equal-rank ties arbitrarily and incrementing the surviving root's rank. After any sequence of unions, \(u\) and \(v\) belong to the same represented block exactly when \(\operatorname{Find}(u)=\operatorname{Find}(v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint-set union maintains a partition under merges; two vertices are connected exactly when their find operations return the same representative.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and elements are introduced before union operations.
The partition evolves only by merging blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) and \(v\) share a block if and only if \(\operatorname{Find}(u)=\operatorname{Find}(v)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and partition invariant are standard and correctly stated, and algorithm is the appropriate content kind, but the record has no citation with an inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Spanning-Forest Maintenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Insertion-only maintenance of a spanning forest using disjoint-set union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(F=(V,\varnothing)\) and a disjoint-set structure with one set per vertex. Upon insertion of an undirected edge \(e=\{u,v\}\), compare \(\operatorname{Find}(u)\) and \(\operatorname{Find}(v)\). If they differ, add \(e\) to \(F\) and execute \(\operatorname{Union}(u,v)\); otherwise leave \(F\) unchanged. After every insertion, \(F\) is acyclic and, for every connected component \(C\) of the current graph, the restriction \(F[C]\) is a spanning tree of \(C\). A connectivity query returns true exactly when the two queried vertices have equal representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insert an edge into the forest exactly when it joins two previously disconnected components; the maintained forest spans every current component.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, undirected, and subject only to edge insertions.
All vertices are known when the structure is initialized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After every insertion, \(F\) is a spanning forest of the current graph.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Spanning Trees and Arborescences p. 133
