knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Forest Replacement Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replacement-edge search after deletion of a maintained forest edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a spanning forest \(F\) of an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\). Deleting a nonforest edge removes it from \(E\) only. Deleting a forest edge \(f\) splits one tree of \(F\) into vertex sets \(A\) and \(B\). Search the remaining edges for an edge \(e\in E\setminus F\) having one endpoint in \(A\) and the other in \(B\). If such an edge is found, link its endpoints by adding \(e\) to \(F\); if none exists, retain the two trees. The resulting \(F\) is again a spanning forest, and the split represents a genuine graph disconnection exactly when the search finds no crossing edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After a tree-edge deletion, search the induced cut for a surviving nonforest edge; link it if found, otherwise preserve the component split.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
Before deletion, \(F\) is a spanning forest of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The repaired \(F\) is a spanning forest, and no replacement exists exactly when no remaining edge crosses \((A,B)\).

notation.meaning: cut created by deleting a forest edge

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The replacement-edge procedure is mathematically correct for a finite undirected graph and fits the algorithm leaf, but no inspectable source supports the fully dynamic replacement-search formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic level-based framework for fully dynamic connectivity in undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed vertex set of size \(n\), the Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup framework maintains connectivity under arbitrary undirected edge insertions and deletions by assigning edges to logarithmically many levels, maintaining nested spanning forests with dynamic-tree operations, and promoting edges when replacement searches fail at lower levels. With the framework's size invariants, a deterministic implementation uses \(O(\log ^2 n)\) amortized time per update and answers connectivity queries in \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) worst-case time, while using near-linear space. These bounds concern the word-RAM/pointer-machine implementation specified by the original framework and require exact maintenance of its level invariants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The HDLT level hierarchy supports deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with logarithmic-squared amortized updates and sublogarithmic-over-loglog connectivity queries.
assumptions_latex: The graph is undirected with a fixed set of \(n\) vertices.
Updates insert or delete one edge at a time.
The prescribed level and forest invariants are maintained exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Updates take \(O(\log ^2 n)\) amortized time and connectivity queries take \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) worst-case time.

notation.meaning: maintained forest at hierarchy level i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated update and query bounds are plausible HDLT bounds, but the original theorem or another authoritative source is required to verify the precise computational model, worst-case versus amortized qualifications, and the unspecified near-linear space claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Cutset Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-sketch recovery of an outgoing edge from a dynamically maintained component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign each dynamic edge an identifier and maintain, for every vertex, a linear turnstile sketch of its incident-edge vector with opposite endpoint signs. Summing the vertex sketches over a component \(C\) cancels edges internal to \(C\) and yields a sketch supported precisely on the cut \(\delta(C)\). Apply an \(\ell_0\)-sampling decoder to this aggregate: if \(\delta(C)\ne\varnothing\), it returns an edge of \(\delta(C)\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\); if the cut is empty, it reports empty. Independent repetitions reduce the failure probability, subject to the randomness and adaptivity model stated for the decoder.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear component sketches cancel internal edges and probabilistically recover an outgoing edge whenever the component cut is nonempty.
assumptions_latex: Edge updates follow the decoder's supported turnstile model.
The sampling randomness satisfies the stated oblivious- or adaptive-adversary convention.
The decoder failure parameter obeys \(0<\delta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonempty cut yields a crossing edge with probability at least \(1-\delta\), while an empty cut is reported empty.

notation.meaning: edges with exactly one endpoint in C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cancellation mechanism is plausible, but the exact turnstile sketch, empty-cut behavior, success probability, repetition rule, and oblivious-versus-adaptive adversary guarantee depend on a particular decoder construction. No source selects or supports that construction.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Edge-Biconnectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic maintenance of pairwise two-edge-connectivity under graph updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected multigraph \(G_t=(V,E_t)\), the dynamic edge-biconnectivity problem maintains, after each permitted edge insertion or deletion, the predicate \(B_t(u,v)\) for distinct vertices \(u,v\in V\). It is defined by \[B_t(u,v)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G_t\text{ contains two edge-disjoint }u\text{--}v\text{ paths}.\] Equivalently, \(B_t(u,v)=1\) exactly when deleting any single edge leaves \(u\) and \(v\) connected. A query must return this predicate for the current graph; a component-reporting variant maintains the maximal vertex blocks induced by the relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain whether two current vertices have two edge-disjoint connecting paths, equivalently whether one edge deletion can separate them.
assumptions_latex: \(G_t\) is a finite undirected multigraph.
Queries concern distinct vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_t(u,v)=1\) exactly when no single-edge deletion separates \(u\) from \(v\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Vertex-Biconnectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic maintenance of pairwise two-vertex-connectivity under graph updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G_t=(V,E_t)\), the dynamic vertex-biconnectivity problem maintains, after each permitted edge insertion or deletion, the predicate \(B_t^{V}(u,v)\) for distinct vertices \(u,v\in V\). It is defined by \[B_t^{V}(u,v)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G_t\text{ contains two internally vertex-disjoint }u\text{--}v\text{ paths}.\] For nonadjacent \(u,v\), this is equivalent to saying that deleting any third vertex leaves them connected. A query returns the predicate in the current graph; block-reporting variants additionally maintain the corresponding biconnected blocks and articulation vertices.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Higher-Order Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized dynamic maintenance of connectivity thresholds above two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer \(k\ge 3\) and a mode \(\sigma\in\{\mathrm{edge},\mathrm{vertex}\}\). For each current finite undirected graph \(G_t\), define \(Q_{t,k}^{\sigma}(u,v)=1\) when there exist at least \(k\) pairwise edge-disjoint \(u\)-to-\(v\) paths if \(\sigma=\mathrm{edge}\), or at least \(k\) internally vertex-disjoint such paths if \(\sigma=\mathrm{vertex}\). The dynamic higher-order connectivity problem maintains this predicate under the specified graph updates. By the corresponding form of Menger's theorem, the predicate is equivalent to every admissible separating cut having cardinality at least \(k\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{t,k}^{\sigma}(u,v)=1\) exactly when the corresponding minimum separating cut has size at least \(k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Minimum Spanning Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle-exchange maintenance of a minimum spanning forest under edge insertions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a minimum spanning forest \(T\) of the current finite weighted undirected graph. When \(e=\{u,v\}\) is inserted, add it to \(T\) if \(u\) and \(v\) lie in different trees. Otherwise, let \(P_T(u,v)\) be their unique tree path and choose a maximum-weight edge \(f\) on that path. If \(w(e)<w(f)\), set \(T\leftarrow T-f+e\); otherwise retain \(T\). Under a fixed deterministic tie convention, an optional equality exchange may be used consistently. After the update, \(T\) is a minimum spanning forest of the augmented graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On insertion, join different components or replace a heaviest edge on the induced tree cycle when the new edge is lighter.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, undirected, and edge-weighted.
Updates only insert edges.
Before insertion, \(T\) is a minimum spanning forest.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After processing \(e\), \(T\) is a minimum spanning forest of the augmented graph.

notation.meaning: unique forest path between the endpoints

knowledge_statements.title: Decremental Minimum Spanning Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-replacement maintenance of a minimum spanning forest under edge deletions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a minimum spanning forest \(T\) of the current finite weighted undirected graph. When an edge \(e\) is deleted, leave \(T\) unchanged if \(e\notin T\). If \(e\in T\), removing it partitions its former tree into vertex sets \(A\) and \(B\). Among all remaining graph edges crossing \((A,B)\), choose an edge \(f\) of minimum weight and set \(T\leftarrow T-e+f\). If no crossing edge exists, set \(T\leftarrow T-e\). With any fixed tie convention, the resulting \(T\) is a minimum spanning forest of the graph after deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting a non-tree edge changes nothing; deleting a tree edge requires the lightest surviving edge across the resulting cut, if one exists.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, undirected, and edge-weighted.
Updates only delete edges.
Before deletion, \(T\) is a minimum spanning forest.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After deleting \(e\) and applying the replacement rule, \(T\) is a minimum spanning forest.

notation.meaning: cut created by deleting a forest edge

children.title: One-Sided Update Asymmetry
children.top_down_role: Structural differences between insertion-only and deletion-only maintenance.

assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, undirected, and edge-weighted.
Immediately before the update, \(T\) is a minimum spanning forest.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An insertion between distinct components joins their trees; an insertion within one component reduces to a path-maximum exchange; and deletion of a tree edge reduces to a cut-minimum replacement search.

notation.meaning: tree path exposed by an insertion within one component

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a minimum spanning forest immediately before a single edge update. If an inserted edge \(e=\{u,v\}\) joins distinct trees of \(T\), repair consists of adding \(e\). If \(u\) and \(v\) already lie in the same tree, insertion can invalidate optimality only on the unique cycle formed by \(T+e\), so repair requires a maximum-weight query on \(P_T(u,v)\). Deleting a tree edge \(f\), by contrast, creates a cut \((A,B)\), so repair requires finding a minimum-weight surviving graph edge crossing that cut; deleting a non-tree edge requires no repair. Thus an insertion within a component is localized to one maintained-tree path, whereas deletion repair searches among non-tree edges crossing a dynamically created cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An insertion between components simply joins their trees; an insertion within a component uses a maximum edge on one tree path, while deletion of a tree edge needs a minimum surviving edge across a newly exposed cut.

assumptions_latex: \(G_t=(V,E_t)\) is a finite connected undirected graph after every update.
Each edge \(e\in E_t\) has a real weight \(w_t(e)\); updates may insert or delete edges and may change weights.

notation.meaning: Total weight of an edge set

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(T_0\) as a minimum spanning tree of \(G_0\). After each insertion, deletion, or weight change, update the maintained edge set to a tree \(T_t\subseteq E_t\) satisfying
\[
|T_t|=|V|-1,\qquad (V,T_t)\text{ is connected},\qquad w_t(T_t)=\min\{w_t(S):S\subseteq E_t,\ (V,S)\text{ is a spanning tree}\}.
\]
A query returns \(T_t\), its weight, or membership of a requested edge. Exactness requires the displayed equality after every update, including when the identity of the optimum changes.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize with a spanning tree \(T_0\) of \(G_0\). Following every edge insertion, deletion, or weight change, output a spanning tree \(T_t\subseteq E_t\) such that
\[
w_t(T_t)\le \alpha\min\{w_t(S):S\subseteq E_t,\ (V,S)\text{ is a spanning tree}\}.
\]
Since every spanning tree has weight at least the minimum, this is equivalently \(\operatorname{MST}(G_t)\le w_t(T_t)\le\alpha\operatorname{MST}(G_t)\). Queries may return \(T_t\), its weight, or edge membership; the guarantee must hold after each completed update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain under edge insertions, deletions, and weight changes a current spanning tree whose weight is at most alpha times the current optimum.

children.title: Accuracy–Update Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between approximation quality and dynamic maintenance cost.

assumptions_latex: Two fully dynamic MST algorithms are evaluated under the same update sequence, computation model, and probability convention.
Algorithm \(i\) guarantees approximation factor \(\alpha_i\) and update bound \(U_i(n,m)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One regime dominates another exactly when it is no worse in both approximation and update cost, and strictly better in at least one.

notation.meaning: Current numbers of vertices and edges

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:Pareto comparison is the canonical formalization of an accuracy-update tradeoff.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto comparison of approximation and update cost; it asserts no particular achievable bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \((n,m)\), regime \(1\) weakly dominates regime \(2\) when
\[
\alpha_1\le\alpha_2\quad\text{and}\quad U_1(n,m)\le U_2(n,m),
\]
with at least one strict inequality for strict dominance. A pair \((\alpha,U)\) is Pareto-optimal within a specified algorithm class if no attainable pair strictly dominates it. Thus exact maintenance is the endpoint \(\alpha=1\), while allowing \(\alpha>1\) enlarges the admissible class but does not by itself imply a smaller update bound; such an improvement requires a separate algorithmic upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accuracy and update time form a Pareto tradeoff: a regime dominates another only if it is no worse in both coordinates and better in one.

children.title: Reachability Update Asymmetry
children.top_down_role: Differences in structure, guarantees, and failure boundaries across one-sided update regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(R_t\) denotes exact reachability in a directed graph on a fixed vertex set.
An incremental sequence inserts one arc per step, whereas a decremental sequence deletes one arc per step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Incremental reachability relations grow monotonically, while decremental reachability relations shrink monotonically.

notation.meaning: Reachability pairs newly created by an insertion
Reachability pairs destroyed by a deletion

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:Reachability monotonicity follows directly from path preservation under edge addition and path loss under deletion.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural asymmetry only; no separation between incremental and decremental complexity is claimed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under an insertion, every previously existing directed path survives, so
\[
R_{t-1}\subseteq R_t,
\qquad
R_t=R_{t-1}\cup\Delta_t^+.
\]
Under a deletion, no new directed path can be created, so
\[
R_t\subseteq R_{t-1},
\qquad
R_t=R_{t-1}\setminus\Delta_t^-.
\]
Consequently an incremental algorithm only adds reachability facts, whereas a decremental algorithm only invalidates them. This monotonic asymmetry permits different maintenance invariants, but it does not alone establish unequal asymptotic update bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insertions can only add reachable pairs, whereas deletions can only remove them; this structural asymmetry supports different maintenance strategies.
knowledge_statements.title: Reachability Update Asymmetry

Initialize a Boolean matrix \(C_0\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) from \(G_0\). After every arc insertion or deletion, update it so that

(C_t)_{uv}=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u=v\text{ or there exists a directed path from }u\text{ to }v\text{ in }G_t.

A query on \((u,v)\) returns \((C_t)_{uv}\); alternatively, the algorithm may output the whole matrix. The update sequence is fully dynamic because either operation type may occur in arbitrary order, and correctness is required after each completed operation.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}\) encodes a directed graph over a field \(\mathbb F\), with indeterminate \(x\).
The inverse is interpreted over the rational-function field \(\mathbb F(x)\), or as a formal power series.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reachability is represented by nonzero entries of \((I-xA)^{-1}\), and a single-edge change is a rank-one matrix update.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:The resolvent expansion and rank-one inverse update are standard algebraic representations for dynamic reachability.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic walk encoding and rank-one inverse maintenance; cancellation-sensitive implementations require additional conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The identity
\[
M=(I-xA)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}x^kA^k
\]
encodes directed walks: when coefficients do not cancel, \(M_{uv}\ne0\) exactly when some directed walk joins \(u\) to \(v\). Changing arc \((i,j)\) by weight \(\delta\) replaces \(I-xA\) by \(I-xA-x\delta e_i e_j^{\mathsf T}\). Whenever the denominator is nonzero, its inverse is updated by
\[
M'=M+\frac{x\delta}{1-x\delta e_j^{\mathsf T}Me_i}Me_i e_j^{\mathsf T}M.
\]

after every deletion. Each vertex level rises at most \(n\) times and each rise scans its incident edges, giving total update time \(O(mn)\), space \(O(m+n)\), and query time \(O(1)\).

children.top_down_role: Reuse and repair of single-source distance information after insertions.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with nonnegative edge weights and known exact source distances \(d(v)\).
A new arc \((a,b)\) of weight \(w\ge0\) is inserted.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Retain all old labels and set
\[
d(b)\leftarrow\min\{d(b),d(a)+w\}.
\]
If this decreases \(d(b)\), insert \(b\) into a min-priority queue. Repeatedly extract a vertex \(u\) of minimum label and relax every outgoing arc \((u,v)\) by \(d(v)\leftarrow\min\{d(v),d(u)+w(u,v)\}\), updating the queue after each decrease. Stop when the queue is empty and output all labels. With nonnegative weights, the resulting labels equal the exact distances from \(s\) in the augmented graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After inserting an edge, seed any improved endpoint distance and propagate decreases with shortest-path relaxations until all exact source distances are restored.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Distance Reoptimization

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2 A Generic Shortest Path Algorithm p. 57
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

children.title: Approximate Dynamic Distances
children.top_down_role: Approximate distance maintenance within dynamic single-source settings.

assumptions_latex: \(G_t\) is a graph with nonnegative edge weights and source \(s\).
The approximation factor is \(\alpha\ge1\), with unreachable vertices assigned \(\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each reported finite label is an upper estimate within factor \(\alpha\) of the current exact source distance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided multiplicative approximation for dynamic single-source distances.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 A Generic Shortest Path Algorithm p. 57
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A dynamic label vector \(\widetilde d_t\) is an \(\alpha\)-approximation to current single-source distances when, after every permitted update and for every \(v\in V\),
\[
\operatorname{dist}_{G_t}(s,v)\le \widetilde d_t(v)\le \alpha\operatorname{dist}_{G_t}(s,v).
\]
The conventions are \(\widetilde d_t(s)=0\) and \(\widetilde d_t(v)=\infty\) exactly when \(v\) is unreachable from \(s\). A query returns \(\widetilde d_t(v)\). For randomized maintenance, the probability with which all required inequalities hold must be stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alpha-approximate dynamic distance estimate never understates the true distance and never exceeds alpha times it.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Dynamic Distances

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2 A Generic Shortest Path Algorithm p. 57
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

children.title: Approximation Under Insertions
children.top_down_role: Accuracy and update-cost tradeoffs specific to insertion-only distance maintenance.

assumptions_latex: \(G_t\) has nonnegative edge weights and evolves only through edge insertions.
Before update \(t\), labels satisfy a multiplicative \(\alpha\)-approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Old upper estimates remain upper bounds after insertion, but must be decreased wherever the factor-\(\alpha\) inequality fails.

notation.meaning: Exact source distance after update t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:Distance monotonicity under edge insertion and its consequence for multiplicative upper estimates are direct and unambiguous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity constraint governing approximate source-distance maintenance under insertions.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 A Generic Shortest Path Algorithm p. 57
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An insertion preserves every old path, hence
\[
d_t(v)\le d_{t-1}(v)
\]
for every \(v\in V\). Consequently retaining \(\widetilde d_{t-1}(v)\) cannot violate the upper-bound condition \(d_t(v)\le\widetilde d_{t-1}(v)\), but it may violate
\[
\widetilde d_{t-1}(v)\le\alpha d_t(v).
\]
An incremental \(\alpha\)-approximate reoptimization procedure must therefore propagate label decreases until \(d_t(v)\le\widetilde d_t(v)\le\alpha d_t(v)\) holds for every vertex, while labels of unaffected vertices may remain unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Insertions only decrease true distances; old estimates stay upper bounds but may need reductions to remain within the approximation factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Under Insertions

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2 A Generic Shortest Path Algorithm p. 57
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

children.title: Exact Dynamic All-Pairs Distances
children.top_down_role: Exact maintenance of distances across every ordered or unordered vertex pair.

assumptions_latex: Each snapshot \(G_t=(V,E_t,w_t)\) is finite and has well-defined shortest-path distances.
An update transforms \(G_{t-1}\) into \(G_t\) before any query at time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every answer equals \(d_{G_t}(u,v)\), including the value \(+\infty\) for unreachable pairs.

notation.meaning: Shortest-path distance in the current snapshot

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: dynamic lifting of the standard exact all-pairs shortest-path specification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness is required after every completed update; preprocessing and update costs are unrestricted here.

source_refs.locator: Section 7.2. Shortest Paths Between All Pairs of Vertices p. 165

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a sequence of graph snapshots \(G_0,G_1,\ldots\), an exact dynamic all-pairs distance structure maintains, after every completed update at time \(t\), a matrix \(D_t\in(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\})^{V\times V}\) satisfying
\[
D_t[u,v]=d_{G_t}(u,v)\qquad\text{for all }(u,v)\in V\times V.
\]
Here \(d_{G_t}(u,v)\) is the minimum weight of a directed \(u\)-to-\(v\) path, or \(+\infty\) if no such path exists. A query \((u,v)\) returns \(D_t[u,v]\) without approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After each graph update, the structure must return the current shortest-path distance for every ordered vertex pair, with infinity for unreachable pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Dynamic All-Pairs Distances

source_witnesses.locator: Section 7.2. Shortest Paths Between All Pairs of Vertices p. 165

children.title: Approximate Dynamic All-Pairs Distances
children.top_down_role: Approximate maintenance of distances across all vertex pairs.

assumptions_latex: Every current distance \(d_{G_t}(u,v)\) is well-defined in \(\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
Parameters satisfy \(\alpha\ge 1\) and \(\beta\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every reachable ordered pair, estimates satisfy \(d_{G_t}(u,v)\le \widetilde d_t(u,v)\le \alpha d_{G_t}(u,v)+\beta\), while unreachable pairs receive \(+\infty\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional noncontractive multiplicative-additive distance guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a noncontractive multiplicative-additive guarantee for nonnegative snapshot distances after each completed update.

source_refs.locator: Section 7.2. Shortest Paths Between All Pairs of Vertices p. 165

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An approximate dynamic all-pairs distance structure with guarantee \((\alpha,\beta)\) returns, after each completed update producing \(G_t\), an estimate \(\widetilde d_t(u,v)\) for every ordered pair \((u,v)\in V\times V\). For every pair with \(d_{G_t}(u,v)<+\infty\), it satisfies
\[
d_{G_t}(u,v)\le \widetilde d_t(u,v)\le \alpha d_{G_t}(u,v)+\beta.
\]
For an unreachable pair it returns \(+\infty\). The special case \((\alpha,\beta)=(1,0)\) is exact dynamic all-pairs distance maintenance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After each update, every reachable-pair estimate lies between the nonnegative true distance and its prescribed multiplicative-additive upper bound, while unreachable pairs receive infinity.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Dynamic All-Pairs Distances

source_witnesses.locator: Section 7.2. Shortest Paths Between All Pairs of Vertices p. 165

children.title: All-Pairs Accuracy Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Relationships among approximation quality, query support, and update cost.

assumptions_latex: All compared structures operate on the same update model, graph class, and query sequence.
Resource costs are compared under a common computation and amortization convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\mathcal F_{\alpha,\beta}\) is the feasible algorithm class, then \(\mathcal F_{\alpha_1,\beta_1}\subseteq\mathcal F_{\alpha_2,\beta_2}\) whenever \(\alpha_1\le\alpha_2\) and \(\beta_1\le\beta_2\).

notation.meaning: Algorithms satisfying a specified accuracy guarantee
Preprocessing, update, query, and space resource vector

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: relaxation enlarges the feasible algorithm class but does not imply a particular complexity improvement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes monotonicity of feasible accuracy regimes, not a specific dynamic APSP lower or upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F_{\alpha,\beta}\) contain all dynamic all-pairs structures satisfying the noncontractive \((\alpha,eta)\) guarantee in a fixed model. If \(1\le\alpha_1\le\alpha_2\) and \(0\le\beta_1\le\beta_2\), then
\[
\mathcal F_{\alpha_1,\beta_1}\subseteq\mathcal F_{\alpha_2,\beta_2}.
\]
Consequently, for any coordinatewise resource objective \(R\), relaxing accuracy cannot increase the optimal attainable resource vector: \(\inf_{A\in\mathcal F_{\alpha_2,\beta_2}}R(A)\preceq\inf_{A\in\mathcal F_{\alpha_1,\beta_1}}R(A)\), whenever these infima are defined. The inclusion alone gives no strict improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weaker accuracy requirements enlarge the feasible algorithm class, so optimal resource costs cannot worsen, although they need not improve strictly.
knowledge_statements.title: All-Pairs Accuracy Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasible-class inclusion is mathematically plausible, but the statement has no citation, uses eta instead of beta, and invokes an infimum of resource vectors under a partial order without defining the optimization convention sufficiently. A dynamic accuracy-tradeoff source and a precise resource-order formulation are required.

children.title: Dynamic Distance Oracles
children.top_down_role: Maintained data structures supporting distance queries under graph updates.

assumptions_latex: Updates and queries are processed online in temporal order.
The current graph snapshot has well-defined distances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maintained state answers each current-pair query with the stipulated exact or approximate distance value.

notation.meaning: Internal maintained state after update t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: online data-structure definition separated into update state and query map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An oracle stores arbitrary state and exposes pair-distance queries rather than an explicit graph representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A dynamic distance oracle consists of an initial state \(S_0\), an update map producing \(S_t=U(S_{t-1},\Delta_t)\), and a query map \(Q\). After update \(\Delta_t\) changes the current graph to \(G_t\), a pair query returns
\[
Q(S_t,u,v)=\widetilde d_t(u,v).
\]
The value is exact when \(\widetilde d_t(u,v)=d_{G_t}(u,v)\); it is an \((\alpha,eta)\)-approximation when \(d_{G_t}(u,v)\le\widetilde d_t(u,v)\le\alpha d_{G_t}(u,v)+\beta\) for every reachable pair, with \(+\infty\) returned for unreachable pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic distance oracle updates arbitrary internal state and answers pair-distance queries for the current graph, exactly or within a stated approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Distance Oracles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oracle formulation fits the leaf, but no source is supplied and the approximation guarantee refers to an undefined eta parameter instead of beta. A source establishing the intended dynamic-oracle model is required before selecting a reliable corrected formulation.

children.title: Dynamic Distance Emulators
children.top_down_role: Maintained surrogate graphs supporting approximate dynamic distance information.

assumptions_latex: The original and emulator graphs share the terminal vertex set \(V\).
All current distances in the original graph are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Shortest-path distances in \(H_t\) approximate those in \(G_t\) simultaneously for all vertex pairs.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: emulator edges may be weighted virtual edges while preserving terminal distances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The emulator is an explicit weighted graph whose edges need not belong to the current input graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a dynamic graph sequence \(G_t=(V,E_t,w_t)\), a dynamic \((\alpha,eta)\)-distance emulator maintains a weighted graph \(H_t=(V,F_t,\ell_t)\), where \(F_t\) may contain edges absent from \(E_t\). After every update and for all \(u,v\in V\),
\[
d_{G_t}(u,v)\le d_{H_t}(u,v)\le \alpha d_{G_t}(u,v)+\beta
\]
whenever \(v\) is reachable from \(u\), and both distances are \(+\infty\) otherwise. Thus ordinary shortest-path computation in \(H_t\) yields valid approximate answers for the current input snapshot.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic emulator explicitly maintains a possibly virtual weighted graph whose all-pairs distances approximate those of the current input graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Distance Emulators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits an emulator leaf, but no source supports the chosen same-vertex-set model or its unreachable-pair convention, and eta is used where beta is intended. Emulator definitions may permit auxiliary vertices, so the exact model needs an authoritative source.

children.title: Query–Representation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between direct query structures and explicit surrogate representations.

assumptions_latex: An emulator \(H_t\) satisfies the required distance guarantee after every update.
A shortest-path routine on an \(s\)-edge representation uses time \(T_{\mathrm{sp}}(s)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The emulator induces an oracle with query time at most \(T_{\mathrm{sp}}(|F_t|)\) and space sufficient to store \(H_t\).

notation.meaning: Shortest-path running time on s edges

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit representation supports queries by shortest-path computation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the generic emulator-to-oracle reduction; no converse representation theorem is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a dynamic emulator maintains \(H_t=(V,F_t,\ell_t)\) using space \(S_H(t)\). Defining the query answer by
\[
Q_t(u,v):=d_{H_t}(u,v)
\]
produces a dynamic distance oracle with the same accuracy guarantee. If distances are computed on demand, its query time is at most \(T_{\mathrm{sp}}(|F_t|)\); storing more derived distance information may reduce query time while increasing representation space and update work. This reduction is one-way: an arbitrary oracle state need not encode any graph \(H_t\) whose shortest-path metric equals its answers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An emulator becomes an oracle by running shortest paths on its maintained graph; faster queries may require more stored information, and arbitrary oracles need not be emulators.
knowledge_statements.title: Query–Representation Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-way emulator-to-oracle reduction is plausible and the property kind fits, but no source supports the query-time formulation or the asserted nonconverse. The dependence of the shortest-path routine on the full representation also requires a sourced computational model.

children.title: Directed Graph Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dynamic path problems where edge direction constrains reachability and distance maintenance.

assumptions_latex: The vertex set \(V\) is fixed and finite.
Each update inserts or deletes an ordered arc, or changes its weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distances minimize weights of direction-respecting paths in the current directed snapshot.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direction makes distances asymmetric and reachability pair-dependent.

source_refs.locator: Section 7.2. Shortest Paths Between All Pairs of Vertices p. 165

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A directed dynamic path regime is a sequence \(G_t=(V,A_t,w_t)\) whose edges are ordered arcs. At time \(t\), a feasible \(u\)-to-\(v\) path must follow arc orientations, and
\[
d_t(u,v)=\min_{P\in\mathcal P_t(u,v)}\sum_{a\in P}w_t(a),
\]
with \(d_t(u,v)=+\infty\) when \(\mathcal P_t(u,v)=\varnothing\). In general \(d_t(u,v)\ne d_t(v,u)\). Insertions, deletions, and weight changes apply to individual ordered arcs before subsequent distance queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the directed regime, updates affect ordered arcs and current distances use only orientation-respecting paths, so reachability and distance may be asymmetric.
knowledge_statements.title: Directed Graph Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Section 7.2. Shortest Paths Between All Pairs of Vertices p. 165

children.title: Weighted Graph Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dynamic path problems with nonuniform edge costs.

assumptions_latex: Every snapshot is a finite graph.
Edge weights lie in a specified numeric domain \(W\subseteq\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Path length is the sum of current edge weights, and distance is the minimum feasible path length.

notation.meaning: Weight of a path at time t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard weighted shortest-path objective applied snapshotwise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allows insertions, deletions, and weight changes; negative weights require the separate negative-cycle boundary.

source_refs.locator: Section 7.2. Shortest Paths Between All Pairs of Vertices p. 165

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A weighted dynamic graph regime assigns each current edge \(e\in E_t\) a weight \(w_t(e)\in W\subseteq\mathbb{R}\). For a feasible path \(P\), its current length is
\[
w_t(P)=\sum_{e\in P}w_t(e),
\]
and \(d_t(u,v)=\min_P w_t(P)\), with value \(+\infty\) if no feasible path exists, provided the minimum is well-defined. An update may insert or delete an edge or replace \(w_{t-1}(e)\) by a new value \(w_t(e)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted dynamic regime measures each current path by the sum of its current edge weights and permits structural or weight updates.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Graph Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Section 7.2. Shortest Paths Between All Pairs of Vertices p. 165

children.title: Negative-Edge Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dynamic distance settings permitting negative edge weights.

assumptions_latex: The current snapshot \(G_t=(V,A_t,w_t)\) is a finite directed graph with real arc weights.
Distances are extended values defined as infima of directed-walk weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The value \(d_t(s,z)\) is finite exactly when \(z\) is reachable from \(s\) and no negative cycle is reachable from \(s\) while also reaching \(z\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reachable negative-cycle characterization of extended shortest-walk distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes finite distances, unreachable pairs, and pairs affected by relevant negative cycles.

source_refs.locator: Section 9.3. Minimum Mean Cycle-Cancelling Algorithm p. 220

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a snapshot \(G_t=(V,A_t,w_t)\) and define \(d_t(s,z)\) as the infimum of the weights of directed \(s\)-to-\(z\) walks. For \(s,z\in V\), the value \(d_t(s,z)\) is finite if and only if \(z\) is reachable from \(s\) and there is no directed cycle \(C\) with \(w_t(C)<0\) that is reachable from \(s\) and from which \(z\) is reachable. If \(z\) is unreachable from \(s\), then \(d_t(s,z)=+\infty\); if such a relevant negative cycle exists, then \(d_t(s,z)=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pair has a finite shortest-walk distance exactly when the target is reachable from the source and no negative cycle lies on a source-to-target walk; unreachable pairs have infinity and negative-cycle-affected pairs have minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Edge Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Section 9.3. Minimum Mean Cycle-Cancelling Algorithm p. 220

children.title: Negative-Cycle Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on dynamic distance semantics and maintenance when negative cycles arise.

assumptions_latex: The current snapshot \(G_t=(V,A_t,w_t)\) is a finite directed graph with real arc weights.
Distances are defined as infima over directed-walk weights.
A completed update creates a directed cycle \(C\) satisfying \(w_t(C)<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(s,z\in V\) such that \(s\) can reach \(C\) and \(C\) can reach \(z\), one has \(d_t(s,z)=-\infty\), so no finite shortest walk exists.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a reachable negative cycle makes affected walk weights unbounded below
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies exactly which ordered pairs lose finite shortest-walk distances after a negative cycle appears.

source_refs.locator: Section 9.3. Minimum Mean Cycle-Cancelling Algorithm p. 220

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a completed update produces a directed cycle \(C\) in \(G_t\) with \(w_t(C)<0\). For every pair \(s,z\in V\) such that \(s\) can reach \(C\) and \(C\) can reach \(z\), the weights of directed \(s\)-to-\(z\) walks are unbounded below and
\[
d_t(s,z)=-\infty.
\]
Consequently, no finite shortest walk exists for any such ordered pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an update creates a negative cycle, every ordered pair that can route from its source through that cycle to its target loses its finite shortest-walk distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Cycle Failure Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: Section 9.3. Minimum Mean Cycle-Cancelling Algorithm p. 220

assumptions_latex: Each arc traversal-time function is defined for every admissible departure time.
Waiting is either forbidden or explicitly included among feasible actions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Earliest arrival is obtained by composing traversal-time functions along feasible paths, with FIFO characterized by monotonic arrival maps.

notation.meaning: Traversal time of arc e when entered at time theta

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses continuous departure time and the FIFO boundary; discrete-time variants require separate conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A time-dependent network assigns each directed arc \(e\) a traversal-time function \(\tau_e:\mathcal T\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\). Entering \(e\\) at time \(\theta\) yields arrival time \(A_e(\theta)=\theta+\tau_e(\theta)\). For a path \(P=(e_1,\ldots,e_k)\) and departure \(\theta_0\), its arrival time is
\[
A_P(\theta_0)=(A_{e_k}\circ\cdots\circ A_{e_1})(\theta_0),
\]
and \(\operatorname{EA}(s,z;\theta_0)=\inf_P A_P(\theta_0)\). The network is FIFO when every \(A_e\) is nondecreasing, so later entry cannot cause earlier exit on the same arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc travel time depends on entry time; path arrival composes arc arrival maps, and FIFO requires each such map to be nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Dependent Network Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied for the continuous-time FIFO model. The expression for entering arc e contains a malformed escaped backslash, and the time domain is not stated to make successive arrival-map compositions admissible. The exact waiting and domain conventions require a source.

children.title: Greedy Matching Repair
children.top_down_role: Local greedy restoration of matching quality or maximality after updates.

assumptions_latex: The initial matching \(M_0\) is maximal.
Updates insert or delete one edge at a time in an undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After each repair, \(M_t\) is a maximal matching of the current graph.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: local greedy restoration of maximal matching after a single-edge update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maintains maximal, not maximum, matching under single-edge updates.

source_refs.locator: Section 10.5. Edmonds' Matching Algorithm p. 259

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with a maximal matching \(M_0\). On insertion of \(e=uv\), set \(M_t=M_{t-1}\cup\{e\}\) if both endpoints are unmatched, and otherwise leave the matching unchanged. On deletion, leave \(M_{t-1}\) unchanged unless \(e\in M_{t-1}\). If \(e\in M_{t-1}\), first set \(M_t=M_{t-1}\setminus\{e\}\); then, for each still-unmatched vertex \(x\in\{u,v\}\), scan \(N_t(x)\) and add one edge \(xy\) whose other endpoint \(y\) is unmatched, if such an edge exists. Output \(M_t\) after the scan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repair a maximal matching locally: accept an inserted edge between free endpoints, and after deleting a matched edge greedily rematch its exposed endpoints.
knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Matching Repair

source_witnesses.locator: Section 10.5. Edmonds' Matching Algorithm p. 259

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local repair algorithm is plausible and the algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the cited static Edmonds maximum-matching section does not specifically support dynamic greedy maintenance of a maximal matching. A dynamic maximal-matching or directly relevant repair source is required.

children.title: Augmenting-Path Matching Repair
children.top_down_role: Matching repair based on locating and applying augmenting paths.

assumptions_latex: The graph is finite and undirected.
Before each update, \(M\) is a matching.
The search limit is \(L\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned set \(M'\) is a matching; if the search exhausts all paths, \(M'\) admits no augmenting path of length at most \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-matching repair after one edge insertion or deletion.

source_refs.locator: Section 5. Cardinality Matching Algorithm p. 193

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an edge update producing \(G'=(V,E')\), first set \(M_0=M\cap E'\). If the inserted edge has two exposed endpoints, it may be added to \(M_0\). Search in \(G'\) for an \(M_0\)-augmenting path \(P\) of length at most \(L\). Whenever such a path is found, replace \(M_0\) by \(M_0\triangle E(P)\) and repeat the search. Stop when no eligible path remains, or after a prescribed repair budget is exhausted, and output the current matching \(M'\). Each augmentation increases the matching cardinality by one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete invalid matched edges, then repeatedly flip bounded-length augmenting paths. Every flip preserves feasibility and increases matching size by one.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmenting-Path Matching Repair

source_witnesses.locator: Section 5. Cardinality Matching Algorithm p. 193

children.title: Repair-Radius Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Relationships among locality, repair depth, maintained quality, and update cost.

assumptions_latex: The graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
The set \(M\subseteq E\) is a matching.
The integer radius parameter satisfies \(r\geq 1\).
The matching \(M\) has no augmenting path containing at most \(2r-1\) edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every maximum-cardinality matching \(M^*\) of \(G\), \(|M^*|\leq (1+1/r)|M|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation guarantee obtained by excluding short augmenting paths; no dynamic search-time bound is asserted.

source_refs.locator: Section 5. Cardinality Matching Algorithm p. 193

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(M\subseteq E\) be a matching, and let \(r\geq 1\) be an integer. If \(M\) has no augmenting path containing at most \(2r-1\) edges, then every maximum-cardinality matching \(M^*\) of \(G\) satisfies \[|M^*|\leq\left(1+\frac{1}{r}\right)|M|.\] Increasing \(r\) strengthens this approximation certificate while enlarging the alternating-path neighborhood that must be excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a matching has no augmenting path of length at most 2r minus 1, its size is within a factor 1 plus 1/r of maximum. A larger radius gives a stronger certificate but requires examining longer alternating paths.
knowledge_statements.title: Repair-Radius Tradeoffs

source_witnesses.locator: Section 5. Cardinality Matching Algorithm p. 193

children.title: Fractional Matching Maintenance
children.top_down_role: Dynamic maintenance through fractional matching structures.

assumptions_latex: The graph is finite and undirected.
The pre-update vector is a feasible fractional matching.
Edges are processed in a fixed deterministic order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(x'\) is feasible and maximal: for every edge \(uv\), at least one of \(u,v\) is saturated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible maximal fractional matching under edge updates.

source_refs.locator: Section 10.1. Bipartite Matching p. 246

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain \(x\in[0,1]^E\) satisfying \(\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\leq 1\) for every vertex \(v\). After an update, delete coordinates of removed edges and initialize every inserted-edge coordinate to zero. Define \(s(v)=1-\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\). Scan the current edges; on processing \(e=uv\), set \(a=\min\{s(u),s(v)\}\), replace \(x_e\) by \(x_e+a\), and reduce both residual capacities by \(a\). Repeat complete scans until no coordinate changes, then output \(x'\). Feasibility is preserved because no update exceeds either endpoint's residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Remove obsolete fractions, initialize new edges at zero, and raise edge values within endpoint slack until every edge has a saturated endpoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Matching Maintenance

source_witnesses.locator: Section 10.1. Bipartite Matching p. 246

children.title: Kernel-Based Matching Maintenance
children.top_down_role: Dynamic matching through maintained sparse kernel subgraphs.

assumptions_latex: The maintained graph is finite and undirected.
Parameters satisfy \(d\geq 1\) and \(0\leq\varepsilon<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a valid matching contained in a bounded-degree maintained subgraph \(H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel maintenance invariant and matching extraction; no approximation factor asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,F)\) such that \(\deg_H(v)\leq d\) for every vertex \(v\), and every excluded edge \(uv\in E\setminus F\) has \(\deg_H(u)\geq(1-\varepsilon)d\) or \(\deg_H(v)\geq(1-\varepsilon)d\). After each insertion or deletion, promote or demote incident edges until these two invariants hold. Maintain a maximal matching \(M_H\) in \(H\): delete invalid matched edges and greedily match newly exposed endpoints along available kernel edges. Output \(M_H\), viewed as a matching of the full graph \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a bounded-degree kernel covering every excluded edge by a nearly full endpoint, then maintain and output a maximal matching inside that kernel.
knowledge_statements.title: Kernel-Based Matching Maintenance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the container, but no source is supplied for the particular kernel invariants or for the assertion that incident-edge promotions and demotions restore them after every update. The maintenance step is also too underspecified to assess termination and correctness without a kernel construction source.

children.title: Local Matching Repair
children.top_down_role: Matching maintenance through bounded neighborhoods affected by updates.

assumptions_latex: The current graph is finite and undirected.
Before the update, \(M\) is a matching.
A repair radius \(R\geq 0\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The output \(M'\
\) is a matching and agrees with \(M\) on every preserved edge outside the repair neighborhood.

notation.meaning: vertices incident to the updated edge
preserved matching outside the repair region

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recomputation restricted to an update-centered neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After an edge update with endpoint set \(S\), form \(B=B_R(S)\), the vertices at graph distance at most \(R\) from \(S\). Let \(M_{\mathrm{out}}\) contain the surviving edges of \(M\) whose endpoints both lie outside \(B\). Remove from \(B\) every vertex incident to \(M_{\mathrm{out}}\), and compute a maximum matching \(N\) in the subgraph induced by the remaining vertices of \(B\). Output \(M'=M_{\mathrm{out}}\cup N\). The construction changes only edges incident to the repair neighborhood; approximation or optimality in the entire graph requires an additional structural invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Freeze surviving matching edges outside an update-centered ball and recompute a maximum matching on the unfrozen vertices inside the ball.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Matching Repair

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this particular update-centered recomputation framework. In addition, the conclusion contains a malformed line break inside the delimited symbol for \(M'\). A source and a syntactically repaired complete record are required before review.

children.title: Incremental Matching Regime
children.top_down_role: Matching maintenance under insertion-only updates.

assumptions_latex: The vertex set is fixed and finite.
Updates only insert previously absent edges, optionally with immutable weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At every time \(t\), the algorithm must output a matching \(M_t\subseteq E_t\) satisfying its declared exact or approximate objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Insertion-only dynamic matching with a fixed vertex set.

source_refs.locator: Section 10.1. Bipartite Matching p. 246

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An incremental matching instance is a sequence \(G_t=(V,E_t)\) with \(E_{t-1}\subseteq E_t\), where each update inserts one edge and no edge is deleted. After processing update \(t\), an algorithm outputs a matching \(M_t\subseteq E_t\). For cardinality matching, an \(\alpha\)-approximate regime requires \(|M_t|\geq\operatorname{OPT}_t/\alpha\). For nonnegative weighted matching, it requires \(w(M_t)\geq\operatorname{OPT}_t/\alpha\). Update time counts computation between receiving an insertion and making \(M_t\) available; preprocessing and query conventions must be stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edges arrive but never depart. After every insertion, the algorithm exposes a feasible matching meeting its declared cardinality or weight guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Matching Regime

source_witnesses.locator: Section 10.1. Bipartite Matching p. 246

children.title: Fully Dynamic Matching Regime
children.top_down_role: Matching maintenance under mixed insertions and deletions.

assumptions_latex: The vertex set is fixed and finite.
Each update inserts or deletes one edge; weighted variants specify how weights change.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After every update \(t\), the output \(M_t\subseteq E_t\) must satisfy feasibility and the stated exact or approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-insertion and edge-deletion dynamic matching.

source_refs.locator: Section 10.5. Edmonds' Matching Algorithm p. 259

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fully dynamic matching instance is a sequence \(G_t=(V,E_t)\) in which each transition inserts one absent edge or deletes one present edge. After every transition, the algorithm outputs a matching \(M_t\subseteq E_t\). For a maximization objective with nonnegative value function \(f_t\), an \(\alpha\)-approximation satisfies \(f_t(M_t)\geq\operatorname{OPT}_t/\alpha\), where \(\operatorname{OPT}_t\) is the maximum value of a matching in \(G_t\). Worst-case or amortized update time, randomization, adversary model, and query time are distinct parts of the regime specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both insertions and deletions are allowed. A feasible matching with the promised objective guarantee must be available after each update.

children.title: Weight-Scaling Methods
children.top_down_role: Dynamic weighted-matching approaches organized by progressive weight scales.

assumptions_latex: The graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
Every edge has a nonnegative weight \(w_e\).
The scaling quantum satisfies \(\Delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned matching \(\widehat M\) satisfies \(w(\widehat M)\geq\operatorname{OPT}_w-\Delta\lfloor |V|/2\rfloor\).

notation.meaning: maximum matching weight under the original weights

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static additive weight scaling usable as a component of dynamic weighted-matching methods; no dynamic repair-cost claim is asserted.

source_refs.locator: Section 11.2. Outline of the Weighted Matching Algorithm p. 280

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with weights \(w_e\geq0\), and let \(\Delta>0\). Define \(\bar w_e=\lfloor w_e/\Delta\rfloor\) for every \(e\in E\). Compute a matching \(\widehat M\) maximizing \(\sum_{e\in M}\bar w_e\) over all matchings \(M\subseteq E\), using an exact integer-weight matching routine. If \(\operatorname{OPT}_w\) denotes the maximum matching weight under \(w\), then the returned matching satisfies \[w(\widehat M)\geq\operatorname{OPT}_w-\Delta\left\lfloor\frac{|V|}{2}\right\rfloor.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round each nonnegative edge weight down by a positive scale quantum and compute an exact maximum matching for the resulting integer weights. The returned matching loses at most one quantum for each edge that a matching can contain.
knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Scaling Methods

source_witnesses.locator: Section 11.2. Outline of the Weighted Matching Algorithm p. 280

children.title: Weight-Bucketing Methods
children.top_down_role: Dynamic weighted-matching approaches grouping edges into weight classes.

assumptions_latex: All edge weights are positive.
The geometric base satisfies \(\beta>1\).
A deterministic within-bucket edge order is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(M\) is a matching, and every accepted edge dominates all later conflicting edges by bucket order.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descending geometric-bucket greedy construction.

source_refs.locator: Section 11.3. Implementation of the Weighted Matching Algorithm p. 283

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the edges into \(B_j=\{e:\beta^j\leq w_e<\beta^{j+1}\}\). Initialize \(M=\varnothing\). Process nonempty buckets in decreasing order of \(j\); within each bucket, inspect edges in the fixed order and add \(e=uv\) exactly when neither \(u\) nor \(v\) is incident to an edge already in \(M\). Stop after the lowest nonempty bucket and output \(M\). Under an update, move the affected edge to its new bucket if necessary and rerun conflict resolution from the affected bucket downward. Any approximation claim requires a separate charging argument and bucket-span assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Group edges geometrically by weight and greedily accept conflict-free edges from heavy buckets to light buckets, repairing lower-priority conflicts after updates.
knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Bucketing Methods

source_witnesses.locator: Section 11.3. Implementation of the Weighted Matching Algorithm p. 283

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The static descending-bucket greedy construction is well defined, but the cited weighted-matching implementation section is not shown to support this geometric bucketing method. The update instruction to rerun conflict resolution from an affected bucket downward is not sufficiently specified to establish restoration of the same global greedy outcome.

children.title: Scale–Bucket Interactions
children.top_down_role: Coordination of scaling schedules with bucket granularity and update behavior.

assumptions_latex: The graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
Every edge has a positive weight \(w_e\).
The geometric base satisfies \(\beta>1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every matching \(\widehat M\) maximizing the rounded weight satisfies \(w(\widehat M)>\operatorname{OPT}_w/\beta\), and hence \(w(\widehat M)\geq\operatorname{OPT}_w/\beta\).

notation.meaning: maximum matching weight under the original weights

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative approximation guarantee induced by rounding positive weights to geometric bucket floors.

source_refs.locator: Section 11.2. Outline of the Weighted Matching Algorithm p. 280

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with weights \(w_e>0\), and let \(\beta>1\). For every \(e\in E\), define \(j(e)=\lfloor\log_\beta w_e\rfloor\) and \(w'_e=\beta^{j(e)}\). If \(\widehat M\) maximizes \(\sum_{e\in M}w'_e\) over all matchings \(M\subseteq E\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}_w\) is the maximum matching weight under \(w\), then \[w(\widehat M)>\frac{1}{\beta}\operatorname{OPT}_w.\] In particular, \(\widehat M\) is a \(\beta\)-approximation under the non-strict convention \(w(\widehat M)\geq\operatorname{OPT}_w/\beta\). Crossing a bucket boundary changes \(w'_e\), whereas a weight change that remains within one bucket leaves \(w'_e\) unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rounding every positive weight down to its geometric bucket floor and optimizing the rounded weights gives a beta-approximation for the original weights. Only crossings of bucket boundaries change rounded coefficients.
knowledge_statements.title: Scale–Bucket Interactions

source_witnesses.locator: Section 11.2. Outline of the Weighted Matching Algorithm p. 280

children.title: Bipartite Graph Regime
children.top_down_role: Dynamic weighted matching specialized to bipartite graph structure.

assumptions_latex: The finite vertex set has a fixed bipartition \(V=L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R\).
At every time \(t\), the current edge set satisfies \(E_t\subseteq L\times R\).
Current edge weights are nonnegative.
When an approximation factor is declared, it satisfies \(\alpha\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After every update \(t\), the algorithm outputs a matching \(M_t\subseteq E_t\) evaluated against the maximum-weight matching in the current bipartite graph.

notation.meaning: fixed left and right vertex classes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic weighted matching restricted to a fixed bipartition; the allowed update and weight-change operations must be specified by the enclosing dynamic model.

source_refs.locator: Section 10.1. Bipartite Matching p. 246

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bipartite dynamic weighted-matching regime is a sequence of finite graphs \(G_t=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E_t)\) with a fixed bipartition, \(E_t\subseteq L\times R\), and nonnegative weight functions \(w_t:E_t\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}\). For a declared factor \(\alpha\geq1\), an \(\alpha\)-approximate regime requires \[w_t(M_t)\geq\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_t}{\alpha}.\] Every update must preserve the fixed bipartition.

children.title: General-Graph Regime
children.top_down_role: Dynamic weighted matching without bipartite restrictions.

assumptions_latex: The vertex set \(V\) is fixed and finite.
Every current graph \(G_t=(V,E_t)\) is finite, undirected, and not assumed bipartite.
Current edge weights are nonnegative.
When an approximation factor is declared, it satisfies \(\alpha\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After every update \(t\), the output is a matching \(M_t\subseteq E_t\) evaluated against the maximum-weight matching in the current general graph; polyhedral formulations must include the relevant odd-set constraints.

edges of the current graph with both endpoints in \(U\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A general-graph dynamic weighted-matching regime is a sequence of finite undirected graphs \(G_t=(V,E_t)\), with no bipartiteness assumption, together with nonnegative weight functions \(w_t:E_t\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}\). After every permitted update, the algorithm outputs a matching \(M_t\subseteq E_t\). Let \(\operatorname{OPT}_t=\max\{w_t(N):N\subseteq E_t\text{ is a matching}\}\). For a declared factor \(\alpha\geq1\), an \(\alpha\)-approximation satisfies \[w_t(M_t)\geq\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_t}{\alpha}.\] In a matching-polytope formulation with edge variables \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}^{E_t}\), every odd-cardinality set \(U\subseteq V\) must satisfy \[\sum_{e\in E_t[U]}x_e\leq\frac{|U|-1}{2},\] where \(E_t[U]=\{uv\in E_t:u,v\in U\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In this regime the evolving weighted graph is an unrestricted finite undirected graph and may contain odd cycles. After every permitted update, the algorithm returns a feasible matching meeting its declared guarantee relative to the current general-graph optimum. children.title: Structural Regime Gap
children.top_down_role: Differences in maintained structures, guarantees, and barriers between the two graph regimes.

assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, undirected, and has nonnegative edge weights.
The bipartite formulation uses only degree constraints and nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{frac}}(C_3)=3/2>1=\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(C_3)\), so odd-set structure is indispensable beyond bipartite graphs.

notation.meaning: The triangle graph on three vertices
Value of the degree-constrained fractional matching relaxation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical odd-cycle obstruction for the matching relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates bipartite matching structure from the odd-set constraints required in general graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign unit weight to every edge of \(C_3\). The degree-constrained fractional matching relaxation is \[\max \left\{\sum_{e\in E(C_3)}x_e: x_e\ge 0,\ \sum_{e\ni v}x_e\le 1\ \text{for every }v\right\}.\] Setting \(x_e=1/2\) for every edge is feasible and has value \(3/2\), whereas every integral matching contains at most one edge and has value \(1\). Thus the degree constraints sufficient for the bipartite matching polytope do not describe the general-graph matching polytope; an odd-set inequality excludes this fractional point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a unit-weight triangle, the degree relaxation has value 3/2 while every integral matching has value 1, exposing the odd-cycle gap between bipartite and general graphs.
knowledge_statements.title: Structural Regime Gap

assumptions_latex: \((G_t)_{t\ge 0}\) is a finite undirected graph sequence produced by single-edge insertions and deletions.
Vertex-cover size is measured in the unweighted cardinality objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t\), \(C_t\) is a vertex cover and \(|C_t|\le 2\tau(G_t)\).

notation.meaning: A maintained maximal matching of the current graph
The endpoints of the maintained matching

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: endpoints of a maximal matching form a factor-two vertex cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant-based fully dynamic, unweighted factor-two vertex cover without an update-time guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(M_0\) by greedily adding edges with two unmatched endpoints. After inserting an edge, add it exactly when both endpoints are unmatched. After deleting an edge outside \(M_t\), retain the matching; after deleting a matched edge, remove it and greedily add available edges until the matching is maximal. After every update output \(C_t=V(M_t)\). Maximality implies that every current edge has an endpoint in \(C_t\), while any vertex cover contains at least one endpoint of each edge of \(M_t\). Consequently \(|C_t|=2|M_t|\le 2\tau(G_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain any maximal matching and output all its endpoints. This is always a vertex cover whose size is at most twice optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Approximate Vertex Cover

assumptions_latex: \((G_t)_{t\ge 0}\) is a finite undirected graph sequence on a fixed vertex set.
Updates insert or delete one edge at a time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(I_t\) is independent and satisfies \(I_t\cup N_{G_t}(I_t)=V\) after every update.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(I_0=\varnothing\), then repeatedly add any vertex having no neighbor in \(I_0\) until no such vertex remains. After an edge insertion whose two endpoints both lie in \(I_{t-1}\), remove one endpoint; otherwise retain the set. After any insertion or deletion, repeatedly add any vertex outside the set having no neighbor in it, stopping when none exists. Output the resulting \(I_t\). Each addition preserves independence, and the stopping condition gives \(I_t\cup N_{G_t}(I_t)=V\), which is equivalent to maximality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repair conflicts after insertions, then greedily add eligible vertices until none remains. The maintained set is independent and inclusion-wise maximal after every update.

Dynamic Graph Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A simple fully dynamic proper-coloring algorithm with no claimed sublinear update bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct \(c_0\) greedily from the palette \(\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}\). Deleting an edge requires no change. Upon inserting \(uv\), retain the coloring if \(c_{t-1}(u)\ne c_{t-1}(v)\). Otherwise choose one endpoint, say \(u\), and assign it a color absent from \(\{c_{t-1}(w):w\in N_{G_t}(u)\}\). Such a color exists because \(u\) has at most \(\Delta\) neighbors. Output the resulting \(c_t\); the recoloring creates no incident monochromatic edge and resolves the only newly possible conflict.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dynamic orientation by recomputation; efficient local-repair bounds are outside this statement.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Source–Sink Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fixed-terminal dynamic source-sink cut by recomputation, without an update-time guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After every update \(k\), enumerate all sets \(S\subseteq V\) satisfying \(s\in S\) and \(z\notin S\). Compute the capacity \(c_k(\delta^+_{G_k}(S))\), choose a minimizing set using fixed deterministic tie-breaking, and output \((S_k,V\setminus S_k)\) and its capacity. children.title: Representation Update Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Update regimes and graph changes that limit stable maintenance of cut representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Update Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An output-sensitivity boundary for explicit all-pairs cut values, not a lower bound for compact cut trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be disjoint vertex sets with \(|A|,|B|=\Theta(n)\) and \(n=|A|+|B|\). Let the induced weighted graphs on \(A\) and \(B\) be connected, and join them by a unique edge \(e\) of weight \(c\ge 0\). Fix \(\varepsilon>0\), and suppose every nontrivial cut of each induced cluster has weight greater than \(c+\varepsilon\). For every \(u\in A\) and \(v\in B\), initially \(\lambda_{u,v}=c\). Increasing only \(w(e)\) from \(c\) to \(c+\varepsilon\) changes all \(|A||B|=\Theta(n^2)\) cross-cluster minimum-cut values to \(c+\varepsilon\). Any representation explicitly materializing every pair value must process this quadratic output change, although a compact cut tree can encode it by changing one edge weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing the unique bridge weight between two large clusters changes quadratically many cross-cluster minimum-cut values, limiting explicit all-pairs tables but not compact cut trees.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, undirected, and has nonnegative edge weights.
\(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint clusters of sizes \(\Theta(n)\), joined by a unique edge \(e\).
The parameters satisfy \(c\ge 0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), and every nontrivial cut inside either induced cluster has weight greater than \(c+\varepsilon\).
An explicit data structure stores every pairwise minimum-cut value separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One edge-weight update changes \(\Theta(n^2)\) explicitly stored pair values, giving a quadratic output-change barrier for such a table.

notation.meaning: Two disjoint vertex clusters of comparable size
The unique edge joining the clusters

children.title: Incremental Flow
children.top_down_role: Flow maintenance under insertion or capacity-increase updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Warm-start incremental maximum flow under capacity increases and arc insertions; no update-time bound is claimed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(f_0\) at the zero flow and repeatedly augment along a residual \(s\)-\(z\) path having the fewest arcs until \(R(G_0,f_0)\) has no directed \(s\)-\(z\) path. After an arc insertion or capacity increase at update \(k\), retain \(f_{k-1}\), which remains feasible, update the residual capacities, and again repeatedly augment along a residual \(s\)-\(z\) path having the fewest arcs by its bottleneck capacity. Stop when no such path exists and output \(f_k\). Breadth-first augmenting-path termination and the absence of a residual terminal path imply that \(f_k\) is a maximum flow in the updated network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity increases preserve the old flow's feasibility. Resume breadth-first residual augmentations from that flow until no source-sink path remains, yielding the new maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: For each update index \(k\ge 0\), \(G_k=(V,A_k,c_k,s,z)\) is a finite directed network with fixed distinct terminals \(s,z\in V\) and finite nonnegative real capacities.
Updates only insert arcs or increase capacities; an inserted arc is treated as previously having capacity zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After each update \(k\), the returned feasible flow \(f_k\) is a maximum \(s\)-\(z\) flow in \(G_k\).

notation.meaning: The maintained feasible source-sink flow after update k
The residual network of the current flow

children.title: Decremental Flow
children.top_down_role: Flow maintenance under deletion or capacity-decrease updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Decremental Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the decremental exact maximum-flow maintenance regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_k=(V,E_k)\) be a directed network with fixed source \(s\), fixed sink \(t\), and capacities \(u_k:E_k\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). A decremental update sequence satisfies \(E_{k+1}\subseteq E_k\) and \(u_{k+1}(e)\le u_k(e)\) for every \(e\in E_{k+1}\). Decremental maximum-flow maintenance requires, after every update \(k\), a feasible flow \(f_k\) satisfying \(|f_k|=\max\{|f|:f\text{ is feasible in }(G_k,u_k)\}\), or requires maintenance of that optimal value alone. Preprocessing time and update time are measured separately over the sequence of edge deletions and capacity decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decremental maximum-flow structure maintains an exact maximum flow or its value while edges are deleted and capacities only decrease.
assumptions_latex: \(V,s,t\) remain fixed throughout the update sequence.
All capacities are finite and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_k\) is feasible and \(|f_k|=\operatorname{MaxFlow}(G_k,u_k)\) after every update \(k\).

notation.meaning: network and capacities after update k

children.title: Flow Update Asymmetry
children.top_down_role: Differences in feasibility repair and performance across one-sided flow updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow Update Asymmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the opposite monotonic effects of incremental and decremental capacity updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed directed network and terminals, let \(F(u)\) denote the maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow value under capacity vector \(u\). If \(u'\ge u\) componentwise, including an inserted edge as an increase from zero capacity, then every flow feasible under \(u\) remains feasible under \(u'\), so \(F(u')\ge F(u)\). If \(u'\le u\), including deletion as reduction to zero, then \(F(u')\le F(u)\), and a previously maintained flow can become infeasible. Thus incremental updates preserve primal feasibility, whereas decremental updates preserve old cut upper bounds but may require primal repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity increases preserve the old flow and cannot lower the optimum; decreases can invalidate that flow and cannot raise the optimum.
assumptions_latex: The vertex set and terminals \(s,t\) are fixed.
Capacity vectors are compared componentwise after assigning absent edges capacity zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u'\ge u\Rightarrow F(u')\ge F(u)\), while \(u'\le u\Rightarrow F(u')\le F(u)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Fully Dynamic Approximate Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines multiplicative approximation under arbitrary capacity increases and decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\). A fully dynamic \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximate maximum-flow algorithm receives an initial capacitated directed network with terminals \(s,t\), followed by arbitrary edge insertions, deletions, and capacity changes. After update \(k\), it returns a flow \(f_k\) feasible for the current network such that \[|f_k|\ge(1-\varepsilon)F_k,\] where \(F_k\) is the current exact maximum-flow value. If only a value estimate \(\widehat F_k\) is maintained, the convention is \((1-\varepsilon)F_k\le\widehat F_k\le F_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After arbitrary graph and capacity updates, the algorithm maintains a feasible flow whose value is at least a specified fraction of the current optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\).
Current capacities are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|f_k|\ge(1-\varepsilon)F_k\) after every update \(k\).

notation.meaning: exact maximum-flow value after update k

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Network Reoptimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Warm-start reoptimization from an integral feasible flow after a network update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a changed capacitated network \((G',u',s,t)\) with finite nonnegative integral capacities and an inherited flow. First repair the inherited flow, if necessary, to obtain an integral feasible flow \(f\) in \((G',u')\). Construct the residual network of \(f\), assigning forward residual capacity \(u'(e)-f(e)\) and reverse residual capacity \(f(e)\) to each original arc \(e\). While an \(s\)-\(t\) residual path \(P\) exists, augment \(f\) along \(P\) by its positive bottleneck residual capacity and update the residual network. When no such path exists, output \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repair the old flow to an integral feasible flow, then augment through its residual network until no source-to-sink residual path remains.
assumptions_latex: All updated capacities are finite nonnegative integers.
The repair step returns an integral feasible flow.
Residual augmentations and comparisons are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure terminates after finitely many augmentations and outputs \(f\) satisfying \(|f|=\operatorname{MaxFlow}(G',u')\).

notation.meaning: an augmenting path in the current residual network
